I just can't justify paying thousands of dollars for a television with features I won't notice, or use.  For our purposes, this one meets or exceeds our expectations, and the price was right.  If you're really picky about technicals, maybe this TV isn't for you.The TV arrived within 48 hours via UPS, shipped by Amazon within a box inside another box, well packed/cushioned to protect the TV from damage in shipment.  Sold by Amazon, with free prime shipping. NOTE: The price had been fluctuating some $200 up and down since Black Friday, so wait it out, and buy it from Amazon.I paired the Samsung 46" with a Sanus VLF525, which is made for much larger TV's, however the Sanus allows me to move the TV completely perpendicular to the wall, a true 90 degree angle.  So I can pull the TV away from the wall, and turn it a full 90 degrees which was a requirement to meet our needs.Setup was relatively easy.  The initial power up walks you though a menu of items.  It connected to my Wifi router about 25 feet away after adding the router password. We subscribe to FIOS, and the Samsung Remote controls the FIOS set top box with very few limitations (power, channel change, STB Menu, and STB Guide, etc. work fine).  However, the FIOS remote doesn't work for controlling most of the Samsung features, so we primarily use the Samsung remote.  Despite what Comcast and FIOS say, they've made watching TV way too complex by forcing STB's and Digital Adapters in the mix.Screen image is crisp and clear, we don't notice any ghosting or motion related issues sitting about 8 to 10 feet from the screen. There is some small level of delay in response to the remote and internet related function, but nothing we're concerned about.

Size and cost figured in too, but reception was the key because I like listening to the radio while I work.Every radio I researched had someone complaining about the horrible reception.  Every single one.  I was paralyzed with fear that I'd pick the wrong one so I just kept looking, hoping to find one where everyone said "Get it, the reception is fantastic!"Finally I realized that reception depends on so many variables that no radio is going to work for everyone everywhere and I was able to quit shopping and actually order the Sangean CL-100.  The price was good and the size was perfect for the space I had in mind.I know you're all waiting with bated breath to hear that the reception, even in an old building where it's difficult to get good cell reception, is spectacularly good.  It even picks up a lot of the smaller and more distant stations.  Tuning and changing settings is relatively simple and the sound quality is good enough for a kitchen radio.  It has some serious volume on it, so I can turn it up and listen while I'm making the bed or cleaning the bathroom.  No the sound isn't great at that distance, but again, it's all a matter of convenience for this radio.If you're like me and want a small, simple-to-operate radio that will (probably, no guarantee) pick up your favorite stations, give the Sangean a shot. review_title: Not really what I was expecting...
review_text: Cabling -First off, I didn't expect much for $12.  However, from the product description, I didn't expect the cording system of these headphones to be designed the way it is.  I prefer a "Y" cording style, meaning that each ear piece has an equal length cable that meets in the middle, and then runs together to the plug.  I have never been a fan of what I refer to as "dependent cabling".  This model has a cable that runs to the left earpiece.  It does have a "Y" in the cabling, but it is relatively close to the left earpiece.  The right earpiece has a longer cable, as I assume is was designed to go around the back of the head to the right ear?  It just seems awkward.  I am not a fan of that, and it doesn't indicate that in the product description.Sound -Again, $12 doesn't get you much.  These earphone sound relatively flat in all areas (mids, highs, and lows).  Don't get me wrong, they are alright, and just fine for the average listener that isn't demanding audiophile-level sound from the ear pieces.Fit / Function -The design is actually pretty cool the way they sit on your ears.  You just flex the ear hook a little bit and rest it on your ear and adjust the foam pad back in towards your ear.  Very easy to place on your ears, and i found them to be very comfortable.  These are "on-ear headphones, and not in-ear.  If you listen at higher volumes, other will be able to hear it, as this style allows a lot of sound "bleed" from the earphone.I would recommend these to anyone that wants a pair of cheap office headphones that they put on and remove frequently.

This Computer is really different! It is like having a great, big Android desktop computer. It is as capable of operating with a mouse and keyboard as fully touch capable. It really is more a desktop computer than a tablet. But it will download and play lots of Android Apps and Games. The powerful speakers make game play more enjoyable. The 21.5 inch screen is bright and readable for my aging eyes. It weighs 10 lbs. so it really is not for your lap. It will tilt from 70 degrees to 20 degrees so if you have lots of desk space you may use it almost lying flat. It is not terribly fast (Quadrant Score = 1800), but it keeps up well and does not appear any slower than some of my faster tablets in Chrome. It has NO sensors (accelerometers, g-sensors, position) so a lot of my previous Apps (99 out of 250) will not load from the Google Play Store (most, I think, for the lack of a position sensor). It will actually display Apps that only work in portrait mode but they are lying on their side. It has 2 full size USB ports, 1 micro USB port, a HDMI port, a Ethernet port, and a micro SD card slot. It has lots of pre-installed Apps including Kindle, Amazon AppStore, Chrome, Facebook, Netflix, Play Store, Polaris Office, Skype, and YouTube. I really like this hybrid and would recommend it to anyone that has some Android experience (I say that because Acer provides absolutely NO Android information). It has a three page Quick start guide that only shows how to hook it up. They provide the User Manual on a CD (this computer doesn't have a drive to view it!). You can go to Acer's Web site to download the PDF file. If, like me, you have been a Windows user all your life  and want to try Android give this computer a try. I think you will like it - I do.

It turned out to be a little more challenging than the one I put on my phone.It doesn't seem to be made exclusively for the Tab 2 7.0 because it has two holes for the camera...one on each side.  While you are trying to put it on the water settles in the second hole.I followed instructions and re-applied the screen protector several times.  I finally got it to lay flat with most of the bubbles out.  But, when it dried the surface between the the Samsung screen and the shield had tiny bumps and streaks.  Even after 24 hours the streaks and bumps didn't go away.When the shield is wet it is easier to work with but I worried about getting too much moisture in my tablet.  It also gives you more bubbles to remove from the surface when you have more moisture.I let it set for two days but I finally decided not to take a chance on whatever was trapped scratching my screen so I took the shield off and threw it away.  I don't think everyone is able to put these screens on properly by themselves.  The screen protector I used on my phone was a different brand.  You didn't use moisture to put it on.The company was quick to deliver the screen protector.  When I emailed them they responded and offered suggestions as to how I could make the screen protector work.  I received several emails from them apologizing and offering to send another screen.  They seem to be very interested in making the customer happy.  They did say that it might take a week or two before all of the imperfections are gone.  I didn't want to wait that long because the one bump under the screen appeared to be something hard that might scratch my screen if I used the tablet.I took my tablet to Best Buy and had them install a screen protector.  I still don't think everyone can do this well.  But, the company was very responsive and if you are able to install the screen yourself it is worth the difference in price for having it done.For someone who has installed one of these screens before it might be a good deal.  After a couple of hours I still couldn't get it to lie flat without bumps and streaks between the protector and the screen of the Samsung Tab.  For me....it didn't work.

review_title: Reasonably priced, gets full Amazon support behind it but makes sure this is what you need
review_text: This is the most common USB cable these days for connecting 'something' to your computer but... beware of the 'Micro-B vs. Mini-B' interface confusion (read below) - if you are to use it with a phone or some other small and 'new' gadget, you may need a 'Micro-B' cable instead.On this specific cable, everything is done right, including the price. It is USB 2.0 certified, meaning that it supports data transfer rates of up to 480Mbps and, if your device accepts a Mini-B plug, this is the cable to get. Maybe the 2-meter length (6+ ft.) is a little bit too much but it does not bother me a lot and there may come a time when a cable this long may come in handy.While USB cables are clearly a commodity item these days, AmazonBasics does have a couple of advantages over the competition.- EASY RETURN - I know because I had to return quite a few items for various reasons. Amazon makes it very easy and, if you are returning the item because it came defective or damaged Amazon pays for shipping.- WARRANTY - these wires come with a 1-year warranty (talking about future-proofing). If a cable performs for one year, the odds that it would stop working after that are pretty close to zero. It's possible that the other vendors back their inexpensive cables too (I never checked) but I am highly confident that Amazon will be around to honor its warranty and I'm not so sure about vendors I know less.- QUALITY ASSURANCE - I've never had any problems with 'cheap' USB or HDMI cables but it may be reassuring to have Amazon's name on a wire. My assumption is that Amazon did insist on some quality checks before they stamped their logo on the product.- PRICE - This cable may appear more expensive than others but keep in mind that, unlike most, it qualifies for SuperSavers and Amazon Prime free shipping.I am awarding this item 5 stars for price and quality - there's nothing to complain. However, I suggest that you look around before you place the order because you just might have one of these already as they tend to ship with many electronic gadgets these days.______________________________________________Notes:Anyone in the market for a USB cable should be very careful because there are at least 6 kinds of USB connectors. If you are buying a cable that connects 'something' to your computer or laptop, the computer end of the cable will always be a USB-A or 'Type A' connector. At the other end, you may have a USB-B/Type B - a nearly square shaped connector used mostly to deliver power to a device but this is rare. Most likely, you will have a Mini-B or a Micro-B. The difference between the 2 is that the Micro-B is half as thick while the width is the same - Mini-B is 3x7mm while Micro-B is 1.5x7mm.If your device (phone, PDA, camera) is a 'new' one and it's using USB, chances are that they will need a Micro-B connector because the industry seems to be adopting the 'Micro' form factor as its standard. If the above sounds simple, you should keep in mind that some devices require Mini-AB or Micro-AB connectors, also known as USB OTG (OnTheGo) devices.My advice: before ordering any cable, make sure that you clearly understand what type of cable you need.Whenever in doubt, do some more research and keep in mind that the 'Micro-B' (very small) is the emerging standard and it's likely to be found on the newer and smaller gadgets - phones, cameras, etc. but, before it we had the 'Mini-B' (this specific cable) so the older devices will need the 'Mini'.

These internal filters provide cleaner power to each device due to filtering out line noise that could be introduced by other equipment plugged into the same surge protector.Each plug is physically situated parallel to each other, so larger transformers have less of a chance of blocking other plugs.  Plug wires hang down the side of the Isobar rather than fall over the top of an adjacent plug.  This is a very nice feature.Isobar makes a quality product. review_title: Overpriced; muddy sound when volume is low
review_text: I'm returning after several months of use to update my review.  In the meantime I've listened to these daily and, very recently, bought a new pair for about the same price, which I will explain momentarily.  My opinion of the Monster NTunes is, if anything, worse than before, and I'm dropping my rating from three stars to two for reasons explained below.  It strikes me that people don't like to read negative reviews: if a potential buyer came to this page, they probably like these headphones and want to justify buying them; and if they like these headphones, they apparently don't want to hear anything negative about them.  But I'm not interested in whether people like my review; I'm interested in giving honest feedback about a product.  So here it goes.SOUND QUALITY.  The Monster NTunes are mediocre on sound quality.  Don't get me wrong: the sound is not bad.  The bass in particular is good.  The sound quality is above average if, say, you were comparing them to other store-brand headphones in the $60 to $80 range.  But there are two major problems that I noticed, both of which should be absent in headphones selling for over $100.  First, the sound (including the bass) is muddy at low volumes.  The highs are muffled out.  The lows and mids are just not as clear as they should be.  Secondly, and worse still, they are terribly fuzzy and distorted at high volume.  Listening to iTunes on my Mac, the sound turns to complete mush when you raise the volume up to the two or three highest notches.  This is not a matter of lack of "burn in," either: I tried this once they had been used for months, and still the sound is full of distortion at high volume while being used with a simple computer amp.  They would NEVER work well plugged into a powerful headphones amplifier.COMFORT.  I grew very frustrated with their comfort level: it is pretty bad.  The headpiece has a bit of padding liner, but it's relatively thin and bothers my head after a while.  Above all, though, the muffs sit directly ON the ear, the material is hard, and they create terrible discomfort after an hour or two of listening.  At first I dismissed the comfort, thinking it was just me, that somehow I was wrong about it, or that the headphones were designed that way (which obviously they were).  I first realized how inferior they are in comfort when I tried my cousin's on-ear Bose headphones, which were very comfortable - like good headphones should be.  The Monsters eventually caused so much discomfort that I decided to buy a new pair for the same price.  I was tired of coming away from two hours' worth of listening with burning red ears and aching cartilage.DESIGN.  There are some definite pros in the design.  First, they look pretty good.  Secondly, I love that you can unplug the cord on the headphones end, which makes it easy to unplug them from the computer and move them out of the way.  Thirdly, they come in nice packaging.  But there are also some major faults.  One has already been suggested above in my comments about comfort.  But another major design flaw is that you cannot fold them up for easy transport or storage.  They come as they are: no folding, no twisting, no adjustment of any kind, really, except in the height of the headpiece.  Finally, they do NOT come with a case or bag of any kind.  How someone is supposed to travel with these things is a bit of a mystery to me.  (Around the neck?  I'm not a teenager.)PRICE.  The price of the NTunes is, in my opinion, the biggest fault of all, and the principal reason for my low rating.  As I mentioned above, after much careful research, I got a new pair of headphones, theAudio-Technica ATH-M50 Professional Studio Monitor Headphones with Coiled Cablefor about the same price.  The new Audio-Technicas are so much better than the NTunes it's like night and day.  The bass is stronger.  The highs are higher.  The entire sound quality is far superior.  And they are much more comfortable.  In short, the price of the NTunes (currently $112) make it seems as if you are getting a serious pair of headphones, when in reality you're getting a hyped brandname that should be selling for about $70.  A comparison of sound quality, comfort, and overall features of another headphone in the same price range (the Audio-Technicas) leaves no doubt whatsoever that the NTunes are nowhere close to being competitive at this price point.My advice?  Save your money and buy a really serious pair of headphones for the same price.  The NTunes are not worth the cost.

I use a laptop that has a touchpad (which I hate), and also has a trackpoint (the "eraser" thing) which can be fatiguing and painful if I'm doing a lot of mousing. When I'm working at a desk, I can use a regular mouse. But when I'm working elsewhere, a mouse doesn't work well at all.I hate a true trackball - tried them many times and they just never work well for me. This concept looked intriguing so I decided to give it a try.First off, my comments would apply to any of a number of models of handheld mouse out there.The concept is interesting - you hold the mouse in your hand, don't have to be right by the machine, don't have to have room for a mouse to move.After several days of using it, my thoughts are:- It's a bit disrupting to have to put the mouse down when you have to use the keyboard. So for someone doing a lot of keyboarding, with the occasional mouse click, this isn't the best choice. It's usable, just a bit intrusive.- The thumb-sized trackball is better than a full-sized trackball for precision, but still can be tougher to get the pointer in just the right spot.  I wish there were a version that had a little thumb-sized touchpad (or better yet, a trackpoint!).- The two buttons which serve for "right-clicking" are below the trackball, on either side of the scroll wheel. It requires a bit of thought when you need to right-click. Presumably that will become more automatic with a bit more practice.- The laser pointer would be useful if you were doing a presentation. It's controlled by the left-hand of the two buttons above the trackball. The righthand button does nothing in this model. Other versions of this device have those buttons working for page-up/down scrolling and double-clicking. The laser pointer is fun (sure wish I had a cat to tease with it) but for me, not terribly useful. Another version (no laser pointer/paintbrush) would have been a better choice for me.Durability: can't really comment as I've just had it a few days. The thing does seem to be holding up well, charge-wise, since its initial charge the day I got it.The documentation is useless. There's a diagram showing the various buttons and what they mean for the different versions, but no instructions. Fortunately it was pretty self-explanatory - I just plugged in the little wireless USB thingy to install the drivers, then plugged in the separate USB cable and let it charge.

These speakers are about as average as you get. Mostly designed for ease of use, Polk clearly put sound quality in the backseat while designing the OWM3's.I will start by giving these speakers credit for what they do well. If you need to wall mount speakers and don't have a ton of flexibility, these speakers may be a good match for you. With 8 different mounting positions(including side and front standing configurations)these are about as versatile as you can get as far as placement goes. The OWM3's are very sturdy and seem to constructed quite well. With a matted black finish and a removable cloth grille, these speakers do look pretty nice. However, performance is not on par with the Polk name despite the somewhat steep price tag considering what these speakers can do.Sound quality on these speakers is average at best. I would not suggest these as front speakers or even rear speakers in a 5.1 setup. You may be able to get away with these as your rears, but I feel that these should be used solely as front height or back rear speakers in a 7.1 setup considering the strengths of this particular model. When using in a 5.1 setup as rears these work ok, but you will definitely notice some of the fallbacks. These speakers don't have a very good frequency response(reaching down to 80hz, and that may be a stretch considering you cannot actually cross them at 80 or even 90hz without straining them considerably)and the mid frequencies can sound somewhat hollow at times. The high end frequencies are ok for the most part but begin to strain a bit in the very high end(20 KHz or so). Like I said above, these speakers would probably work great in a 7.1 setup when they are utilized only to fill in background effects but if you plan to use with a 5.1 setup you can find better speakers than these in this price range.Overall these speakers offer great functionality but seemingly at the expense of sound quality. Do they sound bad? No, but there are certainly better speakers out there for a similar price.

The NIX immediately found the card and began displaying images. Total time from opening the package to beginning to enjoy the pictures was about three minutes.Once it was installed, I used the menu to make two adjustments -- sequence vs. random order and auto fit rather than optimal photo mode, since so many of our images are portrait, rather than landscape mode. There are other settings you can make, all easily understood, but this is all we needed.Image resolution, brightness, color, and contrast are superb -- this from someone who uses Photoshop on a color-corrected monitor.In short, this unit is simple to set up, easy to understand, and provides great image quality.UPDATE: I have answered so many questions about the NIX that I am starting to feel like a shill. Since posting this review, I have purchased two additional units for our children and loaded images of our grandchild on them. (Merry Christmas!) Many of the questions I am fed from Amazon presuppose that this is a highly technical unit. It's not. I have now automated the images for our unit through a Lightroom present, but really all you have to do is plug an SD card into your computer, then drag and drop jpeg or video images onto the card, plug the card into the slot at the back of the unit, and turn it on.Others have pointed out that the menu is sort of kludgy -- well, it is -- but you are likely to meddle with it only once or twice. It is easy to set up, and the video quality is outstanding for a unit in this price range.

RICOH GR DIGITAL III CAMERAThis is a very, very good, high performance 10 MP digital camera with a surprising number of professional features for its diminutive size and weight. It also has a couple of unfortunate shortcomings. The most important lack is an optical zoom (there is only a 4X digital zoom). There is also no image stabilization. However, if you can live without these two features, which are present in almost all point-and-shoots being sold today, read on.PHYSICAL CHARACTERISTICSThis is one of the few small cameras that has a built-in hot shoe for accessories such as an external flash unit or an external  viewfinder. It has a superb fixed 6.0mm lens (equivalent to a 28mm lens on a 35mm camera) that opens to a nice, wide f1.9 aperture. Because of this, the lens is outstanding in low light situations. Focus range is from 30CM to infinity and in the Macro setting, it will focus down to 1CM - one-quarter inch. Autofocus is very fast with almost no lag time. The camera is very compact and lightweight - 7.5 oz. (only 2 oz. more that my mobile phone!) The reason for this is the well-built magnesium body - very sturdy feeling with a secure, wide rubberized gripping surface. It has an incredibly sharp 3 inch LCD screen that can be adjusted for brightness.OPERATION AND EXPOSUREThere are several modes - Aperture priority, Shutter priority, a Program Shift mode that ranges properly exposed settings combining various apertures and shutter speeds. In addition there are six "MY" settings where custom configurations to match various shooting conditions can be set up and saved. There is also a completely manual setting for times when no auto program will do. The versatility of available settings is very impressive - exposure compensation, flash synchro settings, noise reduction, ISO settings, level adjustment/correction, white balance compensation and several more. In addition, there are two function buttons that can be set to control any of the above adjustments that the operator uses most. There are four `scene' settings - HDR combines two exposures to optimize high contrast scenes. In this case, the HDR combination is saved as well as the normal exposure. There is a Skew Correction feature where the camera attempts to reduce perspective distortion with varying success. There is a Text setting that makes high contrast exposures for capturing printed text, whiteboard charts and written notes. The camera takes VGA size movies as well, not HD. The camera will take bracketed exposures in 1/3 or  stop increments. The exposures can be set to all color (Auto-bracketing), White Balance bracketing and Color bracketing, a black and white and a color exposure for each shutter press. There is an interval timer so with a tripod, an exposure every minute or a user-selectable time interval is possible. When a photo is being set up, there is a Tilt Sensor that displays on the LED screen assuring that the camera is level, with or without an audible cue. The camera saves RAW image data which is rare in small cameras.FOCUSFocus features built into this camera are many and varied. The auto-focus is lightning quick and in cases when even this is too slow, Ricoh utilizes their convenient Snap feature. Set the focal distance and when the shutter is pressed all the way down in one motion, the camera uses that focal length, if it is pressed halfway down first, the normal auto-focus process is used. This is excellent for shooting, say, a sports event where the focus can be preset on the players so there is no delay waiting for auto-focusing. In addition, there is a Pre-AF feature. When this is active, the camera continuously focuses as the camera is moved into position for a shot - ready to shoot at the press of the shutter. This camera also can be set to show a depth of field guideline or a nice levels graph for each aperture on its LED screen.BOTTOM LINEThe Ricoh GR Digital III is a joy to use and with its truly professional features, it is uniquely positioned - small, compact and exceptionally powerful. Without an optical zoom and image stabilization, it is not really a family point-and-shoot and as such, it seems a little overpriced. However, for the serious photographer who wants a feature-rich but pocketable camera, this may just be the one that fills the bill. Highly recommended.

review_title: This or the Canon 70-200 2.8 IS II? - A Wedding Photographer's Perspective
review_text: This is a very difficult question.  Here are the qualities that both lenses have:1) Amazing image quality2) Very fast, accurate, and consistent autofocus3) Wide(r-ish) available aperturesYeeeah...Let's get into the fine differences of these lenses.  Okay,so there are two difference that are not exactly fine, but very large.  The 70-200 boasts consistently excellent image quality throughout a 70-200 range AND it has a robust image stabilization.  From the few times I've rented it, I feel like I could snap sharp photos of a deer while chasing it through the forest with this one.  So is the image stabilization and wide focal range give the victory to the 70-200?  In my humble opinion, not necessarily and here are my reasons:1) The 135 is around $1500 less than the 70-2002) The 135 is f/2 - unique look3) The 135 is about half the weight of the 70-2004) The 135 is widely considered to be the sharpest lens made by CanonAs a shooter who spends most of his time using a 50L, I don't find myself needing telephoto ranges very much.  When I do, the 135 does the trick and leaves more money in my pocket for other gear ($1500 can easily buy you an L prime).  The 135 is definitely not as easy to use as the 70-200 because it lacks image stabilization, but it forces you to develop a steady hand.This wasn't an easy review to write since I love using both of these lenses, being an owner of the 135 and having rented the 70-200.  If I photographed more wildlife or if I ever went on a safari, I would surely look to pack the 70-200 in my bag.  But if it's just weddings,the 135 is sufficient for my needs.

review_title: Wired Creative Fatal1ty USB (aka HS-1000) vs. Wireless HS-1200
review_text: TheFatal1ty USB Headset (also known as HS-1000), which usually is worth for about $30 less, and this newer model, HS-1200, are both gaming headsets made by Creative and endorsed by "professional gamer" Jonathan "Fatal1ty" (if that means anything to you - personally, I can care less about that). They both connect via USB; however, the obvious main difference is that one is wired (HS-1000) and the other is wireless (HS-1200). Is it worth the extra money for the wireless luxury? Well, it all depends on your needs.Although both headsets have the same frequency response/audio specs (20Hz ~ 20kHz, 40mm Neodymium drivers, Impedance: 32ohm), they do NOT sound the same. It's just like if you were take the same speakers and listen to it in different environments/position (a garage compared to a living room), it will definitely sound different, right? Well, I believe it's mainly because the wired HS-1000 cups are much larger and covers the entire ear, giving a more secluded, dynamic feel -- like being in a theater. However, the HS-1200 ear-cups are much smaller and does not cover the ear entirely -- it's more like the sound is produced directly to the ear; it sounds like actually being out there in the open than sitting in a theater. It does sound more clear (like removing the front covers of the speakers), but then again, it also doesn't have that confined feel of being in a large room/theater. So it all depends what you're looking for. Overall, for music and videos, and considering comfort as well (especially if you're going to be wearing it for a long time), I like the wired, more confined sound of the HS-1000 better. Personally, however, when playing Crysis and Call of Duty 4, I actually prefer the sounds of the HS-1200, as it sounds a little more clear and direct. It's just too bad the HS-1200 isn't as comfortable to wear.I think the whole point of wireless should be that you don't have to deal with cords AT ALL. Well, you still have to deal with wires with the receiver - not only the USB wire to connect to the computer, but also another wire is coming out of the receiver for charging the headset. It would have been much nicer if the receiver just had a USB sticking out (no cords) or be the size of those laptop mouse receivers (like Logitech's wireless headset's receiver), and simply just include a USB extension cable as an extra.When the battery is running low on the HS-1200, the headphone will start to beep. Make sure you hold the ON/OFF button for 3-seconds to turn it off after each use.The headphones worked without installing any software (Plug-and-Play) on Windows XP, but you will need to install the Creative Software if you want to take advantage of the X-Fi Crystalizer and CMSS-3D. It seems like a gimmick feature, but they both actually make it sound better.Advantages against the two headphones:HS-1000 (aka Creative Fatal1ty USB Gaming Headset)- Much better comfort against the HS-1200 - NO QUESTION!- Sound is more like being in a theater/confined.- No need to worry about charging.- Better overall for other uses besides gaming: music and movies.- Can completely detach the microphone.- Comes with a bag to put in.HS-1200* Wireless* Sound is more direct and clear/sharper.* When you swivel the microphone down, it will automatically enable it. (and turn off when you put it up)* Volume controls are on the right side of the headphones (although it can be annoying to the ear when you press the buttons on the headphones while wearing; like when you crunch on food when wearing earplugs)For most gamers, when it comes to mouse and keyboard, wired is still the way to go. It's just nice not having to worry about recharging the batteries ever (or the the batteries not holding a charge anymore, for that matter) or any frequency interruption. The wired HS-1000 only has one wire on the left side of the earphone, so it really isn't a big deal to deal with one wire. (whereas the HS-1200 has two wires sticking out of the receiver, even though the headset is wireless.)Personally, if I were to only keep one between the two, I would stick with the wired HS-1000. However, if you often do a lot of gaming -- granted, you also own a wireless controller or keyboard/mouse -- from your bed or couch late at night (and don't want to disturb others), then the wireless headset can be a nice addition. I still think wired is still the way to go for gaming (keyboard, mouse, headphones).Although I have been disappointed with Creative Fatal1ity's gaming mouse (Fatal1ty 1010), I have to say Creative knows what they're doing when it comes to sound. I also own a SteelSeries 4H gaming headset and both Creative HS-1000 and HS-1200 sound a lot better. Both headphones have their own advantages and weak points, so it all depends what is important to you the most.Definitely not a 5-star product, but I give this a 3 1/2 stars.Pros:* Clear, direct sound.* Works with PS3. (you hear the other player's voice and not the in-game sounds)Cons:* Headset cannot adjust/turn inward or outward* Not too comfortable (also because of first con). The cups are very small. I have small ears, yet it feels quite tight even after adjusting.* Receiver has two wires (kind of defeats the purpose of being all wireless) coming out of it (USB and Charging line)* Cannot wear the headset around the house. (However, it works fine in the same room).* I really don't like having to hold on the power button for a few seconds just to turn on/off. This has really annoyed me in the long run. It needs a quick on/off switch.* Slightly inconvenient having to restart certain applications (or games) if the headphones aren't connected before (no sound). [But I'm sure this is a common problem with any USB audio devices]

What I wanted in a keyboard were:* Thin* Lightweight (very important!)* Inexpensive* Excellent wireless range* A full-sized layout since I'm also playing some games (especially FPS's) on itThis keyboard met every one of those requirements.  First, this keyboard is unbelievably thin.  Next to a lot of other keyboards, it's sort of like comparing a Macbook Air to a conventional notebook. When I pick it up from beside me to use, picking it up one-handed even, it doesn't break my arm to lift it over to my lap.  I must emphasize what a big deal this is. I actually bought mine at Fry's for $34 and felt like I was getting a bargain for the package.  I expected to spend that on a decent lightweight wireless keyboard alone, and the mouse was a real bonus.  Wireless range was critical, as a couple of heavier desktop keyboards I had at home already were fizzling out more than a few feet from the computer.  This one just works fine all the way across the room.  One small annoyance:  It didn't work quite as smoothly when the USB dongle was plugged into the back of the computer which sits on the floor.  It sometimes missed a beat.  Running a short $3 USB extension cable to place that dongle up about 3' from the ground and without a computer and other junk between me and it, but without moving it any closer to me, totally solved that.  Now I can lean back and it never misses anything.Finally, I had mulled over the idea of getting a smaller compact keyboard as originally this was STRICTLY a HTPC and you don't generally need a full keyboard for one of those.  As I had also caved into the temptation to put a high performance video card in the system for some big-screen gaming, I figured I would probably need a full keyboard.  For this, it works splendidly.  I can play Left4Dead 2 or Fallout Vegas as comfortably as at my desk and enjoy the gigantic view of my 50" TV.  As for the feel of the keys, it has the right amount of tactile feel, responds brilliantly (some cheap keyboards miss a keypress now and then or don't depress smoothly), and generally feels very solid.  I'd be pleased to have this on my desk if I weren't already used to the Microsoft Natural Ergonomic "Humpback" model 4000 keyboard with the split in the middle, which I've been using for many years.On the mouse:  It doesn't have the assortment of extra side buttons that I like on my Logitech mouse that is at my desk, nor the nice variable-spinability scrollwheel that can be made to be clutched or to spin freely.  It's pretty much a basic 3 button laser mouse with scrollwheel, but for that, it works beautifully.  A laser mouse tends to work better on more surfaces than your old-school red-eye LED mouse, and this one certainly works on nearly everything.  That is, it works on any mousepad, the end table, the coffee table, the couch, a piece of paper, a newspaper, a magazine, my thigh with or without long pants, the front of my shirt... whatever I need it to work on to get that pointer over to the XBMC icon to get it kicked on so that my Harmony remote can take over.  If I need to use it for a while, though, it gets the job done very competently.This is a combination that I recommend to anyone.  I wish I'd have gotten mine for the price this is currently listed on Amazon, which at the moment is about $10 less than I paid at my local Atlanta Fry's.As for durability, I've been using it heavily for 9 months so far and it still works like new.  Of course, I do tend to use a keyboard for pretty much a decade or more, so hopefully this one will live up to that expectation.

review_title: FAST LENS!!!!  Great Value,  you can't afford not to own this lens
review_text: I've owned this lens for about 3 years, please look at [...] or our FB page for examples.  I'll also add one to the product images.As one of, if not, the cheapest lenses in the L series line up you might think it's going to be a bit sub-par.  Well, you'd be wrong if you though that.  This is a Canon L series 70-200.  Possibly one of the most utilized focal length ranges on the planet and Canon did not take the F/4 non-IS version lightly.  When I bought this lens, I bought it to augment my motorcycle track day photography kit which was primarily my 7D and 100-400 L.  This lens quickly became as utilized if not more than the 100-400 depending on the track.  If I don't need the reach of my 100-400, I'm using the 70-200 F4.  It's sharper, and faster and lighter, in fact this lens is not big at all which makes hand holding it very easy.  This means panning for those motion shots becomes a breeze even if you don't have IS.Basically, at around $600, you CAN NOT beat this lens.  I'm not saying the 70-200 F/2.8s are not better.  They are, after all they are F/2.8, 2.8 is better than 4.  But is the 2.8 sharper or faster?  Maybe a little sharper, not sure, but I've shot with both and it didn't seem to be faster to me and the sharpness difference was marginal.  The basic advantage I saw with the 2.8 was, 2.8.  But at over $2k for the 2.8 IS II, that's over 3x the cost of this lens.  I have not shot the 2.8 non IS which is cheaper but word on the street is the non IS 2.8 is being discontinued and support for the lens by CPS is also going away.  The one thing I will concede that I liked a bit better on the 2.8 was the color quality.  This is not to say that my F4 is bad, it's not, and again for $600 it's amazing, but let me reiterate.  I've shot this F4 lens, and the 70-200 F/2.8 IS version 2.  We are talking about a $1600 difference in price.  $600 vs. $2200.  Sure I want the F/2.8 and may buy one eventually but when you can get 80-90% of the quality at 1/3 the price, you just can't afford not to buy it.  On the other hand, if you have money coming out your ears, or maybe you only want to buy 1 BA lens and that's it, sure buy the 2.8, but if you are trying to assemble a comprehensive kit for your needs and your budget is limited, the F/4 will not disappoint.With the new DSLRs ISO performance increasing more and more these F/4 lenses are becoming very attractive, and not just from a price perspective.  The lens is lighter, less imposing and much more likely to end up in your bag on a trip where you can't bring everything.  You still get decent background separation with the DOF provided by F/4 @ 200mm, and like I said before, the keeper rate with this lens is on par with the 2.8.  The AF is blazing fast, probably because it's just got those tiny little lens elements to move around right?  I shoot motorcycles going around corners at over 100mph and I'm telling you, using the Al Servo mode AF on my 7D with this lens I don't miss, and I'm not trying to tout my talent, the combination of the 7Ds AF and this lens is killer.Anyway,  I bought this lens because it was cheap and I thought it would be a good addition, turns out, it's one of my primary go to sports lenses.  You can't afford not to put one of these in your kit.  It's too good and too cheap not to.So.... if you are weekend warrior like me, part time pro, and money IS an object, you are ON a budget, this lens is gonna deliver so much bang for the buck that you'll want to tell everyone you know and they'll be annoyed about it because they have no idea what  you are talking about.... so try to reserve all that enthusiasm for your photography buddies, everyone else doesn't get it.  :)

review_text: This is a good looking iPad case for earlier generations of iPads.  More recent versions don't fit.The case can hold your iPad at four different viewing angles. The strap is wide and not too tight...it's comfortable to use for extended periods of time.The only real complaint is that the screen doesn't automatically turn off when you close the cover.  Case manufacturers can add in a small magnet to trigger the off switch, but there isn't one in this cover.  The magnet inside the strap would probably work if oriented correctly, but it isn't in my sample.The lack of the screen shutoff dropped my rating from five stars to four.  I have my iPad set to shut off the screen after a couple of minutes of inactivity, but it's still an unnecessary waste of battery power.  Outside of that, I really like the look and feel of this case and wouldn't hesitate to buy it.

review_title: Legs can be used to make a great travel tripod
review_text: Looking for a travel tripod that is very short collapsed but not a table top; light enough and short enough to put in my bag and carry as my standard set of equipment.  This tripod gets down to just under 11 inches; or you can take the pan head off and it is 10 1/4".  This is short enough for either of my travel bags.  Although it's a bit wobbly, I have had great success with it when using a timed or external shutter release.  Run a cord to the ground and use you foot to hold it down, and it stabilizes well.There are two problems with this tripod.  First, the pan head is small and flimsy, and doesn't lock the tilt very well.  A large camera will drift up or down.  Second, it is nearly impossible to level the camera with the horizon.  Although it is possible to open fewer than all 8 sections on any leg, the legs do not have fine adjustment on the length, .  And the legs really need to be spread out to be stable.  So there is not enough flexibility to get a precise level.You can attach a ball head onto the pan head, and put the camera on the ball head; that solves the leveling issue but not the drift issue, and adds weight.  What I did was remove the pan head and attach the ball head directly to the tripod legs.  I used a 1/4-20 x 3/8 Socket Cap Screw, a Heavy Duty 1/4" Female to 3/8" Male Bushing Adapter, and a Redged Professional R-0 Ball Head.  This holds my Panasonic FZ-200 without problem.  And I've even used it to hold the FZ-200 with 1.7x tele adapter, but with a tripod mount ring attached to the adapter tube to balance weight.  Total cost for this modified tripod is less than $60.  And it's light, long, and sturdy enough to use as an extender arm as well (with a remote shutter release).Now my standard kit is the camera, a filter pouch (with polarizer, ND400, ND8, graduated ND, +3 macro), remote shutter release, extra battery, ball head and modified tripod legs, and Metz 28 CS-2 with Ultra-Pod.  Super compact, light, and ready for nearly any kind of shot.  If you like this kind of photography, then this is the tripod to get.

review_title: Installed in 2 minutes; superior range & power
review_text: This NETGEAR N450 wireless router replaced a Ubee DDW3611 wireless router that Time Warner installed a couple of years ago. Time Warner charged me $5.99 rent per month for that router and over the past 24 months that totals $143.76.But in addition to the long-term cost savings, the NETGEAR N450 has superior range and maximizes the power of my Internet connection compared with the Ubee -- important since I enjoy Xbox One and Xbox 360 games (Xbox Live) and my wife and I also both work from home and are both on our computers way more then I care to think about.Installation was incredible easy. I just swapped out the same connections (I did replace the ethernet cable to the router with the new one included with the NETGEAR unit). Then I placed a call to Time Warner and it was up and running in a couple minutes.The following devices are on our wireless network:* 3 computers (2 PowerBooks and one iMac)* 2 iPhones* 2 Dish Network Hoppers (DVRS) and 2 Joeys (wireless boxes that link to the 2 Hoppers)* 1 Kindle Fire HD* 1 Apple TV* 1 Xbox 360* 1 Xbox One* 1 Playstation 3* 5 wireless security cameras* 2 Sony HD televisionsOur house is 3,200 square feet and the NETGEAR N450 is in my wife's home office located in the center of the house. My office is at the other side of the house and the "man cave" (where the Xbox's and Playstation are located) are on the opposite side from that, over the garage (the bonus room).Here's the results of a network speed test from my home office ... which is some 100 feet away from the router:* Download speed: 55Mbps* Upload speed: 5.69 Mbps* Ping: 31msWith the Ubee, the speeds fluctuated wildly from day to day. Sometimes I'd notice super-slow speeds and do a test where I'd see 30Mbps downloads; 3.9Mbps uploads and a ping of 55ms. On the best days it would be around 45Mbps downloads; 4.4Mbps uploads and the ping at 30+ms.For me one of the biggest improvements is in one Xbox One game play (Xbox Live), Titanfall, Call of Duty, etc. The console, and the games, show your connection in terms of 1-5 bars. With the old modem mine was usually at a 3... 4 on really good days with all the doors open. Now I can leave all of the door closed and still get 5 bars every time.I've been testing this router for over one month and haven't had to reset it once. Accessing the router's settings (to make adjustments) is easy... just open a web browser and enter 192.168.0.1 That will allow you to change the name of your network (SSID), adjust security options and much more. Most of the settings have a good explanation of what they are for right there in the interface. It's very user friendly and one of the better modem interfaces I've seen.I give the NETGEAR N450 wireless router two thumbs way up. It's the best wireless router I've tested to date.

review_text: The SD870 IS is about everything you could want in a compact point and shoot digital camera.  It offers excellent image quality, a large vivid LCD display, intelligent defaults, fine low-light sensitivity, a high quality movie mode (with sound), an outstanding wide-angle lens and (most importantly for me) a photo capture speed that leaves many other digital cameras in the dust.I cover a fair amount of electronics trade shows such as CES and CEDIA for my home theater site (Big Picture Big Sound), so I need a camera that is quick on the draw, has a good macro feature for close-ups, and has good low light sensitivity and zoom for distance shots at press conferences.  But portability is also key, as I need to carry the camera around in my pocket along with other gadgets for note-taking.  I've owned a Canon S400 Digital Elph for a number of years, and it has served me well, but the lag time between pushing the shutter button and actually getting a picture (particularly indoors) was frustrating, and the low light sensitivity is also fairly poor.The SD870 retains all of the positive features of the earlier ELPH models, yet improves on the weaknesses.  You can go from power up to pictures snapped in about a second.  And once the camera is powered up and ready, you can capture shots in 1/2 second or less (depending on lighting conditions).  For taking pictures in low lighting, the "Night Scene" mode (along with built-in optical image stabilization) is excellent, enabling me to capture on-stage action at a press event from 20 or 30 feet away (ISO sensitivity on the camera goes all the way up to 1600, but you can expect some graininess when the camera goes above ISO 400).  Other scene modes such as "portrait" are also handy when you're going in for a close-up shot and want to capture a posed or candid pic of a loved one with an "artistic" out-of-focus background.In terms of size, the camera is very small, yet comfortable in the hand.  The camera's aluminum frame feels solid without being weighty and controls are logically laid out so you can be up and running without cracking the manual.  Unfortunately the small size means it does not take standard AA batteries, but the Lithium Ion battery that comes with it will last through a couple of hundred shots in normal use.  You will want to buy a spare battery however, as there is not always a lot of warning between when the on-screen low battery indicator starts flashing and the camera powers itself down (hint, get the Lenmar NB-5L equivalent - it will last about as long as the Canon for about 1/3 the price).All in all, I'm very pleased with my purchase of the SD870 IS and am looking forward to using it to snap high quality pics of the latest gadgets at next year's Consumer Electronics Show.Update (2/23/08) - Coming home from a party one night, I was mortified to find that the SD870 lens was halfway extended inside its case, inside my pocket.  Apparently the power button was activated while inside my pocket and the lens motor has no safety so it tried to extend itself and the mechanism broke when it met resistance.  So the lens would no longer fully extend and the image was perpetually out of focus.  Sending it to Canon, I got a letter back saying it would cost $100 (flat fee) to repair even though it was under warranty.  I argued that the camera was not abused or dropped and eventually they relented and covered the repair.However this design flaw in the lens motor would lower my score of the camera to 4 stars if I could edit the score.  What good is a portable camera that can't be carried inside a pocket?  My advice would be to take the battery out if you're going to pack this inside luggage or transport it somewhere it could be jostled about.  And I hope Canon addresses this with a safety retract mechanism (or a recessed power button) in future models.

review_title: Fast is good; with RAW images it's essential...
review_text: Getting fast SD cards for your digital camera is relatively simple here on Amazon or even at your neighborhood drugstore these days. You just look for the Class 10 rating on the card or the package, insert it into your digital camera and format the card. It's that easy. But if you have a digital camera that writes RAW images to the card, the storage time can take much longer, and for those cameras that are equipped to write RAW images, you might want to consider a much faster card.ThisSanDisk Extreme Pro 8 GB SDHC Class 10 UHS-1 Flash Memory Card 95MB/sis one of those SDHC cards that is better for shooting fast sequential photos, RAW images or full HD videos due to it's faster write time. These SDHC are available in capacities of 8GB, 16GB, 32GB, or as 64GB SDXC (Secure Digital eXtended Capacity) cards. The 8GB size is a personal standard as I'm a "card swapper," a habit that goes back to 35mm camera days when we would change film for color transparencies, color prints, b&w;, etc. If I was shooting more videos, I wouldn't hesitate to get the largerSanDisk Extreme Pro 32 GB SDHC Class 10 UHS-1 Flash Memory Card 95MB/sfrom the results that I've seen from this 8GB card, and I have a few of these. But these SDHC (Secure Digital High Capacity) cards are more costly than a standard SD card, and there are a few things that you need to be aware of before you get one of these:1. Check your camera's documentation to be sure that it will work.2. Format the card in the camera in which you intend to use it.Older digital cameras may (or may not) be able to handle the capabilities of these cards, so that's why it's crucial to check the documentation for your individual camera. You can also look it up online at most of the better camera manufacturers' Web sites if in doubt. Once you have verified this, it's absolutely essential to format the SDHC card in the camera in which you intend to use it. It's not advisable to format these cards in your computer, as you may have a loss of images, or it just may not function at all.Regarding the UHS-1 (Ultra High Speed - 1) rating, this is a speed class for SDHC and SXDC memory cards. It's the fastest category of SD cards available today, and will work in any SDHC compatible digital camera at lower speeds, but to take advantage of the UHS-I speed, a UHS-I compatible camera (or device) device is necessary. In other words, even if you don't currently have a camera that supports the UHS-1 standard, this card will still work and is backwards compatible with SDHC and SHXC devices. Just be aware that the card will be functioning at regular Class 10 speeds.This card is really designed for those who take RAW images or shoot high-speed sequential photos, such as sporting events, action shots and the like. If you're more into snapshots or a casual shooter who takes just a handful of photos in a given day, then you might be better off to consider picking up a couple of theseSanDisk 8 GB Class 4 SD Flash Memory Cards, as you'll be money ahead. Still have a few of these that I use as backups and for one of my compact digital cameras, and they're find for that type of use.ThisSanDisk Extreme Pro 8 GB SDHC Class 10 UHS-1 Flash Memory Card 95MB/sis one of the best that I've found on the market today for shooting RAW images and for high-speed work, as noted above. That's what makes it easy to recommend, and why I've just bought a couple more of them.11/17/2012

review_title: A HUGE UPGRADE!!! ELECTRIC84 Electric Projection Screen (84 Inch 16:9 AR)
review_text: I've had HD projectors for about 10 years.  The whole time has been with a painted wall.  I've read several reviews touting screens and doubted very much that they were worth the money.  I had my setup with the painted wall in the living room where my fiancee graciously allowed the wall space.  I wanted her to have a "normal" wall with say a mirror or large picture above the fireplace.  I started looking into screens.  I thought one with an electric motor would be cost prohibitive...until I started looking at the Elite line of screens.  I wanted a smaller screen, less than the size I had painted.  I found the 84" with an electric motor for an astonishing $149.  I just had to try it, especially after reading all the glowing reviews.  I was skeptical about how much better it could be, but several reviewers said it would be a noticable..."night and day" even.  The setup was incredibly easy.  Basically 2 screws required for wall mounting.  This makes it very flush to the wall, the one where the mirror or picture was supposed to go.  I ended up mounting it using shelving brackets and an S hook to project it out a little farther.  Again, very easy to do.So finally (sorry) the good part.  Since I just upgraded my system to 3D, I wanted to watch something 3D.  Titanic would work.  The picture did look great, but not really "night and day".  That wasn't until the next night when I agreed to watch something 2D to appease my 3D saturated fiancee.  It was a "chic flick" I got from Netflix..."One Day" with Anne Hathaway.  I was thinking, "I finally have my dream system and I'm watching a mediocre movie".  Was I wrong.  I noticed even with OK content, the difference with the screen (rather than the painted wall) was literally "night and day".  From even the credits and opening sceens, the picture was bright, crisp and highly detailed.  I kept (actually we) WOWing at the picture quality...almost like 3D without the glasses.  I've watched streaming content from Netflix and Amazon Prime with an equal WOW factor.If you're either starting a home theater and you've read the many blog about screens versus walls, ignore them and buy one of these screens.  If you want to upgrade, don't hesitate.  You won't be disappointed.  No matter what components you have or projector, it will definitely look the best it can with one of these babies.

I purchased this radio principally for SW use. I received it yesterday and had already been testing a Grundig G3 since last weekend. The external antenna included with the 909X makes the signal even stronger.  I am in northern NJ about 30 miles from NYC, although at a relatively higher elevation.  I easily pick up several foreign stations--RHC, CRI, RHC, REE and VOR.  Today, I picked India at a weak signal.  I pick Radio Japan at a good strength also but have not listened to English programming as of yet.  The 909X comes with preset stations labeled by countries, which makes it easy to update the memory as you find stations in your area.  It is a little less portable than the G3, but it is definitely a portable unit.  For its bigger size you get superior sound, LCD display,  a rotary tuning dial that is much more efficient than the tuning knob on the G3 for SW tuning, and larger and comfortable digit inputs.  The LCD display is extremely legible without turning the backlight on.  The FM sound is very pleasing.  The only advantage I give the G3 over the 909X is that when you auto tune, the G3 scans from one band to the next, while the 909X only scans within each band, a minor inconvenience.I wish the radio had Bluetooth for headphone use and the ability to scan through stations on the memory.Following my quick side by side test, I  did not wait and returned the G3 to Radio Shack last night.  This is after I inquired from two RS stores and left a voicemail with their regional manager to see if they could match the price Grunding/Eton sells the radio in its own website.  It did not seem right to pay 30% mark up for the radio.  By the way, RS is still selling the 909X for the original MSRP  of $499.

review_title: Just the Thing for an Aged Dell Laptop
review_text: 2006. Six years ago. An eternity in Internet time. This laptop had sat unused and unloved for so long its keyboard had started to degrade, and as a result was nearly unusable, despite having the horsepower to run Windows 7 with aplomb.Enter the replacement keyboard here, and all is now well. The instructions were clear, and the process was easy. I can now type at 50 WPM on the unit, and it's got a new life as my primary writing machine.Excellent product.
I got it to be able to download pictures off my cell phone to my desktop w/o having to dig up a cable each time. Once the setup and pairing was done , it worked as expected.

Sony generally makes good products, and the HDR-CX190 is no exception. It is durable and works as advertised.Pros- Compact, portable, and easily fits in the palm of your hand.- Zoom works well.- Image stabilization works well.- Shoots full HD (not as good as a movie studio HD, but still very good).- Audio records loud and clear.- Fits on standard tri-pods.- You can transfer the videos to your computer without the Sony software. Simply plug in the camera via USB and drag and drop the files (at least in Windows 7).- The lens cap is manual and built into the camera so you can't possibly lose it.- It has a USB cable attached to the camera at all times, so you always have one (but it isn't very long so I normally have to use the extension cable that it came with).- Great price!Cons- Definitely buy additional batteries. The battery this camera comes with lasts up to an hour (maybe) when recording full HD.- The zoom is kind of noisy and can be heard during playback.- There's no light on the camera, so make sure there's plenty of light when recording or else the video quality degrades and becomes grainy.- You can get hand cramps when recording for extended periods of time due to the camera's small size, so get a tri-pod.- You can't take a still-image while recording full HD.- The default recording setting isn't full HD, so make sure to change it before you start recording.

This is our first HD camera, so we didn't really know what to expect. (Note that for video review, we played the output via HDMI to our Sony Bravia 46" HD TV.) In full light, the picture is fantastic; you get some blur and artifacts during movement or in shadows, but I don't know if that is normal or not for an HD camera, so I'll take that at face value. Night shooting without the IR light (Nightshot) is pretty grainy, even with an add-on light. The Nightshot IR functionality works great and is a lot of fun to play with. The built-in IR light seems to work well up to 7 or 8 feet and then drops off.Still shots are pretty poor; even in picture mode, they look like video captures; the contrast and color balance are bad compared to a dedicated still camera, but that seems to be common with most if not all dual use cameras so, again, take it at face value. Note that it does have a built-in flash (I couldn't find that documented anywhere).It is small and light; you can almost stick it in your pocket, even with an extended life battery. Contrary to the CNET review, I didn't have any issues with the touch screen functionality.Video and still import work fine; I had to buy a different firewire cable (the one included has the small end on each side, my PC has a large firewire connection). The Picture Motion Browser did not work; it crashed with an error when trying to open on Vista. Sony were absolutely no help; they just kept sending me to knowledge base articles that were of no use, and refused to make any effort to help (given that I just dropped $1500 on camera and accessories, you'd think there would be more love there).On the whole, I'm pretty happy with the camera, although I'm disappointed that I have to carry two devices to get quality stills, and I'm very frustrated with Sony's support for their worthless software. But, at the end of the day, I paid for an HD video camera, not a still camera or software...so, four stars for the video functionality.

review_title: Okay for the price, but has some annoying quirks
review_text: I used to have aMiccus Mini-jack RX: Bluetooth Music Receiverbut when I got a new car with built-in bluetooth, I gave it to my husband. But then I found I wanted a similar device for myself to use with headphones and other speakers. Since I have aLifeProof Caseon my iPhone, it is not easy to access the headphone jack, so I like to use bluetooth whenever possible. This device serves that purpose well enough considering the price, but it definitely has some quirks and annoying aspects.First off, the charging port looks like an ordinary micro-USB port, but there must be something special about it, because EVERY time I have used a charging cord other than the one that came with it, it has killed the device. The first time this happened I thought it was defective, and I arranged for a return through the seller. But as I was packing it up to return, I noticed it had a couple of small holes--one on the top, and one on the side--like those found on many devices to perform a 'reset' by inserting a paper clip into the hole. I tried this, and the receiver turned on and worked again!After that, I tried all the Micro-USB cables I had, and all of them caused the same problem except for the short one that came with the device. Putting the paper clip in the side hole always brought the device back to life, but I don't want to risk damaging the device permanently by using other cables. I'm not sure what the hole on the front is for.I mostly use this receiver with ear buds for listening to audiobooks. In most apps, pressing the button once will cause the audio to pause, but then pressing it again does not always resume the audio playback. With some apps it will resume and others it won't. Pressing the button twice quickly will skip to the next track in some apps, but not all. I don't think these functions are documented.One very annoying feature of this receiver is that it beeps--LOUDLY--when you turn it on and off, and when the battery is getting low. It's dangerously loud if you have it connected to earbuds or headphones. I have to be careful to remove the buds from my ears when turning it on and off. And when the battery is low it also emits a very loud, obnoxious beep. The warning beep is every few seconds so you can forget about using it until you go and charge it. It does work while being charged but since the charging cord is so short it usually isn't practical to do so.The indicator lights on the receiver are part of the button. This makes it difficult to see the what the lights are doing as you are pressing the button. Bad design decision. I have to press the button with my thumbnail in order to see what is going on with the indicator lights.I found the directions were not entirely accurate about turning it off and on. To turn it on, I press and hold the button for about 5-6 seconds, until the blue light starts flashing slowly. To turn it off, I press and hold the button for about 7-8 seconds until the blue and red lights both appear, and then you have to immediately release the button, or you'll end up turning it back on again if you hold it for too long.When you plug it in to charge, it will display a solid red light while charging, and then a red and blue light after it is fully charged. I've never timed the battery life, but it's probably around 5-6 hours, which is about half that of the Miccus BluBridge.Helpful hints:- Only use the short charging cord that came with this receiver.- If the receiver will not turn on, try resetting it by inserting a paper clip into the small hole on the side for a few seconds. Then try turning it on.- Remove any attached headphones from your ears before turning it off and on.For my limited use, this worked out okay for the price, but if you don't mind spending a little bit more, theMiccus BluBridge Mini-jack RXis a better device. It has better controls and indicators, longer battery life, works more reliably in various apps, and seems to be of higher quality. If I was using this receiver in the car, I think the annoyances would be too much to put up with.

review_title: Not bad for the price, but it's got some issues
review_text: I purchased these speakers on sale for $50, and since they are a outgoing model it shouldn't be too hard to find these for a great sale price. Overall if you're getting them on sale, they aren't bad speakers. I've detailed some of the pros and cons I've had in using them over the last several months.Pros- Compact design: they fit great on my desk and take up only a moderate amount of space for the sound output they offer.- Convenient headphones/microphone input: They offer the ports on the right side of the right speaker to plug in your headset. This is particularly convenient when you've got them hooked in to a desktop/are using up the audio-out on your laptop or tablet.- Gets quite loud: This 2.0 system puts out plenty of volume for a bedroom or small apartment. It's not enough to throw a small party, but it's more than enough for individual listening.Cons- There is an imbalance between the right and left audio: I notice that the right and left speakers aren't completely in sync at all volumes, meaning that sometimes the right or left sound "louder" than the other when it's at a particular volume. I don't know if this is a defect with my individual unit or something more general.- No Bass: Despite the claims Logitech may make, I knew I wasn't going to get much bass and I don't hear much of anything on the low end. I bought this set because I didn't have room for a sub, so I was willing to make the compromise for portability. For bass lovers out there, buy a different set of speakers or a quality pair of headphones.For Games: The lack of the low-end really comes out when you play games, but I still enjoyed playing Diablo 3 and others even without the boomy bass. As long as you're reasonable about your expectations from a 2.0 setup, you won't be disappointed.For Movies: I've watched a number of movies across various genres, and overall this has been an admirably performing set. For the price, it does a great job with the highs and mids. The lows are obviously missing, but it hasn't significantly impacted my movie enjoyment.All in all, these are a solid set of 2.0 speakers. I think they will work great for someone looking for a compact yet loud setup to use for general computer purposes.

I have one of these on the door leading to my company's datacenter.  It feels well built and has not had any problems.  I didn't install it (yay for maintenance staff) but it didn't look all that difficult to install.  It almost always accepts my fingerprint and it's forgiving enough that your finger doesn't have to be positioned exactly perfect.  At the same time it has not yet given a single false positive.  The glass on the scanner does need to be wiped clean every now and then but that's hardly a huge deal.My only complaint is with the PIN code feature.  You can program it with a single six digit PIN code (no multiple codes) in case you need to give someone access and haven't yet enrolled their biometrics.  However, setting and entering the PIN code is convoluted without a numpad, and the display on the screen makes it confusing.So let's say you have a PIN of 654321.  To enter the first digit you press the + and - buttons until you have chosen the correct number.  The screen will show "6-".  Then you press # to move on to the next digit, and after choosing the correct number the screen will show "65".  Then you press # and the display changes to "5-", then "54", then "4-", and so on.  After thinking about it I can understand the logic behind it, but seeing it for the first time is confusing and makes you second-guess whether you're entering the correct numbers.Having said that, I so rarely use the PIN feature that it doesn't bother me, and clearly the lock's bread and butter is reading fingerprints and the PIN code is a throw-in feature that is useful in the occasional unexpected circumstance.  It excels at what it was designed for, so it's hard to hold the PIN shortcomings against it.  I highly recommend this lock.

review_title: Great wiring harness for 2006 Hyundai Sonata, with a couple of fixes (tl;dr: order two of these!)
review_text: I just used this wiring harness yesterday to install an aftermarket stereo on my 2006 Hyundai Sonata and I want to point out a couple of things.This harness is missing a couple of wires that are important for 2006 Hyundai Sonata owners. It also actually has a couple of extra wires too, that won't end up being connected to anything in the factory stereo wiring harness, but those can be just capped off and ignored. But what's more concerning for those of us with a 2006 Hyundai Sonata is that it's missing a larger spade connection at factory harness location 24 for the power antenna, and also a smaller wire connection at factory harness location 19, which is the remote control ground (required if you want to have your steering wheel radio controls work on your new, aftermarket stereo).Also note that this is the same wiring harness as the Metra 70-5520 Radio Wiring Harness, except the FD23B adds an extra wire (the 70-5520 has 18 wires and this one has 19 wires, IIRC), but it adds it add the wrong location for the 2006 Hyundai Sonata. I'll explain below...As "jasper pipestone" points out in his review of the Metra 70-5520 Radio Wiring Harness, a large wire is missing for the power antenna. He mistakenly refers to this as factory wiring harness location 13 in his review, but it's actually factory wiring harness location 24. Factory Harness location 13 is the black (common ground), so don't remove that one!. You actually want to match up with the funky green colored wire on the factory wiring harness for the power antenna line, which is at factory harness location 24, on the opposite side from the big black and gray wires (black == common ground and grey == battery/constant power). I did what he suggested and bought an extra wiring harness because I knew I'd be short a couple of wires, and these wiring harnesses are cheap. I popped the red wire retainer out from both harnesses. Then I lifted the little plastic clip on the inside of the wiring harness that holds down one of the bigger spade wires and removed it from one harness and then put it into the other harness, solving the location 24 problem.Also, this harness does not have a wire that matches up with factory harness location 19, which is the remote control ground, which is required if you plan on hooking your after market stereo up to a steering wheel control interface like the Axxess ASWC that I used. To solve this problem, I removed another (smaller) wire from my second/spare harness and put it into location 19 in the wiring harness I used to install my aftermarket stereo. Then I reinstalled both of the red wiring harness retaining clips. It works perfectly!I've uploaded a REALLY helpful wiring diagram for the 2006 Hyundai Sonata car stereo factory wiring harness here: [...]After adding the two missing wires to this wiring harness, I was able to connect all of my factory wiring harness wires to my aftermarket stereo with little problem.Hope this helps somebody else out there. =:)

Small external USB batteries like this Energizer model are extremely useful for additional power for phones, iPods, handheld games devices, and the like. I've gone through several over the years, and functionally, this is one of the nicer ones.It has a recessed on/off switch that is reasonably protected from accidental pushes, it has a four-stage blue LED indicating how much charge it has left, and if you're charging it, how much it's charged so far. It uses a standard micro-USB cable for charging, so you don't need to keep track of a specific AC adapter - any USB AC adapter or laptop USB port will work. The included 27" cable is about the right size for travel, and the magnetic clips are kind of snazzy.The issue is that this battery is only 9 watt-hours (2500 millamp hours @ 3.7v). Which is not a bad size, since an iPhone 5's battery is 5.4 watt-hours (1440 mAh @ 3.7v), so you can expect almost two charges with this. However, there are a lot of batteries with about the same physical dimensions with twice the capacity, such as thePowerGen 5200mAh batterythat I own, and if you price them on Amazon you'll find they're cheaper. The Energizer battery is 1" x 2" x 3", and I really expected something smaller given the capacity. The Powergen battery is 0.87" x 1.62" x 3.75", which is actually slightly smaller in total volume, and competing batteries are similar.  I'd be fine with the smaller capacity if the battery were really slim, but it's not.This will charge an iPad, which is an issue since some USB power sources won't. I experimented with my iPad 3, and found that this would restore about 25% of the battery, which is about right since since the iPad battery is 45 watt-hours.While I'll certainly be using this battery, you're really better off buying one the higher-capacity batteries from Powergen or New Trent. They're just as solidly built, and less expensive.
