Windows people - this has nothing for you. Move along - nothing to see here. 8-)I set the cameras up physically and attached them to a test network on a 192.168.1.x IP range CAT5 connected. I haven't tried the wireless it supports. I set up a dhcp server on a box and had the cameras find any old IP address just to get them connected so I could access them and then modify their IP information manually. Thereafter, I took down the dhcp server as I didn't need it any longer. I used nmap to find the new IP's for the cameras and their associated mac addresses.I never opened the Foscam users manual as what to do is fairly obvious to anyone that's worked with router, firewalls, AP's, etc. It's all the same stuff. Don't complain about the product if it's your own lack of knowledge that is giving you trouble.I used Firefox to get to each cameras internal web server and completed the setup. Just followed down the list of available buttons and made my selections. Using Firefox to see what the cameras were seeing is a snap. Video quality is good, low light operations are good and it has an automatic cut filter to sense light versus low light conditions. What more could you want for the price? The gadgets themselves are fine.On Fedora 17, fully patched, I installed mysql and zoneminder. I followed the zoneminder site instructions for Fedora 17 and was up in about 2 hours. I have zoneminder recording what the cameras see via motion detection and zoneminder is doing a great job. I gathered some statistics during this period to see how much disk space I needed to store the video events.Both cameras operating at 5 frames/sec on motion detect consumed quite a bit of space. I had both cameras pointing at me while I worked so they saw me typing, moving, etc at random. They consumed about 1Gig per 90 minutes. Therefore in my case I'm installing a 4T drive in a box to hold quite a long time worth of video.Actual usage in my business will change the disk consumption, I'm sure, but now I know what range of usage to expect. Those hardware DVR's with 500G of disk space are a joke. If I doubled up on cameras, I'd double up on disk space required, so those DVR's with little disk space and multiple cameras make no sense to me.Issues:Selinux and zoneminder don't get along too well. I have some bugzilla incidents reported and Fedora 18 does not appear to be any better than 17.The zoneminder startup script is also using the old chkconfig method as opposed to systemctl so on a normal boot sequence zoneminder attempts to start before mysql is up and fails. There are several work arounds available and I did my own so that zoneminder attempts to start only after mysql is up.The zoneminder error log was getting lots of buffer overruns primarily because I was using an old box with a relatively slow cpu chip. I followed the instructions for increasing buffer space and ultimately created the file /etc/sysctl.d/60-kernel-shm.conf containing:kernel.shmmax=536870912I also went into each cameras setup and increased buffers from the default of 40 to 100. That got buffer overruns down to 1 every few hours. RAM is cheap, so I didn't spend too much time trying to optimize these settings.I have a new mobo, I5 chip, and 8G RAM on order with the 4T drive. That's going to be my surveillance box.I believe I'm getting more of these cameras as they're inexpensive and great for my application.

review_title: Loved my Garmin FR 305; this one goes way beyond it
review_text: I've had my Garmin FR 305 for 6 years and still going strong.  So why did I see a need to go further?  It was prompted by my getting into interval training (run/walk, run/walk, etc.)  I could not hear the transition points with the somewhat muted tone of the 305.  So I figured there was some other way to get the transition message, maybe bluetooth.  I didn't even think about vibration.In my search, I happened upon this Garmin FR 310XT for around $200.  There was an even later release of the 910 for around $450, but that would be overkill for my purposes (I'm not into decathlon-type activities).My primary motivator for the purchase of the 310 was the ability to feel the vibration at the transition points.  Perfect.  I can be running and walking along, listening to my music through earphones, and know exactly when to do the next leg of the workout.OK.  That said, it was worth every bit the price just for the vibration.  But I discovered that almost everything about the 310XT was an improvement over the 305.  Where do I begin?  The chest strap for heart-rate monitoring is vastly improved from a comfort standpoint.  Setting values, such as setting the intervals, is so much easier than it was in the 305.  Many of the other improvements are covered by many other reviews, such as longer battery life and the ability to see remaining battery life (after two days of workouts, I was at 97% capacity remaining), quicker connection to satellites (never was a big deal with 305, but nice to get the connection quicker in order to get going), slightly smaller footprint without sacrificing the 4-readings per page capability, waterproof (not that I will swim with it, but comforting to know that getting stuck in the rain will not harm the watch), etc.  It retains all the great features that are present in the 305, so nothing is sacrificed.One more key point to make about the vibration.  Without vibration, for intervals I was needing to watch the screen count down as it got closer to the transition.  With the vibration, I can be viewing other screens if I want to see other indicators like avg speed, heart rate, etc., and the vibration will let me know it's time.  Or if you want, you can do the entire workout without ever having to look at the GPS watch.I have yet to try it when bicycling.  I know that I'm going to want to do interval training with the bicycle, which would have been difficult without the vibration.Net, net, a must have.

review_title: I love it so much that I did it again!
review_text: I've never networked anything before using this, and I have successfully created two different wireless networks.  I used the BEFW11S4 to set up a wireless network in my two story house (~1500 square feet), and I don't have a dead spot in the entire house.  Not only that, but I am able to use my laptop at the pool, over 100 feet away.  It was a little bit tricky to set up because the router had the same IP as my modem.  But after getting this figured out and simply changing the IP of the router (which is extremely easy with the setup utility), the network worked very well.Now I am in a house in Mexico which is made out of solid concrete and rebar.  This does create an issue with distance, but we fixed that by setting up the router in the middle of the house, that way we still get our 11 Mbps here in the office and on the other side of the house.  The greatest benefit of the router, though was its MAC address cloning ability.  Even though our ISP here limits our access to a single computer which it recognizes (I learned after a couple hours of messing around with different options) by the MAC address of the network adapter card, we were able to connect an entire house of computers (>5) with the hub by simply (again using the awesome configuration utility) having the Linksys router change its MAC address to match the network adapter of the old computer.  Now we have wireless access in the states, and we can bring the laptop to my parents house here in Mexico and instantly get service here.PROS*Can use inexpensive ISP service to a single computer to give internet and network access to multiple computers.*Can offer both wireless and wired (up to 4 computers wirelessly) connectivity.*Maintains speed up to 50 feet away through 3 6-inch walls filled with concrete and rebar.*Easy to set up.*Great configuration/setup utility which is accessable through a web browser (firmware is also upgradable by downloading an update from the website.)CONS*It does show a loss in speed or even in connectivity in certain "dead spots" in the house.  (To fix this, you just scoot over like 3 feet in either direction and it goes from 0% to 50%).*Poor customer support over the phone.I bought a second one based on my experience with the first one.  As I discover more and more about what this unit is capable of doing, it makes me more and more willing to recommend it.  So that's what I'm doing: "I recommend that you get this router/WAP."

I've used this with a couple Win7 64-bit machines.  I got this dock after my latest NewerTech dock died within 15 minutes, I was slightly hesitant due to the lack of reviews but I wanted eSATA+USB3, and how much worse could I do?  So far I'm quite pleased with it, using USB 3 and spinning drives I'm getting transfer speeds on par with internal SATA indicating the drives are the limiting factor.  The fan is a nice feature, I usually use a separate USB fan with my other docks, this is nicely incorporated into the dock.  It feels solid -- from the images I was afraid it might be a somewhat flaky add-on, but no.  The placement means that in addition to cooling the drive it acts to shield the drive's circuit board.  On mine it's quiet even on the max setting (I can't hear it over the drive at least) and at that setting keeps the drive fairly cool (just barely warm to the touch after copying 1TB onto a 2TB WD Caviar Black drive).  The dock shuts off when you "eject" it in Windows which is a nice feature -- some other docks I have when I eject the drive in the dock I find the drive suddenly spinning up again.  So far I'm pleased, if I have any problems in the future I'll update this.

If your camera doesn't allow that, it's not the monitor's fault. Several canon EOS DSLR cameras automatically switch to 480p when you roll. The Canon 7d doesnt, but others do. That would make racking focus much more difficult visually. You'd have to measure out the actors' distances, spike them on the ground, and grease the marks on your focus wheel, traditional film-style. That's a good habit anyhow. Then this monitor would still be good for framing and composition.I wish it had a HDMI pass through and headphone outputs. When you playback footage from the Nikon DSLR, it defaults to play through HDMI if a monitor is connected. Meaning, you have to listen through the internal speaker rather than the camera headphone jack. It's a minor inconvenience.Also, buy an extra battery Lilliput 2200mah Lithium Battery for 668gl-70np/h/y to get through a production day, and power down the monitor when not in use. You'll find the monitor battery will then last much longer.The monitor has unusual features. Read the manual. The rocker switch on the back is for toggling "charging". Switch it to "on" to "charge". Very unusual...

I decided on this unit because it supported Miracast and because it was one of the handful of 2014 models (all Sony) that supported Amazon streaming.It works very well, producing a fine picture.  Amazon streaming at 5.1 (or 7.0 for 'ST: Enterprise' that I tested) is a welcome change from the LG, which was two-channel only.  This Sony's interface is clean and it was a straightforward matter of a few minutes to scan through the device's setup menu and configure each option.  There are apparently a great variety of internet video and audio sources available, although I tried only Netflix and Amazon.  The remote is quite simple and easy to use, with fewer buttons than I am used to but all the function is there.<RANT>I did not try the built-in wireless because I have had such poor luck with on board wireless that I don't bother anymore, I just hardwire everything.  For devices that cost a little more than $100 to have a wireless solution worth a damn, it would have to be a very large fraction of the cost,  but it isn't and so they aren't.  I also haven't tried the 4k upscaling yet because that TV is in another room, and I don't expect miracles.  Genuine 4k content on 4k is great, but the best I hope for with upscaling is that it doesn't get too screwed up.</RANT>The bad:1) The styling is silly, frankly - just hide it under something better looking.2) It can not connect to SMB/CIFS network shares, only DLNA and although this worked well enough, you won't be using this device for that; DLNA is just too cumbersome.  WDTV or Roku are your options there, the LG was great for that as well.3) My unit was discounted (open box-priced item at a local retailer) and came set to HDMI control (CEC) which apparently precludes local power-on control from the remote or the power button on the unit, an /incredibly/ stupid problem if it wasn't so easily fixed by disabling HDMI control from the setup menu. review_title: IO Crest VGA to HDMI Convertor with Audio support (SY-ADA31025)
review_text: There seems to be no way to display my PC's entire HD screen in HD format on a HD TV. The video ends up having both much less resolution and in a 5:4 aspect ratio. I would have been very disappointed if I wanted to use my TV as a monitor for my laptop. Using this adapter is acceptable to me only because I use it to play video using VLC. It's VLC's flexibility that makes this possible and not the adapter's. Your mileage may vary quite a bit depending on both your particular PC and TV models. Maybe the more expensive VGA-to-HDMI adapters have a hardware video scaler in them to avoid this problem.My particular laptop has its VGA connector on the opposite side from the audio output jack and I wish the convertor's audio input cable was about 16 inches longer for this 15.6" laptop. A 1/8 inch connector 'extension cable' (male plug-female jack)  is needed and the only one I have at the moment is 6 feet long ! (The term 'female jack' is not a pun - think about this for a moment.)The convertor works well once its limitations are compensated by the VLC media player program run on my PC. My laptop 's screen resolution set to 1366 X 768 which is the proper HD video aspect ratio. I use VLC to play both HD and SD videos. Yet, when this adapter is plugged in the laptop, the laptop automatically changes its screen resolution to 1024 X 768, an SD video aspect ratio of 4:3 (Go figure that...). I'm guessing this happens because the convertor doesn't have a built-in 'hardware video scaler', so the PC display changes to the highest compatible resolution that both the PC screen hardware and the convertor have in common. This is HDMI's way of finding compatibility between a video source and an HDMI display device.A decent work-around seems to be setting VLC's aspect ratio to compensate for the adapter's and/or PC's shortcomings. I set the TV's display mode  to 'Stretch' rather than 'Normal'. The rest of the video size readjustment is done using VLC: When playing an HD movie I set VLC's aspect ratio to be 16:9 and when playing SD video I set VLC to the 5:4 aspect ratio.This works very well, but is a bit annoying since it has to be set every time for each video. HD video played by VLC then completely fills the TV screen. SD video appears with the normal left and right side black bars. I haven't yet played around with VLC's video sizing to get SD video to fill the TV's screen which would magnify the image and cut off the top and bottom edges, but this should be possible, too.The problem with this and every other VGA-HDMI adapter is that both the adapter and the PC are capable of supporting only a fixed number of resolutions regardless of the TV being used. Whether or not HD is displayed correctly without adjustments is a matter of both the adapter and the PC having an HD aspect ratio capability in common. Some people's PCs do, many people like myself happen not to have any compatible screen resolution. I think this is why expensive PCs have an upper resolution of 1920 X 1080. The vertical resolution of 1080 is exactly the resolution od 1080p HD TVs and all converters claiming to have 1080p capability is gauranteed to share this resolution with the PC, and so, video will always appear right without adjustmnents being necessary.More expensive adapters may have a wider selection of resolutions to choose from, but, ultimately, there will be some PCs that can never naturally display correctly with any particular adapter model.

I’m using this as a baby monitor so I don’t really mind (in fact prefer) that it can’t be viewed via the internet.This was NO easy system to set up… there’s several steps that had to be taken and many of these steps were NOT spelled out in the instructions.  For example, my home network name had a space between two words (home network).  The system didn’t like this but didn’t specifically tell you, it just gave you an error message during setup and you had to guess what the error was.  There was no indication anywhere in the instruction either that this would cause a problem.  After a lot of trouble shooting I deduced the problem and I re-named my network without the space (homenetwork).  The system suddenly worked.  I also noticed during the trouble shooting process that in the set-up, you will often times have to enter the information twice or even 3 times for it to “take”.  I’d enter the information and the system would come back with an error; I’d enter it again, and sometimes again, and it would suddenly accept the info.The instructions are not very easy to follow and there is essentially NO tech support for this product.  At certain points during the setup it would say “contact dealer”.  I’m pretty sure if I called Amazon for help I’d be out of luck.  There is a phone number to call but it’s in Hong Kong and unless you used Skype (or similar) the call itself would likely cost you more than the camera.I have no idea whether the Foscam is any better but next time I would probably pay the few extra bucks and get it over the Tenvis.

review_title: Super useful, works great! User tip inside!
review_text: I have a box full of IDE hard drives that goes back 15 years.  I think there's a 240 MB drive in that box.  I bought this IDE to SATA adapter so I could use my SATA USB dock with these drives to off-load the data before I throw them out.  I didn't want to buy a brand new IDE USB dock so I got this adapter.  Basically, you attach the IDE drive with a data cable and power cable (included), screw in two small screws on the back and now you've converted your IDE drive to a SATA drive.  Then you can put the entire drive into your USB doc.Tip: Since the power cable and IDE cable between this adapter and the IDE drive is flexible, you MUST screw in two tiny screws on the back of the adapter to the hard drive to keep everything together.  These two screws are tiny and require a small screwdriver set to attach.  This is fine if you are going to do one or two drives, but in my case, I am transferring 20+ drives.  I found two old computer case thumb screws that look like this:Solid Brass CPU Case Thumbscrews, 6 Packand use them to attach this adapter to the drive much faster.  No tiny screws, no need for a screwdriver.  Fast and easy.Thanks to StarTech for continuing to make useful if not esoteric products like this.

review_title: Belkin Easy Transfer Does Not Transfer Programs
review_text: If you're looking for a cable that will transfer your programs as well as your files, this isn't it.  I didn't expect it to do that when I bought it, but I hoped that it would.  Shame on me, because I bought it without doing the research first.  There are two products on the market that will migrate your programs as well as your files: one is Zinstall, which offers two versions, and the better of the two (XP7) is presently on sale - you can view a nice video on their website; the other is LapLink, which has received lukewarm or not so warm reviews.If you have all your old programs on CD's as well as their product keys on hand, however, you might be able to install the programs manually and still use the Belkin Transfer Cable to transfer your files from the old computer.  When I tried to manually install my MS Office 2007, which was an upgrade that I could use on up to two computers and for which I had the product key, the Windows 7 on the new computer would not accept it because it couldn't detect a previous copy on the new computer.  The new computer came with an incomplete version of MS OFfice 2010, which isn't a PREVIOUS copy, but a more advanced copy, so it appeared that I was out of luck.  I solved the problem with Zinstall XP7, which cost me $89 and allowed me to transfer files, settngs, and programs without needing any special cables.  With Zinstall, you can use any type of computer cable- DSL, USB, whatever you have available.  When the files are transfered, you're actually placing fresh copies of them onto the new computer; the original files remain on the old computer.  So, if you plan to toss that old computer or donate it, and don't want anyone to inherit your personal business, you still need to delete those files from the old machine.The Belkin Easy Transfer Cable for Windows 7 allows you to transfer the files from an XP, Vista, or 7 computer to a Windows 7.  It comes with a CD that, similar to Znstall, you have to install onto the old computer and the target computer.  You then follow very easy steps before you connect the cable.  After you're instructed to connect the cable, you do just that and follow a few more steps.  Because I used Zinstall, the Belkin software and cable were of no use to me.UPDATE: On Windows Vista, I recently noticed an entry for transferring files and settings in the Control Panel.  I haven't tried it, but I mention it in case readers are interested in following that link.

I bought one of its predecessor models about four years ago, and it still works, while a newer and more capable Sony died after a year. But I can't say that I love it. Some have said nice things about its video quality, but in a side-by-side comparison with the IPhone 5 (importing video from both into Final Cut Pro) the IPhone 5 produces noticeably better video (of course, without the benefit of the ZS25's flexibility). The ZS25's quality on still photos is likewise acceptable, but one can do better, especially for images shot at higher ASAs, for about the same money or perhaps just a bit more. What you probably can't find, at least at this price point, is a camera that offers the ZS25's particular combination of advantages -- the 20X lens, the compact size, a well-thought out interface and decent image and video quality. I wish the image quality was better, and I wish the ZS25 was even more compact. But for the price, and since I own a couple of DSLRs and several camcorders, nothing suits my needs for a casual, walkaround camera better.  If I hadn't bought the ZS25, I'd been leaning toward a Canon SX280, which might be a step up in image quality and offers its own advantages But it's typically at least $75 more, and it's also thicker and heavier than the Panasonic.

review_title: Works exactly as specified.  Highly recommended.
review_text: I've owned several of the AudioSource monoblock amps and one of the pre-amps for about ten years.  AudioSource's products have been faithful servants --- first class manufacturing and exceeding the written specs.The 100 watt power amplifier is a little different.  Designed to hit a lower selling point, the weight and feel of this amplifier does match the upper end design of the above products.But looks are deceiving.  This amp works exactly as specified for my application; and at an outstanding price.  I would purchase this unit again if I had a similar application.Pros:- Simple design.  Flat frequency response. Small footprint.  Set and forget.- The amp is installed in a cabinet with limited ventilation.  The circuitry is very efficient, producing minimal heat.- The auto off when there is no input on channel 2 works as specified.  Saves energy and prevents heat buildup.- Power is sufficient to drive a pair of B+W in-wall speakers at reasonable volume with no noticeable distortion.Cons (and these are very minor for my application):- The speaker binding posts on the rear are cheap.  No thru-hole, and no ability to unscrew the binding nut completely.  Not helpful for large gauge cables.- Speaker labeling is backwards.  Right speaker is on the left set of binding posts, and left on the right.- Input channel 1 vs. 2 - already discussed.  Not a problem, just read the manual.UPDATE - 14 January 2014 - Channel 1 connection to iPad via AirPlay - 5 starsAttached the audio output from an Apple Airport Express to the channel 1 input of the AudioSource amplifier, and enabled AirPlay over the Airport Express from a nearby iPad.  The AudioSource worked as specified, cutting out the audio input from channel 2 (television) and switching on channel 1 (AirPlay).  When the iPad music source stopped (and after several seconds), the channel 2 audio input resumed to the speakers.  Oscar Peterson never sounded better. Again, five stars to AudioSource !!

I'm looking at the screen... but feel like a premium device... is super thin... and lightweight.. Yep.. the Ipad look more premium with the metal cases.. but the Galaxy tab S doesn't feel cheap like other samsung tablets like the galaxy tab 3...Power: The octa core processor work great.. I'm giving this device a very heavy use so far and I haven't felt any major hiccup or lag... yes sometimes It doesn't response right away like when you exit out of an app and want to open other app right away... but is just normal like any other premium android device... unfortunately this is how the OS works... don't get me wrong... is really fast and these so called hiccups or lag are barely noticeable and even if you noticed, its for about 2 secs then the tablet response is normally... It happened sometimes on my retina display Ipad as well... I guess this is normal for any device with... well.. ram... even computers have the same problem for over years...Interface / OS: This has been the main problem with androids.. the ecosystem is not a fancy and good looking as the IOS and samsung touchwiz is not well optimized and look dull... The magazine interface is good, but is laking of widget and customization.. I'm hoping on future versions that they allow us to select free feeds to add to the widgets since they only have a couple "categories" that I don't care that much like culture, bussiness, living, photos, travel.. etc... I don't see gaming or movies like on flipboard... and they only have twitter as a feed, I don't see facebook or instagram...Apps: IOS has more tablet dedicated apps, but is not noticeable for my usage, email, youtube and browser are tablet friendly and that is what I use the most... facebook and all other work fine... even if they are phone versions... look and feel better than on my galaxy S4... android had the same problem with apps vs the app store a few years back and they catch up... they will do the same shortly with tablets.... Some apps doesn't work on my country like paper garden, milk music and most of the "gift apps" that come with the table... but is not a big deal for me...Camera: haven't use it... I don't care about it..FingerPrint scanner: This is a feature that I don't care that much but it Work 95% of the time... is a good ratio if you asked me... I heard some bad reviews that It never works... but is working fine for me...Multi-Users: this is great... you can have 2 users on the same tablet like on computers... I'm not sure if there is a feature like this on IOS but is perfect for me, since I can have 2 accounts... one for me and one for my GF....Multi tasking/ multi windows: Work perfect... this is another thing that IOS is missing... I was considering buying an Ipad Air over this... but even on IOS 8 there is no multi tasking... I use this a lot since I translate some documents... I had the translator app on top and the word app at the bottom and do my work directly from my galaxy tab S without even open my computer...Battery: I head so many great things... but I had to say that battery is average.... I will say same or even a little less than the Ipad... don't get me wrong.. it last the whole day with normal usage... but it drain out the battery fast when I use my torrent app... or when I download anything...Usage: perfect laptop replacement... I download some movies on it.. and watch them on any format... I just simply copy them to my SD card.. and that's it... since I have Tab S I haven't use my computer only to do this review since involve a lot of typing... review_title: Munitio COD Phones with Comply Tips
review_text: I won a pair of these through a giveaway that Comply Foam Nation was doing through their Facebook fan page. I was really excited to win a pair, they looked fairly good, they came with Comply tips(yay!), and they were free. As a reference, my other two pairs are a pair of UE 350s, and Sony MDR-V6s, both excellent in their own right for different reasons.So I opened the package when it arrived, put in the ear buds with the supplied tips, and thought, wow these are extremely uncomfortable. They are modeled after 9mm bullets, I felt like I put a metal bullet in my ear canal. They may look cool from the outside, but because the silicone tips provide no cushion, they are easily the most uncomfortable in-ear phones I have ever worn. So I swapped out the tips for the supplied T400 Comply tips. This is the reason we buy foam tips, they increased the comfort 500% easily. Good seal, no metal feeling against my skin, great.So I plug them in, and give them a listen. I listened over a three day period for probably 16-20 hours, to allow for some burn-in time(if you believe in such a thing, which I do). My overall impression is the base is out of control in these. My UE 350s are fairly bass driven, but these are another beast all together. Bass doesn't have a real sense of impact, it more covers every other range. Mids are extremely recessed, highs are non-existent. If I were a bass-head, these might be good choices, but as the bass is all consuming, and doesn't let any other elements shine through, I would look elsewhere.So in summary, out of a free pair of phones, really the only thing worth having were the Comply tips, at least that's something.

review_title: Digital signal means no signal loss
review_text: This "review" is broken into three parts.1) Digital cables and signal loss--a myth.2) Audio over DVI--it is possible in some cases3) The cable itself--buy it if it is cheapestI'll start by saying when you're buying digital cables (HDMI, DVI, TOSLINK, etc) buy the cheapest cable available that is not built like crap.  If the cable is not literally falling apart, it will perform as well as the $75 cables Monster sells.  With digital signals you're either going to get all* or nothing.  If there is a color on the pixel, the cable is performing at its best.  There are some times where a bad connection will cause a picture to look like there is snow in the picture, but its exceedingly rare that a cable will will "snow" and still give you a partial picture.  In most circumstances, you will either get a 100% perfect signal, or absolutely nothing will display.  When buying digital cables, build quality is the ONLY thing you should consider.Still with me?  Next thing.  DVI CAN transmit audio.  BUT you may not want to rely solely on DVI.  Look at it this way, buy just this cable and see if it works.  If it does not do not get upset.  Think of audio transmission as a bonus.  There are some sources that refuse to output audio over DVI.  For example some nVidia graphics cards do not, but myMSI GeForce GTX 560 Ti with 448 Coresdoes output audio over DVI to HDMI cables.  If the monitor/TV/reciever makes it known that it can accept an audio signal (and it should), and the output device allow it, you will get audio.As far as the cable itself, it is solidly built.  There are stress relief portions between the connectors and the wires.  The casing is acceptable.  It is nothing special, but I would not worry over the cable falling apart in normal use cases.  It is flexible enough.  I'm using it to connect my computer monitor to my desktop.  I have it at some 90 degree angles with a slight bend to it, it was not at all difficult to run this cable.  I will say it is FAR more flexible than Monster cables I have used (they were free...)  As I stated in the first part of this "review" it is a digital cable, so every one is going to be similar.  Buy whatever is cheapest.

review_title: Very good - Not True Audiophile Performance
review_text: I am an audiophile. Prove it you say? I think records sound better than CDs. I pay extra for hi resolution downloads of music I really like. my turntable costs more than my car. I have tubes in my preamp. ALL of the components in my stereo were made in the US. So when somebody says that a consumer product is "audiophile" quality, I usually feel they are engaged in hyperbole. That is the case here, but it does not mean the ZVOZ 580 is not worth the money. IT IS!The sound from the TV in my bedroom was so bad to my ears, I could not even watch the news in bed. Wide screen TVs are getting smaller and less expensive, so something has to give. THE SOUND. I needed an answer and quick. I first started looking for a pair of powered speakers, but could not find something that sounded good and would turn on automatically when the TV was powered up and would shut down when it was off. Sure there were some solutions like the Tannoy powered speakers, but the cost was very high. I could also get an receiver and some traditional speakers and have good sound that way. But that was complex and took up to much room. I started to feel the sound I wanted was still far off and I was starting to blow the budget. Then I saw this ad in Stereophile Magazine and there was hope!Here was my criteria:- Less than $500- Easy enough for my wife to use- Low profile- REALLY GOOD SOUND - remember the audiophile part?- Did not stay powered up all the timeThe ZVOX 580 seemed to fit the criteria so I ordered one from Amazon to try it out. It came in two days in a large banged up box, but the ZBOX was in perfect shape. It took about 10 minutes for me to place it under the Panasonic HDTV, although the unit did not include the SPDIF fiber cable. So I hooked up my iPad and listened to some music.MUSIC:It sounded nice, well balanced, very good extension, good dynamics and a good soundstage. While listening to music, the sound stage did not extend far beyond the edge of the box. If you have listened to a Bose Wave radio, it sounds MUCH better than that.  In fact, I would recommend this as a nice low cost hifi system for anyone. After all it has two analog inputs, two digital inputs on the back and an additional input on the front. The rear inputs are switchable from the front or the remote. For less than $500 this would be a hard system to beat as a stereo. One complaint, the high end is a little directional. As you move your head off axis, the sound changes in the high end. Going up or down, or hard left or right, there is a drop off in direct high end frequency response. My guess, is the speakers used to produce the high end are full range cone type and not dedicated tweeters. I will say, because the apparent lack of a crossover in the critical music frequencies (my guess is the crossover is close to 200 HZ) the sound is very nice with little or no phase error. After it playing it for a while, it even sounded better. If this were a table top stereo, it would be among the best available. Yes MUCH better than the Bose and better than both B&W; systems. I may have to get one of these for my office.VIDEO:After a trip to Radio Shack for a fiber cable I was ready for video. The video sound is very good. On content with surround information the soundstage does get wide and can even give you a bit of a 3D feeling. However, it is not close to a real 5.1, 7.1 or even 4.1 system. That being said, for the money and size, it is pretty remarkable. Dialog is quite good, bass is extended and tight and the highs are crystal clear with none of the usual shimmer you get in low cost solutions. My bedroom is large, and it easily fills the room with sound. The bass is pretty impressive without being boomy, however it will not shake you to the bone. The system will learn your remote so it will come on with your TV and turn off when you power off your TV. It will even shut off after inactivity. I love saving power and it passes the "easy for my wife to use"PROBLEMS:1. You need to be in front of this thing for it to sound its best. It sounds fine off axis, but the sound is BEST when you are in front. Not a problem when listening to the TV because you will be sitting where you need to be. The thing is because it sounds is so good, I use it as the stereo in our bedroom and I can tell when I move off axis, it is just not as clear.2. When changing the volumes, it feels like there are 3 db steps and the taper seems to be linear, not an audio taper. So at lower levels say below 12, I find myself wanting to use a volume of 10.5 rather than 10 or 11. There is just too much of a difference between the levels for me. The volume needs to move in smaller increments.NICE STUFF:Looks good, well designed and the remote is easy to use. However, you may not need it once you get it setup because it works with the TV remote and the front panel controls are easy to access. it has that nice "American" sound. You know that kind of sound that Henri Kloss made famous. It does feature bass/treble adjustments, compression (sound leveling), dialog enhancement and 3D enhancer on the remote. I left it flat, no need to adjust the bass or treble. I turned on the sound leveling to not to bother the kids with loud parts of the broadcast and keep the volume of the ads down. I keep the 3D enhance on 2 and left off the dialog enhancer. You can't use the dialog enhancer and the 3D magic at the same time anyway.IN SUMMARY:Easy to setup. Looks nice, SOUNDS REAL GOOD (not audiophile), plays loud and is well worth the $500. If you are looking for better sound than the usual sound bar/plastic sub combo and need something easy for your wife to use - this is your answer.

review_title: They got it right with v.3
review_text: I'm reviewing v.3... which is the same as v.2... but now with 1080p.If you see my review for v.2 you should disregard it as they've made significant improvements to the user interface.In short... I love my AppleTVs.  One in the living room and one in my bedroom.  You can "mirror" your Apple's Mac to ALL your connected AppelTVs, so if you're running a movie for a bunch of friends through your mac (like I have a few times) you can have some of them in the living room and some of them in the bedroom watching the same thing.Enough about my life... the product itself is very intuitive to use, the interface is simple and sleek, and allows for iCloud information to be passed to your ATV (bought music on iTunes but don't have iMatch? No problem. All your music that you bought through iTunes now shows up on your ATV and you can play your music to your hearts content). Bought a movie or TV show from iTunes? It plays it via streaming.  They used to only stream rented movies, but NOW you can play any movies or tv shows that you've fully purchased via iTunes.What it DOESN'T do is allow you to play any iTunes extras (the added features that some iTunes movies comes with).  You'll need to run them through your Mac and send the "broadcast" over to your AppleTV.I also love the fact that it pairs up nicely with my Logitech Harmony remote. As simple as the included remote for ATV is, I like everything to be controlled through ONE remote... ONE remote to rule them all... and Apple TV plays nicely in that respect.Why ATV vs. Roku? Quite simply.... simplicity.  My roommate has my old Roku box.  And what I didn't like about it is that there were a plethora of "channels" to choose from, however, most of them had the same content that I could find on the Apple TV box and those apps (Netflix movies and shows, HuluPlus movies and shows, rental items from iTunes, sports apps, etc). You have to wade through all their "channels" to see what they were about and how useful they are to you. I found a majority of the channels NOT useful to me... even less useful when I found out that you had to pay a subscription services for a majority of those channels. And so this is why my roommate ended up with my Roku box.  He don't care. He's happy to have something for free.

review_title: Best Choice in the Price Range
review_text: I got this TV recently and couldn't find that much on the internet about it in terms of reviews, so I want to share my experience. I had previously owned a 720p LG and bought the Samsung LN46A550 because of a great deal and great reviews. Once I got the Samsung I was happy, but when I spend over a grand on something I need to be ecstatic. So... since I was in the window to take the TV back, I did some research. I came to where there were two TVs in my price range that I was interested in, the Samsung LN46A650 and this TV. I went with this TV because the Samsung seemed to have more issues based on online posts (AVS Forums) and the picture looked a bit better to me in the store. So... here is my review:Setup: I had heard that with this TV you have to attach the stand, but you don't. Its with the smaller models I believe, but this one is was new out of the box and the stand was attached. It was as easy as it should be (instructions are included on how to detach the stand).Look: It has a really classy look. There is a dim light that's red when its off and blue when it's on in the bottom right of the frame, but you can turn it off if you don't like it (I like it). There is red on the trim, but I haven't noticed it since I set it up. I really like that the input/channel/vol buttons are basically touch sensitive.Audio: What you would expect from an LCD. Not that great, but not bad. In my opinion you shouldn't be using the TVs sound if you're going to spend this much on a TV unless you have to... but that's my opinion. I've got mine running through my 5.1.Picture: WOW! HD looks stunning! The contrast compared to the Samsung 550 series is incredible. Blu-Ray is absolutely beautiful. If you like things simple, you can just use one of their many preset options. Plus, the TV does pretty well with the intellisensor. However, if you are a complete videophile, you can calibrate it with the expert setting and control many things (search for this model in the AVS Forum and you can get different people's calibration settings to try if you want to go more in depth). I'm not totally into the Trumotion (its good with sports and a few movies), but turning it off is easy enough. I will tell you though, when you watch true HD content (not just stuff on the HD channels, but the stuff recorded for the HD channels... usually the newer stuff), the picture is hard to beat. The blacks are about 9/10 (compared to other HDTVs), but the colors are 10/10... easy. Standard-def looks about the same as the 550, but not bad enough to make me like this TV any less.CONS: (because everything has them)1. The remote is horrid. If you're going to sell such a great item... spend some time on the remote! However, it doesn't matter to me because I use the Harmony universal remote. Don't have one? Check them out... mine is a cheaper one and I could never ever go back. I can't imagine what he expensive ones are like.2. This isn't much of a con for me, but it would be for some; when you change inputs it takes about 2-3 seconds to come up to that input and another second for the sound.3. The side inputs aren't 100% on the side. They are a bit further back than most TVs have them. However, not too big a deal if you ask me.4. You have to enter settings to turn on/off Trumotion. As I said, there are a few things that it works great with... wish the remote could turn it on/off so I could program my Harmony to do it.That's it... all my cons...I strongly recommend the 47LG70 vs the Samsung A550 or A650 series... well I just recommend it overall. I mean, even the settings menu is pretty. Plus, my last LG shows me that this brand is reliable. It kept going and going and never died... not even after several years and many moves (I'm in the Navy and move a lot). If you have questions check out AVS Forums and search for this TV. It's free and someone on there will answer your question. Go on... buy it already!

review_title: Myeh - Lack of Support and Mortal Nav Board
review_text: I have installed two of these DNX-6160's.  I also have two of the previous 2009 models, the DNX-6140's.  I have encouraged others to buy Kenwood Nav receivers based on their functionality and features along with a fairly good experience (I post to a handful of automotive forums).Well, it would seem that what you have read here is true.  Kenwood really doesn't expect to stand behind it's products or make their customers feel good about the brand.One day out of the blue this 6160 had a message that it "Cannot unlock maps".  An examination of the "info" screen on the map section of the nav area showed only a blank screen.  No Text. No version number whatsoever.  I updated the Kenwood head unit software followed by the latest Garmin nav software.  No change.  A call to Kenwood cust support gave an answer that the unit must be bad and I should send it in to a national service center to be fixed.  I called Garmin and asked if I could buy a map update and unlock the maps on the unit.  Garmin said it would not work because the original unlock was not in place so the upgrade would not take.  I then called the Kenwood National Service Center and explained the situation and the fellow on the line said it sounded like I needed a new "nav" board.  He'd heard it all before. He said the board would be around $350 and labor was charged at $75 per hour and it would take an hour and a half.  So with shipping back and forth I should be out just shy of $500 on a one-year old head unit that can be purchased for less than that new and just over half of that used on the internet.Is it any wonder that Android devices, with their internal Google maps that update daily and work flawlessly (including real street views), will effectively shut down stand-alone navigators?  I am done with dash-mount navigators.  And with Kenwood.  And for the most part Garmin automotive devices (I do have their equipment in an airplane).  I even have OEM navigation in a Toyota Tundra and at this point discourage anybody from getting in-dash nav as it's really not worth it anymore.  Go for a rear camera monitor (mirror or stand alone) and then use a smart phone for nav.  And save lots and lots of money and frustration.

review_title: Probably used or not genuine from Alfatronix, Good as New Electronics, or EXCELSHOTS.
review_text: UPDATE: Januay 2013I purchased a battery to replace the one I bought from Alphatronix that failed.  I purchased it from Good as New Electronics.  It was sold as a New battery.  When I received it, it appeared that someone had previously ripped the package open and the whole thing had been under water.  The packaging was stuck to the battery.  So I returned it and purchased one from EXCELTSHOTS; again a NEW battery.  The packaging on this one was in decent shape.  BUT it had been opened carefully and all the edges taped closed again.CONCLUSION:  I believe many of the NP-45A batteries being sold by the vendors on Amazon as NEW are either knock-offs or USED batteries placed in original packaging.  So be VERY CAREFUL.  Do not accept any NEW battery that is not in original UNOPENED packaging.  For this reason, I only purchase items sold or fulfilled by Amazon.  It is much easier to return defective products to Amazon.ORIGINAL REVIEW:I purchased 2 "Fujifilm NP-45A Li-Ion Battery - Retail Packaging" batteries from Alfatronix about 6 months ago.  If you are purchasing this battery from a vendor other than Alfatronix, this review may not be relevant. The batteries look very similar to my original battery that came with my camera--but not exactly.  They both worked fine for several months.  Then one failed and wouldn't hold a charge.  I contacted Alfatronix and they told me it only had a 30-day return warranty.  When I see other sellers offering aftermarket batteries with a 3 year warranty, I expect that a NEW, Fuji branded battery should have at least a year.  A 30 day warranty screams to me that this is a knock-off or used battery.

The Belkin Folio iPad2 case offers a wireless Bluetooth keyboard and the option to use your iPad either with the keyboard or without.  The keyboard is nice and clicky, but as the case is somewhat awkwardly shaped, the whole package is a little clunky.PROS:There are lots of case combos that offer a keyboard, but few that still allow you to use your iPad as an actual tablet.  Most cases are constructed with the keyboard folding onto the iPad screen, just like a laptop, which means the keys are touching the screen. For this circumstance, in order to use the iPad as a tablet, you have to let the keyboard part hang off the side or try to fold it underneath.  The Belkin people seem to have remembered that although iPad users might want the typing ease of a tactile keyboard (since how many of us can really type efficiently with the on-screen keyboard...c'mon, you know you can't really do it for long emails or documents), we still bought the iPad because we wanted a sleek touch screen device that can rest comfortably on our laps while we surf the web from the couch or check emails during meetings at the office.Although the design of the case is definitely an advantage, what matters most to me is the way the keyboard feels and responds, i.e., the clicky-ness factor.  Because at the end of the day, if you don't like typing on it, then what's the point?  And this thing is great.  Very clicky, very easy to use, and the keys are a good size and nicely spaced out.  And the biggest thing I missed about using the on-screen iPad keyboard was the arrow keys.  Never fear - this keyboard brings all 4 dimensions of arrow-scrolling back into your life...it's glorious.The last pro is the battery.  It lasts a long time.  I've only had to charge it twice in a month.  It uses a micro-USB port to charge.  Belkin supplies a micro-USB cable, but not an AC adapter.  So you can either plug the supplied USB cable into a computer's USB port and charge the keyboard that way, or you can use an existing USB AC adapter (I have one for my phone and it works well).CONS:I know I said earlier that the design of the case lets you use your iPad as an iPad, but that does not come without a price.  Because the keyboard is velcro-ed behind your iPad, the case sort of juts out in the back in the shape of a keyboard.  Makes sense that it would happen that way, but it leaves the whole case/iPad package a little asymmetric and awkward looking.  It still sits flat on a table, but it does cause some packing issues when trying to jam this in between file folders in your work bag. Additionally, the velcro causes a bit of a ruckus when trying to covertly use your iPad during meetings.  Once you peel the velcro off to release the keyboard, everyone will stop to stare as you flip the case up and around to assemble it for use.  It looks cool once it's ready to go, but you definitely do not look cool doing it.The material used to make the case is a bit cheesy.  It's not the fact that it's not leather that's the problem, because I actually like the synthetic feel to the case.  What makes it feel cheap is the rounded stitched corners, and the chemical smell.  Like a new Sharpie, at first the smell is kind of intoxicating, but after a while you start to feel a little queasy.All in all, a 4 out of 5.  The case isn't perfect, but it is a lot better than the other keyboard options on the market.  It offers the best of both worlds - gives you a better keyboard than the iPad does, without forgetting that sometimes you still want to use your iPad as an iPad.

I have had this Toshiba TV since late July 2011 and so far have been extremely pleased with my purchase. It seems to be unjustifiably underrated. Crutchfield likes this set and they're no technology dummies!I purchased this television after first having had a look at the comparable 47" passive 3D LG TV (Model: LG Infinia 47LW6500 47 Cinema 3D 1080p 240 Hz LED-LCD HDTV) which - overall - did not impress me as much as I expected based on the opinions of certain overly enthusiastic members of the LG True Believers Club here on Amazon.com who are apparently experiencing something akin to an ersatz orgasm as they continue to post monotonously uncritical, over-the-top, positive reviews about this set."How many ways can I say wonderful and amazing? Oh dearest LG, let me count the ways!" I think that some of these people must be paid or unpaid shills intentionally getting the good word out for LG on the Internet.Although the 47" 3D LG TV does indeed have a beautiful picture, I personally disliked the following and thus would rank it a neutral 3 out of 5 stars:1) Stand quality/design - especially flimsy and wobbly plastic with removal problems - not an easy on or off. Attach the stand and you may very well not be able to remove it in the future due to an apparent mismatch between the screws provided and the drilled holes.2) WIFI implementation via external dongle with suboptimal throughput - the LG would repeatedly ask me to establish my Internet connection when this had been done successfully a long time ago.3) The second remote provided with the LG is essentially superfluous; there's rarely a need for more than one remote per electronic device. Why unnecessarily contribute to the multiplication of remotes around the house?4) Both LG remotes also did interfere with some other electronic devices that I have in my living room, turning them on and/or off when this was not desired (digital picture frame, Internet radio, etc.). Panasonic and Toshiba remotes do not cause this problem.NOW CONCERNING THE TOSHIBA:The integrated WIFI connection on the Toshiba TV is rock solid. I have had absolutely no problems with having to repeatedly input my network information due to a lost wireless connection or anything of this sort. Just set up the WIFI connection once and then forget it. Streaming from the Internet - either through the TV itself or via my WIFI-enabled Panasonic Blu-ray player - is smooth and flawless, which it should be with the now 50 Mbps download speed that I have available at home (as of May 2013). And the integrated WIFI means that both of the provided USB ports are available for other things - no need for a USB WIFI dongle on this set!Picture quality is great as far as I am concerned. I am by no means claiming that this TV has the absolute best picture quality available anywhere and this is unnecessary. I don't get too obsessed about the picture of one TV being technically 10 - 30% better than that of another. In most cases we're not dealing with truly good versus bad image quality, just different levels of goodness. Choose the set that's good enough for you overall; that's all that matters.When first receiving this TV be sure to perform the software upgrade/update and then do NOT leave the television on the default AutoSave picture settings which emphasize energy savings over picture quality. Instead select the Standard picture settings. If you do all of this, you should end up with a very nice picture. And if you are so inclined, the Toshiba has a large number of settings that you can tweak to approach whatever your idea of picture perfection may be. Personally, I'd rather spend my time doing other things, but the potential to do this is readily available.The Toshiba TV certainly more than meets my needs of watching the occasional over-the-air TV program and then streaming on-demand content from the Internet via WIFI. I have also had the opportunity to try out the passive 3D effect/experience of the set and it is very realistic; the images appear to pop right out of the screen - works fine for me.Sound quality - although acceptable for built-in TV speakers - certainly can be improved and I have done so by adding a soundbar system with wireless subwoofer to the set (Panasonic SC-HTB520 2.1-Channel SoundBar Speaker System with Wireless Kelton Subwoofer, see my review). The combination works like a charm, a great sound upgrade! And everything can be controlled with the Toshiba's single remote control.I give this Toshiba TV a rating of 4 out of 5 stars in light of the following things that I felt could be improved:1) Stand implementation could be better. I would prefer a stand with more metal parts and less plastic (see Panasonic TVs) that attaches to the bottom/base of the LCD panel - better weight-bearing functionality and less strain (again see Panasonic) - instead of a stand that attaches directly to the back of the LCD panel. If one of the attaching screws does not come out easily, you may have difficulty removing the stand if you ever want to wall mount the TV in the future.2) The design/layout of the Toshiba remote control is not optimized. Of the two remotes that I regularly use (Toshiba & Panasonic), I like the Panasonic remote much better: There are fewer buttons overall and they are larger, more colorful and easier to actuate while the Toshiba remote for the most part has smaller, monotonic black buttons making it difficult to find the desired function. In short it takes longer to get properly oriented with the Toshiba remote control, but it's not an insurmountable problem and you'll get used to it.3) Changing channels is a bit too slow for my taste (as another reviewer already has mentioned). They do all switch, but the time delay is longer than expected or needed. The original start-up of the set from a cold start at about 27 seconds or so is also on the long side. You might wonder whether or not anything is happening during this time: nothing but a soft click is heard after hitting the power button on the remote and then a tiny green light - as the only sign of life - starts flashing after some 15 seconds have elapsed. These are essentially minor inconveniences - not deal breakers.4) The Internet apps provided with the Net TV function need to be expanded. The selection so far is very limited, but this does not bother me, because I have other streaming-enabled devices (Blu-ray player, etc.) available to provide additional choices. This is something that Toshiba can -and hopefully will - improve in the near future.STATUS UPDATE ON 11/20/2012I have now been using this Toshiba LED TV daily for about 16 months - no problems whatsoever, no repairs. It is still going strong just like on the day in July 2011 that I first plugged it in.STATUS UPDATE ON 07/20/2013After 2 years of regular daily use, this Toshiba LED TV still continues to function flawlessly - no service needed.STATUS UPDATE ON 02/02/2014After more than 2.5 years of daily use, this Toshiba TV is still going strong just like the Energizer Bunny - no problems, no repairs!

review_title: Pleased overall, but a very mixed bag
review_text: I was really looking forward to installing this item, since I'm geeky enough (22 years in IT, designed large wireless networks) to appreciate what it could do. But it was not all as I might have hoped.First the bad: It was a little bit hard to install the driver for 64-bit Windows 7. You'll have to watch the video that's on the enclosed mini-CD to see how to get that done. Once it was installed and running, Windows gave me a sort of alarm sound every 5 seconds it was plugged in, because it was apparently drawing more power than the USB standard considers kosher (500 mA). In order to get around that, I had to revert to using the EU version of the driver, which dropped it to 100 mW (as opposed to 1000 mW) transmit power. The only other workaround would be to attach it to an external USB hub. With the 9 dBi antenna, 100 mW is ample, but you should know that it may wind up limited to 1/10 its theoretical limit.The bad, under Linux: The drivers need to be compiled, the source code is 3 years old, and will not compile on a 64-bit Ubuntu system. Since Ubuntu is the world's most popular Linux distribution, it's definitely a misstatement to say that it supports all 2.6-kernel Linux. At this point, it may not even support most.Now the good: On Windows, once I did get it working, I went from being able to pick up a handful of access points, most of them fairly weakly, to being able to pick up 26, half of them with at least "good" signal strength & quality.Since I was evaluating it primarily for use in a Linux-based network, I could consider this gizmo to be a complete and total failure. Had I not figured out how to get it to work in W7, or that it was in danger of frying my USB ports, I could consider it a disaster there, too. But, if you work around the problems, DANG. It's an amazingly effective device, particularly at under $40. If they could work out their driver problems, and limit transmit power so that it wouldn't fry USB ports, I'd give it an A+ without a second thought. For now, they'll have to settle for a C.

review_title: Poor Choice for Modern NiMH C and D Cells
review_text: The problem here is that a good NiMH D cell is 9000-10000 mAh. Look at the spec sheet for this charger: a C/D cell is listed as 3000 mAh. So a good D cell has 3 times the capacity listed in the specs for this charger. So the specs say it can charge a 3000 mAh battery in 8 hours, but what about a 9000 mAh battery? The charger shuts off after 8 hours so leaving the battery in longer hoping for a full charge isn't the answer. Three cycles, taking them out and putting them back in every 8 hours?A good Tenergy C cell is 5000 mAh and a good Tenergy D cell is 10000 mAh. Of course, there are other brands comparable to Tenergy; Rayovac is not one of them. For those who use just AA/AAAs or low end, cheap C and D NiMH cells this charger will be fine, but slow. For the rest of us, it'll collect dust once replaced with something decent.For AA or AAA cells the Sony BCG-34HRMF4 is a much better charger in this price range: batteries don't have to be charged in pairs, there is an independent status indication for each battery, and it fits easily in luggage.I'm replacing my Rayovac Platinum with a Tenergy Advanced Universal Charger TN190, which I'll review soon after it arrives.

review_title: If you listen to pop music, have a small head, and have money to burn, these are the headphones for you
review_text: I'm not a huge fan of Bose due to their high price and lower quality sound (generally speaking) but I decided to give these a go to see the quality that they are pumping out lately.DesignI like the overall design of these headphones. The headband/earphone placement is slightly uncomfortable but you get used to it. The earphones do not have replaceable covers and seem to be made out of imitation leather, but they are quite comfortable. The headband is so small I can barely wrap it around my head extended all the way out. The headphones fold to be very small indeed and fit nicely into the cardboard/imitation leather pouch (cheap quality, but works well). The color is tacky, but I kinda like it. One really nice feature is that the headphone cable plugs into the headphones, so if the cable goes bad you can just plug in another one instead of replacing the whole unit.SoundThe good news is that you don't have to break these headphones in. Out of the box they sound as good as they are ever going to. The bad news is that while the sound hides flaw (static, pops, poor mastering) quite well, it also is lacking in detail, accuracy, warmth, and range. Listening to pop music, they sound great. I played a bunch of pop/rock songs and thought they sounded fantastic. The trouble started when I listened to some film scores and electronic music. Daft Punk's score for TRON Legacy lacked bass and sounded muddy. Orchestral recordings by the Prague lacked power and clarity. The highs certainly are bright, and the mid-range is fine. But the lower end is pretty much non-existent. If you are one of those people who complain that your Sennheisers don't have the bass of a pair of Beats you are going to absolutely hate these. Likewise I wouldn't use them for movies or gaming because the bass simply isn't there.OverallThese are a nice pair of headphones if you aren't picky about sound quality and don't mind that the price is easily  triple what they are worth. If you are on a budget, or appreciate sound quality over brand name (and especially if both), buy the Sennheiser HD 239 Headphones instead. The price is a third, the sound quality is triple, and they come with a two year warranty.Update 05/08/14: I've downgraded these headphones to 3 stars instead of four. Over time it has become more noticable how muted and muffled the sound of these headphones is (kind of like listening from a pillow). Also, the volume is very low. Despite how they seem to improve the sound of pop music, these flaws bother me to the point where I see this product as merely good instead of great (regardless of price).

review_title: Great replacement on my Mid 2010 MBP 15" Unibody
review_text: The HD on my Mid 2010 15" MacBook Pro was going out.  I could hear (click, click) the hard drive head flying all over the disk trying to find data.  I was fortunate to get one last Time Machine backup with the help of placing cold compresses above and below my HD to cool it down (old freeze hard drive recovery trick).  I ordered one day service and got it FedEx on a Saturday! YES! Thanks Amazon!  Received in a padded envelope.  Not a big deal since the SSD is light and more shockproof than regular hard drive.  Additionally, the box allows for reasonable cushion as well.  Good that minimal packaging was used.  I hate when packaging is unnecessarily 10 times bigger than the actual product.  Such waste!  From there it was a reformat and restore from Time Machine.  Everything went well and operated like any other HD.My choice to go to SSD was not very deeply researched.  I knew SSD have been around for a while and I knew of the performance and durability it provides.  I know that the ruggedized laptops at work were running SSD.  If those guys are using them in rough conditions then it should be ok.  Since I believe heat was the reason my original drive went, I decided to just go for SSD because of durability reasons.  I knew it was supposed to be faster but didn't know what to expect.  I wasn't paying attention to load times before so I wasn't very impressed initially.  I then used a friend's laptop with similar specs and saw the difference.  The startup and program load up time are definitely shorter.  It just seems like the programs are on the starting line waiting for your click to sprint to the finish line of loading the program.  I did notice the laptop seems to run cooler.  I do photo editing and I did a test to export a set of pictures.  I didn't measure times but I believe time was cut in half.  So far everything is running well!  Some are worried about degraded performance but I think by that time it would be time to get another SSD anyway.  However, I will be mindful of my SSD usage as I say that... haha!I am glad I spent the extra money to get the SSD.

review_title: Great device if you have a strong need for it.  Otherwise, pass.
review_text: This product is priced pretty high for what it does so many would hesitate to purchase unless they could be reassured on its capabilities. I've therefore broken down the components most likely to be analyzed:Robustness & quality - this measures how physically durable the product is.  An important point because this unit is unlikely to be used inside your home (think about it), but rather be taken on trips and in the outdoors. The entire contraption with its cable is about 13 oz or just slightly under 1lb.  If you're day backpacking this can be significant weight so might want to reconsider.  On the other hand, longer trips this isn't a whole lot of weight.  The battery itself can be removed from the solar panel and it has its own USB terminals that are slotted with a rubber cover to protect against moisture.  Panel itself is plastic and slightly rubberized.  Of course, there's a large solar surface but it doesn't appear to be glass, but rather, plastic.  This should help keep the unit from breaking inside your pack.Charge time from solar - Supposedly it takes anywhere from 16-30 hours to charge up from dead to full.  That's a lot of time, as it's 30 hours in the sun, so you can't count the night darkness times. Especially in the winter where the sun is out less.  Best exposure of a panel is to place it facing south and of course to ensure it is free from obstructions.  Naturally, this device is unlikely to be permanently mounted anywhere, but on the go, so placement may not always be optimal sinec you'll want to just lay it down near you rather than climb a tree or roof.  My charge time after about 6 hours in the sun was on the mark with about 25% of the unit charged up.  I did have strong sun available. I'd hope to do more testing as it's otherwise been overcast where I'm at and I know that will not produce great results.Charge time to device - I used a fully charged panel battery to charge my Samsung Note 3 phone, which charged up just about the same amount of time as using the plug.  This tells me that the 2amp rated output is true to word.  So if you have bigger devices, rest assured it will charge without taking forever.  And of course smaller devices like flip phones will just thrive.Durability - unable to be assessed because this takes a longer period of time to review, which I don't have.  Cheaper battery packs tend to have cells that don't last, so it's a concern.  Solar panels don't typically fail but it's not unheard of.  Will have to report back on this finding later.One other point to mention is how the battery is removable.  The battery itself is very thin and I find this to be a plus because other battery packs I've seen tend to be brick-like thick.Overall, is the product worth its price?  I'd say only for those who are going to be going on longer trips, where some extra weight will be worth it.  You might think about just getting a regular charge pack as they are much cheaper and in a lot more sizes that meet your needs. However, for those who are in fact out in the woods at days at a time, this is a great device to have.

review_title: Love this 'better than a point and shoot' camera
review_text: I've been using this camera for a couple of months now. Got it for Christmas 2012. So far everything i wanted plus a little more.Pros:1.  Nice size which helps with holding it steady at super zoom distances. But can still carry it in my pocket.2.  Very nice 16 mp shots. The bigger the better.3.  Super zoom to get close up shots from far away. (This replaced a 3x zoom camera).4.  Lots and lots of manual adjustments. Anywhere from full manual to full automatic and everything in between.5.  AA batteries for easy replacement on the go.6.  Cool flash pop up.7.  Price for what you get.Negatives: I was aware of these prior to purchase, thus why no stars off.1.  Drains batteries fairly quickly.2.  Somewhat slow between flash shots, can be up to 7 sec while flash recharges.3.  Low def display screen.This is by far the best digital camera I've owned. I love the larger size. It actually makes you look like a semi-pro photographer ;). DSLR is too big for me at this time. I didn't want to carry around a camera bag and be constantly worried about a $900 investment. This camera is not an investment at $150, it cost less than most smartphones, but the image quality and ability far exceeds any phone camera.  I can take it out of it's small bag and just carry it in my pocket, which is soooo nice and convenient. Easy to quickly put away while needing both hands for something else.Portraits and family shots are why I got it. It excels at those. Motion shots can get blurry, but half of a quality motion shot has to do with the photographer.  That being said, I've taken very nice motion shots. If the motion is predictable and the lighting is good you can get decent shots. I actually had an easier time getting quality motion shots when the motion was side to side relative to me. Motion towards or away from me meant I needed a quick trigger to get a good shot. The auto focus could not keep up with objects changing depth.  One way around this is to pre focus at the desired depth, wait for the object to get back to the predicted position then shoot. This worked for a kid on a swing and is one example of what I meant by predictable motion.  It does take patience, several shots and 'living through' the camera; what I mean by that, is spending a lot of time viewing the action through the camera display instead of in the real world.  But there are good shots to be had, it just takes a little work. Don't let all the negative reviews convince you that the world has to stop while you set up the shot.Picture quality is excellent. Although some of the auto setting do need manual tweaking. For instance with a bright background some photos tend to be be washed out. Auto white balance is not compensating enough. Auto focus sometimes focuses on the wrong object at the incorrect depth.  But being digital you can take as many shots as you want and ditch the bad ones.  The burst shots are a little slow. More like a shot every one-half to full second.I'm very happy with its appearance, performance, manual options and picture quality and for $150 it's really not reasonable to expect $900 performance.  Even with its limitations due to being a budget camera, it is the best one I've ever owned.

review_title: A decent screen protector with partial anti-glare properties
review_text: Installation of this Moshi screen protector sheet is fairly quick and easy, and there is a short video showing this on the product page. First clean the screen with the cleaning cloth that comes in the package, then place the protective sheet on the Kindle Fire.This product has 2 great features that other manufacturers will hopefully emulate:It offers bubble-free installation and also is designed to be repeatedly removed and reused. This is needed because many people will probably not want to always leave this on because image quality is slightly diminished due to its anti-glare properties.I'd like to see UV protection added for future versions of this product, and all screen protectors should include that feature. Some already do have it.This Moshi sheet does not entirely remove glare but is the best screen protector I've seen for reading outdoors or under overhead lighting. Personally, I will only use this sheet for anti-glare purposes at those times. I won't use it when I'm indoors away from overhead lights.For those people who still have complaints about using Kindle Fire in sunlight, one suggestion might be to contact an optometrist to see if they can make heplpful recommendations to at least alleviate the problem to a greater degree. Maybe there are types of anti-glare eyeglasses that would be more effective. Or you might like to consider getting other types of Kindles that work better outdoors.For gamers who'd like to know the effects of this protective sheet, I've tried playing games and find that the touch screen is not affected by the sheet.Aside from the installation process, it's quite instructive to read reviews of screen protectors because it is not uncommon for people to have contrasting opinions. This is natural because no one's eyesight is the same and we also use the devices in different ways (reading, movies, games) and in quite varied environments. This is a good screen protector so you should give it a try and see how well it works for your needs and preferences.

Despite what you may have heard, all HDMI cables are not created equal. A $1 HDMI cable is not the same as a $25 cable or a $100 cable.  But this doesn't mean that a $100 cable is better, or that you need expensive (or even high quality) HDMI cables for all purposes.  Construction quality, cable design, cable thickness (gauge) and connector quality can all play a role in the success you'll have with an HDMI cable. And the longer your cable requirement (and the higher your bandwidth needs), the more important the cable construction.Yes, HDMI is a digital signal but this does NOT mean that you either "have a signal or you don't." Cheaply constructed HDMI cables can have not only mechanical failures (worn out solder joints over time, ill-fitting connectors), but electrical failures as well, and these can be represented either by visible distortion ("sparklies," lines, dropouts or pixilation), or by incompatibilities with certain high bandwidth HDMI sources and displays.This is not to say that you need to pay $50, $100 or more on well-known brand HDMI cables in order to get good results, but when you buy "no name" cables (particularly from unknown marketplace sellers), you're taking a risk - you might get something decent, or you might not. And is it really worth it, to save a couple of dollars on the cable, when it may cost you hours of debugging to determine exactly what's wrong with your picture or sound in your high end home theater system?As the editor of a home theater publication (Big Picture Big Sound), I've had the opportunity to own, evaluate and use many high-end high definition components and displays as well as a variety of HDMI and component video cables. I've used high-end name brand cables as well as no-name plain plastic-wrapped HDMI cables made in China. Some of the cables I've ordered via Amazon marketplace sellers don't even match the picture of the item.But the "Cables To Go" HDMI cables I've bought from Amazon have been consistently high quality, with strong mechanical connections and excellent reliability.  This specific cable (5 meter "Velocity" model), is currently happily in use between an HD cable box and a Sanyo HD projector in one of our writers' home theater systems.  It hasn't caused us one lick of trouble.Cables to Go (aka "Impact Acoustics") is an American company, based in Ohio, specializing in all types of cables, connectors and switching components. They may not be a household name, but they're a solid brand with a proven track record of quality and reliability.Many of the "cheaper" cables offered by marketplace sellers come with hidden costs that you won't see until check-out, namely high shipping and handling fees. But Cables To Go cables bought from Amazon.com can be shipped free (orders over $25), which brings their price down to an extremely reasonable level.Don't be taken in by the claims of high-priced cable manufacturers, but neither should you believe that a $1 or $2 no-name cable is going to be the equivalent of a cable from a reputable brand.  The truth lies somewhere in between.
