review_title: Okay for the money, but it has some annoying factors to it
review_text: First off, this isn't that bad of a machine. However, it had some annoying features that caused me to return it. I would really rate this between 2 and 3 stars, but since you only get whole stars, I went 2 on it. But, that 2 is just because of what I found wrong with this machine as far as what I wanted from it.First off, the picture is not that bad. Also, playback is not noisy and the picture and sound is pretty good. Having audio inputs on the front is great. Also, the programmeable timer options are great.But, I had some problems with this machine. Two of them are not fixeable due to the design. The other might be due to a bad machine, but I'm not sure. However, the first two points I cover are the reasons why I returned this unit and gave it a 2 star rating.Reason 1 why this machine went back - in order for the timer recording to work, you have to press a TIMER button on the remote. Hello! This is NOT the 1980's. Yes, that is what the OLD VCRs did, but in this day and age, you normally just program the time you want to record and then turn the VCR off. It wouldn't be so bad with the timer button IF it were on the machine as well, but you have to do it from the remote. If you lose the remote, you're out of luck. This alone was the major deciding factor in why I returned this unit. Plus, since my wife is the primary user of this machine, she found that to be annoying. She doesn't want to have to hunt for the "other" remote just to turn off the machine and put it back into timer mode. You see, I have it set up to record her Y&R on a daily basis. If we stayed with this machine and she just hit the power button on the remote (as she has done for 10+ years on our previous VCR), the timer would never kick off and record the show for the next day. Oh boy. If THAT happened, I would NEVER hear the end of it! ;)Reason 2 - The remote ONLY works with JVC TVs. You CANNOT program it to work with other TVs. On top of that, I could NOT for the life of me get this VCR to work with my universal remote that I already own. I use that remote for my TV, the cable box as well as the old VCR. Now, I normally probably wouldn't care too much about this, but since my wife is the main user of this VCR, she DOES care about it. She doesn't like having to hunt for multiple remotes.Reason 3 - This didn't necessarily cause me to return it, but it is an annoyance and possibly, it was due to a faulty machine. But, reasons 1 and 2 had already made me decide to return it, but I wanted to let people know about this possible problem. The auto-tracking is VERY slow and some tapes that I have that I KNOW work fine in HiFi mode apparently could not be adjusted to stop noisy playback. The tracking seemed off and the HiFi sound was awful for some tapes. Playing them in another machine resulted in clear playback. Also, it seemed at the beginning of a recording, the picture was bad for about 10 seconds as if the tracking were off and then it finally fixed itself. This is kind of annoying if you can't see the beginning of your recording. Normally, when I program the timer, I give myself 5 minutes before and after the program's time. However, there are times when something comes on that I want to see and I have to hit the record button right there. With this machine, I would possibly have to sit through 10+ seconds of snowy picture before it clears up. This seemed to happen time and time again as I tested the recording function. Again, this might be due to a faulty machine. I even ran a head cleaner through the machine and that didn't help.However, if annoyances 1 and 2 mean nothing to you, then this machine is not that bad of a buy. Some stated it ate tapes as soon as they got it home. Others have stated noisy playback from the machine itself. I experienced no such problems, but of course, I only had the machine for 1 night and exchanged it for a Panasonic, which DOESN'T require you to hit a timer button AND it's remote could control my TV AND my universal remote can be programmed to control the Panasonic VCR.I guess the best bet is to try it out for yourself. I myself didn't like some of the "features" it had and returned it promptly.

review_title: fast, small, efficient, but not perfect
review_text: Some brief impressions with more to follow:Pros:-well built, quiet and low power consumption. Has a plastic faceplate but otherwise quite solid.-very small footprint. It's almost impossible to get any smaller for a 2 drive unit.-robust online support with all the necessary drivers and utilities (albeit not as easy to download as it should be)-fast transfer speeds - the fast CPU helps delivering the Gigabit speed promise.-hardware switch that recovers itself if UPS/power fails.Cons:-needs product serial number to download basic software and utilities required for use--a real pain.-some incompatibilities in FTP software such as unable to display/handle some unicode file name correctly.-the UI is a bit slow, if not clumsy. Updates never fixed it. A cleaner and leaner control UI would be much appreciated.-waking from "sleep" takes about as long as booting, which is pretty long--over a minute.-the windows management utility is rather limited in function. All it does is find and map the NAS. Need a way to control the sleep mode for more flexibility.-Cannot exit sleep mode other than using the Buffalo utility software, which makes it a bit proprietary unless put into always-on mode. The utility also installs a service that keeps the unit on as long as the PC is on, and the service can't be controlled easily except by going into the services administrative control in windows. Also not quite sure how to wake the unit up remotely without leaving it in constant-on mode.-I would appreciate a spin-down feature as mine is used at home without constant need for access, but it's not offered as an option. I manually turn off the windows service just to put it to sleep.-Remote access to the unit has not always been problem free.I wish for a more open and customizable firmware with more flexible power saving features such as disk spin-downs, and better ftp/remote access daemons; the latter hadn't been working as well for me. It's otherwise a very clean, reliable, efficient and fast unit, which delivers the gigabit promise without any issues. Reliability has been great in the 18 months that I've used it, though I was a bit worried about the included seagate drives--which hadn't been the most reliable for me in recent years--in raid-0 configuration. I will update with more findings.

review_title: Head to Head for Bluetooth Speakers
review_text: I am writing this review as a head to head comparison of the three bluetooth speakers I have used right now: theBose SoundLink Bluetooth Mobile Speaker II - Nylon, theSony Bluetooth Wireless Speaker system, Blackand theEton Rugged Rukus All-Terrain Portable Solar Wireless Sound System (Green).I will cover the physical aspects, ease of use, battery life, sound, and miscellaneous for each speaker.Physically, the largest and heaviest is the Sony at almost 18 inches long and almost 5 pounds, not including the charger and carrying case; the Bose is next at 9 1/2 inches and almost 3 pounds, including the carrying cover but not the charger; lastly, the Rukus is a flat 6x6 1/2 inches weighing in at 1.2 pounds, no charger - it's solar.Ease of use is about equal, power buttons, bluetooth sync, volume, etc. are all readily accessible and usable, no rocket science here. All shut down after a suitable period if not in use to conserve battery.Battery life is a differentiator, the Sony is by far the longevity winner with at least 8 hours between charges, the Bose claims eight hours but I have felt lucky to get 4-6 hours, the Rukus will play for ever in direct sunlight and about 4-6 on charge (if only playing music not charging another device).Both the Sony and Bose offer great sound, I'd be hard pressed to select one over the other (I'm sure there are those out there with better ears, I'm not one of them). The Bose might offer slightly better range and the Sony offers better bass, but that's just my opinion. The Rukus is a far cry below in sound quality, more like a portable radio than a stereo speaker set.Misc. qualities - the Bose has its cover built in, which doubles as its stand; the Sony can charge your devices, the Rukus is SOLAR and can also charge your devices (though the battery life is suitably reduced).Ultimately, each of these devices has its prime use, the Sony is great for outdoor use if you need extended play time and don't need to carry it too far, the Bose is suitable for shorter outings and offers easier portability, the Rukus is for extended trip or camping where electricity is at a premium or non-existent and rugged construction is at a premium. The user will have to decide upon their priorities and select the appropriate speaker. P-)

I purchased this to use as a transmitter for audio from my bedroom television so I could watch TV if my wife was sleeping.  It is very small, about the size of pack of cigarettes.  It has an 1/8" stereo jacks for  audio input and output. It appears to turn itself off when it is not synced to a device (which is fine with me since I don't need it on continuously).  I found it broadcast the sound clearly and stayed in sync with the TV video.  I was concerned because the instructions stated it required an amplified audio source (such as a headphone jack on a TV or MP3 player) and the use of RCA line-out jacks may cause the audio to be distorted.  Luckily my FIOS box allows you to configure the audio out on the box so it is amplified; as a result I can turn the volume all the way down on the TV itself, but audio fed to this unit from the cable box is a constant volume and the volume can be adjusted at the headset.  I could also see this coming in handy if you wanted to use wireless headphones with home stereo source or broadcast music from an iPhone to a stereo.  I chose the Bluetooth system over Infra-red because IR required line of sight clearance and Bluetooth did not.  It functions exactly as promised and appears to be very durable.  I did find because it is so compact that traditional straight 1/8" plugs work best; right angle style plugs do not seat well in the unit.

review_title: Simple, that's the word to describe it.
review_text: This is my very first netbook, so I'll start by saying that this netbook is good for what it was meant to be, and whenever you're lounging in your room and just want to check your favorite websites do your homework late at night, watch a few videos, reply on forums...that's about it. This review will be based about the "use" of the netbook. I'm not going to point out Windows 7 features because this is not a review for an Operating System, as I will not compare it to the performance of a laptop or notebook.Before pointing out the strong, neutral and weak points of this laptop I'll note what I did after opening it from the box. First, I unpacked the netbook and charged the battery (It comes discharged, read the instructions), I turned it on after a few minutes, set up Windows 7 in about 15 minutes, uninstalled all the junk-ware it has (Norton, toolbars, Office 2007 trial, games...etc.) and installed Google Chrome, the latest Flash Player and Avast Antivirus. So far here's what I have to say about this little netbook (I will update later):PROS:- The packaging is very solid, the box is small and not heavy.- It's great for everyday tasks, browsing, video-watching, music-listening, photos...etc.- Runs Office 2007 without problems when you work with few documents at the same time.- Slightly faster compared to other brands of netbooks that I have tried, thanks to the Atom N280.- Long battery life, with normal use and standard battery setting (not Eco-Mode) it can hold up to 6-7 hours.- I really like the overall design of the laptop, the power button in the middle is cool for turning it on without having to open the netbook.NEUTRAL:- YouTube videos run smoothly; however, they tend to "crack" when I try to view them in HQ.- Glossy finish on the top, if you're used to these fingerprint magnets it won't trouble you. However, it has matte finish on the inside.- The battery takes good 2-3 hours to charge (If not in use, else about 3-4 hours), but for a good 7-8 hours of real battery life I won't complain.CONS:- It can get considerably hot, not good for prolonged use on your lap; mind you, it will not burn you, but it's very uncomfortable.- It has no Bluetooth connectivity, I bought a small Bluetooth dongle adapter separately. They're not expensive though.- The sound coming from the speakers is horrible and very quiet(set at it's highest), you can listen to the sound but it won't sound pretty or normal; instead, get a pair of headphones or earphones.- The trackpad gets in your way several times, it's too sensitive and whenever you type your palm can mess up what you were writting.

review_title: Not built quite as well as Canon's, but still very good
review_text: The NEEWER battery grip for the 70D isn't built quite as well as the one from Canon, but it is still a great product, especially considering the price difference.  It is built well enough to hold up to difficult conditions, and the attached camera is more fragile and would probably be damaged before the grip is.  This is the perfect product for someone who wants to shoot vertical or double their battery life without shelling out hundreds of dollars for Canon's version.  It is so much cheaper that if it does break or get damaged you can replace it many times over and still spend less than you would if you bought Canon's.Being able to run the camera with two batteries is great, but my favorite part of all vertical grips is being able to shoot in portrait orientation without twisting my wrist into uncomfortable positions for long periods of time.For those fearing damage to their cameras from an aftermarket add-on, these vertical grips are passive devices -- there aren't any electronics inside to damage your camera.  It is just a bunch of connections to simple button switches and encoders that wouldn't be able to damage the camera.  So it should be entirely safe to use.

review_title: Samsung UN55D7000 Review from 3D TV Buying Guide
review_text: Picture Quality: 9/10No one can deny a few facts about the UND7000 picture performance. 1) It is extremely bright with tremendous light (especially in scenes with sunlight streaming into the picture). 2) Colors are vibrant to the point of over saturation unless you are careful with the Picture Mode (the preset Movie picture mode is best) and the picture settings (see our calibrated settings on the next page). 3) Black levels from the Ultra Clear panel are very good. 4) With the proper set up, you can obtain a fantastic picture quality with both HD and SD resolutions. 5) One must be careful to properly tune the Auto Motion Plus feature to get the best combination of attributes. 6) Contrast still decreases at around 25 degrees off center, but not as much as before.With regards to #5 above our recommendation is to tune the Auto Motion Plus (found in the Picture Options settings) feature to the Custom setting. Adjust the Judder reduction section of this feature to the #2 level (down from 5). This will prevent deletion of natural background blur while still allowing for a smooth motion appearance during on-screen fast action. This setting proved very good results in our HQV tests. We also highly recommend turning off the Digital Noise Reduction and MPEG Movie Filter features due to unwelcome shuttering effects.3D TV Glasses: The model is one of Samsung's newest (SSG-3300GR). Unlike some, these glasses are rechargeable using the included USB connection cables. The glasses are light and comfortable but as mentioned above do produce some glare off the sides of the lenses. Samsung includes 2 pair of 3D glasses in the box. Costs for extra sets will run you approximately $79.Features: 8.5/10Design: People either love or hate the UND7000 table top stand. For those that will be wall mounting, this is not an issue anyway. It could be called obnoxious, but I like that it's different and it swivels 20 degrees. It's functional, cool design. The super thin trim framing this TV is only .35" in width all the way around the screen. It has a chrome silver finish on the edges. One thing I also like about the appearance is the jet black screen when the TV is off. This is Ultra Clear Panel which absorbs light and has a incredible depth.Menu Function and Remote Control: Samsung's new menu for the D7000 is quick and has a handy description of each function out beside the highlighted feature. As one would expect from this level of TV, you get a full 10 point white balance adjustment option and lots of extra features. The Smart LED feature is the option for Samsung's new micro-dimming technology. We noticed a very slight flicker occasionally when the micro dimming feature adjusts one part of the screen to enhance contrast. It's really not distracting, but picture purists will probably prefer it off. There are tons of optional picture settings in the Advanced and Picture Options settings. We've done the work for you on which of these to use. See our recommendations below in the picture section.One of the key differences of the UND7000 from the highest end UND8000 is the normal remote control that comes with the UND7000. It's backlit, functional, and has a special Smart Hub key for accessing Samsung's Smart Hub Internet TV features.Audio Output: Unlike most very slim LED-LCD TVs the D7000's 15 X 15 watt speakers performed solidly. Voice is well separated and clear and volume was sufficient to fill a large room. Overall sound is just well separated and there is also ample bass which is especially surprising considering the speaker housing size. The D7000 also has a Auto Volume leveler for to help reduce those annoying advertising volume increases.See the full review at 3D TV Buying Guide

review_title: Lower your already low expectation for this tablet
review_text: I have this tablet for several weeks now. I use it mainly as a tablet, but it took sometime to adjust to its' shortcomings. I've own both iPad and Androids, size big and small. This Windows tablet with an atom processor is a very different kind of tablet.Unlike the Surface, the atom just doesn't have enough processing power to run IE and the news reader App on metro mode. This means that I actually spend most of my time on desktop mode using it in portrait view after disabling all the graphical animations and effects. For web browsing, I only use IE on desktop mode, which has limited gesture support and stalls before web pages are fully loaded. Yes, this does get extremely annoying. But once loaded, the pages glide smoothly and doesn't look broken. If you have too much tabs or other programs in the background, the tablet will just freeze. This happens about 20% of the time. You CAN watch 1080p videos on YouTube, but the controls might be hard to use, and the site and video will stutter before everything plays smoothly. You can forget about Chrome (desktop and metro), FireFox, or Opera. These browser are not smooth at all, they are just not optimize for touch control on an atom processor, though they maybe fine if you have a mouse.The pen is way better than any stylus you can get for an iPad or Android, I use Onenote and it works great, although the screen size maybe limited compared to an actual notebook. The pressure sensitivity works fine too, but it's useless since this tablet cannot handle Photoshop. The stylus is not without problems though. The palm rejection only activates when your pen is about 2 inches or less away from the screen, so sometimes your palm will accidentally register. However, you can disable the touch screen completely in the Device Manager when using the pen. The calibration of the pen is off near the edge of the screen and on portrait orientation, maybe 1/10 of an inch off, but it is noticeable enough to get annoying. I have already tried recalibrating it with the official Wacom driver on different orientation, but still can't fix it. I found the pen too small to hold as well, and I don't have big hands. However, the pen comes in handy when using desktop applications, and completely hides inside the tablet.If you use MS Office a lot, I assure you that this tablet can run any Office 2013 applications quickly without any problems. The virtual keyboard also comes in simplify and full keyboard mode so that you have every key even the F1-12 keys, but the auto-correction is nowhere as good as in iOS. You can also use the handwriting keyboard which immediately converts your handwriting to keyboard inputs. The virtual keyboards are actually good enough to do word processing and even programming. Just remember that all the virtual keyboard, pen, and touch-screen will never be as fast as a real keyboard or as accurate as a real mouse.The built quality is cheap, but I don't think it will break anytime soon. The built does seem weak enough that I suspect something on the case will snap one-day. There are already scratches on all four edges. As you know, the tablet is very light weight. You may still not want to hold this with one hand for a long time, but it will feel like nothing in a backpack. I estimate the battery life to be about 8 hours. It is enough for all-day of occasional web browsing, taking notes in class, reading, work processing, music, movies, etc. assuming you don't actually have it on all-day. Charging this tablet is very slow, but remember you are charging a fully capable Windows machine through a USB port.I was worried that the screen would look bad, but the screen looks just as good as the best tablets out there today. The resolutions is small enough to keep everything on desktop mode, touch friendly, and doesn't overburden the very weak video card on this tablet. However, the resolution is big enough so you won't notice any pixelation.As for performance, the fact that this thing has problems browsing web page, don't expect it to run anything more than Office or play any video near 1080P quality. If you want to play 1080P video, it will run fine as long as it is on the right codec, which is mp4 I'm assuming. But it is sure nice to be able to have VLC player and k-codec installed on a tablet. Unfortunately XMBC is too overpowering on this tablet.

review_title: Works well for indoor use, terrible for outdoor daytime use.
review_text: I purchased this despite the very well documented issue with complex scenes, hoping that I'd receive a working version.After first setting it up the evening I received the camera I was pleased to see it working well inside my home and excited to test the night-vision via the infrared LED illumination. Over-night the camera worked well and I had a new-found insight into the nocturnal life of our cat (bathing, sleeping, occasionally running like crazy).The next morning, before work, I setup the camera to point out of a front window as I wanted to monitor the mailbox and various deliveries throughout the day. Once at work I connected to the camera to see what was going and was confused to find that I'd get a few frames of video and then lose connection. I initially blamed this on my phone and the WiFi signal at the office, as when I got home in the evening the camera was working perfectly again.It wasn't until the next day that I was able to observe the camera first-hand running during daylight. When the camera was facing the interior of the house it worked fine, but as soon as it was panned to point out the window it would immediately freeze. I was able to easily repeat this by holding the camera and manually pointing it out the window. Every time the bushes and grass came into shot the camera would freeze displaying a black frame. If the camera was quickly pointed away from the window it would recover and start streaming video, and once pointed back outside it would immediately lock up again.The only way I was able to operate the camera while pointing out of the front-window was to reduce the resolution down from 640x480 to 320x240. Once the resolution was reduced the camera worked perfectly, but the resolution was now so low it was impossible to identify anyone via the footage.When not freezing due to complex scenes the camera and it's PTZ mechanism worked well. When pointed out the window it failed dramatically.This camera didn't work for my intended use, I've now re-purposed it for use monitoring the interior of our home during the day and night. In this role it works perfectly.All-in-all this camera works well if you play to it's strengths.PROs:- Cheap- Wireless- Pan-Tilt-Zoom functionality- Two-way audioCONs:- Completely freezes and reboots when displaying complex scenes- Quite noisy image- MJPEG is a horribly inefficient compression method which uses way more bandwidth than needed.The only reason I gave this three stars instead of less is that when running inside the home it works as expected.

review_title: It worked for two days. Unimpressive performance.
review_text: I regret I bought this (Sandisk SSD 128Gb). It worked for two days with little increase of overall system performance and then died suddenly.I took care in installing it. I turned on AHCI in bios settings; I set the 1 kb alignment and then I cloned the C: drive with Macrium. I turned off defrag and hybernation, but not the page file. review_title: Altec 326 vs. Altec 326NP: There's only one, possibly the best IEM out there.
review_text: [12/9/12  These phones continue to perform with the best IEM phones ever made, remaining among my favorites.  I'm noticing that increasingly cables are becoming thinner and flimsierdB Logic EP-100 Earbud Headphones (Green), resulting in excessive kinks and even "unknotting" prior to each use.  Moreover, the intrusive unmusical interference of these extremely lightweight cables exceeds, by far, the rubbing or bouncing sounds that so many reviewers found objectionable about the Altec UHP326 Backbeat Titaniums, which remain among the top 3 IEM phones I've heard--whether listening to finely nuanced chamber music or the most fully textured orchestral passages of symphonic music.]Original Review:These are the headphones that the leading consumer's magazine recently rated above phones (full-sized and "in-ear" style) listing at 3-4 times the price.  First of all, lest there be any confusion (though Amazon has apparently fixed the problem), these phones formerly were being listed on separate Amazon pages (and at different prices) as the Altec 326 and the Altec 326NP.  The 326 claimed to use "Ultimate Ears" technology whereas no mention of that was made with the 326NP.  ("Ultimate Ears" is the company that makes true audiophile IEM phones at ultra-high prices.) Some quick research yielded the conclusion that the two Altecs listed on different pages are the same headphones--from the cloth-mesh cable to the noise-isolation feature to the 8-piece fit kit and, above all, to the "Titanium-enhanced speakers."  Altec's website confirms it: there's only one set of "Backbeat Titanium" earphones.The Altec Titaniums are mid-priced, excellent-sounding earphones.  The most frequent complaint--extra noise interference attributed to the cloth mesh covering--is exaggerated, in my opinion. Indeed, you become aware of a thicker, heavier cord as well as its different "feel" from that of other headphones, but I detect no unusual or conspicuous microphonics unless I rub the upper section where the cord branches off into right and left channels. But unwanted, extra-musical sounds are no problem for me, as I'm usually quite inactive while listening to music. Runners and mobile listeners may notice it more than with a pair of phones using thin rubber wire.  Despite this caveat, the Altec Titaniums excell in handling bass frequencies: the somewhat muddy and mushy tones I was occasionally conscious of with my Sennheiser 300's are clearly defined pitches on this Altec model, even during the accompaniment supplied by acoustic walking bass (and there's no "boominess"--that artificial spiking of the lower mid-range that appeals to some wearers).  Listeners who would never dream of spending over a hundred on earphones probably shouldn't.  J-Buds and Coby's will generally perform quite well on compressed audio source material (e.g. MP3 or AAC files at bit rates of 128kbps).  Moreover, an active wearer can break one of the low-end phones without breaking the bank.  But in testing a wide variety earphones on non-compressed, full-frequency source material, the cheap phones soon distinguish themselves from the ones designed and manufactured to the most exacting standards. The Altec Titaniums compare favorably with (and, in some cases, surpass) audiophile phones I've acquired or had the pleasure of using--by Klipsch, AKG, Shure, Sony, Sleek Audio, Phillips  Woodees, Phillips SHE-9850.  Moreover, as currently priced, a user could be forgiven for wearing them while running or doing manual work--should damage occur, it's not the end of the world.  (It's not that unusual to snag a cable or to trample on a phone that suddenly pops loose.) One solution is to have a pair of "everyday phones" for the treadmill, etc., and a pair of "Sunday phones" for serious listening, which is when the Titaniums really shine.[Later: I've had to raise my rating from 4 to 5 stars after breaking them in.  In the case of the Altecs, I found that Comply Foam tips made a difference for the better. Without them, the bass was a bit over-emphasized while the mids lacked in natural presence and the highs didn't have the clean, ringing ride cymbal sound I like to hear.  With the foam tips, everything is balanced and the fit especially secure. If the Titaniums are a tad larger than some earphones, they're richer-sounding because of it. They're slightly heavier in the ear and less sensitive than my light and bright CX300s (i.e. they require setting the gain higher for comparable loudness, shortening the life of batteries--a welcome trade-off for sound this good). But with the Altec Titaniums you don't merely hear the bass: you feel the acoustic instrument's soundboard and cabinetry, practically moving the ground beneath you (the Klipsch Image S4's came up woefully short; even the Sony MDR-EX700's, with a 16mm driver, couldn't muster the same might and muscle.  Moreover, the fragile thin wire of my Sennheiser's already shows signs of fraying--but not a chance with the rugged cable of the Altecs. The worst I can say about them is that the "Left" and "Right" channel designations (black on black) are the least conspicuous I've ever seen on a pair of headphones--virtually invisible and useless.In sum, you can find plenty of appealing, highly acceptable earphones for under $50 (even $20), some of which you'll most likely initially prefer to the Altecs.  But it's doubtful you'll find a more "expensive-sounding" or better-built pair of phones than the Altec Titaniums in this price range. Update: 05/19/2012: Belkin sent the second replacement. Same issue as the first. The magnet feature works very unreliable as described below. Too unreliable to be of any use. If you can live without it, it is a great case, though. One star for Belkin's failure to address the issue.Update: 04/18/2012: Belkin sent a replacement. This one had the magnet upside down. One star for incompetence on Belkin's side. I would hold off until Belkin figured out the magnet issue.Before, I start, I wanted to mention that I also experienced the magnet issue. I think there are two different issues with that magnet: some people reported upside-down magnets which did not work at all and even switched the iPad off when the cover was bent back. Other reported misaligned magnets which did work, but unreliably.I had the later issue. The new iPad only shuts off when the lid was pressed perfectly straight. The new iPad was switching itself on when it was just laying on a table from the little bend in the top cover. It also switched itself on when the cover was shifted just 1 mm to the top, but worked actually reliably when the cover was shifted like 5 mm to the bottom. That tells me that the magnet is positioned about a 1/4" too high.Belkin admits to an issue on its Website. I contacted Belkin customer service who is sending me a replacement, and a prepaid shipping label to send mine back once I get the replacement. Belkin says the issue had been fixed.And now to the review, the positive:I think, the Belkin Cinema folio is the best compromise between size and protection. I am spending a lot of time in the air and was looking for something which can protect the iPad from moderately rough handling while on the road. I think the Cinema folio does that without being too bulky. I never used any phone condoms and my gadgets do show signs of road worrier wear. The iPad, however, looks much more fragile than my trusty Thinkpad T. I needed a case adding sufficient protection not from scratches but from destruction.The blue part on the outside of the Belkin Cinema feels rubbery which provides a good grip, and the black part feels like craft foam. The inside consists of some fleece material which feels nice to the touch. The Belkin Cinema holds very comfortably in the hand opened or closed without having to fear that the folio slips out of sweaty hands. The case has some new-car-smell to it but not to an extent that it would bother me. I kinda like it actually.The cover can be swung back with the magnetic latch used to secure the cover on the back while reading and also keeps the latch out of the way.I particularly like that the iPad itself is held by rubber corners instead of a sleeve. I do not like the sleeve solution because I want to feel and watch the entire surface of the iPad without something getting in the way around the display area. The rubber corner mounts are a snug fit and feel save without having to be afraid that the iPad may slip out. The rubber mounts also provide much needed protection around the edges.The stand feature appears to work sufficiently well. You can either do it as Belkin demonstrates on their Web site or alternatively, also put the lid to the back and secure the cover in a little cutout there. The later solution orients the iPad almost into a 90 degree angle without having anything in the front getting into the way, for instance when using a keyboard, but feels less stable. I tried the first stand feature having the iPad on my lap while sitting on the coach which worked. However, I probably will not use the stand feature in my lap at the airport because I think it is not stable enough for that when being bumped and such. Either one just works in landscape orientation. It will be saved for table top surfaces.The Cinema makes your iPad look like an old fashioned paper notebooks, one of those sales people like to carry around. Since I am working in the field, I actually like that look.To mention is also that the dock connector is readily accessible to connect an HDMI adapter, a serial cable, or whatever else you like to use. Many cases I saw only have a narrow cutout. The back camera cutout is big enough not to interfere.The negative:There is not much which I dislike. I found was that the iPad becomes really hot when used in the case outside in the TX sun. The new iPad has anyway much higher battery consumption and with that higher heat emission. The case appears to make this issue worse in hot weather but then also makes the iPad more comfortable to hold in the hand. I am not sure how nicely the material wipes clean. The rubbery part probably nicely, but I could see that the outside foam part and particularly the inside fleece part could become icky and not easily cleanable with rubbing alcohol which I use to keep my gadgets clean of finger prints, smudges, and road bugs. The case is a tight fit and there is no place for a stylus.I will update the post, once I get the replacement to report back on the magnet issue.

review_title: Great price for a great router
review_text: The setup for this router was extremely simple. Plug the device into a power outlet and Modem, boot up your computer, toss in the included disk, follow a few instructions, and you're set.During the setup, a Router Monitoring program is installed. This gives you quick and easy access to options should you wish to access more advanced setings. It is not necessary if you stick to the default.I had previously attempted to setup a Buffalo WZR-HP-G300NH, which was highly recommended to me by friends who have used it successfully. After nearly pulling out all my hair, I ended up returning the device. For some reason the wireless signal would not detect properly. I returned it as recommended by Buffalo support and tried another. Same issue, so I sent the second back as well.From there I went with a D-Link DIR-655. It took some tweaking and manual channel switching before it would work, but at least it worked.After hooking up the Belkin N150, I was amazed to see that, after following the setup instructions, it was up and running! I successfully connected my MyTouch 4G phone, iPad 2, and Gateway laptop. I didn't have to tweak anything. Oddly enough it also had a stronger signal than my D-Link DIR-655 (which has three antennas). All the devices gave me 4bars at the farthest location in my house, where the D-Link DIR-655 often moves down to three or lower.Out of curiosity, I checked the internet speed between the Belkin N150 and D-Link DIR-655. The D-Link DIR-655 gave me a download speed of 7414kbps with a 1417kbps upload speed. The Belkin N150 gave me a 8785kbps download speed with a 1140kbps upload speed (I used the integra Telecom speed test and have Comcast as my internet provider). This tells me that their internet speed is pretty much the same, as the speed tests in general tend to fluctuate a bit.One negative about the Belkin N150 is that the LAN ports on the back are only 10/100 whereas the D-Link DIR-655 is 10/100/1000. That said, for the price, I was extremely impressed with the Belkin N150 and will be recommending it to friends and family who are looking for a good buy.

review_title: Records well but a little too large, no pocket clip, and has bad user interface
review_text: On paper the ICD-PX312 has a good feature set, has USB & microSD slot for more storage. But the user interface is not very good compared to older models, particularly the Olympus VN-240.THE GOOD:+ Batteries are included. Also a a mini-USB to USB cable is included for transfer.+ Using the onboard memory (no external microSD) you can record for over 20 hours on SHQ mode.THE BAD:- Just as in previous Sony recorders I find the Recording interface is dumb. There are 2 large buttons: one labelled "PLAY/STOP", the other "REC/PAUSE". To start recording you press "REC/PAUSE" and recording starts. So far so good, right? The problem is stopping recording - if you press the large conveniently labelled "PLAY/STOP" button recording will stop BUT IMMEDIATELY PLAYBACK which is most cases is NOT what you wanted. To stop recording without playing back you have to hit the small unlabelled square icon "stop" button (located in the middle of 3 buttons). For the life of me I don't understand why it doesn't stop recording (without playback) when "PLAY/STOP" is momentarily pressed. If the user wanted to really review the just-completed recording he could just press "PLAY/STOP" one more time to playback. This would be a much better solution, because many people use a recorder for quick "to me" notes or lectures. When you stop recording you don't want to attract unwanted attention (in a lecture) or hear the note you just recorded, both of which will happen if you press the wrong stop button.- After stopping a recording there is a slight delay (about 1-2 seconds) while the recorder processes the recording ("ACCESSING" is displayed during this time). There was no delay with the VN-240.- I wish I could say the bad UI design stopped there but there's more. Like most recorders there is a "HOLD" lock to prevent inadvertent presses from starting recording or playback (i.e. if you put it in a pocket). The problem is when the recorder is locked it only displays "HOLD" on a blank screen for 4 seconds THEN reverts back to the normal display so there is no way to know if it is locked after the 4 seconds pass! Oh sure, you could press a button and see if it displays "HOLD" when pressed (or look at the HOLD switch) but a better way to handle this is what the Olympus VN-240 does in HOLD: it blanks the display completely so it is obvious that the device is locked. One way around this problem is to power off the recorder instead of using HOLD - the display will be blank and of course it will not respond to button presses. The only downside of doing this is that the recorder takes 3-4 seconds to power on (from off).- By default, the recorder will power off in 10 minutes. This means that even if you have the recorder on and 10 minutes elapse after last using it, it will power off and you will have to turn it on before proceeding (after the power-up delay wait). Fortunately this auto-power off time is adjustable to 5/10/30/60/OFF.- The volume control is implemented as two digital buttons (VOL+ and VOL-). I prefer a old-style volume dial because it is faster/easier to adjust volume that way. (The VN-240 had a volume dial)- The device is taller than it feel it should be (it is 1/2" taller than the VN-240). This makes it more noticeable in a shirt pocket. More importantly there is no pocket clip (as on the VN-240) so it will not stay upright in a shirt pocket.STATE OF THE RECORDER INDUSTRY:I find that the older Olympus models (like the VN-240, sadly no longer made) had a optimal interface (not to mention a pocket clip). Somehow manufacturers are making products that are worse than the older ones despite advances in technology! Even newer Olympus models aren't the same. For instance I cannot find any USB recorder with a shirt pocket clip. The ICD-PX312 could have been a 5-star product if these flaws didn't exist.Instead, I would recommend theOlympus VN-702PCas it has the same features but a better user interface (still no shirt pocket clip though).I hope you found this review helpful!

review_title: Was an inexpensive "beast" when originally released
review_text: While this card was never considered top of the line, it was fairly capable and affordable when released.  There are normally just two types of video cards - the inexpensive, good enough to surf, but nothing else types - and the oh my god, this is beautiful, but I can't afford to eat any longer type.  Thankfully, this mid-range of card became popular around this time and actually produced respectable frame rates, included SLI functionality and had 2 DVI ports (something that wasn't very common at this price point).That being said, nVidia has always produced a pretty good reference board and XFX seems to have cracked the nut on juicing that reference up a bit and giving it to customers at a decent value.  Being able to play most games at "moderate" graphics and still able to achieve 60fps or more is respectable.  No, you don't get to see the game in all its glory, but it is close enough.  If you want lower frame rates, you can certainly tune this up a bit - and I haven't even tried to overclock this puppy.The card only takes a single slot, which is fairly nice in a smaller case, but at the same time is fairly long, so don't expect to go plopping this thing into a micro/mini case anytime soon.  Exact specs on size can be viewed in the above product description - but know what you're buying before you jump in.  It runs fairly quiet, but under full load, you can definitely hear the fan a little.  As for additional information - this card is PCI-E (not to be confused with old PCI and AGP slots).  Please make sure you have that slot on your board before buying this.  Also, this card will require a 6-pin power drop to work properly - not all PSUs have this, so make sure yours does before buying.  Otherwise, the card was easy to install, configure and with a simple download of the latest driver from nVidia's website, performed superbly.This card, unfortunately, just stopped working for me (this is after years of faithful service), so I am now going through the task of seeing if XFX's lifetime warranty still applies.  They recently switched from nVidia cards to AMD cards, so I'm not sure how I'm going to make this happen.  "Lifetime warranties" are a weird beast - as some imply for the lifetime of the individual that purchased it (way cool) and others for the lifetime of the product line (not so cool, but not bad either).  This second option is what worries me - since XFX no longer designs nVidia cards, they may claim that the "lifetime" of that card is now passed and no warranty.  Granted, it served me for many years, so I'm not upset with the company or the product - and getting a replacement would just be a bonus.

review_title: Provides Great Protection For Treasured Photos & Documents
review_text: When it comes to saving your unreplaceable photos, documents or videos, nothing is as secure as a memory vault. With a memory vault, you have a totally sealed compartment compared to a Plug In, which has an open end. I have used a SanDisk Image Mate for downloading my photos for over a decade now. SanDisk is a name brand I trust completely, as I have to have the best photos with sharp, great detail for family history and magazine articles. SanDisk's transfers are the sharpest and clearest giving me perfect photos for my photo programs.This SanDisk Memory Vault stores my photos and videos in the clearest sharpest state and with the totally sealed vault, they will stay that way. The vault comes with a separate USB plug in cord and a cloth storage bag. There is a rubber cover over the Plug In USB port on the vault that you must remove to plug in the USB cord, before downloading your photos, videos or files. When you are finished you simply put the rubber plug back on sealing your photos for probably longer than your lifetime. With a comparable Plug In USB flash drive, such as a PNY Attache 8 GB for $20.00, you only have a 1 year warranty. Printing your photos is also a big difference. The Vault prints the sharpest prints possible, but the Plug Ins are not as clear. The Plug Ins get too much damage with the open plug- even simple dust, pollution or humidity damages the photos, not to mention the open plug itself can get damaged.I have stored photos on everything from CD's to Plug Ins to Vaults over the last decade. CD's and Vaults store and print the best photos. This SanDisk vault is a wonderful fully sealed protection for your photos and well worth the money if you are looking to protect your treasured photos, videos or other important documents for many, many decades to come. There is one important thing you should know, that these vaults even with a rubber plug are not waterproof, so if you want to protect it from being damaged should it ever be submerged in water- keep it in a waterproof container.

review_title: Great Program if it's What You Need
review_text: Curious as to the name X3?  No, it's not a spaceship from 50s sci-fi classic, it's a cutesy reworking of the Roman numeral XIII, or 13 as we know it.As the program goes, it's a very capable painting and artistic program for those in fields requring such or having one or more as hobbies that fall into these categories.  For those looking for cheaper alternatives there is ArtRage (free to $50, depending upon options) and Inkscape (free) but beyond that I don't know of much else (Illustrator I won't mention since it's basically a monthly service now).Which brings me to the point I briefly touched upon above - cost.  At $400+ this isn't a cheap program; however, it's cheaper than Illustrator and in line with what one might expect in such a supercharged program.I could bore you with trite details but I'll cut to part you want by stating if it can be drawn, painted, mind-mapped or otherwise creatively put together, this program will probably do it.  Really suck at painting or drawing?  This program might help you out there, too.  Want to see what watercolor and oil paints do when mixed on canvas (it ain't pretty, folks)?  This will do that, too, along with anything else your mind is set on doing.Here's a listing of virtues and vices, in no particular order:Virtue: If given the option, go for the download.  The total program is only about 140MB although it does fatten quite a bit when installed.  The DVD is only as good as its age whereas the download is usually kept up to date.Neutral: There is a learning curve that isn't as steep as the big boys but will probably confuse some of the newbies until they learn the ins and outs of palettes, brushes, textures, etc.  Truthfully, I had most of it figured out within an hour but I'm possibly more experienced than some out there.Vice: Installation is something of a bear, especially given the size download.  Plan on kissing at least an hour goodbye while this puppy goes through the motions.  Do have to admit, though, most programs like this have a tendency to be really slow on the install end.  Those used to Photoshop know what I'm talking about.Vice: Slow to open, and I do mean slow.  I believe the best time I've ever had is around 15 seconds with some instances creeping up to a half minute or so.  Quite obvious this program is sucking resources and RAM because I'm pushing an Intel I3 with 8GB RAM, more than sufficient for anything else I'm running.  In fact, it's such a hog at before fully booting the window often reads "not responding" when it was really grinding its way through a slew of commands.Virtue: Once running the user can literally tweak this program any way they want it with palettes galore that includes brushes never thought of by Van Gogh or his contemporaries.  In fact, you could technically blot out your screen for all the palettes that could open if you click too much.Virtue: Impressive set of secondary items such as perspective snap (keeps your picture in perspective no matter how much you fool around with it) and "jitter" brushes, a rather unique addition in which the brushes can reproduce imperfections such as blobs or smears that would be present if you hesitated during painting or took an abrupt turn.Vice: This is a big screen proposition, those with small screens had better look elsewhere.  It's definitely better looking on my 25 inch screen versus my 12 inch, but that's a given.  The problem here is that the program is literally useless on the smaller screen if you open palettes to any great degree.  In short, plan on tweaking palettes if you switch back and forth between large and small screens (tweaking as in hiding or deleting).  In the age of smaller screens this could prove troublesome.Virtue: Quick clone is a boon.  Any image or photograph can be quickly cloned so you can perform surgery on the copy without damaging the original.  What?  You say most programs like Photoshop have this?  Of course they do.  Actually used it recently?  Quick is not a word you use to describe that process, but with Painter it is.  Withing seconds you have a quick clone you can alter to your heart's desire.Is Painter X3 worth the money?  I've known students, architects and engineers that swear by this product; however, casual users are a different story.  For them it costs a bit too much and they'd be better served with the freeware mentioned before.  If your idea of painting is to do an occasional watercolor sunflower, go somewhere else.  If you're doing a field of sunflowers and each one has to be meticulous, this is the program you want.For those on the fence, i.e., undecided as to whether to fork over the $400, you can do one of two things.  You can see if you qualify for the academic version since it runs around $89 or, if you don't, download the free but full 30 day version via the website.  This gives you a fair amount of time to evaluate the product before buying.

review_title: The crap is in the the razer ware
review_text: I loved my N50, loved my n52, loved my n52teWow did razer seriously f'up a good thing. This device has some nice upgraded physical features over the 52te such as a fiber coated usb cable and I believe they re-enforced the thumb control and wheel button some more. Even the software itself looked promising as it had some nice new features for mapping single keys that use shift/control/alt combinations without using macros.But the problems seem to come in when pressing key combinations especially with the single shift/alt/control combinations and when using modifier keys to switch profiles. Key states stick! And stick annoyingly so. The shifted profile states will stick and you'll end up on the wrong set of mappings and keys themselves will be in a stuck down state. I get this a lot on the thumb control and here you are in a pvp situation endlessly moving in circles. Even pressing that direction on the controller again seldom turns off the 'stuck' state and I have to hit the appropriate key on my regular keyboard to 'unstick' it.  I can't tell you how many times this has interrupted my game play.I tried contacting their technical support and they were totally useless, suggesting I send the hardware back for what I am certain is a software issue. They don't want to listen to what I'm telling them in regards to the problem and give the general pat questions/answers. "Are you on the latest firmware? Are you using the latest UI?" Um, yeah I wouldn't bug you until I'd tried all that.Razer successfully turned one of the best game controllers into a useless PoS in my opinion and until those software issues are fixed, I would avoid the nostromo line like a plague.

review_title: Flipping Cool! My Favorite Flying thing.
review_text: The coolest flying "toy" just got better! Compared to the original, nearly everything has improved. The new drone is more stable in flight, especially at higher altitudes. Ive been piloting with my iPad for the past month, about 50 flights so far and its still doing great.New features like the HD camera, additional sensors and FLIP work well. Video quality is much better than the original and really comes in handy when piloting via camera & screen.The core functionality is solid but there are some bugs to be addressed with video recording. Would have given it 5 stars if the USB recording was perfect but it seems to be problematic and degrades the video quality. I recorded about 10 flights to USB then it started acting up. Wifi recording mode seems to be better quality but flight range is decreased.Thanks to Parrot for producing such a unique product. I am shocked that it still has NO competition from other manufacturers.Cons:1. Requires An iOS or Android Device to work. If you don't have an iPod Touch, iPhone, iPad or Android Device this will not work. (put phones in Airplane mode prior to flying to help avoid disconnection)2. Limited WiFi recording range3. USB recording mode issues4. Spare batteries and Parts are a good idea, I suggest getting a set of spare gears & shafts, They are the most likely parts to damage in a bad crash.5. If video stream stops while wifi recording, stop the recording and the video comes back.6. Beware of Higher capacity batteries, the drone was designed for the battery it comes with, running for longer than intended may damage components like the motor or CPU.

review_title: Good bass, but not deep bass
review_text: I recieved these headphones tonight and listened to them on my mp3 player for 3 hours.  The sound was full range, but not excessively deep in bass, but still punchy.  The only drawback was that the volume had to be excessive to get good bass response.  Bass was greatly diminished at lower volume settings, even with the EQ set as 'BASS' setting.  They were a little tight fitting but were tolerable after sliding them backward a bit.  Only half of my songs had appreciable bass response, but that was better than my sony headset and much better than the sets that come with most MP3 players.  I think I'll stay with my mid-level Koss headphones that are more comfy and bass goes down to 20Hz.  I ordered some Audiology Extreme Bass headphones with a subwoofer amplifier.  They did not have real bass, from 20 to 100 hertz.  The only bass was a fake vibration that occurs when there is a bass hit from a bass drum, explosions, thunder, etc..  I really don't recommend them except they're fun for movies or video players.

review_title: Tough time choosing this rating part 1
review_text: I say this in the title because I'm not quite sure if it's the fault of the Rosewill Challenger case or the Gigabyte GA-970A-D3 motherboard I used, but I had some isssues with the build on my new PC regarding them, so I'll first duplicate this part for both products then move on to the individual pieces themselves.The outstanding dealbreaker for me that prevented a 5-star review was the actual installation of the motherboard.  Of the 6 screw slots on the mobo, I could not use 2 of them and had an issue with the 3rd (This description will be if you were looking at the case/mobo from the left-hand side of the case opening, which places the I/Os on the mobo in the upper left-hand corner): The lower right corner screw spins freely for me, as if there is nothing below it to hook onto, the left-middle screw on the other hand tilts at an extreme angle and won't seat despite several attempts at insertion, and though the upper left screw caught in the case hole I was forced to leave it rather loosely seated because any attempt at tightening it further pulls that part of the mobo to the left, causing all of the IOs on the rear of the case to not match up with the IO panel that came with the mobo.  In summary, I have a diagonal (more or less) line from the lower right to upper left of the mobo that I either could not attach or had to leave very loose.  The other 3 screws seated perfectly and the board seems to be secure, so though it's not causing any issues at the present I hope that trend continues. I had 1 wiring issue as well, but that's probably due to my PSU being of the non-modular variety, but with the placement of the PSU now being in the bottom the 12v power connector for the CPU was ~3" too short, and had to be spliced in order to reach the slot.Now that that's out of the way, the rest of the case is very well made, and for me at least there was ample room for wire management behind the opposite panel which of course is also removable. The installed fans are working very well so far, and though I just got my order in today for the other 2 remaining fan slots I'm fairly certain I could've done without them, at least thusfar.  While working this morning (which by no means is akin to playing something like Crysis 3 on ultra settings or some such), my CPU core temps registered ~20 degrees cooler than my old case, and actually 6-7 cooler than room temperature for that matter.Obviously the issues I mentioned above are unique to my particular case/mobo/psu setup...yours of course may vary if you deviate from that.  Overall I'd have to say it's a good case but I can't in good conscience give it or the mobo a 5 star rating.  Thanks :)

review_title: Best Antenna Yet for Old Analog TV That Uses Digital Converter Box
review_text: The Winegard Digital FlatWave Antenna is the best antenna yet for my ancient Panasonic TV/VCR combination set!  After the digital changeover, the old analog TV works fine with a Zinio set-top digital converter box, but it still needs a very good antenna to pull in digital signals off the airwaves.  (The area around my home is quite hilly.)The Winegard FlatWave antenna gives better reception on all channels than my other generally satisfactory digital antenna (Philips SDV2780 TV Indoor Antenna).  The Winegard antenna finds all the same channels (except for a couple of bad-signal local shopping channels)--and also finds one network channel that I'd never been able to get before!  With the FlatWave antenna, the SD picture is generally sharper, and is more stable (breaks up less often).The FlatWave antenna is thin and flexible, sort of like a mouse pad (the kind without foam backing).  I was surprised at how large the antenna is (roughly a foot square, measuring 11-3/4" x 13"); you need to allow some space for it.  One side is white, the other black, so the antenna will blend into almost any background (depending on which side faces out).  Because the antenna comes with a generous 15-foot coaxial cable, it can be placed in many different locations (in a window, on a wall, or laid flat on a table), with different orientations.  Mine gets the best reception when laid flat on a window table, but it also works well propped up between a couple of cushions, or placed on a wall.  (Double-sided sticky mounts are included with the antenna.)Installation of the antenna is supremely easy.  Just plug the coaxial cable into your converter box (or digital TV), and run the channel finder setup utility.  Your TV will find all the available channels, and you'll be ready to go.

review_title: Yamaha RX-V575?  So far, so good...
review_text: I bought this receiver to replace a 4 year old Pioneer 7.1 receiver that lost all of its audio channels suddenly and simultaneously.  I've only had the Yamaha for about a month, but, hopefully, it'll give me better service than did the Pioneer.  The 575 is an outdated model now, having been supplanted by the 577, but I didn't need or want built in wireless WiFi, and I certainly didn't want to pay an additional $170 for a receiver that otherwise had nearly identical specs.  I was glad to find that Amazon still had the 575 in stock at a good price.The Yamaha receiver doesn't look as snazzy as the Pioneer, but I liked it just the same.  All of my input device connections (Blu Ray player, DVD recorder, TV, attic mounted AM/FM antennas and LAN ethernet) transferred directly to the back of the 575.I'm not interested in using Bluetooth or my phone with this rig, so wireless capability for playback and control is a moot point with me.  The receiver is hardwired to my Asus router, as is my Blu Ray player and TV.  The receiver immediately found my router and configured itself before I could even call up the page to look at the settings.  Internet radio is easy to use and works like a dream.  There are tons of stations available in many genres, depending upon your tastes.  Right now, I'm listening to some peaceful Celtic tunes.Automatic speaker setup using the YPAO routine is also fast and easy.  After running the setup routine, I find that the sound from my surround speakers is more noticeable and full than it was with the Pioneer, and the sub seems to have found some new energy, as well.  The menu offers me the capability of going in and making changes to my speaker and sound settings (such as EQ), but I doubt that I'll need to fiddle with them.  Overall, I am entirely pleased with the quality of sound from this receiver.While there are many features available from this unit, the vast majority of people will use only a few of them.  I've found that the ones that I've needed are simple to use and setup, and provide a good level of adjustment and choices for sound quality.  I've found that the "Enhancer" feature for use with MP3's and other compressed soundstreams (such as streaming movies from Netflix or Vudu) works very well.  I also like that maximum volume levels can be set via a menu.  This might come in handy for someone who lives in an apartment.  The menu item for lip sync adjustments can also easily be found, which was not the case with my Pioneer.My TV is connected to the receiver via an optical Toslink cable to the receiver's AV4 input, which I have relabeled "TV".  The receiver selects AV4 as its default input for sound from a TV, so all I had to do was rename that input.  The hot button labeled "TV" on the remote pulls that input up with 1 touch, and audio is there.  The same thing is true for Blu Ray (BD), internet radio (Net) and the radio tuner.Speaking of remotes, I can understand how the remote might seem a bit complicated and over populated for many people.  Personally, I like it.  Believe it or not, it's a huge step up from my Pioneer remote, which was almost insane for the the amount of tiny buttons and cryptic, nearly invisible labels that it had on it.  I won't miss that.  I'm not a fan of trying to make 1 remote do everything with everything, so I prefer to use the remote that came with the machine.  I keep them all in a drawer, out of sight in the center section of my loveseat.Even though I've had the RX-V575 for a short while, I'm liking what I see.  If it lasts, I think I'll be happy with it for quite some time.

Even at its relatively cheap price, I still struggle to see the value in this thing if you already own a Roku, smart TV, game console, Apple TV, etc. If somehow you don't have any of the above in 2014, then this will do the job and allow you to stream Netflix, Hulu, and YouTube by receiving it from your laptop, phone or tablet--but be sure that your device is compatible, as there are still a lot of kinks that Google has yet to work out in terms of compatibility. Amazon video or many other apps that devices like Roku allow are not available.It's fully capable of streaming all of your local media from all of your devices, but Google blocks this ability and offers no alternative of their own, not yet anyway. Google has crippled this technology, as this device is capable of so much more. Even if it could stream anything and everything on your devices, I already have HDMI cables for my phone and laptop (even cheaper solutions), so again, I don't see the value in owning this device unless you don't have a smart TV and/or devices that are already capable of streaming video.EDIT: Well, I'm revising this review as Google has since addressed many of my concerns with the release of the Chromecast SDK. Additionally, compatibility has improved and there are quite a few apps that support Chromecast (including Aereo soon), now making it a viable competitor to Roku. I also prefer using my existing mobile device as a remote control rather than having yet another remote. Additionally, using the app's interface on my phone is far easier to me than navigating it on the TV with a little remote.I don't feel there is anything mind-blowing that developers have done yet, but the ability to stream local media is a huge plus that bumps my original rating up by a few stars. I'm excited to see what others can do with the SDK. I think there is a lot of untapped potential and it's a steal of a deal for what you may get in the future, and it's quite good for what you get out of the box as well.Amazon Instant Video is still not supported, which is a shame, but I have other devices that can stream this, so it's not a dealbreaker. Tabcasting needs work and is quite a memory hog on the PC, but I've primarily been using it to stream Comcast Xfinity (live TV channels, on demand content) and it generally works well with a few hiccups.Overall, I'm glad that Google has listened and that things are looking up for the Chromecast. Hopefully the support continues and we'll also continue to see new apps churn out for the device.

review_title: Now if I only had some artistic ability
review_text: When used with the Paper by Fifty-Three app, Pencil is the best iPad stylus I've ever used.  It can be a bit finicky to get working, but once it is, it really is the closest thing I've ever felt to just drawing on a tablet.  Physically, the stylus feels properly built, unlike some, where it's felt like the rubber tip is always just about to rip off and leave who knows what scratched across my iPad's screen.  The squared-off shape is easy to hold, and it just feels solid all the way around.Previously, the best stylus I had ever used was the Cosmonaut, which is built like a big crayon and felt that way when drawing.  The Cosmonaut works well, but doesn't fit my hand in the same, precise way as a pen or (real) pencil.  Pencil does.  Combined with the special features it has--flip to erase, palm rejection, essentially getting free in-app purchases with the Paper app for extra drawing tools--it really works well when you want to sketch something out on the iPad.It is not perfect, however:* It has to be recharged.  Unlike most styluses, which are just not-quite-pointy sticks of rubber and plastic, this one connects via Bluetooth and has to be charged.  So far, it doesn't have to be charged all that often, but you may have an idea for sketching something and not be able to sync with the Paper app because you need a recharge.* The neat features are finicky.  I particularly like the idea of treating the rear of the stylus like a pencil eraser and erasing when it is used.  In my experience, this feature works almost, but not quite, all the time.  Sometimes, it still thinks you're trying to draw.  (I've never had it go the other way, where it thought I was trying to erase when I was trying to draw.)  Blending with your fingers seems hit-or-miss, too--again, it almost always works, but occasionally not.  The good news is that palm rejection seems to work without a problem.* Right now, at least, it is utterly dependent on the Paper app on the iPad.  If you try to use it with any other app (or with any other tablet), it works fine, but all the neat advertised features won't work at all.  Supposedly, there is some effort to try to get other app developers on board, but there are no other apps that use the special features that I've seen so far, and I'd recommend not relying on that hope when making a buying decision.* You also need to have the right iPad.  The compatibility list (iPad 3, 4, Air, Mini) isn't for show.  The syncing and special features do not work with an iPad 2 (or, presumably, an original iPad).  It still works as a dumb stylus, but it's too expensive to recommend without its special features in the Paper app.In sum, it's a really nice drawing stylus (with a few quirks) when used with the Paper app, and a good, solid (but expensive) stylus when used with anything else.  It makes me wish I had a smidgeon of artistic ability, but it helps me get the best out of what little I have.

review_title: Not impressed and a little frustrated. Updated: 10/18/2012
review_text: 10/29/2012 update - Yeah, I've had this thing crash on me far too many times. This isn't a system I can live with, it's far too cheaply made for me. It's going back. Good riddance.You know the built-in media player that seemingly every electronics device has built-in now? Like the Youtube player on most modern TVs, or the internet browser bundled in your DVD player? That's what this interface feels like. The menus are inconsistent from one section to the next, the navigation is sluggish, often causing me to sit there and wonder if I should press the button again or just wait another minute to see if it's really doing something.While it might seem nitpicky to ding a product for not having a perfectly translated interface on a $99 HTPC, it always bothers me when a company goes through the trouble of doing something but not doing it well. These are simple fixes that should have been zapped in the first round of GA, but here we are, ten months after the latest firmware update and it still says "Dolby TureHD" and "Transmission PT" instead of BT. The verbiage, tense, and capitalization is inconsistent, even within the same menu, and just lacks the togetherness that I was expecting. Scrolling through the main menu "drags" a portion of the background image along with it. When you format an internal hard drive, if you press a button during the operation it says "DON'T INTERRUPT". When it's done, it says "CONGRATULATION'. Congratulation. No serious device should celebrate doing the task that it's supposed to. My toaster doesn't throw confetti when it turns my bread a golden brown. It just sits there with a tri-colored circle made out of arrows spins around dumbly. No progress bar, no time estimate. Would someone please just give the user interface a once-over and fix all of the broken stuff?But ok, hey wordy internet reviewer guy, I don't care what all of that stuff says, I'll figure it out, I just want it to download stuff 24/7 and play me some phatty phatty 1080p videos. Once the hardware actually starts getting fed a stream of data, it's great. A certain 17.7GB mkv file of a certain 70's shark movie looks outstanding. Problem is, none of the navigation options seem to work. All of the sudden, all I can do is fast-forward 1.5 or 2x. Typing "30" into the remote no longer zips me ahead to the movie's 30% mark, and while pressing the forward/backward arrows moves the little slider across a little bar, indicating that it should let you skip ahead to a specific spot, it does nothing. It just kinda hangs there. Apparently there's a "goto" function that I didn't think to use, which I'll try when I get some time later, but I would expect that functions that aren't supported wouldn't even show up. Or maybe it should yell "DON'T INTERRUPT" at me again.10/18/2012 update: This problem seems local to this certain file. I have been able to skip around in other full 1080p movies with no problem.Whatever version of Transmission they have installed seems to get hung up quite often, forcing a reboot before I can access the web interface again. There's no way to update this other than to wait for the next firmware version... hopefully? SMB and FTP work nice, and there is a telnet server running by default, which gets you a BusyBox prompt. Unexpected, but a nice way to poke around and at least see what processed are running. Sometimes doing one thing (FTP) causes something else (BT) to slow down or pause. Also worth mentioning that whenever new files are added, they don't show up automatically. You have to "rescan" before they are ready to play. While I have the option checked for this to happen automatically, I still found myself having to press the green button to start this operation. Of course, you can't do anything else while it is scanning for new media, but you can press the stop button to stop it.Seriously, this thing looks really cool on the outside with its tiny shape, cool time display and sleek finish, but it's incredibly frustrating, and just ten minutes in, my wife said "I miss the popcorn hour". I'll give this another few days to see if it levels out or I can find a few tricks to make it behave better, but I made a point of pulling the box out of the recycling pile just in case it needs to go back. They made a device that works, but in between "working" and "not breaking" there's a lot of room to explore. This thing falls on its face far more often than I can deal with.10/18/2012 update: After changing a few of the options, the interface is a lot more tolerable. List view instead of big icons is a nice start, and the fact that it's sortable by all sorts of different fields is *very* nice.

review_title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
review_text: THE GOOD here, and there is good, is a well made bit of hardware with excellent sound, long battery life, compact size, etc. I didn't even mind Sony's digital rights management, designed to ensure you don't go into production of MD discs full of other people's music.THE BAD is that, while the device is fairly well optimized for ripping CDs, and at that, the DRM isn't a hinderance to anyone making copies for all their friend (as opposed to all of the East Coast). But it's huge hinderance for field recording, a perfectly legal pursuit. I can download YOUR music from CD at up to 32x over USB, or via optical TOSlink in realtime, but I can't upload MY recording digitally to a PC. Period. Only output is analog.THE UGLY is that you are intentionally deceived. None of the MD players support anything but ATRAC or ATRAC3 on-disc. The DRM software has to convert MP3 or WMA files to ATRAC/ATRAC3 for download, dropping in quality vs. pure MP3. The current version of their DRM doesn't support VBR MP3s, period, and seems to choke on most  ID tags. So even in transcoding, it's not MP3 compliant (VBR is a requirement of the MP3 spec, and supported on virtually any player you'll find). Your 5-hour playing time is only by way of LP4, which is 66Kb/s ATRAC3. Maybe not as cheesy and full of artifacts as WMA, but questionable for music.

review_title: NO SUPPORT - buy at your own peril
review_text: I had the external version of this (Hauppauge HD PVR 1212) for four years then it just died and stopped responding. It had served me well, so even though I was very annoyed that it just died, I came back to buy another and decided to try the Colossus, the new internal version. I popped it in, installed the drivers, and no sound. Since then I have tried everything, I reinstalled Windows from scratch thinking maybe my old drivers were causing a conflict, exchanged the card thinking maybe I just had a defective one, I've tried to contact their support, I've posted on their forums, I've posted on TheGreenButton forums. The reinstall didn't do anything except waste my time. Still no sound in WinTV, ArcSoft Showbiz, or Windows Media Center. This was through the Toslink connector which I had working fine for years with the 1212 so its not my hardware. I did try analog audio through the RCA connectors and that did work with ShowBiz but not with WinTV. And yes, I had the settings to all of these programs set to use the digital input when I had the Toslink plugged in, and the RCA connectors when I had those plugged in. Even if the RCA connectors worked, I don't want analog 2-channel audio, I want the 5.1 AC3 audio that I paid for.Anyways, the real reason to stay away from this card and Hauppauge in general is their complete lack of support. I submitted a ticket weeks ago when I bought the original Colossus and heard nothing back, so I exchanged for a new one. When I also couldn't get that one to work, I emailed them. Still heard nothing back. So a week later I emailed them again, told them they had 48 hours to respond or I was returning the card and they were losing a customer. Well it's been over 48 hours so I am returning the card because they obviously have no technical support. So purchase at your own peril, but my advice is to find an alternative and stay far far away from Hauppauge.
