review_title: A Bomb-Proof Mobile Charging Device that Packs a Punch
review_text: I've been using the NT120R for about a week and I've been able to put it through it's paces pretty well. Touting a waterproof rating up to 15 feet underwater, dust and dirt proof shell, and a ruggedized case this is the battery pack I've been waiting for. I spend a great deal of time outdoors camping, hunting, fishing, and working and so I need something I can throw in a pack and forget about it until I need it. The NT120R is just that device. It's light, compact, and rugged enough not to worry about when it's bouncing around in a pack or even the floor of your truck, plus it packs enough power to charge your phone or tablet enough to get you through a week's worth of work.The device it came in a very well thought out box with a cool seemingly magnetic flap behind which are some of the specs on the device. It comes with a white micro-USB cord but no wall adapter; a nice carabiner with a lanyard containing a compass; and a velcro strap with which you can keep the micro-USB cord wrapped up. Some nice extras that you don't typically see with most devices.The outside of the pack is very rugged plastic with a rubberized banding all around. The USB port compartment is accessible from a rubberized plastic flap that has a gasket on the back to prevent water fro seeping in when the device is not in use (the battery pack is not waterproof when you are charging your device(s). There are two USB charging ports which are labeled on the outside of the flap as 5V1A and 5V2.1A respectively. Charging two devices at one time works flawlessly and does not seem to slow down the charge time of either device however, it does drain the battery rather quickly (as you would expect).When I first received the NT120R the first thing I did was test the waterproofing. I placed the device in a bowl of water (with the USB compartment flap closed of course) where it could be submerged in water. The device sunk to the bottom of the bowl where I let it sit for a few minutes. After removing it from the water and drying the outside off I opened the USB compartment flap and there was some water in there but no water reached the USB ports (which is due to the design of the gasket and something that I expected). I then plugged my iPhone into the battery pack and it charged it up with no problems. This thing is awesome!!As I mentioned above, I'v only had this device for about a week but in that time I used it to charge my iPhone and iPad every time they needed to be charged. I charge y iPhone every day and my iPad about every other day and with that charging scheme The fully charged NT120R lasted for 3 iPhone charges and 2 iPad charges. This is actually better performance than I expected to get out of this device.In the end I am very impressed with this battery pack. It performs as well as they say in the description; if not better. Congratulations to NewTrent on another stellar product! If you have not heard of this company check out their website for other great products - [...]

review_title: From Apple Earbuds to Solo Beats hD
review_text: Firstly, I'm an average listener who listens to music every day from my iPhone ( currently 4S ) - I'm not an audiophile.First Impressions :First encounters with Beats were with the earbud versions from a friend maybe 2 years ago on the NYC subway, I was impressed with the sound. Second encounter was with this exact version 2 months ago from a different friend as well , also on the subway and I was also impressed. These are my first over head headphones. My major concerns was always carrying convenience. Ear buds are great  but hated in-ear earbuds ( for hygiene and hearing health reasons) so i was stuck because I didn't like big over head headphones. My eyes darted to the Solos because it seemed like a great size compared to the regular ones.I always felt Beats were overrated because these are so popular and I thought it was just a trend but aesthetically they're very well designed headphones so I couldn't deny that. Despite my thoughts , yesterday, months ( and years ) later I decided to treat myself.Sound:When I got home my first impressions with my own pair were some what disappointing. I was looking forward to more boom in the bass without any preset equalizers. It's likely that both my friend's had preset equalizers and I didn't know ( because I didn't ask ) . I don't hate my apple ear buds so It wasn't like I was complaining. However, I considered returning these  back to the apple store but I honestly didn't want to so did a head to head comparison to be fair to myself. From my iPhone 4S , with sound check off, EQ off and volume the same , I noticed the difference is the audio balance.  Immediately , I noticed the earbuds were louder but it definitely not as clear -- there was a lot more ' noise ' and there is more treble than bass. The Beats play at a lower volume but the audio is more balanced : bass , tremble , all of that. Also , of course because of the padding it blocks out exterior sounds and allows for more music to enter your ear.I went to my computer ( iMac early-2008 )  to do a slightly more technical test. It's important to consider bit-rates. With the Apple headphones, I was never able to properly hear distinct differences in the bit-rates unless it was comparing 64kbps ( and lower)  to 256kbps ( and higher) then the difference is obvious, but for the first time with Beats I was able to tell the difference between a much smaller range. If you unknowingly play a song in the 192-kbps (and below) with these from your iPhone/ iPod you may think the headphones are unclear or average but it's really outputting extremely close what the song is outputting. You can test for your self in iTunes, enable the bit-rate column and choose songs ranging in bit rates.I hope I gave an understanding of the kind of leap you're going to be taking if you buy these. I find myself enjoying my music a lot more than I did before. I'm sure I can enable a preset EQ when I'm ready but as of now, because the bass and treble are so balanced, I don't need to turn on any EQs. At this point, It will sound completely crazy to me to hear anyone ever compare apple earbuds to Beats and didn't notice the difference. I was content with the apple ones and I'm not an audiophile so I had to prove it to myself they were worth it.PortabilityI've always been concerned with how I'm going to carry these around. I usually carry a knapsack with me to work , gym , etc and these come with a carrying case so that makes protecting and carrying it it a little easier. If not, around my neck it will stay.The folding feature also makes it just that much more portable and easy to store away. I'm slightly scared to bring these in 'rough ' places, considering that I go in and out of NYC frequently. I wouldn't think about falling asleep with these on.ErgonomicsThe control for the iPhone / iPods work great. Easy to make deliberate choices for functions as you would on the original apple headphones, a much appreciated design. I've used other headphones with the control and they don't compare to this design , especially if it's round.I've been having a slight issue with ear fatigue after maybe 2 hours, especially on my left ear. Even with the apple earbuds, they were much loser in that ear...so Im not sure if my ear, or how i'm placing the earbuds and the beats. My only gripe with these is that it's LEFT handed ! The controls are on the left side of the headset.it's not a big deal at all but being use to the right handed earbuds, its something new but not a trade off at all.ExtraIt comes with a case as i mentioned before, an extra cable that does not include the control, and a microfiber cloth ( not sure how useful that's going to be).PriceI paid regular price cause I wanted these right away, amazon offers them for much less , which is great. If you're patient, (unlike myself ) then shop around.Overall, I'm happy with them, especially after doing some testing to actually see for myself. Design , great, portability , great for the class of headphones its in. 5 stars.

review_title: Good Surround Sound For The Money!
review_text: After reading all the reviews and comparing, I made my decision to get this Panasonic theater system.  Out of the box I was pleased.  It has an easy setup that took me about 40 minutes due to rearranging my room.  Speaker connection is super easy.  The guide isn't even needed.  Two wires, ones white, and the other has a blue stripe.  The back of the speakers have + and - that are colored blue and white.  Obviously white goes with white and Wht/blue goes with blue.  Now on to it's features.  The system comes with a total of 6 speaker units.  2 front, 2 rear, 1 center, and a sub.  It has a total of 7 ports. 1 HDMI, 1 Digital port, 2 USB ports(ones for the wireless lan connection and the other is ipod/music), internet cable port, AUX input, and an SD card reader.  Once started, I recommend that you change the equalizer setting to heavy.  I have my sound effects on digital tube 4 which give a powerful, but clear sound.  In the settings they have multiple sound effects to choose from.  Their description is in the guide booklet.  Choose which one suits you.  With that being said, the sound quality is pretty good after messing with the settings and effects.  The speakers are loud and clear, and the sub delivers powerful bass.  I have multiple settings on like whisper mode, which helps raise dialogue under low volume, and center focus which sends most of the sound towards the center speaker.  The bass is adjustable and it ranges from level 1-4. Also, don't forget to set the surround effects to Dolby Pro logic II.  I haven't tried the Blu Ray functionality on it yet so I have no comments to make on it.  The network service is pretty basic.  You have your apps like netflix, hulu, youtube, skype, and amazon instant video.  Navigation is a little on the slow side for the menu network screen.  My only complaint is the lack of a headphone port.  It is a pain to play music through my phone via usb connectivity as I have to back out every folder to look for new songs to play and it doesn't give me the control I want.  This was easily resolved for me, as I have the Earforce DSS box which allows me to connect it via digital output.  The music feature pretty much works better with an ipod as it has its own menu.  all in all this is a great system for the money.  The retail price is $299.99, but amazon like always has it for cheaper.  I am very pleased with the product.The Good: Easy setup, Ton of different sound effects to suit your needs, simple menu navigation, great sound.The Bad: No headphone jack.

review_text: This thing is awesome.  It is a little larger, so make sure you have a spot for it!  Also, make sure you know how sound waves work.  Imagine an ocean wave.  The top of the wave will be much more  powerful than the bottom!  This is the same for a sound wave.  Putting the subwoofer in a corner will reduce the amount of times you hit the "bottom of the wave."  Position it somewhere where you hear those deep frequencies right at your couch.  This thing gets very loud as well.  I have used it for music at parties and it pounds!  I recommend getting a good speaker set up with good woofers that have decently low frequency response.  Then you turn the frequency response on this subwoofer to pretty low so it's not interfering with the other speakers.  It does have an option to reverse your sound wave though.  Just in case you need to be out of phase with other speakers, or if you are unable to hit "the top of the wave" at your couch.Definitely worth it.  I love this thing, and it has lasted me years so far.  Don't hesitate if you're looking for an awesome addition to your home theater setup.

With the increased availability of GPS and computing technology at an ever lowering price, Escort has combined those technologies with their continued top-end radar / laser (LIDAR) detecting technology. The continued support and incorporation of the Safety Warning System was also a selling point for me. Pre-warning me of DOT construction, school and church zones, vision / hearing / mobility impaired zones, etc. gives me another warning of areas where caution in driving is required. I chose the Escort for it's ability to filter false signals and memorize them using it's 'AutoLearn' feature that ultimately disables the 'false positives' from alarming in the vehicle.With regard to the actual radar performance, I was surprised at how far away from the radar source you are when the Escort starts warning you .... in two cases on a flat, level, relatively open right-of-way, wide median State highway in Florida, I was warned of an active Ka band site at least a mile from the source. Once I got closer (within 1/4 mile) the Escort Ka warning was 'pegged' into a solid tone. I have not experienced any of the 'POP' radar (aka 'instant on') alerts or a laser alert yet, but it doesn't matter - if you're alone or not in traffic and receive one of those alerts and are speeding, you might as well consider it an alert to find a place to pull over and await the LEO to arrive. Nothing in this unit will prevent you from getting cited. It's a 'radar' detector, not a 'police' detector. :)I like the 'auto-mute' feature that lowers the volume of the detector alarm signal once an alert is registered - you don't have to hit the 'mute' button to silence it completely - I found that it drops to a still present but not obnoxiously loud alarm signal.Operations - easy. Turn it on and go. The default setting for sensitivity is 'Highway' which will give you maximum sensitivity but will cause a lot of alarms while driving around town. I went into the setup menu and selected 'Auto' which will automatically adjust sensitivity based on vehicle speed - you have to make sure the GPS feature has a signal to ensure you're vehicle speed can be monitored.The only 'issue' I have had so far was due to the users manual not being updated. In order to update the detectors database of redlight cameras and speed cameras, you have to use a usb cord that is NOT provided. I found this to be a shortcoming with a '$400+ detector' from a company that is famous for quality service and products. The other issue I had with this particular update process is that the manual (page 26) states that you have to update the unit with it powered on, and that you should take your laptop to the vehicle to do this. I thought 'really??' - how far do they think my apartment WiFi goes? I found that to be a ridiculous manner when most GPS units (Tom-Tom / Garmin) all have the ability to be powered on and updated from a computer in the home. I called Escort tech support and was told you can update it with a usb cord in the home. When I pointed out what the tech manual said, they said they were surprised about that since it was only the 'older' units that needed to be in the vehicle to update. Here's the 9500iX model (does the 'i' stand for 'internet'??) with an out of date manual. Again -for a $400+ detector, I would expect an updated users manual, especially when it deals with database and firmware updates! So instead of a $4 usb cable, they provide everything packaged in a very nice lined box that will never see the light of day once you have this in your vehicle. Marketing and Communications needs to update their priorities. If this is the 'Cadillac' of detectors, provide an up to date manual and a cord to update the unit easily. I would suffer with a less expensive box that looks more like a presentation gift box.Ability to use the unit is simple in the 'auto' mode once you have everything set the way you want. It's 'hands off' once set and sitting in the vehicle. I'm using the included coiled 'Smart Cord' but may move to the optional wiring system to hardwire the unit to the power source and free up an accessory plug. The provided coiled power cord is long enough to go from my accessory power units in the truck (low - just above the center console) all the way to the detector unit positioned at the bottom of the windshield - over the deep dash - lots of distance from the power plug to the unit and it's fine - taught, but not overly and not 'loosely' hanging.Overall, it gets a '4' star rating due to lack of provided usb cord and errors in the users manual that required a phone call to tech support. Operationally, it gets a good review because it's been working fine for me so far. I'm glad I got it, I've had it a week but driven over 300 miles with it already on the full range of roads to expose it to all radar sources. It's picked them all up and either discounted them, stored them as 'false positives', or alerted me to real and viable radar sources. I'd recommend it to others but would caution them to get the required usb update cord first and understand that they do NOT need to have it in their vehicle with a laptop to conduct updates.

I purchased a second Ziotek adapter as I anticipate a friend will soon want an upgrade to his PC and I will be faced with a similar situation when I do that work.

review_title: A worthy successor to the original Fire
review_text: I was an early adopter of the original Kindle Fire in November 2011. I loved the Fire, but it was a bit clunky in some tasks, and it sadly lacked some desirable hardware features. I'm happy to say that I've had my Kindle Fire HD for a few hours, and my initial impressions are very positive. Clearly, Amazon listened to customers and addressed many of their comments. For starters:1. There's an external volume control. This was my single biggest gripe with the original Fire.2. There's a built-in microphone. That means you can Skype and use cool apps like Soundhound and Shazam. With the front-facing camera, you can do video Skyping, which is a big plus. The lack of a microphone or mic input was my second biggest gripe with the original Fire.3. An HDMI port means you can connect your Fire HD directly to most TV sets. I have a Roku, so that's not as big of a deal to me, but the HDMI puts the Fire HD out in front of almost every other tablet. I definitely want to try streaming Amazon instant video to a hotel TV the next time I travel.4. The video is noticeably crisper for videos.5. Bluetooth is a great new feature. It opens the possibility of wirelessly connecting the Fire HD to a myriad of products. I've been using a small, portable Bluetooth speaker to amplify my original Fire's sound. That works, but only with a cable connecting the Fire and the speaker. With the Fire HD, it only took a minute to activate the Bluetooth, find the speaker, and pair it with the Fire HD.6. The sound quality is very noticeably better. So far I haven't encountered an MP3 or video where I had to strain to hear, and oftentimes I'm having to back down on the volume.7. The web browser appears to be a little faster, although I won't really know how much faster until I upgrade my wireless router to a newer, dual band model. The wi-fi reception is quite good. When I connected the HD to our home network, the HD detected ten other networks in near-by houses, which is more than our laptop PC can detect.8. In the original Fire, using the graphic handles to select text was awkward and not always very responsive, especially with text in emails. The HD appears to have improved considerably the ease of selecting text.9. Unlike the original Fire, the memory is not partitioned, so it appears you can use all the user-available memory (12.63 GB) for anything - books, video, music, photos, etc. This is a big improvement.10. The virtual keyboard has been restored to something closer to the original Fire. Once again, there are separate periods and commas, so you don't have to hold down the period to type a comma. This was a real improvement.11. Text-to-Speech for books has returned to the HD. There aren't any settings - the voice is either on or off, and there's only a female voice - but it sounds more like a human voice and less like a computer than before.The HD was delivered already registered to me, so about all I had to do was connect with my wi-fi, set up my Gmail account (less than one minute) and set my favorites for the web browser, then download some of my books, magazines, videos, and apps from the Cloud. With 8GB of memory in the original Fire, I often had to delete apps before downloading any new apps. With 16GB in the Fire HD, that's much less critical.Because the size is different and the controls and ports have been moved around, cases for the original Kindle Fire won't work. The padded envelope sleeve that I had for the original Kindle Fire does work, although it's not a perfect fit.One annoyance: the Kindle Fire HD displays color advertisements on its lock screen, so every time you turn on the HD, you see advertisements for a Kindle e-book, a video, Amazon MP3 music, and such. Amazon has announced that owners can opt-out of the ads for $15. After using the HD for a few days, if the ads are too annoying, I may opt-out. Update: Apparently only the rotating lock screen ads can be removed by opting out. The targeted "suggestions" that show up when you're in the Amazon Store won't go away, so I don't know if it's worth $15 to opt-out. You'll have to decide that. You can do this at any time from your "Manage My Kindle" page.Invariably, the Kindle Fire HD is going to be compared to the Nexus 7, its closest competition in size, performance, and price. The HD weighs 13.9 oz. vs. 12 oz. for the Nexus (the original Fire weighed 14.6 oz.). That weight difference is at least partially offset by longer claimed battery life: 11 hours for the HD vs. 8 hours for the Nexus. Screen resolution is 1280x800 for both tablets (the original Fire's resolution was 1024x600). Most of the new features of the HD, like the front-facing camera and the microphone, are common to both tablets, but the HDMI port on the HD is a very nice feature that the Nexus can't match. I've used a Nexus 7, and it's a wonderful tablet, but based on my initial impressions, my slight favorite is the Kindle Fire HD, mainly for its ability to stream Amazon instant videos (which the Nexus can't, at least not without some finagling).Overall, the HD appears to be a worthy successor to the original Kindle Fire.-------------------------------------------Update (September 15, 2012):* At first, the layout of the various screens is somewhat different from the original Fire, but after playing around for a while, I'm getting used to it, and learning how everything works is pretty intuitive.* I'm reading on forums that some folks are having problems running some of the apps they had on the original Kindle Fire. For example, I'm having problems with MapQuest - it starts up, but crashes within a minute or so. It's probably just some glitches that will be fixed with the first OS upgrade.* The power button and volume control switch are flush with the case. It's not a big deal, but I wish they stuck out a millimeter or so to make it easier to feel them.* The original Fire was noticeably rectangular, so I used it mostly in the portrait position. The HD is more square, and it seems more natural to use it in the landscape position.

review_title: Decent widescreen monitor but not ideal
review_text: I'm very picky about my computer displays, having owned many CRT and LCD monitors which I spend way too many hours in front of.  Unfortunately, LCD monitor reviews seem to invariably consist of either people who just got their first LCD, or those explaining basic LCD technology.  What I usually want to know is if it's a good LCD compared to OTHER comparable models.  So I'll keep this short and focused solely on that topic.I found the 225BW crisp, clear, and functional, with a couple of dead pixels.  However, there is considerable backlight bleed-through at the top and bottom of the display.  This is most visible when the screen is displaying solid black; I can usually ignore it during normal use, but it would be distracting while watching a DVD.The narrow bevel means this monitor takes a minimal amount of space.  Controls are easy to reach and non-obtrusive.The viewing angle from left-to-right is good, but top-to-bottom is another story.  The display doesn't appear entirely crisp at most angles,  the crispest view is in a very narrow viewing angle.I have my 225BW sitting next to the newerSamsung 226BW 22-Inch Digital/Analog Widescreen LCD Monitor (Black).  By comparison, the 226BW has a much broader top-to-bottom viewing angle, although it also looks fuzzy if you stand in front of the LCD at desk-height and look down at the display.  The 226BW is much brighter and cleaner looking, without much backlight bleed-through.  However, the 226BW doesn't have an adjustable neck, and surrounding bevel is much thicker, making the whole monitor larger.  The 226BW's bright blue power light  may also be a distraction during DVD viewing.The 225BW works well and is relatively cheap for 22" brand-name displays, so I still give this LCD 4 stars and recommend it for its price, Samsung reliability, and adjustable neck.  But the backlight bleed-through and relatively poor contrast ratio suggest the newerSamsung 226BW 22-Inch Digital/Analog Widescreen LCD Monitor (Black)as an alternative if you don't need the adjustable neck.

review_title: For the Price, My New Favorite
review_text: The advent of the uber-easy-to-use Canon 600 flashes with built-in wireless, this Wescott is the perfect match for beautiful diffused light anywhere you need it. The clamp has a good amount of adjustable range up-and-down and in-and-out to pretty much accommodate any hot shoe flash. Third, it includes a carrying case which is great. Last and MOST important is the light: when you add the small beauty dish wish throws the light back onto the "umbrella", and then it passes through the removable diffusion cover, you're getting some nicely diffused modified light. As a fill for an outdoor portrait or even as a main light outside to achieve a darkened background, the size and portability make this a great setup. For outdoor portraits you often need the light source really close if you're not using $3000 ProPhoto packs with 1200 watt light. Because this Wescott is 26" and very portable, your assistant can lean the softbox JUST off frame and get it real close which will get you enough power for all but the brightest of sunny days (and that's a challenge here in Phoenix, lol!). Great unit, definitely buying a second one.

review_title: Should be reliable, good choice for home backup power for pc's and related equipment
review_text: I've been buying APCC back up systems for home use for many years.  An older ES350 with a battery barely over a year old died and instead of buying a new battery I spent a tiny bit more and bought a new, bigger UPS.  I've gotten this model before but this one looks different, and finally, after decades of having telephone RJ11/RJ14 plugs for surge suppression, it now takes ethernet cables.  Just where APCC needed to be - 20 years ago.  Except that according to the manual these are for 10-100 mbps ethernet.  Unfortunately, those are a long since obsolete ethernet standard.Another issue the batter cables are so short they are very hard to connect.  You connect them, start to put the battery in, and they pop back off.  Also, there is no clear way to tell what is going on with the UPS.  A coule LED's hopefully tell you whether the unit is working.  And the alarm can't be shut off without a computer to do it from.  The unit did not come with a cd for the monitoring software.  Hopefully that's not a problem since one should be able to download the software from the apcc site, where a new version shows up once every several years.  The software works but is badly inadequate in terms of telling you what has been going on with your line current in detail.BTW, this unit has a different purpose; to maintain power for a cable modem and a router.  Which means I've no way to see how the unit is holding up.  My feeling is at this price range a small LCD should be included with status info.  Keeping in mind that small LCD based calculators are available for under $1, this should not be an issue, except that APCC products - while they tend to work well, are decades behind in their abilities.  Not enough outlets, especially for bricks, and no APCC product optimized for this type of use - cable modems, routers, etc. that use low power and lots of powered outlets and a good display.Still, if you need backup power at home, this is a good choice.

review_title: Proof that more expensive doesn't equal better quality.
review_text: I bought these on a whim.  I'd been using a set of Sennheiser MX500's, earphones that are a fraction of the price of the Sony's.  I figured I'd try something new.In terms of comfort, the Sony's are better, and that's the only reason these things get a 2-star rating.  They are very comfortable to wear (they even come with different sized earpieces so you can choose the most comfortable ones).  They also eliminate outside noise almost completely, way better than the Sennheisers do.In terms of design, the Sony's are awful.  Due to the design, the weight is not distributed equally.  The cable coming from the right earbud is 3x as long as the cable coming from the left earbud.  One ear gets pulled on more than the other.  The cable is ridiculously too short--fine for if your music player is in your shirt pocket, but inadequate if you want to carry it in your hand or in a pants pocket.  They give an extension cable with the unit, but it's far too LONG.  If I attach the cable and put the buds in my ear, the cable almost reaches the floor (and I'm six feet tall).  Poor, poor design.Finally and most importantly, in terms of sound quality, the Sony's don't hold a candle to the Sennheisers.  Very tinny and shrill sounding.  They hurt my ears even at low volume.  They sound like a cheap set of phones.Save some cash--if you're looking for a good pair of earbuds at a good price, skip the Sony's and get the Sennheisers (which Amazon sells by the way).

I am a layperson when it comes to photography. I take pictures of my family around the house and on vacation. I tend to stick with the modes that automatically adjust color settings, exposure, white balance, etc. because I am usually satisfied with the picture quality. I tell you this so you can gauge the utility of my review accordingly.This camera is not a pocket camera. It houses a substantial 26x optical zoom. The "H" in H200 indicates it is a high zoom model from Sony. The trade-off for the size is the zoom capability and it features Optical "steady shot" to correct for unintentional movement so you can shoot a decent photo while moving a bit. The size also accords better handling - I love the way the camera feels in my hands. I am right -handed so the protrusion with the shutter button on the right side of the camera, and its subtle, finger grooves in front, offer a nice feel and grip. With two hands it is easy to steady the camera, and it is also easy to zoom and shoot with one hand, especially if you are right handed.You can only frame your shots via the 3-inch, high resolution LCD view screen on the back of the camera. There is no small viewfinder for you to look through with your eye. The screen is huge and bright and easy to see even in daylight.  There is no case so you'll need to pick one up if you don't already have an extra.I would carefully consider how you expect to use your camera before you buy this or any camera. My usual preference is a small camera with a built-in rechargeable battery because I like to keep it in my shirt pocket or on my belt in a small case for easy access and carrying convenience. (I use the Sony DSC-WX150 for this purpose). If you likewise want a small point and shoot then this is not the camera for you unless you don't mind carrying it in a carry case or from around your neck. If you don't mind the larger size, and expect you will be photographing distant subjects (kids in sports, animals on vacation, etc.) that will really benefit from the super zoom, then this camera is a good choice.Keep in mind this camera uses AA batteries rather than a built-in battery. To me, this has pros and cons. The pros include easy access to additional batteries on vacation wherever you are. The cons include the increased size of the camera to accommodate the batteries, and the need to carry extra batteries in your bag in case your charge dies while you are out shooting pictures. You also have the extra expense of purchasing batteries for the life of the camera unless you purchase rechargeable AA batteries.  But, when travelling, you won't need to bring a charger or voltage adapter, nor worry about keeping the battery charged as long as you have access to AA batteries.Intelligent auto shooting mode chooses a scene mode based on what the camera detects in your scene. I love this mode - you just point and shoot and the camera determines the optimal settings. Within this mode you can add a secondary level that, when it senses a certain type of scene (low light, etc.) it will take two pictures with slightly different settings. You can then decide which one you like the best. Nice.Program mode is also automatic, but offers some setting controls that you can research with the built in help guide.  There is also a full manual mode if you really want to do your own settings. There is also a Scene Mode where you can select the best preset mode based on your settings: Soft Skin (which enhances skin), Soft Snap, Landscape, Night Portrait, Night Scene, High Sensitivity, Gourmet, Pet, Beach, Snow and Fireworks. There is also a Panorama Mode which allows you to pan the camera while you move in a 360 degree circle and it stitches the images together for you. I used this quite a bit on vacation and the stitching is flawless. You can choose the direction of movement (left or right), whether to use standard mode or wide mode, and the degree of the panoramic sweep. Again, very nice.The camera can shoot video at 720p HD.  The video quality you can get from the camera is pretty amazing. Keep in mind video takes up a ton of space, so you will need a class 10 SD card or higher speed Memory Stick Pro Duo card. I like the class 10 SD cards sold here on Amazon. I would get at least a 16GB card (preferably a few of them) to make sure you don't run out of space on vacation while shooting movies and pictures.  There is a small, not terribly powerful flash. If I was shooting indoors and didn't need the zoom of this camera, I would just use my smaller Sony.This is a nice, affordable camera that produces high quality images and movies. It has the look and feel of a DSLR but without the attendant price tag. I took a ton of pictures with this camera on vacation and was very impressed with the image quality. I'll upload some samples for viewing up above. The noise level, even on super zoom pics, was not noticeable to my untrained eye. I also really like the built in help guide. You simply press the question mark button on the back of the camera and a very intuitive guide shows you the answer to whatever you need to know about operating the camera. With a ton of features and options (including an easy mode that makes picture taking idiot-proof), you can be as involved or uninvolved in the camera settings as you like. I used the automatic modes while learning about all the other features as I went along and was quite pleased with the results.While the size is still a bit large to me, all around me on vacation were people with much larger cameras (DSLR cameras) or sadly, just their smart phones. I intend on bringing both this and my smaller Sony with me on vacation, and will take whichever one best meets the needs of that day.You can't really go wrong with this high-zoom camera at this price.

I have the ER4P for a month now and have written a review on it but decided to delete the review because my original review gave the ER4P a five star but now decided that its really a 4 star.  Please note that I subtracted a star because of comfort and extra accessories requirements.Pro:1) Price. I payed $164 for the ER4P and I believe that you'll have a hard time finding another headphone that can deliver the same clarity for that price.2) Sounds as good as your source.  I frequently find myself plugging the ER4P in my home theater system because I notice that the portable cd player I have does not have a clean sound as I thought it had and the ER4P revealed that!3) Real to life sounds.  When I first got this I tried my best to see if I can detect coloration or fakeness in the sounds of the instruments coming out of the ER4P and I can't.  The ER4P is very accurate in my own opinion.4)  Low volume listening is possible because of noise isolation.  Plus, other people can't hear your music because the ER4P is in your ears.5)  Portability.Cons:1) The foam plugs are the ones that are the most comfortable to me and they need to be replace because they will lose their resiliency.  You would also need to replace the filters on the ER4P.  These items you have to replace are inexpensive but can be a hassle after awhile.2) These are basically earplugs with a very good transducer in them so all the hassle and discomfort you associate with foam or triple flange earplugs will be present in the ER4P.3) Micro phonics on the cords.In conclusion, The ER4P is a good buy and if they ever get lost or breaks I'm sure I'll be shopping right away for another set of high quality earphones in the $150 to $199 dollar range.

My other bag which is a back-pack design I now primarily use for times that require long hikes.  Comparing the two design, I feel this Caselogic bag offers easier access.  Whereas the back-pack provides better weight-distribution when carried on both shoulders.My only caution for interested buyers is to be careful when selecting between the Case Logic SLRC 202 and 203 for proper size. The latter, which is the content of this review, is in my opinion much more spacious after trying both on for size.  I actually ordered the 202 (medium) bag first and found the main compartment interior a little snug for my D90 with kit lens and after-market thick strap, while the side pockets too tight for mid or larger sized lenses.  For reference, I have a Tokina 11-16 ultrawide and it does NOT fit in the side pockets when the camera is also housed in the main (on the 202).  On the other hand, the 203 side pockets are deep & wide and the zippers go all the way down front to back (NoDrop tm), giving great access. The larger bag looks barely bigger than the medium one and yet it still weighs nothing.  When loaded with the camera, a flash and 3 lenses, it feels supremely capable for the job.  I have not done any measuring, but I doubt a nikon or canon 70-200 2.8 will fit in the side pockets or the main when connected to the body.  Finally 203 can carry a tripod.A strong yet light bag.  Highly recommend.--------------It's now Oct 2010 the bag is in great condition - like new.  I use it all the time and now occasionally attach a tripod/monopod to it.  Solid bag.

review_text: I have been wanting a macro lens, but the price of a real macro at 200mm is alot. I decided to try extention tubes before I took the leap to a real macro lens. review_title: Addictive but be aware of the work you will create using the clips!
review_text: This isn't a review of the features and performance of the camera. I am not an expert at comparing it to others. This is a review of what you can do with the files that you create.I got this camera and the 16gb memory duo card. So far so good. It stores between 2 and 5 times the life of a single battery in video.. hours and hours unless you pick the highest bit rate.The challenges come after you get your files home.1. Sony VegasProbably this is the best solution for workflow from this camera, but it is windows only. Moving right along ..2. PS3Happily you can either insert the card into your PS3 (or into a multi-card reader via USB - a recent one, not an old one, as high capacity memory sticks can't be read by older multi-card readers). The PS3 sees the clips, shows moving previews, and they look fantastic. You can also put them on a media server (such as MediaTomb mac/linux) and connect to it from the PS3. Not quite as nice, as the thumbnails lack preview, but workable.3. Connecting the camera to your Mac via the included dockThis works fine and I'll sub-divide what you can do at this point:3a. Using Final Cut Express (or Final Cut Pro).Neither of these programs will deal directly with the MTS files (which are AVCHD and 5.1 ac3) without the full directory structure of the card present! so don't copy the MTS files off, and delete them if you want to use FCE! At any rate, use FCE to import the clips, they are decompressed and blown up to an apple format that uses heaps more space! you can't edit natively in AVCHD using FCE. It isn't clear to me that you can even edit natively in FC Pro. Note, FCE down-mixes to 2 channel stereo during import!3b. Not using Final Cut Express - using other tools (linux users read this too)You can't play these MTS files reliably using Quicktime or Quicktime Pro despite the claim that quicktime pro can play h264 video. You can't even use the Perian codecs (which are available free and based on the open source libraries used by ffmpeg). They claim h264 compatibility but unfortunately they do not read the sony h264 stream properly. You may see various problems: missed frames, half speed, crashing or lots of errors. It may be that a SD camera setting on this camera is more reliably usable, I got bored trying so many different things. This also means you can't use ffmpeg or mencoder under linux, despite their flexibility. The latest version as of time of this review just does not deal with all your clips. It might deal with some, reading and re-encoding if necessary to mpeg4 or whatever, but you WILL get frustrated. The same problems apply to mplayer, vlc, MPEG Streamclip, and so on, as they also depend on the same libraries.Note: xportdev will demux MTS files and TMPGenc will decode the video correctly, you CAN use these two tools to create mpeg4 or whatever.see [...] this forum for more info.3c. Not using Final Cut Express - using VoltaicHDVoltaicHD will convert the clips properly but there are no options to speak of. It creates much larger mov files that can be used in typical mac utilities, quicktime, etc.3d. Using Toast TitaniumI believe this produce accepts AVCHD files. I haven't tested it, obviously you have to buy the product. It appears to be capable of writing DVDs or even bluray discs after the edit is done.4. Uploading to vimeo (the HD version of youtube)Vimeo does not accept MTS files, it tries to accept h264 video if packaged in an avi or whatever, but will not process them correctly. It accepts mpeg4, or re-encoded h264 as output by mencoder. It probably also accepts mov files from VoltaicHD and obviously you can get FCE to output a file that vimeo will take.The problem I have with this is the chain of encoding and decoding:image --> camera --> encoded to avchd --> decoded in voltaicHD or FCE --> re-encoded to mpeg4 or whatever --> uploaded to vimeo --> decoded --> re-encoded to their On2 codec --> played by flash.As you can see this chain is ridiculous and the result will not look as good as the ideal, which is:image --> camera --> encoded to avchd --> playedMy conclusion is that your frustration level will vary according to what you want out of your clips. The camera offers very limited editing: you can chop a clip into two and delete any clip, so you can basically throw away bits you won't want to waste time on.If you want to show them off on your HDTV via the PS3, without mixing them into a "movie" then everything is great. They look really good.. the interlacing is really not visible when the PS3 plays them, resolution is outstanding at least depending on how high a bit rate you pick.If you want to burn DVDs then I expect Toast Titanium or FCE will be reasonable but there is some quality loss from the inevitable decode - reencode cycle.If you want them on the web at vimeo, although the result is heaps better than youtube, it certainly isn't high definition. I believe the vimeo bit rate is limited to 2000 kbit, for example.

I have a 30gb ipod I like to watch video on at work. Video burns the battery up very quickly so the booster is a big help. As for space, this unit is very small - easy to fit in a purse or pocket with no worries. I like the idea of having one piece of plastic serve two purposes; flash drive and battery pack.I have another battery booster that works for ipod or any device that connects to usb. It's huge. It was a big help on an extended bus ride to visit relatives during the great gas panic of 2008. I did not like dragging the thing around. It took up twice as much space as my ipod and was clumsy to use. This is small and elegant. I also like that its small footprint makes it easier to recycle. I hate having a dozen bits of plastic that serve one purpose when they could all be easily be combined.What would make this better is if you could get the files off the flash drive without having to plug both units into a computer. I don't count this as a failure of the device. That's a functionality issue specific to Apple. However, IF this unit were also made for Sansa, or any unit that enables you to drag and drop files independent of software, it would really help with portability. Like if you could go to one computer, get what you need then boost it up to your device where there is more storage. Flash drives are great for documents because you can plug them directly into printers. They are also great for media, like movies and music, because most modern televisions and dvd players have usb connectors. Depending on your player or TV, different codecs and compressions are easily rendered without first having to re-encode and burn to disk media. This saves space and eliminates the need for yet more plastic.I would like to see more flexibility in this area, which would make multifunction devices like the Powerlink more relevant. One of the great joys of having a mass storage device is that you can keep a library of stuff all in one place where you can use it whenever you want. This appeals to my sense of conservation. So good effort, Powerlink. We'll just have to wait until device manufacturers catch up with you.

review_title: This thing has a bad rap. I love mine.

Fits like a glove now, and not a baseball glove. The P7000 is a BIG point and shoot camera. It's not a DSLR and it's not a pocket camera. Same goes for this case. It's styled like a point and shoot case. I personally love the magnetic closure, which most reviewers despise. I don't have to bother unsnapping something or fiddling with a trigger latch or pulling a strip of velcro that gets the subject's attention. Instead, I just tear the camera from the case by pulling the the neck strap and dropping the featherweight case to the ground. It's kind of like having a gun in a holster, always ready to quick draw and shoot. I understand everyone's complaints, and they are entirely valid. But there are certain circumstances in which these shortcomings can be advantages, too. It now fits my camera very well, gives a reasonable measure of protection, and doesn't get in the way when I'm ready to shoot. I don't leave many reviews but I thought I'd live a devil's advocate review on this one. Hope somebody finds it helpful.

The audio sounds crystal clear with no cracks or clipping when set around volume level 25 (which is now my favorite volume level for this unit).My iPhone Models & Compatibility.I am using an old retired iPhone to keep plugged into this unit (a 3GS) I had recently upgrade to a 4S  and was looking for something useful to do with that old unit anyhow. I filled it up with all music like a glorified ipod touch and now I am going to use this as my alarm clock music player too. (Side Note: This dock also charges the 4S without a problem, I tested that too) Please note...both of my iPhone's charged and playled audio flawlessly with no glitches or errors at all on my phones.Docking Port Info:The dock at the top of the unit has a little flip open bay that can hide the dock connector when not in use. review_title: Really great product with a horrible (but fixable) flaw
review_text: Given the new trend for Macs being not upgrade friendly for storage (see iMac), this is a really great option to have.[Good]Speed: Thunderbolt does make a huge difference in this department. It feels like this drive is an internal drive, speed wise.  I can only imagine what this product line's future will be like once SSDs go down in price.Security: I now also don't care as much when I bring in to get my machines repaired for whatever reason. All of my sensitive files will be on this drive instead of on the computer itself.Upgradable: To me given the price of thunderbolt, this is the most innovative part of this product. You can separate the hard drive from the thunderbolt adapter. Theoretically you can buy larger drive sizes in the future and just use the same adapter. I don't know if other thunderbolt drives have this, but in my mind this is the feature that makes me remember this product.Portable: It's the smaller drive, but you can bring it to the office.Daisy Chaining: You can keep adding Thunderbolt devices. (I didn't try this feature.)[Bad]Price: Of course for all this great tech, there's a price. It's approximately double the price of a traditional USB external drive with the same size. This is understandable given the technology.Size: It's about twice as big as a comparable USB external drive. In my opinion, I don't really see this as a big deal. Most people use bags for work anyways.Pre-loaded Crapware: The bloatware included with this drive is really horrible. Every time I even tried looking at the new drive through Finder, my Mac would crash and reboot (iMac 16 GB, Mountain Lion with the latest updates). There's really no excuse for this on the Mac platform given that there's not a lot of hardware variety and even less software variety. Did anyone at Seagate test it on more than one Mac? My guess is their program would try loading when I started to browse the drive, and for some reason it would cause a kernal panic in  Mountain Lion and make it reboot. This definitely fails the non-techie Mom / Dad test. If I wasn't technical, I would probably rate this product way below 4 stars given that it causes your Mac to reboot.As a techie, the solution to this problem is really simple: reformat the drive with Disk Utility (included with OSX). After that quick fix this product is just awesome. I would have probably given this 5 stars, if it didn't have the crapware. Seagate if you're reading this, there's a really easy fix for any new drives being manufactured ;)Even if this software worked no one needs it. Macs already have a backup program and non-techies don't need something new to learn.[Verdict]If you're a techie, I highly recommend this product. It is worth the extra money. If you're buying this for a normal person, you're going to have to do some cleanup for them but it's still worth it if they're running out of room on their default config iMac.If you're a normal person and you don't have access to a techie, I would wait until Seagate fixes things; unless you don't mind using a simple utility that's included on your Mac (Disk Utility).

review_title: A great design a decade ago, and still great
review_text: The original PSone dualshock controller was practically revolutionary when it was first introduced. The series, 1, 2 and 3, have never offered anything particularly new or unique, but they've all managed to package great functionality into a good package, and the DualShock 3 continues the delightful trend.The good? Same familiar feel and layout that most everyone can hold comfortably, same pressure sensitive (analog input) buttons across the board, same rumble package. New here are separated L2 and R2 trigger buttons that easily allow for progressive input, which I find especially great in racing games. Wireless connection is via Bluetooth, with a rechargeable onboard battery. Sony added it's in-house 'SIXAXIS' controls, which is something of a cousin to a Wii controller. The battery life is quite surprisingly good, giving me at least 12 hours of any game with full and frequent rumble. It's also nearly indestructible and refuses to die-- I've bought additional units, but my original that was packaged in with the PS3 well over 2 years ago is still 100% reliable and functional.More on the 'SIXAXIS' feature... it's not particularly meant to track movement (this is the territory of the Playstation Move add-on), but rather to be used as a floating motion sensor. Few games support it, but those that do (Heavy Rain does it very well) include down or upward snaps as actions, a tilting camera view based on your tilting, and generally natural-feeling motions that would otherwise be done with the hand such as opening a sliding door, twisting a key in a lock, etc. ...Honestly, it's hit-or-miss and doesn't really add much value to the device, but since you're not particularly paying any extra for it, there's no harm in it being available.The bad? Ergonomics could use an upgrade, to be honest. For particular hand sizes/shapes extended use will give stiff fingers, and any kind of extended use with a very firm hold (in my case, running into this while concentrating my hardest to push in the racers Gran Tourismo and F1 2010) may well end in some pain on finger bones. This "should" lower my review score, but I freely confess this is my own problem that I could correct by better controlling my grip or taking more small breaks. 95%+ of users will never run into this, and it is preventable. I can't fault Sony for not making the device comfortable to play with for an indefinite length of continuous play!More than anything, I'm shocked how incredibly light the thing is and feels almost weightless when held firmly. I have no clue how Sony managed to pack in all it offers, especially the battery life. The bluetooth connection means third party controllers will probably never happen (or be any less expensive), but thankfully Sony doesn't leave the window open for anyone else to ever offer additional features or alternate designs that would work any better. It's rare that your only choice isn't at all painful to be stuck with. Thumbs up all around.

After a bit of research online reading reviews and watching some tech videos on another site I thought the 812dru would be a great upgrade for my home wireless network with the idea of "future-proofing" my network for what I thought would be some years.  As a lot of the other reviews have mentioned it is a very easy setup especially if you've worked with any routers in the past and have had to set up any specialized applications or administrative functions within the router's menus. It's not a WRT setup but still has lots of options and way more than I would really need in my simple home wifi network.  My home printer hooked up easily and was on the network with no issues either (using Ethernet cable) and my wife's ipad hooked up without a hitch.Then the trouble began....  Within the first day of operation we kept experiencing lost internet connections.  We always had full bars showing on the windows wifi connection but the "server cannot be found" web page kept reappearing.  This would happen at random times, but mostly about 3-5 minutes after logging on to the internet for the first time of the day.  This went on for a couple of days and thinking that I had done something wrong in my setup I finally contacted customer support using one of the links provided by trendnet customer support following one of the not-so-good reviews another customer had written on this product page.  I had a response the same day, which was really shocking to me but they described how negative reviews can impact their brand and they really tried to address all customer complaints as quickly as possible. Working with Steve (an actual tendnet engineer) we went back and forth trying different setups and scenario's for about two weeks, which was driving my wife crazy cause she kept losing her internet connection, and finally came to the conclusion that it must be a faulty piece of equipment.  So instead of sending it back through the retailer I had it sent directly to trendnet and had a new one cross shipped to me (of course they charge your credit card for this and this is my only gripe because it took them over a month to send my refund back).  Upon receiving the new router, the setup was again easy, (and I will say that when this thing worked it was quick, quick, quick, very fast) and was up and running in a matter of minutes. For the next couple of hours there was not problems, I thought that maybe it was just a bad unit, until....  the dreaded "server cannot be found" pages started appearing again.  Meantime, the original one I sent in for troubleshooting was having no problems whatsoever at their test facilities which made my situation a bit of a conundrum.  Upon more troubleshooting at home, using my old dir601 and connecting the 812dru to one of the Ethernet jacks and visa-verse, it seemed to work perfectly when it was plugged into the dir601 but not when the trendnet router was hooked up directly to the internet.  Very strange indeed. The trendnet engineer was talking about "pipes" being broken and the such, which I have no clue on, but the basic conclusion was that this router was incompatible with my Isp.  Being that my Isp is timewarnercable  i wondered how many others were being effected this way so i kept checking back to the product forums to see what people were experiencing  with this router.  It does look like more people were having this type of problem but never went to the lengths that I did to try to figure out the issues.  My takeaway from all this is, I learned a heck of a lot more about routers than I did previously and I wouldn't think twice about buying another product from trendnet because of the level of customer service i got from them in trying to troubleshoot this equipment.  In the end I did return the second router to them and will wait till they get all the issues ironed out before I try to upgrade again.  And I will look at trendnet first before other brands when I do try it again. Thanks again for all your help Trendnet.

review_title: Great looking case design, lousy implementation...
review_text: The Netgear SC101 Storage Central device holds a lot of promise and offers a nice looking case design. In fact, I referred to mine as a "network toaster" since that is kind of what it looked like.Unfortunately, "beauty is only skin deep" when it comes to this unit.Netgear did get some things right--the ability to buy just the enclosure and add your own hard disks is great. Anyone who has worked on computers for some time will undoubtedly have some perfectly serviceable hard drives sitting around. This unit gives you the ability to put at least some of those drives to use.Installation and use of the device--when it works, which it doesn't always do--are both easy and definitely geared to new and inexperienced computer users who just want something that works.What Netgear missed with this device, however, is the ability for more advanced users (or people who have multiple computers with different operating systems) to take this device further. It offers no web based interface and no file sharing protocols outside of the proprietary software (for Windows 2000/XP only). This is a serious flaw to an otherwise great idea.The hard drives are also loose inside the device when you install them. There's nothing to hold them in place or keep them stable other than some blocks of foam. I could see this leading to electrical shorting from the circuit board on the drive to the case and even serious disk damage in the event that this unit would fall. The interior of the case is also quite sharp, so watch out not to cut or slice yourself while installing drives (or taking it apart to see what's inside).All things and limitations considered, I returned mine after five minutes of using it. It's just too limited for the power user, hobbyist or tinkerer. If you pay full retail price (~$100), it's also quite pricey for such a limited piece of hardware. If Netgear were to come out with a more powerful version that offered true network attached storage functionality, I'd certainly give serious thought to buying it. As it is right now, the product was an expensive disappointment to me.

review_title: Love the keyboard; hate the mouse
review_text: I picked this set up because I wanted a second one of the keyboard (which I love, see my reviewLogitech K350 2.4Ghz Wireless Keyboard), and figured the mouse was a bonus. ... Not.The mouse is full-sized and full-featured. Very flexible with the software as far as reprogramming the buttons. However, there are two features of this mouse that will cause me to either put it in a drawer for emergency replacements or just give it away.1. The scroll wheel: I have two other Logitech mice that I use most of the time: an MX Revolution and a Darkfield Performance MX. Both have VERY fast scroll wheels. Once you get used to that, you never want to go back. This mouse is PAINFULLY slow in comparison, and, although via the software you can reprogram it to two other scroll modes, both require moving the mouse on the desktop rather than just moving the scroll wheel.2. This is the real deal-breaker: The finish on the top of the mouse is gritty and irritates my palm. I used this mouse for about 4 hours, doing normal "stuff." My right hand was back and forth between the keyboard and the mouse, but mostly I was clicking around the web and my system. At the end of the time, the palm of my hand, in the quadrant under my pinky and toward the heel, was irritated. I couldn't figure out why. Then I compared the finish on the M510 to my other two and realized that the others are MUCH smoother. I checked my husband's stash of sandpaper, and I would say that the M510 has a finish on the top that is just a bit smoother that 600 grit wet or dry sandpaper. Apparently I don't settle my hand all the way down on the body of the mouse all the time. Part of my hand hovers just high enough that it "brushes" over the surface of the mouse. I never realized that before, but now that I know, I'll never buy a mouse without a smooth top surface again.If your mousing technique is different from mine, this could be a great mouse for you, but not for me.

review_title: Another great product from the already awesome line up of Anker Products
review_text: I use Anker products on a daily basis. I use the Anker S4 battery in my T-Mobile Galaxy S4, an Anker router as my homes main router, and an Anker laptop battery in the Asus K52F laptop that I am using to write this review. So needless to say I was thrilled to be able to solve another possible issue with an Anker product. And that possible issue is running out of juice when you need your mobile product to work. In this case it was with my Galaxy S4 with an Anker 2600mah battery as my main cell phone battery. I received this item as part of Ankers power user program for test and evaluation, and I promised that my review is fair and honest. So now onto the review.I received the item well packaged with no dents, or any other problems regarding packaging. I opened the box and saw all that it comes with. In the box is the Charging Power Pack itself, a short USB cable, Mesh Protection Sleeve, a 30-pin apple adapter (not the Lightning Type), and the instruction manual.The charge pack arrived at about 50% charge. This device starts the charge process using a shake to start system, which I am guessing uses an accelerometer. To be honest I would prefer a simple start button, but this is a minor gripe. It took a couple hours to charge it to 100%. You can use several ways to charge the pack. I used my stock Galaxy S4 charger which has an output of 2 amps. You can use basically anything with a USB port, and the charge time of the charge pack will vary depending on the output of whatever method or charger you are using. The packs indicator for how full it is is a circle of LED lights. While it is charging the lights will show you how empty or full it is, and when it is full the whole circle of lights blink simultaneously.As a test I ran my Galaxy S4 down to empty with my Anker S4 battery in it. I did this because I wanted to see how long it would take to charge from 0%, and to see if the charge pack would allow me to use my S4 while it was charging. So I hooked it up and was able to turn on and use my S4 if I needed to, but for the purpose of this test I just left it on, but did not use it while it was charging. It has 2 charging ports, one smart port (5V / 2.4A max), and one universal port (5V / 3A max). I used the Smart Port for this test. It took 3 hours and 4 minutes to charge from 0% to Full 100%. And the pack itself still had about 65-70% available charge left.And by using a little math this actually seems exactly what should be left. The S4 has a 2600mah battery. The Anker pack is a 9000mah pack. 9000 minus 2600 is 6400, and 6400 is about 71% of 9000. So a 2600mah battery should get about 3 full charges from the Power Pack before a recharge is needed. If you had a smaller pack like the 2200mah stock, or 2300mah Anker packs that are available for the Galaxy S3, or the HTC One's built in 2300mah battery you could most likely get close to 4 full charges. Now of course your mileage may vary, especially if you plan on using the phone while it is charging, but I figured these stats might help someone doing research.And if you are familiar with Anker batteries you know that their cells are top notch. So I'm sure I will get a lot of use from this awesome pack. And I now no longer need to worry about running out of juice with no way to charge. If you are looking for a great quality Portable Power pack for one of your devices you definitely cant go wrong here. I highly recommend it. And as far as customer service goes I can honestly say I have never seen a company that does more to make sure their customers are satisfied.I have also added several pics to the item details page if you want to see exactly what you get.

review_text: ok first things first. i know there are various versions of this product by different companies like apple tv, etc. i wasn't a particularly fan of any of them or roku going in. so here's my quick hones review. the thing is way smaller than you'd imagine, i mean seriously it's tiny. i think the power cable might be bigger than the actual roku box. ok probably not, but still it's small. that's good and bad i think. good because it doesn't take up a lot of room, but bad because sometimes people want their electronic components like this to be sort of presentation like in the living room. from the pictures the box looked really cool, but in reality you barely even see it sitting there. overall, it's better that the footprint is small. ok now on to the price, the only reason i really ordered the highest price one (the XS one) is because it's the only one with the ethernet cable in the back. ok this review is not short anymore! ok so having that ethernet cable in the back of the device is actually a big deal (and annoying that you have to buy the highest price version to get that). the reason it's a big deal even if you have high speed internet and wireless is that (and you've probably noticed this) when you're on wireless at home it's definitely a good amount slower than if you're plugged into straight via the ethernet cord. just check on speedtest.net if you don't believe. this is course varies based on the security level you've set on your wireless. the more secure the slower. ok so onto the actual use of the device after the ethernet cable is plugged in and you see how small the box is. the setup is really quick. you actually have to get on our computer and go to roku.com/netflix or something like that to actually activate it which is sort of funny since the box is advertised as a streaming device that allows you to not use a computer. but seriously that's a serious nitpick. it took like 2 minutes. oh and clever roku makes you enter your credit card information in case you ever buy something. but they make it part of the signup process, clever clever but little annoying. don't worry i haven't been charged. they're legit on not screwing with you on this. the menu is good, not insanely great, but good. ok so now onto what really matters. how does the darn thing perform if you have a fast internet connection and the ethernet cable plugged in. beautiful is the answer, freaking beautiful. hasn't hickuped or slowed down once yet! i've only had it for about 4 days, but i've watched a lot of netflix since then. the box stays on all the time and i've heard people complain about it, but if you see the size of the box the thing barely uses any power so who cares. and plus it turns out to be a good thing because when i turn on my computer, bam it's on! so this review sounds i'm giving it a pretty good rating, so why did i give it 5 stars you ask. because i just like being a bit critical in general on these reviews. the reason i even bothered to write this review is because this device rules! love it. buy it. just make sure to follow my advice on even if you have fast internet connection to get the one with the ethernet plug (the xs). oh and if you're not sure if you have a high speed connection, you probably don't have one. go to speedtest.net. if it doesn't say like 4-5 mb download speed most of the time, it's not high speed. oh and the remote is pretty cool. oh and ignore the crap about angry birds, they actually use that as a selling point for the XS. it's stupid, not the game just the fact that's it's on there and used as a selling point. the XS model is good because of the ethernet port and because it plays HD content well. oh yeah totally forgot that. high definition content on netflix plays awesome. make sure of course you have an high definition television. i bought a high definition TCL tv for $328 on walmart.com and it works awesome on it. $328, isn't that insane. wait maybe they won't post the review now since amazon has the same tv in its electronics section. it's just that it was cheaper on walmart.com. but in general shopping on amazon is waaaay better. crazy how this device is $89 and the tv was $328. weird times. oh so last thing, cool little thing the box does. during the 1st few seconds of high definition content, it actually granulates the video just a pit (i.e looks low resolution) and then suddenly kicks into high definition. i think it does this to avoid putting up a buffering message. the logic being instead of showing the user a buffering message, just show lower quality video to the user while the device catches up and downloads the high def information is the background. clever i thought. would of course rather it just that right off the bat, but i'm good with it. so yeah roku roks! i'm not sure if apple tv is good, i'm sure it rules as well because well it's apple, but i don't know i guess i didn't look at it because i just assumed apple would loop me into this thing where i pay for every little thing i get through itunes, etc. ok so how was that short review, eh! how many times did i say ethernet?!

review_title: Perfect stereo separation as a splitter; turn it around to merge 2 signals
review_text: First of all, the reviewer who gave this product 1 star because he thought it failed to preserve the stereo signal was dead wrong.  He must have received a different product (a stereo channel separator?) because I purchased two of these units and each female connector puts out the same perfect 2-channel stereo signal that goes into the male plug.  The male and female connectors are all standard mini-stereo, ie: 3.5 mm or 1/8 inch in diameter.  I leave this splitter plugged into my MP3 player at all times to prevent wear and tear on the MP3 player's built-in female mini connector, which would be difficult to replace.One more use for this product: turn it around and this splitter becomes a signal merger.  I have a Samsung Chromebook which has a single 3.5 mm input jack for audio headsets, combining the microphone input with the earphone output on a single jack.  All of my headsets had separate 3.5 mm plugs for earphones and microphone.  This splitter (when turned around into a merger) serves to merge the 2 headset lines into the single combined line with a 3.5 mm plug which is required for the Chromebook.

First of all, you should know that I own a Nokia N800 - not the N810.  I encourage you to read my review of the N800 for more information on that device.The N800 is identical to the N810 with only two exceptions.  The N810 has a GPS receiver and built-in slide-down keyboard.  The N800 has a FM radio and no hardware keyboard.  There are some differences on memory capacity as well, but these will almost certainly change as Nokia releases OS2008 performance updates.While I do not own the N810, but I have had the opportunity to play with one for an hour or two at the Nokia store in downtown Chicago.  The internet is where I make my living, so I try to experiment with any portable device that will allow me the freedom to work away from my desk.The N800 is sold with OS2007.  The N810 is delivered with OS2008.  The OS2008 performance upgrade is now available for the N800, allowing you to have most of the features of the $400+ N810 in the now sub-$300 N800 tablet.  If you do not need a GPS receiver (or already own a bluetooth GPS receiver), you can use the N800 to perform the exact same tasks as the more expensive N810.  Consider your needs and then decide what's works best for you.On the plus side, the N810 is slightly smaller than the N800.  The N810's keyboard is much easier to use than the on-screen touch keyboard I'm stuck with.  The N810 casing is all metal and feels a bit more durable than the N800.Whichever device you choose, the new operating system and browser are excellent and allow easy browsing of most websites.  The Mozilla browser with Flash9 renders most websites beautifully on the small screen.  The user interface is a lot more intuitive in OS2008 and it's very easy to email, chat and browse.  It won't completely replace my laptop - neither the N800 or N810 can print without extensive modification - but you truly can carry the web with you wherever you go!I hope you found this review helpful!

review_title: NETGEAR N450 WiFi DOCSIS 3.0 Cable Modem Router (N450-100NAS)
review_text: Bright-House compatible and very easy to set up.  I replaced my cable company supplied modem and my wireless router with this one unit just before Bright House was going to start charging a monthly rental fee, which means that not only do I now have better equipment, in terms of quality and performance, but it will pay for itself in about two years as well.  I had to call tech support at the cable co. and give them the model number (CG3000Dv2) to check that it was compatible with their network -it was, the modem is compatible with pretty much every cable company, and in about 10 minutes they had me ready to roll with everything working. I then had to set up my personal preferences for my home network and the modem security settings on my end.Installation:  There is no manual other than a three flap fold out that comes in the box.  It should be all you need if you have already set up a wireless router before.  The settings 'webpage" for the modem/router is user friendly and provides descriptions for each setting that you are browsing through.  The manufacturer may have more info on their website, but I didn't even need to look.  If you have never set one up before, you may want to check out their website.  Your cable company tech support should be able to talk you through most, if not all, of the setup, however.Neither my former modem nor router were wired for more than 100 Mbps, though my router was an N band wireless. This unit is wired with gigabit (1000Mbps) ports at the switch and N band wireless.  The modem component should also no longer be throttling my overall connection, which is a plus.  So far no issues with VOIP, streaming or the number of active connections, so I'll chalk that up to the new modem itself, because I had issues before the switch.  Overall, I am impressed with the unit overall: easy to set up, one unit instead of two, it out performs my old setup -what else could I ask for.

review_title: It's a new day in the world of radio. Get with it!
review_text: Okay, I admit it. I'm a radio junkie. Some read trashy novel after trashy novel. Others watch TV until they're diabetic. Me? I listen to radio. It brings me up to the minute news. It offers me an enormous range of perspective AND I can get all this while doing something else! So what's the difference between regular radio and WiFi Radio? WiFi radio pulls in 20,000 stations from everywhere in the word with crystal clarity, that's what. All you need is a WiFi internet connection and from the minute you take delivery to the time you're listening to the radio, MAYBE ten minutes will have gone by.I have five WiFi Radios throughout the house and they include the CCrane, two no longer available "Acoustic Energy" radios and another brand with an internal battery that no longer exists. My favorite, by far, is the ccrane WiFi. It connects as flawlessly as one can expect of what amounts to an audio web browser. It's got a BUNCH of presets, and trust me, you'll need them given the variety of stations you'll want to listen to, it's got a remote control devise that is much like the one you get with the Bose radio, it's incredibly easy to set up, it's small and it looks like a radio. On top of all this, it's cheap!Listen: Even if all you want to do is listen to your local stations, which is NOT what you'll want to do in short order after getting this devise, get one of these if your reception is less than perfect where you listen to radio. Reception will be crystal clear with this radio. And if you want to expand your radio listening horizons, you are going to LOVE this.BUT! suppose you're not sure this is for you? Want to find out before spending serious money? Do this. If you've got an IPod with or without a docking station, download the Reciva app for $3 and use your IPod as a WiFi Radio. It'll work just the same, pull in just as many stations, get great reception, offer a place to bookmark your presets and demonstrate how WiFi radio works for you. Then you can get the CCrane WiFi when you're sure.Enjoy.
