review_title: Good sound, great features, but too big to stay on/in my smaller lady ears!
review_text: *Update*Since writing my original review, I've handed these over to a male friend of mine to test 'em out, and he gives these an enthusiastic thumbs up! He spent the whole first day with them listening to Pandora and music from his Samsung Galaxy II, and couldn't say enough great things about these! Being that he's over six feet tall, and a larger build than me by quite a bit, he had no issues with these staying in his ears, and doing so comfortably. I DO have to say that the call sound quality on these leaves MUCH to be desired, however, as we were on the phone as he wore these, and, as the person on the other end of the line, I can unequivocally say that these made his voice truly sound like he was in a tunnel, and talking from across it as wind whipped through it. Badly distorted, distant, poor-quality call audio. For listening to music, the radio, and working out, though, these, in HIS opinion, were pretty spectacular. So, one star added back for those of you that can comfortably wear these, but still a one star penalty for call quality, and the wearability of these when it comes to smaller ears...~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~Since way back when I got my first cellphone, I've been a loyal fan of Jabra products since, for the most part, they've proven themselves reliable in the creation of quality cellphone headsets (I'm still not sure with regards to their in-car Bluetooth speakers, but their headsets have always been great). Really, this headset does not necessarily skew from that path, outside of the fact that it's meant to be worn while working out, and the over-the-ear pieces just won't stay in or on my ears. Really, I thought I was doing something wrong, until I saw that others have mentioned the same issue with theirs (which prompted me to think, "OH! It's NOT just me!!!"). Since then, I've taken note of the fact that a fairly sizable-looking man is pictured both on the product packaging and in the product page images here. Noticing those details, I'm thinking that these are marketed somewhat more strongly for men, or those who happen to have ears that are larger than my average-sized-for-a-woman ears...The features offered by this stereo headset really are great, and it seems to me that Jabra has thought of just about everything one might be looking for in a Bluetooth headset to work out with. Since you don't need me to reiterate the features of this headset, I will say that I found the flat yellow cord attaching the two earpieces to be a bit short and uncomfortable for my taste. It did feel a LOT like having a rubber band strapped against the back of my neck, and I found the cord lightly pulling against my longer hair - which wasn't necessarily pleasant - but I don't see that affecting any of the men out there that have short enough hair that it doesn't hang down over the band. Overall, I found myself wishing that the band was made of a softer, longer, adjustable-length fabric-coated cord. The control buttons (all located on the right earpiece) are low-profile, but not so difficult to find as the ones on my HTC Rezound, and they're well thought-out, so they cover all the bases (and then some) for the purpose(s) that these are intended.Additionally, if you tend to wear glasses while working out, you may find yourself adjusting the headset to properly accommodate any thicker arms(/temples), due to the girth of the ear pieces.At this point, I guess it's time to hand these over to my guy, and see what he thinks of them, and how well they fit, and stay, in his ears during his morning runs... If he feels they work better for him, I'll be sure to update this review.

Had to tape down one controller to keep it form doing this.  I play heavy-handed though.- Will not recognize more than 3 macro presses simultaneously.  However you can bypass this by adding simple button combinations.- Advanced scripting is not supported.After 3 years of using this product,  I can say this was well worth the $[...] I spent on it.  I can't tell you how much this pad has saved my hide in PvP games.  I even bought the Logitech G13 when it came out, but I still use this one for its ease of programmability and button layout.  Too bad Belkin customer support is non-existent.  They should really try to support the products which have a huge fan-base such as this.

I saw this on sale for $160 and took another look at it and decided to buy it.Setting this up was a little problematic, but it was partially my fault.  I have two wireless networks in my house.  One is my personal network running on 802.11n, the other is a guest network running on 802.11g.  Since this is 802.11g only, I decided to set it up on the guest network.  The problem was, I forgot the guest network password when I got to that part of the configuration.  I recommend that you have that information handy before you start.The iOS app that is used for setup can be a bit cumbersome if things go wrong.  You may want to consider using Safari to set it up instead.  Also, the app is only useful for setup.  Other than that, it is useless, so don't stress if you don't have it.  Just download the manual in PDF format and follow the instructions on how to do the configuration with Safari.Also, I had to use the reset button a couple times during the setup.  At first I was not holding the button down long enough.  I read the manual and learned that you had to wait for the WiFi LED to turn red before you let it go.  The problem I had is that it turns red briefly, then turns blue.  I was was releasing the button when it turns red.  What I learned through trial and error was that 10 seconds after it turns blue, it turns solid red and stays that way while you are holding the reset button.  That is the time when you should let the button go.Setup probably would have been easier if they had put an ethernet port on this device.  Sometimes a good old fashioned wired connection is easier.When I finally got it set up, I was a little disappointed with the sound quality.  It was really muddled and soft.  I was able to fix this using the equalizer (Settings - Music - EQ).  Oddly enough, my favorite setting was "Spoken Word", which is fine because I listen to audiobooks when I am commuting.To setup the sound, I played some songs that really test the full range of sound.  One song I recommend is LL Cool J's "We're the Greatest".  With the thumping base and Eddie van Halen's guitar, you get a good range to test the sound.Using AirPlay works fine with my MacBook, iPad, iPod, and iPhone.  I did experience some skipping, but I was able to resolve it by giving my device a direct line of sight to the router.  The router is on the opposite side of the house and the signal has to go through a lot of rooms to get to the speaker.  The skipping seems to only happen when both the phone and the speakers are in an area with limited connectivity.To resolve the skipping, I am going to move the guest router to a central location that is a lot closer to the speaker.  For now, I have an old iPod touch hooked directly up to it.UPDATE: I have been trying unsuccessfully to update the firmware.  My system was shipped with version 3.8.93.3700 (2100-10-30).  The latest version is 3.8.97.3700.After you get to the Firmware Update page with your browser, you are supposed to click the Apply button to put the speakers into an edit mode.  This process is supposed to take a few seconds according to the instructions.  My speakers do not go into edit mode.  The WiFi LEDs just blink red and I have to reboot the speakers.  I can never get beyond that step.UPDATE: If you want to use these speakers for playing games over AirPlay, don't bother.  AirPlay has too much latency.  There is a three second delay from the time you pull the trigger to the time you hear the gunshot.

review_title: Elegant but pricey speakers sound great but are not portable and there are better options at this price point.
review_text: Overview: these elegant speakers work and sound great, but are pricey. They are not really portable, and work on Bluetooth technology, which is inferior to speakers like Sonos and the forthcoming Denon HEOS system that work over wireless networks.The Harmon Kardon Nova speakers are great looking. With their clear covering and white accents, they just look cool.The speakers also sound great. The bass thumps and the highs are clear. Great stuff.But: they are powered through AC with no battery backup. That means that they are stationary. And for any stationary solution, I think the era of bluetooth has passed in favor of wireless internet.A few months ago, I would have been completely in awe of the bluetooth technology that allows you to play music from your phone. But, since then, I've become a convert toSONOS PLAY:1 Compact Wireless Speaker for Streaming Music - (Black)and I just don't think a bluetooth based speaker system makes a whole lot of sense at this price point and relative lack of portability. (IF you click on my name, you can see my review of the SONOS system.)The SONOS ecosystem has become very affordable (especially relative to the price of these speakers) with the introduction of the SONOS Play 1.Conversely, if you want a portable soundbar, there are cheaper options than the Harmon Kardon speakers. They sound much worse, yes. And they don't look nearly as elegant. But they are designed to be carried around. Here's a well reviewed example, for under a hundred bucks.iLuv Mo 'Beats HD High Definition Portable Bluetooth Speaker with Viewing Cradle(If you're really dedicated, look for my August 19, 2013 review where I express my awe for bluetooth technology. Sigh. Sorry Harmon Kardon, a year is a long time in the world of technology.)And if you want a semi-permanent solution and you have a wireless network, a single SONOS Play 1 sounds almost as good as the Harmon Kardon speakers for less money. (A single Play-3 is at least comparable.) Two SONOS Play-1s blow them out of the water.The niche that that leaves for the Harmon Karden (at its current price point)is situations in which you have no wireless network or, for whatever reason, don't want to use it.The other issue with Bluetooth is that it plays everything that comes through your device. That means that if you're playing music and you get a text message, you will get a loud text message noise through your speakers. This can be disconcerting and even harsh.The pace of technology is unforgiving. The ability to wirelessly play music through Bluetooth is like magic--but it is already practically obsolete outside certain situations.So, even though these are amazing speakers as a stand alone item, my reluctant conclusion is that they are simply not the best option on the market. Either go for greater portability if you want a speaker you can take to the beach, or look seriously at SONOS if you want a permanent solution in your home.

review_title: Ask yourself- What has happened every time I've gambled on cheap camera gear?
review_text: This review will not be about zippers coming unzipped because someone met the zippers in the middle at the top of the bag instead of zipping them all the way to one side so their camera fell out as many reviewers have complained about. If you don't know that a bag will unzip when left in that position, you deserve to be taught an expensive lesson! Now, for my actual review- Six months ago I bought a Tamrac Evolution 8 for $176 and found it to be functional but slightly cumbersome and quite uncomfortable while wearing it. So, I decided to trust the good reviews on this bag and take a chance. Yikes, when will I learn?! If you are a somewhat seasoned beginner, a novice or even a pro, you have to ask yourself this; what has happened nearly every time I've decided to go cheap on camera equipment? EXACTLY! Sure we get lucky sometimes but when it comes to cheap gear I have learned one fast and hard lesson- you really do get (or do not get) what you pay for. Also, a bag might be best bought or at least tried on, worn and inspected in a store. The moment I took this out of the box I grabbed a hold of the Canon emblem on the front just to see how it was attached because I knew I would want to remove it as most of us do in hopes to deter thieves. Well, the moment I grabbed it - the cheap prongs that pierce the bag to hold it bent and it pulled right off (I think I almost had myself convinced that Canon had purposely constructed it to be easily removed). I didn't give it a second thought and was happy with how comfortable it felt when filled with all the gear that was once in my Tamrac (it's only about 2/3 the height of the Tamrac and it does not have a pocket for a laptop). After transferring all my gear and being uber-excited to attach my tripod. The Tamrac's tripod mount is an absolute joke for anything over 15 inches so I couldn't wait to attach it and be on my way. Yikes again! The top strap to hold the tripod will not stay tight to save a life and the pocket for the foot is far too big and sloppy- offering no stability or support. Now, for day 3. I was zipping the small front pocket after putting some papers in there and the zipper handle (which I believe must be made of die-cast metal) broke like brittle plastic. I couldn't believe it but I decided not to make a big deal of it because, although sharp and jagged, there was enough handle left to operate the zipper. It is now one month later and while zipping the main camera compartment- it happened again. The zipper broke in the exact fashion as the first. This time I could not dismiss it as it was the most used "function" on the bag. It is now on it's way back to Amazon. I have to say that Amazon was great about allowing me to return it for a credit even though the window for return had lapsed. If you get a defective product- Amazon always supports their customers and I think I can speak for all of us when I say it is very much appreciated. I'm glad many others have had a positive experience with this product but I can not in good faith trust this bag to hold my expensive gear.In a nutshell-  I know I mentioned the Tamrac bag often in this review but it was to compare (or contrast in this case) but despite the Tamrac's design flaws, it is a quality built product that still looks and operates as if I just bought it today. So, when it comes to gear I am adopting a new philosophy- CRY ONCE! Meaning, rather than go thru the hassle of buying cheap and wasting money and time, I'm gonna drop the bucks on the good stuff and be done.

review_title: Good bag if you are looking for a backpack
review_text: This is a great backpack.  It is well-built, has a ton of space, and is cheap to boot!  Buying something cheap in the photography world usually means its either poor quality or a knockoff of some patended item, but not in this case.  Being one of the cheapest bags around, this backpack certainly holds its own.  As many have said, it can hold a LOT of stuff, such is evidenced by the member photos.  Mine (which is pictured in the member photos) held a flash, 3 lenses, 1 35mm SLR, a digital SLR, CF's, and other small accessories.  It is really quite incredible how much fits in this bag which looks fairly small.I have encountered no problems with rips or tears in the year that I have been using it, and I always have about 10 lbs of equipment in it.  THe zipper is well-constructed, and there have been no problems with it.I would not recommend carrinying around a lot of equipment constantly though, not because the bag can't handle it, but because the padding on the back isn't as thick as other bags, and it really begins to hurt your back after about 10-15 minutes.And though I praise the backpack, I don't use this bag anymore.  There is one thing you should definitely consider when thinking about purchasing this bag:  how well will it actually serve what you are wanting to do with it?  Yes, it carries all my equipment, but it is barely accessible.  Anyone who needs their equipment on the go should consider an alternate type of bag to a backpack.  If you have time to stop, pull off your backpack, open it up, and grab your equipment, then throw your bag back on, then by all means go for this bag, but if you are looking for something you can just unzip and have everything right there, consider another type of bag such as a reporter or shoulder bag.

review_title: Worst Logitech Mouse I've Ever Bought, Unfortunately
review_text: I've owned quite a few mice made by Logitech, and I normally swear by them.  Both of the USB mini-mice I used with my previous laptop were made by them, as are the larger ones I use on my desktops at both work and home.  Never had a serious problem with any of them, except when they wear out from use.I cannot say the same of this one, sadly.  I've had this mouse for about 10 weeks now, and I've had a lot of issues that are just annoying enough to bug me constantly without quite having prompted me to return it.  Occasionally, when I wake my laptop from sleep, it will fail to reconnect to the mouse and I have to either re-pair it or restart my bluetooth controller.  Sometimes this appears to be the fault of the laptop, because other bluetooth devices also don't work, but others it's just the mouse.  This is minor, and doesn't happen that often.  If it were the only issue, I'd not be at all annoyed, really.Unfortunately, the laser sensor also doesn't work well.  I use my laptop primarily in our living room, with the mouse sitting on the arm of my chair.  I believe that the slight texture in the upholstery confuses the sensor, because the cursor tends to wobble and jump around on the screen, making it somewhat difficult to use.  This was not a problem for either of the previous mice I have used with a laptop, so I don't know why it would be now.  Irritatingly, if I try to use it on a more uniform surface, while the cursor no longer wobbles, it moves VERY slowly, requiring huge movements to get across the screen.  I'm not certain, but I think these problems may be worsening.  I may try contacting Logitech Technical Support and see if anything can be done to resolve it--perhaps I was unlucky enough to get a faulty unit.

This is a reliable workhorse of a projector for a very reasonable price. It starts up quickly, runs flawlessly for hours at a time without overheating, and has a bright, crisp picture. It is easy to use with intuitive controls using both the panel on the top of the projector and the remote (which includes a laser pointer!). The quality of the build is relatively high, with solid exterior plastic unibody, with a highly polished piano black exterior.Unfortunately the height adjustment front leg and the adjustable balancing leg both are not as high quality. I am a little disappointed with the functionality for balancing: one of the two rear legs screws in or out and levels the unit. The problem is that it can get screwed in too tight (or get stuck over time) and getting it unscrewed is tough since the leg is just a rubber pad that provides little leverage for gripping. The front height/angle adjustment leg is not very sturdy and made of plastic. I wish it was thicker and made of metal, since it gets constant use.Image quality is very high. Slide presentations, even those including many images and videos, all look very nice. While this is not a high resolution projector, the 800x600 native resolution is ideal for slide presentations. I do find it a bit laughable that Vivtek's marketing materials mention using projector for a home theater set-up--that would be a very sub-optimal home theater arrangement! I use this project for PowerPoint presentations and it performs really well in that role.Start-up and cool-down for this projector are very quick. From powering on to showing an image, the unit only takes about 25-30 seconds of wait time. That's much faster than my old projector, an InFocus model. I appreciate that I don't have to wait minutes at a time for the projector to do it's thing. Shutting down leads to a very brief cool-down cycle of approximately 10 seconds.This is a very nice projector for the money. While it isn't perfect (resolution being only adequate and a few issues with the support legs) it produces high quality images onscreen and is a solid purchase for business applications. 4/5 Stars.

review_title: excellent tv. important tech info in this one. fan info.
review_text: This tv is the reference tv for critics this year. my friend who works at a av shop has had several of these returned due to loud fan noise. The fans enginers are loud, they hum on most models. but it's not so loud that you would hear it while their is volume on your tv. but if there's a silent moment you will hear huma huma huma, barely.  still this does distract some evidently.  noone else is mentioning this but it is that way on every tv. so while watching a silent scene you'll hear that slight hmmn nmmma hmmma noise. panasonic said that they had to install these type of fans which are louder to due to the fact that the tv is so thin.  if you don't believe me turn off all volume on your speakers and sit in front you will hear something.  I don't care about wify and all that stuff but the picture is the best ever seen on a tv. And that's not just my opinion , the blacks are the best, the picture is the most natural , the tv is ultra slim and light too. The tv has many features on it and it does 24 frames per second so that your blu ray looks correct and less jerky. It has 2500  hz motion smoother that really works well on movies. that you are using on a blu ray at 24fps. if you use the motion smoother on cable or a dvd that isn't a blu ray it will cause jerky motion. So it is only for use on blu rays or live sport events in hd at most. even then a blu ray that isn't set for 24fps will then be overcorrected and jerky. You set the 24 frame per second on your blu ray player then set on advanced settings under picture 94 hz. there is another setting for when you use the tv as a computer screen. al input 1080p , if you are not using the tv as pc screen then do not set that to on. the ambient light control that responds to your room lighting will make the tv fainter if the overhead lights are on. I turned that off. the mosquito option is a good one for keeping off noise artifacts. It took me a day to figure out these aavanced controls. As the manual doesn't tell you about them. Take my word on it though , only set motion smoother when using blu rays set at the dvd player at 24fps. This tv is wirelsss and lan ready too. So you can connect to the net with it, but I wouldn't use this as my pc screen.  I would NOT do the 3-d feature though on any show that is NOT in 3-d. Use the 3-d for 3-d film and tv and don't bother with it otherwise. Few people do this but it's not what a 3-d tv was designed for really. (watching non 3-d in 3-d) this tv is expensive but for at least the next 8 years at least, it should be well worth using as your main tv,  even if they go to higher resolution their is no medium of anything at that resolution anyway!.  oled tv is here now but like led it is much brighter than plasma and the picture will never be as realistic as what you see on this one.  I don't plan to grab another tv for at least 8 years or more so I grabbed this fantastic set.  Will next years model be better than this years? sure. But there come a point where you have to settle on a great tv and just stay with it for many years. This is that tv. And frankly my 2009 vt-10  was that tv. I had no reason other than the lack of 3-d to go on to this model that's how good vt plasmas are. This is worth your money and with it's excellent picture and 3-d feature this IS good enough to be your main tv for many years to come. It has antiburnin features and improved gas elements too. This set leaps forward from the past plasmas in that regard. So this is another break in tech power to hold you over for many  years.  Sure wall and window tv's will be here in the future for  you to buy. But for absolutely the best most realistic picture you will want a panasonic plasma for your living room tv.

review_title: The large touchscreen is great with Windows 8
review_text: It's been several years since I've had a laptop computer. The desktop, smartphone and Kindles have gotten me by, but I'm realizing now how much I've missed using a laptop for the portability and the processing power that tablets just can't fit into their small sizes. This laptop comes with Windows 8 installed and it opens a whole new world in laptops for me. With the touchscreen it has the "hands on" feeling of a tablet where I can expand windows or text using my fingers or touching the spot where I want the cursor to go, but it has a big, beautiful 15.6 inch screen and lots more processing power and memory than a tablet or smartphone.I love my desktop computer but it sure is nice to be able to work anywhere I want to, and in fact be able to communicate with the desktop from other locations. The built-in Wi-Fi works very well with our home network and stays connected without any problems. It communicates with our wireless printer and also has Bluetooth. It isn't a real sleek little laptop, it weighs 6 pounds according to my scale although it's shown here as 5.1 lbs. And at 10.20 x 14.80 x 0.98 inches you aren't going to be tossing this into your backpack, but hey, that's what a tablet is for. This is a serious computer and it has a nice, solid feel. I'm also impressed with the speakers which are surprisingly good for a laptopI wasn't sure if I was going to like Windows 8 since I've been using 7 and hadn't had a chance to try it before. This laptop came with it installed and 8.1 is available through the Microsoft Windows Store as a free product update so I downloaded and installed it the day after I received the computer. One word of warning: allow a lot of time for the upgrade. It's a huge install file, something like 3.2 GB. And once you've got it downloaded it seems to take forever to install. I started it around midnight with a pretty fast Wi-Fi cable connection and didn't want to go to bed while it was downloading and installing. It didn't take any work on my part, I just watched it whirring away, but it was at least an hour and a half before it was finished. I'm really liking Windows 8.1 so far on this laptop. The touchscreen is very responsive and I love being able to go back and forth between the screen and the keyboard. Everything feels very fast and now that I'm getting used to it, it's easy to navigate. Being able to just start typing the name of a program anywhere and have it open is very cool. And it's always fun to have something new and different when it comes to operating systems.I like the solid feel and speed and since we've had several Dell computers over the years I'm expecting this to be dependable like the others. Two thumbs up so far!

review_title: Perfect for an upgrade from an older point and shoot
review_text: If you're still using a point and shoot camera that's more than a few years old and you're tired of pushing the button and holding it down waiting forever for the damn thing to take a picture then this is a great next camera for you.Our old digital camera was fine for throwing in our pocket when we went on trips, but the shutter delay was so horrible that we'd miss fast paced moments or people would get tired of smiling as they hold a pose anxiously waiting for that flash. We had a few trips planned this summer and wanted an upgrade that would take clearer faster pictures generally for photo books and online viewing.I did TONS of research online and got all tangled up in megapixels and optical zoom and features that I probably would never use anyway. I'm not advanced enough to move up to a SLR camera, but I wanted something that was a step up from the camera I have now. After getting dizzy from all the online reviews I finally just went to some big box stores and played around with the cameras on display. I used them like I would use them on a trip and I even brought along my wife to make sure that she was comfortable using it.Based on the reviews I was all set to buy a Panasonic Lumix model, but there were too many dials and settings and it wasn't user friendly when actually holding and playing with the camera. I honestly hadn't even seen a review for this Sony WX150 camera, but it was so easy to use and was much smaller than some of the other "travel zoom" cameras. It has three basic modes that you could easily toggle with a button - camera, movie and panorama.Camera is where you spend most of your time and on here 95% of the time we live it on "auto". There are several scenes you can select if you want to optimize something for a specific setting. For example, if you're shooting through glass in low light you can set it to that it doesn't flash. If you're moving around a lot you can set it for extreme anti-blur where it takes like 5 pictures super fast and then puts them all together for a crisp image. Most importantly it's easy to toggle between the settings and you don't have to scroll through countless menu/info screens to find things.Panorama mode seems awesome when you read about it, but in practice it's been tough to get to actually work out well. The pictures always end up getting cut off pretty short. Maybe they'll look good on the computer when you blow them up, but on the camera screen it's a little disappointing.I haven't used movie mode yet so I can't speak to that feature.So this camera doesn't have GPS (which I think is just a battery drain) and it doesn't have wifi (another battery drain) but it has everything else you could probably want for the best of both worlds between point and shoot and travel zoom. Sure you can probably find more zoom or more megapixels, but if you play around with this camera I guarantee you'll appreciate how easy it is to use, how compact and lightweight it is, and how fast and clear it takes pictures.

The build quality of the Canon EW-60C Lens Hood is simply top-notch. You are paying a premium not only for the Canon name, but for a high quality and impeccably constructed component.Form----The inner side of the hood is specially coated to reduce glare. This coating, called "flock," gives the inner surface a non-reflective matte texture.The EW-60C is designed specifically for theEF-S 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6(AKA the "kit" lens), theEF-S 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 USM, theEF-S 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 IS, the EF 28-90mm f/4-5.6 USM, the f/4-5.6 III/II USM, the EF 28-80mm f/3.5-5.6, the EF 28-80mm f/3.5-5.6 III/II, and the EF 28-80mm f/3.5-5.6 IV USM/ V USM lenses. The optical properties of these lenses is taken into account in the design (such as the depth and shape) of the lens hood.Do not try to fit your lens with hoods designed for lenses with different focal lengths or you might run into a problem with vignetting (a phenomenon where the edges of a picture are darkened). Although there are "cooler" looking lens hoods, such as one with a"petal" design, they will not work properly unless they are designed for your lens.There are also "generic" (or "knock off") versions of this hood made by other manufacturers, such asFotodiox,Opteka,HDE, Janco, andAdorama. These should work just fine.Function--------So how well does the lens hood fare in reducing glare or flare? To be honest, I find the pictures taken with the hood and those taken without the hood look virtually indistinguishable. On the plus side, the lens hood does offer some protection for your lens from accidental knocks because it protrudes slightly above your lens. If nothing else, the Canon EW-60C definitely helps to give your lens an added appearance of sophistication that will impress your friends ;)An Aside--------Seriously, a polarized filter does much more to reduce glare and improve the quality of your picture. I use theB+W 58mm Circular Polarizer MRC Filterand the difference it makes is simply phenomenal! Blue skies are bluer. Foliage in direct sunlight are greener because the filter eliminates any harsh reflection. It also "cuts through" the haze on a smoggy day.---When all is said and done, the EW-60C definitely has some functional and aesthetic value. I personally have no regrets about getting it. Recommended.

Since I really like the original version, I wanted to give this newer model a try.Regarding comfort: It is a bit bulkier than the original, the cups are almost doubled in thickness (a bit exaggerated, but if you got used to the size of the original you will be really surprised when you see the newer version), I think they wanted to increase the comfort around the ears with that. But, they forgot that bigger means heavier, and it puts more pressure on the head compared to the original.  Around the ears I don't feel much discomfort, but with this design, the upper part of the head is most affected. For longer usage that may become a concern for some.Regarding sound quality: I couldn't figure out a difference if not a small increase in the quality. So, if you enjoyed the sound quality of the original, then you won't be surprised with this one either.Regarding noise cancellation: It is as good as the original, maybe a bit better (in a quieter environment, it felt that way, at different frequencies the response might vary). But, since ATH produced models with varying hissing levels (I am sure of that), I don't think the performance may be a good indicator. One of the originals that I had almost gave a barely noticeable hissing, whereas the other was quite noticeable. This one is in the middle, which of course masks some outside noise. That is why all I can say is it is as good as the original, and this is never a bad thing.Regarding leakage: Comparing to the original, I think this one is better. Yes, there is still leakage, but as long as you don't listen at high volume it won't be a problem, and in a noisy environment, no one will notice it much, and you won't be in a position to care much either.Other issues: The battery location has changed thanks to the increase in size. They moved to the right cup, and the battery location can be opened by just turning the silver colored outside layer. This makes it a bit easier and lessens the risk of breaking something while changing the batteries. The carrying bag is as compact as the original, they didn't seem to reflect the change in size of the headphone on the size of the carrying bag ( only the inside is a bit different to accommodate the bigger cups). It comes with two cables instead of one, a regular-sizes one and a shorter-sized one.In short, as of now, I don't see a lot of reason to go with the newer model, unless you had discomfort issues with the original one around the ears. If you had, then you might have better results with this one. Considering this, it wouldn't be wrong to consider this headphone as ATH-ANC7-big&tall.; On the other hand, if you liked the original and happy with it, then let the original be your choice, there is really no need to go for the newer model.

review_title: Excellent audio quality excellent upgrade from onboard
review_text: The Creative Sound Blaster Z SBX is an excellent upgrade from most onboard motherboard sound chips. It has a 116dB SNR which is the signal-to-noise ratio, meaning the louder you crank the volume there will be less background noise/unwanted signal. The card has audiophile grade capacitors and several inputs and outputs including TOSLINK digital optical and 3.5mm gold plated microphone and 5.1 speaker inputs. Don't get me wrong, these are definitely tuned to bias toward the low end, but not so much that it drowns out everything else.I've had Shures and Grados so I'm not going to kid you in saying that the highs are accurate and brilliant. They aren't, but if you're considering these headphones, you're probably looking for reasonably clear mids and highs. Which is what these headphones provide.My Tracks HD headphones are only comfortable enough to wear for about an hour at a time. Maybe two at the most. I've had these Master Tracks on for an entire work day without feeling the slightest of pressure discomfort. That's not to say it can't be improved, however. The only reason I don't give it 5 stars is because the ear cushions only swivel in one direction.Take note that if you don't use an Apple iDevice, the buttons may not perform the function that you expect. I use these headphones with my iPod so the volume, play/pause and track skip functions work as expected. But they're practically useless with my phones (Galaxy S4, Nexus 5 & Nexus 4).

I know tablets, from the hardware to the firmware. With the exception of GPS (which this unit lacks), this tablet is an EXTREME buy for the price. Also, the HDMI output worked surprisingly well. However, what i said about the GPS, there is a saving grace here. One could buy a "bluetooth" GPS and use it with this tablet and it would almost be perfect.As for everything else, i put this tablet through some SERIOUS paces and it came through with flying colors. I have owned many tablets, many from Hong Kong, name brand units like Archos, Viewsonic, & Dell and other eastern name brands with most people have never even heard of. For the price, this tablet beats most competition, hands-down.Whoever designed this tablet got the "right" configuration. When i say this, i mean they put things like USB, power, TF slot, SIM, and HDMI on the "side" rather than on the bottom (a common habit among Asian tablet makers) so it's not uncomfortable to use this unit even when it's charging.I will say this, i had some "modified" firmware installed on the tablet in order to harness ALL of it's gifts. With this, i was allowed a few gems that most people didn't get like Android Market. I sincerely hope they will develop Android 2.3 (Gingerbread) for this unit because it's even more impressive than 2.2Now, no review is really complete without a little complaining and here is mine: In a semi-loud room (we're talking TV and/or kids being loud) the tablet almost can't be heard. But this is a common problem among MANY tablets because of the size of the speakers...they're just too small to get any really impressive sound. HOWEVER, one could buy blue-tooth loudspeakers and get a wireless relief from this problem. I read the initial firmware had some bugs in it, like the wireless cutting off but i never experienced the problem because i upgraded it as soon as i got it.I field-tested this unit by logging into my Windows 7 machine and transferring files with absolute EASE (Thanks in part to the app called "File Expert" on Android market and very free). I streamed music & videos between my tablet to Windows 7 and my XBOX 360 with a little app called "Double-Twist Air Sync", it's a GREAT alternative to i Tunes. Another little gem was the "blinking" LED to let someone know that the unit was still on, that one was a great extra for me because i tend to just set something down and leave it running for hours.Another good thing about this tablet was the designers were SMART enough to give it a rubber-like back side where it could be easier to hold on to. Too many tablet builders create "smooth" backed tablets and the result is....they slip, fall, and turn into an expensive (but broken) door-stop.Now, i won't waste a lot of people's time by going into deep tech-slang because it just makes most people irate when others do but this is one seriously well-made tablet. I played lots of games on it and it handled the graphics like a champ.Frugal buyer who want the most bang for their buck....GET THIS TABLET. For what it is, the Elocity A7 is the best pad for the money.

review_title: It works... but is NOT Power over Ethernet (PoE)
review_text: These units are actually the Chinese knock off versions of the PPoE (notice the two P's) injector/splitters. For the most part, these items work as intended and, for shorter distances like mine, can supply continuous power without any issues. Longer distances require stronger power units. Only time will tell how long the units last.One word of caution, though, to anyone who is looking to purchase these units: PPoE != PoE (does not equal). These units are not 802.3af. Rather, they implement a proprietary Mode B of 802.3af. What this means is that if your devices are true 802.3af (PoE) compliant, 9 times out of 10, these devices will not power them on as the power levels will not match. This is because PPoE devices do not negotiate power requirements (as required by 802.3af). Rather, they simply send out exactly what they get in from the power supply (which is usually less than what is sent across 802.3af). Essentially, what this means is that in order for these units to power your device, your device (PoE or not) will need the following:1 x Power Cable for your device (and the size needs to be 5.5mm x 2.1mm DC)1 x set of PPoE connectors (this set includes both the splitter and the injector and you will need them both)1 x Cat5e (or Cat 6) cableWith all of that in place, you will be able to power your device. If your device is PoE only (802.3af), such as the Polycom IP Sound Station phone (or any other device for which there is no DC jack), these PPoE connectors will not work. Also note that because PPoE requires the original power cable, these connectors will actually work on any device.

Very simple once you figure it out but not at all obvious without directions.  Next step is the firmware update which several other reviewers have posted instructions on.  To their directions I would add that saving the file to "the root" means the root directory of the FILM CARD, not the camera since the camera itself has no internal memory.Once that is done, you can actually start learning how to use the camera.  First off let me stress: do not buy this camera if you're not a tech savvy person.  The user interface is not very friendly and it took me a long time to figure out basic tasks.  To cram everything into such a small package, just a couple of buttons control a multitude of tasks and without any LCD display, you pretty much have to memorize what you're doing rather than be able to follow prompts.  HERE'S A BIG TIP THOUGH: If you have a smart phone, download the GoPro app before you do anything with the camera.  The menu in the app is much easier to navigate than the one on the camera and it will be easier to set the camera up the way you want it with a menu you can actually see.  The app does have a bit of a delay when framing a shot but that is understandable.After you get through the cumbersome set up, you're ready to rock and roll.....for about an hour.  I am a cyclist, so I bought a bike mount and took the camera on a few short rides.  The first ride, I took non-stop pictures and video, and the camera was dead in an hour.  On the second ride, I tried to be more selective and got it to last about two hours.  I brought it with me on this year's STP (Seattle to Portland bike ride, for those not familiar...).  Out of 204 miles, I got 26 usable pictures.  Now, granted they are 26 shots that I wouldn't have been able to get without the GoPro, but the battery life isn't suited to endurance activities.I took one video at the start line and it turned out very choppy.  Not because of the bouncing on the bike but because of a problem with the recording device.  I assume there is some sort of update that will solve this problem, but I haven't looked into it.In short, if you're looking to get this camera for short duration activities or instances where you can carry many extra batteries, it's a cool gadget.  If you're doing an endurance activity, you'd better invest in lots of batteries.  I recommend the Wasabi Power set, sold on Amazon, that comes with two batteries and a car/wall charger. Note however that the battery door is not hinged or connected in any way and comes completely off the camera to change the battery.  Good luck keeping track of that if you're changing batteries on the fly!  Be advised you also need to buy a micro SD card and might need different mounts for your intended use.

review_title: A first rate TV for the money
review_text: We've had our 5265 for a few days now, and I've had some time to adjust and tweak the settings to where color, brightness and black details are pretty good. That's kind of an understatement as there is a big WOW factor when it's all set up well. A very important factor with a tv this large is the quality of the signal being fed to it. If your provider uses heavy compression on the signal being fet to you, you're going to see macro-blocking artifacts and other such noise. Our tv is plugged into cable directly out of the wall, and the built-in tuner takes care of the rest. HD from NBC and others is very cool. We watch DVDs on an upscaling Sony with HDMI, and the picture is very enjoyable. HD-DVD or BluRay would be a real treat.I only have a couple of relatively small issues that keep me from giving it 5 stars. One is that when auto-programming cable channels, the tv would freeze-up and turn itself off whenever it got to channel 108 for some reason. Then, after a moment, it would turn itself back on and repeat as long as it was on 108. There's nothing on 108 for us, so to bypass this, I just unplugged the cable as it reached 108 and plugged it back in after it was past it, and everything works fine. Now, to be honest, I'm not sure it's the fault of the tv or the feed from the cable company, but it didn't happen with our smaller tv.The second problem (minor) is that sometimes in dark scenes, it seems like the tv can't figure out how to properly display the darkness. I'll say it again: only sometimes. It happens so infrequently that most people would probably not notice, but it shows up as lighter shades of gray eminating from the sides of the tv inward. 9 times out of 10 the tv shows solid black, but sometimes (mostly depending on the disc being watched) it shows these lighter side areas in a scene that's very dark or has darkness with little other detail. I'm a bit paranoid about these big LCDs since I'm a former owner of another brand that had terrible banding problems. On the 5265, though, it is seemingly so small a problem that I hesitate to mention it, but it's there, and some people have a harder time with it than others.On the plus side, again - the picture is amazing and even standard definition played off of our home video camera looks really nice. Also, the screen is glossy compared to most LCDs. If you don't like reflections (think near tube-tv reflection) or have sunny windows facing where you'll put this tv, it could cause you problems. I happen to really enjoy the glossy screen, however, as it ads a real feel of... oh, I don't know how to explain it - visual "POP", I guess. A very nice tv for the price. I'm looking forward to enjoying ours for a long time.

I'll surf the internet while watching TV at night (so I won't have to steal my wife's iPad---which is probably why she got me the Kindle Fire HD in the first place), read my books at times, check e-mail and maybe watch some movies.Viewing movies from Amazon Prime is very simple and the audio and display are awesome.  The ability to obtain IMDB information easily while viewing the movie is a real plus as well.  Similarly viewing movies from YouTube is a pleasure with the display and audio.I do not find the interface with the various applications, web, videos, etc as intuitive as on the iPad but I am getting used to it.  Again the Kindle is NO WHERE CLOSE to being a true tablet computer and is NOT an iPad in terms of functionality or availability of apps to download.  Skype is nice and ePocrates drug database is very good.My camera did not function at first on the device but I contacted Amazon customer service and had to do a 'reboot' that seemed to fix the problem, so now my wife and I can skype easily (me with my Kindle Fire HD and she with her iPhone 4S).I would STRONGLY recommend shelling out the bucks to get a case for the device and a stylus.  The keyboard is rather small and if you are going to do any typing (at least with my fat fingers) you will be hitting 2 keys at once even holding it in landscape format.  The stylus (Belkin Professional Capacitive Tip Stylus for Kindle Fire, Black) has made responding to e-mails on the Kindle Fire HD a much more pleasent experience.  The case (Amazon Kindle Fire HD 7" Standing Leather Case, Ink Blue) makes the device easier to hold and protects it well.  I LOVE the fact that the case will automatically turn off and turn on the device with closing or opening the cover.  Before I got the case I just could NEVER remember where the on/off button was located on the Kindle Fire HD as all the buttons are flush with the device so I was stroking all over the edges to try to find the buttons...now I don't need to worry.So bottom line:  It is no iPad but it is a very slick and functional device and will work very well for its intended uses...plus it is a wonder to behold its display and very easy to carry due to its size.

And since I worked with Far East market frequently on commercial/magazine assignment, this type of lens work out very well and indeed became workhorse of my production.You have to be mindful, 35mm focal length is bit tricky to do portrait.  So, you have to be careful with type of model you are using.It is also very useful for low available light situation, so I see some wedding photographer used them.Some of events photographer also love to use this for similar reason, and it seemed to work well with capturing child etc.However, I only see limited satisfied amateur user of this lens... while I am teaching photography lesson.It is may be because it makes very little economic sense for amateur user who are shooting landscape or family portrait.This 35mm lens focal length are well covered by many reputable L zoom lens including 16-35, 17-40, 24-105, 24-70 and other. All of them are excellent L lens, and will do wonder for the most of landscape or portrait project.  Zoom lens actually makes better economic argument in many occasion.As far as difference from L zoom lens concern, you won't notice much until you started to enlarge to considerable size.To be honest, not all of my 35mm focal length shoot on commercial assignment used this prime lens either... and that is even for the people who shoot staged subject in studio.  So, you can guess how often prime lens is used for journalistic type of photography.So, be sure you need this particular lens or you will be disappointed.Faster Aperture alone normally won't justify this lens.But if you know you need this lens, and your assignment or project demand this lens. Why wait.You really have to look at its performance when it is stop down to f2.8~f4 where many of money shot using this lens are created.For people who are not sure about taking plunge to the L prime lens, I strongly suggest to rent this lens for a week or more, so you will be sure you needed this lens for your particular style.Major Advantage are:1. F1.4 Aperture really help for low available light portrait situation, and ideal for indoor use.2. Very nice portrait lens for particular type of production.3. Work wonderfully on both full size sensor camera as well as 1.6x body.4. Build quality is excellent5. Very sharp, sharp enough to convince you that your L lens prime is worth the price.  Very useful for spread or any other large assignment.Major Disadvantage are:1.Cost as much as L zoom lens that does not sit well for many people.2.Prime lens is inherently limited as a workaround lens, so I wold go for L zoom lens if I have to choose lens on the travel.3.35mm is not going to work well with particular type of people as head portrait lens, so if you are going to buy your first L prime lens for portrait purpose, it is might be safer to buy 50/f1.2 or 85/f1.2

review_title: It's a Manfrotto product, but this is their worst item
review_text: I just finished writing a review for the Sirui L-10 and then thought I'd write a review for this monopod tilt head too. I don't like writing harsh reviews, but it's fair to review the good with the bad so here I go.This mount head was the second head I ever bought for any one of my 'pods. I needed something for my monopod and thought I'd give this a try. I was very disappointed for a few reasons and ultimately disposed of the head.The first problem is this head doesn't handle very much weight. Only 5.5 pounds (2.5 kg). That is barely a camera body and lens. Mounting a telephoto on this actually feels like it might stress the head to the point of breaking because you'll come within a pound of the weight limit or exceed it if you're using any professional glass. And with shorter focal lengths, a monopod isn't necessary unless doing HDR work. So basically, you're only buying this because you're trying to stabilize a telephoto lens and camera body, but it's not really rated to handle the weight of a telephoto lens and camera body.The second problem is that the tilt doesn't lock tightly enough without feeling like I'm going to strip something and torque the plastic adjustment knob to the point of breaking. This was actually the specific reason I stopped using the head. I could never get the tilt tight enough to the point where the lens and camera wouldn't creep forward or backward eventually.The third problem is the 200PL-14 mount plate that comes with this head is a little too small and doesn't appear to lock solidly to the head. Every time I used this I was afraid that I would accidentally hit the release clamp and then lose my lens and camera in a fall.I love Manfrotto, but this is the only product they make that I actually felt like it wasn't safe to use. I'm honestly confused why there are so many positive reviews for this product. I can understand that the price point may work for a lot of people but it just wasn't worth taking the risk with my equipment. If you are one of the people that loved this product, then try some other stuff out! Maybe you haven't had experience with other gear and don't realize the limitations of this piece of equipment. This really isn't a good product by Manfrotto (which otherwise makes some of the best stuff) and there are much better tilt heads available by other manufacturers.The reason for 2 stars: I gave some leeway because the product is priced affordable but I took most of the stars away because I don't think the design was very good.

This is one of the best purchases I've made in a long time. I now have 3 Roku players, and have dropped satellite service and am saving the $90 a month I was spending previously. I get everything I need through Netflix and Amazon, so no need to pay for cable or satellite anymore for me.I already had a Netflix membership, so the Roku player was an very nice  extension of it.The Roku player is extremely simple to setup and use. One of the easiest things to setup I've dealt with in a long time. I have two connected directly with ethernet cables (using Linksys AC powerline connections, which are awesome as well), and 1 connected wirelessly. I have 10Mb DSL, so bandwidth is not an issue. That said, the players would sometime not select the highest quality stream (especially my wireless connected one). I resolved this by forcing the highest quality stream by using the debug mode (you press Home 5x, then rewind 3x, then FF 2X, all about a half second apart and that gets you to a debug screen. From there you can select a connect speed and override the automatic speed selection). Now I'm always running the best quality, and have never seen a reload like some other mention. HD looks great when it is available.So note that your broadband speed will make a difference in video quality. My 10Mb is fine, but if you have less than ~3Mb or so, you will likely pull lower quality streams.As for connection, I have used all of them (HDMI, component, and composite). No issues with any of them.The remote also works great, and does not need to be pointed at the box to work like the old style remotes used to require. So you can hide away the Roku player and it will still work with the remote.All and all, this has been a great purchase for us.

review_title: Excellent sound & functions. Could use better iPhone/Touch docking.
review_text: I wanted to replace my clock radio for one that charges my iPod Touch & has decent sound. After sampling several models at the Apple Store & researching online, I picked this one. As a note, there is a previous model of this unit & there are some major differences. Since both are still available as of 1/14/10, you might want to decide which one works better for you. The differences are:-The old one was shorter, designed for regular ipods. The Touch & the iPhone stuck out higher then the radio, which meant when reaching for the snooze or other buttons, you may hit the iphone/touch and knock it off.-The old one has a smaller clock display.-The old one had a BETTER ipod dock. It actually had a rest behind where the ipod stands, which could be adjusted from the back to go in or out. This to me was an amazing & rather unique solution.The one I bought, the new one described in this item listing, has a bigger clock display & is taller so the touch and iphone no longer stick out on top. However, the dock no longer has the adjustable backrest like the older model. Instead, it comes with 2 plates, one for the iphone, one for the Touch. If you have another ipod, you'll have to bring your own dock plate.The main problem with this dock plate solution is that my Touch doesn't fit with the protective case on (I use an Agent 18). Since taking the Touch out of the case everyday is not something I wish to do, I have to use this without any dock plates. The problem with that is the only support the Touch has is the dock port. This is obviously not a good thing in the long term. It makes using the Touch while it is docked a 2 hand operation; one to stabilize the Touch & keep it from pushing back & the other hand to make the adjustments. This is doubly frustrating since they had a much better docking solution in the older model.I plan on glueing a piece of foam or other material on the radio behind where the Touch would be to support it.Even with this caveat, I would still recommend this Sony. The price to benefit ratio, to me at least, is great. The sound quality and clock radio functions are excellent, especially when you factor in the price you paid.Things I like:-Excellent sound-Lots of options for the clock radio; 2 alarms, different days of the week, can wake up to ipod, buzzer, or clock.-Sleep function also works with listening to iPod-Comes with external AM & FM antennas. Picks up stations I listen to without a problem.-Electronic tuning for radio stations with presets-Plays Pandora & other sound apps through the system also-Buzzer for alarm works great. Starts off slow and low volume. Then increases in intensity after every hit of the Snooze bar.-Clock auto sets & remembers time if unplugged. Only have to set time zone when you first set it up.-Remote works with iPod and has decent range.Things I don't like:-Docking solution is a regression compared to the older modelOverall, I recommend this unit. If you don't use a case with your iPhone or Touch, than it would get 5 stars, IMO.

As expected, the Domke F-1x follows the same tradition of quality design manufacturing and simplicity as other Domke bags. Having owned a variety of camera bags from manufacturers such as LowePro, Tenba, Tamrac, Timbuk 2, Opteka, and others, I am familiar with many design and manufacturing aspects affecting practical usability and wear in the field. Throughout the years, Domke took many of these issues into consideration.The F-1x, as it's extended name implies, is a "Little Bit Bigger Bag."  I specifically compare the F-1x to theDomke 700-02A F-2 Bag (Brown Waxwear Finish)and it is in fact a "Little Bit Bigger." However, in my opinion, it still maintains the nearly same sleek design as the F-2.  It does not feel or look bulky, but it sure carries more gear.  The construction of the bag is near military specs in my opinion. Heavy duty stitching, quality workmanship, heavy canvas, strong hardware, etc...  This bag, as many people report of other Domke bags, will last many years under the roughest conditions.  The strap, in my opinion, does not need any padding because it is wide enough. Some might still prefer to use aDomke 725-310 FA-031 U.S. Post Office Shoulder Pad, which I actually own but rarely use.  The underside of the strap provides some type of rubber grip that will keep it from sliding and it does a good job.The genius of Domke bags is the streamline approach (simplicity) and limited padding.  This helps the bag avoid becoming cumbersome like theLowepro Stealth Reporter D400 AW Camera Bag. However, it is a tradeoff in gear protection and bag structure. Since the bag is canvas and with limited internal padding, when empty, the bag loses it's structure.  But really, who cares? And while Domke does provide theDomke 720-240 FA-240 4 Compartment Insert (Green), it's flexibility, size, and protection leave a lot to be desired. In fact, I replaced it with theCiesta Flexible Camera Insert Partition for DSLR SLR Lens (Brown / Large), which I found better suited for my partcular needs.  The Ciesta insert also provides better weather and dust protection since the F-1x does not come with a raincover.The bag provides a very large main compartment, two front pockets (flapped), two side pockets (flapped), and a magazine pocket backside.  The external pockets allow you to load them with a large amount or gear.What's in my bag today:-Nikon D300s w/ grip-Nikon D7000 w/o grip-4 Nikon prime lenses-Tokina 12-24-2 Nikon SB-900's-2 Pocket Wizards (in a Nikon case)-2 LensPens-Moleskine and pen-Small Giottos Rocket blower-Lowepro Memory Card Wallet-8 AA batteries (in 2xStoracell by PowerPax SlimLine 4 AA Battery Caddy Yellow - Holds 4 "AA" Batteries)-Camera Strap-Iphone-Grey card-Small reflector-Lumiquest BounceBesides being able to hold a ton of gear, the bag actually feels good to carry AND it does not scream "camera bag!" on first or even second glance. It is subtle and professional. The selection of a camera bag is a highly personal and studied task by most photographers. In my case, moving to the Domke F-1x and F-2 is more evolutionary than revolutionary. I eventually found my Lowepro bags were incredibly bulky and overly padded for carrying downtown, though they protect the equipment perhaps like no other. Now, I simply use the F-2 for street shooting and quick moving scenarios, the F-1x when I have to bring more gear for a generally static or slow moving situation, the F-1x or F-2 and theDomke Rolling Propack 220 Camera Bag - Blackwhen I have to bring all my gear to a static location shoot. My lighting gear (stands, umbrellas, grip, etc.) is all carried in a duffle type roller and only brought to static locations.As a side note, a cheaper alternative to this bag for some may be theOpteka Excursion Series C900 Full-Size Weatherproof Canvas Bag for Photo and Video Cameras, which is similar in design and possibly even bigger (I do not own it). And, for those concerned with the open (to the elements) aspect of the F-1x main compartment, the Opteka addresses this concern with an internal flap, under the main flap, that zips shut.

review_title: Excellent value for the current price...great P&S camera!
review_text: For the current price of about $200...the Panasonic Lumix DMC FX700 is an excellent value for this little super-compact, multi-function, and multi-featured P&S; camera...as long as you don't expect the image quality is the same as that from a DSLR, because it is not a DSLR! If you want a super image quality camera, then go buy a DSLR if you like to carry big/heavy camera with different lenses and equipment plus spending lots of $$$!When I first started my photographic hobby many years ago, I used SLR cameras along with telephoto & wide-angle lenses....I got tired of them so, I changed to smaller super-zoom models, such as Panasonic Lumix DMC FZ models. Even that, I still feel they are too bulky to carry all the time during traveling...I missed quite a bit opportunities because I didn't have the camera with me in some occations. So, I decided to carry good quality super-compact models for most my travelings.....the FX700 is just the ticket for me!I really like the 24mm super-wide-angle lense (with f2.2....do you realize how expensive that lense would cost if it is for a DSLR???)....it is perfect for taking scenery photos while traveling! I also like the fact it offers many manual settings besides just all auto settings (like most P&S; do)....very few super-compact cameras can say that! The LCD touch-screen is fun and functional, very easy to get used to...although it is measured 3" but, it seems a little smaller than my older camera's 3" LCD...I think it is due to the newer shape (newer 3:2 vs. older 4:3???). The new Panasonic FX78 model features a new 3.5" touch LCD...that should be better than the current 3" LCD!All I want to point out is don't let the image quality discussions stop you from buying this great little camera....the image quality is on-par with all P&S; super-compacts, if not better (the key is not to set ISO too high for better pictures)! But, with all the features it packed, no other camera in the same class can touch it for the current price ($200+/-)! Best of all, I can carry it all the time and don't even feel a thing! Once awhile, if I really want great image quality photos, I can always use the Canon 7D I bought for my daughter....but, I would never carry it for my traveling trips!

review_title: Excellent tone & volume for most casual listening. Not recommended for CD player use.
review_text: I bought this recently for 2 main reasons: I can listen to my iPod w/o using earbuds (while reading, e.g.) or when I'm on the patio with others & want to share the music; I play guitar & wanted to use it with my portable CD player (a relic, I know) when learning new songs w/o moving my Bose radio into my music room.With the iPod, it just works great. you can really crank the volume, but that level of loudness does make the speaker "dance" across the tabletop, something others have mentioned as well; also, it tends to distort when volume is pushed too high. However, I gives enough volume to be easily heard at a distance w/o cranking it up to the max. It uses a Lithium-Ion battery which, at a modest $15 surprised me. Lithium-ion batts hold almost a full charge for extended periods of time, are long-lasting and don't have "memory" issues as other battery types do. Using my iPod, I ran this (with a full charge) for 2 1/2 hours straight, at a moderate volume, without it needing recharging (I did recharge it, tho, which took under an hour). You can also use the speaker while it is recharging. That said, I'll mention that I use a separate Apple 5v USB wall-plug recharger rather than plugging it into my computer. It charges the speaker more quickly and lets me charge it anywhere.The speaker didn't work as I had hoped with my Sony portable player. When plugged into the "phones" jack, the CD player's volume control worked but, even set to the max, could not drive the speaker to anything other than a very low volume. Not surprising: it's an impedance issue not worth discussing here; when plugged into the CD palyer's "external" jack, the volume control on the player did not work (also normal) and the speaker was driven at "max" volume. In other words, without some sort of in-line volume control, the speaker is pretty much useless for use with a portable CD player. Nevertheless, this is no fault of the iHome product, and I expected as much. If iHome incorporated a slide volume control, as some earbuds do, it would solve the problem & be an improvement to my mind.NOTE: This is a "Mono" speaker. It can be combined with a second speaker, but only to provide "simulated" stereo.PROS:  Compact & lightweightGreat for travellingExcellent volume & toneLong lasting rechargeable Li-ion batteryInexpensive way to share MP3 music source with other listenersCONS:  Lacks integrated volume controlMono only unless connected to separate L/R speaker outputsAll-in-all, this is an excellent, sturdily constructed product well worth its price. Highly recommended for MP3 players!

review_title: High-end Mobo for Middle Class Cost
review_text: First I must state that I was building this for a friend, and he was very pleased with the result at a final price of $712 (Without OS) for a gaming PC that can make Crysis 2 and Skyrim cry.  I will include the exact specs below.  When I built this PC, it was the first one I was told to pay specific attention to looks on.  My pal doesn't know a thing about computer hardware, so I just picked as much AMD things as I could and tried to make everything red.  There are no red mobos out thee right now for less than $200, and that's a little too much for a color.  I had previously settled for a black Gigabyte board for around $120. I've had the opportunity (due to day job) to use lots of mobile speakers including several brands of this form factor of speaker (ones that open like an accordian) and I can say very clearly that these are the best I've used so far. (In fact, if you look on Amazon or a local store you'll see just how many speakers look very similar to this one.) Like most of the others, this speaker comes with an audio jack attached to the bottom and a charger via USB. But that's where the similarities end.XBOOM's USB charger is a Y cable that plugs in to the Smartphone or music source and the speaker leaving the attached audio jack free to daisy chain another speaker to it for more dynamic sound. In fact, one thing that really sets this brand apart is how they work together out of the box. If you aren't using the USB, the box also included an additional audio jack. The box also came with a travel pouch. A final touch on presentation is how the box looks so much better than the others I've worked with/ used. This speaker looks great in the package and would be a nice gift.The sound was outstanding. I love how these speakers work for both music and audio books. I played Dan Brown's Inferno (great book, BTW) over headphones and phone speaker then plugged in this XBOOM and was amazed that I was able to walk around a large room (30 by 15, with obstructions) leaving the speaker in the far corner without any loss in clarity or depth of voice. I could do chores while still listening to the book with no effort. Music sounds even better. On the loudest rock song - I tested it on Pour Some Sugar on Me by Def Leppard (because it rocks with very high sounds and some slightly heavy bass) - and could make out lyrics and riffs easily all around the room without distortion. As far as portable speakers go this one works great for what I use it for.The only thing I didn't like was that I chose pink (I was thinking of my daughter and how she plays her iPod Touch all the time) and the LED was blue. I'd have liked the LED to match the color of the XBOOM. Minor complaint, but I'm just being honest here.Overall, I'm really satisfied with this speaker and it has become my default budget (under $40) speaker.I was provided a test device by the manufacturer for this review.

review_title: Limited in function, but a beautiful product
review_text: FiftyThree's Paper is one of the best drawing apps for the iPad, being very simple and yet capable of rich creativity. It's that simplicity that makes it so fun - your tools are limited to a small number of drawing styles (pen, pencil, marker, watercolor, etc.) - and line weight is controlled by the speed at which you draw. It's this last aspect that many saw the Pencil tool that FiftyThree created as having more control over, probably due to expectations set by Wacom's long-revered line of pressure-sensitive drawing tablets.Let's cut to the chase: that is not how Pencil works. In fact, Pencil functions mostly as a typical stylus, which do have their merits over simply using your finger. There's no pressure sensitivity available (more on that in a moment) but Pencil does open up one capability that your finger cannot. When paired with Paper (by poking the tip at a circle in the tool drawer of the app), Pencil is the input device while your finger is a smudge stick. Draw a line, lift Pencil from the screen, and you can then smudge that line into a blurry mess, much the way one can with a line drawn on real paper, but this works for all tools in Paper. It also includes a handy eraser on the end opposite the tip.Pencil is beautifully designed, shaped like a carpenter's pencil (wide and flat on two sides, with a chisel-shaped tip) and, in the case of the model I have, crafted out of rich walnut wood. It's a pricy joy to hold and use. Pulling on the tip reveals a thin plastic case inside, the heart of Pencil where the battery and electronics are stored. One end of this terminates in a USB plug, from which the built-in battery is charged. The rubbery tip is removable and replaceable, as is the eraser, and the attractive cardboard tube the Pencil comes in contains one extra of each.But back to pressure sensitivity, as promised. FiftyThree has just announced that with the upcoming iOS 8 for the iPad comes the ability to enable pressure sensitivity. This is a game-changing feature that will make the Pencil a must have, transforming what is an exaggerated stylus into a truly useful tool, and a feature that will likely be built into, or activated in other styli. At that time, I might consider updating my review and, hopefully, adding 2 stars to my current 3 star rating.

Pros:The case is well made and the trays are easy to put in and take out.The unit comes with a pair of SATA-II cables and an entry level Highpoint Raid Controller.The Highpoint 622 Raid Controller drivers and management software work under Linux although the software is somewhat limited.Cons:This is was my third RAID configuration using WD20EARS 2TB drives which I have found to be very reliable and a bargain at around $67 each.The first RAID array is a RAID 5 configuration 4xWD20EARS connected to a 3ware 9650SE, this array has been running flawlessly for 2 years.The second RAID is 6xWD20EARS in a Cooler Master COSMOS case in a RAID 10 software configuration based on Ubuntu Linux. This has been running flawlessly for 6 months.I configured the TR8M in a JBOD configuration and created an 8xWD20EARS  software RAID 10 configuration on the same system as my existing Linux RAID box.During the RAID build one of the drives dropped out showing removed status.I did manage eventually to assemble the array but when I started copying data to it the array fell apart after an hour. I tried replacing drives swapping cables drivers etc etc.I contacted Sans Digital tech support, they told me they only support Enterprise RAID drives e.g. WD RE4-GP (8x$229.00) = $1832Oher Thoughts:The host machine can't see the SMART data, it's only available via the Highpoint UI. I verified the SMART data showed no errors for any of the band new WD20EARS drives I tried in this unit.Sans Digital did respond (after a week) to my email, however they were unwilling to pursue the problem any further once they discovered I was not using enterprise RAID drives.Why would you have a $65 RAID controller in a box that costs $1832+tax+shipping to populate?This unit should clearly state in the specification that it only supports Enterprise RAID drives. I am bummed that I have to pay significant RMA shipping and restocking fees for this unit which is technically flawed since the WD20EARS drives work fine on a regular PC SATA controller.
