review_title: Great features, works wonderfully (when it works)
review_text: I've had 2 of these units so far, and I'm about to return the second one. The first I shipped back immediately (love you, Amazon) because I had no video output from the HDMI output. I thought it was operator error, but I tried absolutely everything and followed the instructions in every way they could be interpreted, but could not get the on-screen display to come up. If I recall correctly, I even upgraded the firmware via USB to no avail.I have had the second unit for 7 or so months, and when I first got it, I noticed that any local EMI (electromagnetic interference) event (example: turning on the switch for a light within 50ft of the unit) would cause the HDMI output to lose synch with the TV, and I would end up with multicolored snow. Fortunately this was only an inconvenience, because changing inputs and changing back resolved the issue without fail.Unfortunately, a few days ago, the system lost its ability to properly interface with either my laptop, my TV, or both. My TV will detect a connection, lose it and start searching again, and repeats ad infinitum. It's not my laptop or TV's fault, because when I connect the two directly, everything works. Other reviews suggest that the HDMI interface boards in these units have both an infant mortality rate and limited lifespans, and I think my second unit just croaked.With all of that said, though, when this thing works, it is almost a religious experience. The sound quality is great, and I have a pretty keen ear for distortions. There is a reason Pioneer has been making audio devices for so long, and they've brought their best design practices to the audio section of this product. Oddly enough, I bought this product for the networking features it boasts (they are the most numerous among all home theater systems up to twice the cost of this unit), but I never found the time to set them up. The binding posts for the speaker outputs in the back feel a little cheap, but man do they make it easy to wire up when your speakers have banana plug ends!For the gamers in the audience, don't pass the video from your game to the unit. If you can (and with most newer systems, you can indeed), pass the audio to the home theater via optical (to the "TV" input) and pass your video straight to your TV. If you feed the video to the home theater, it introduces a teeny bit of lag, which can be enough to drive you nuts. It's worse if you have component outputs from your game (Y/Cb/Cr), because the conversion to HDMI takes some time.It all boils down to the title of my review. This thing is awesome, if it isn't DOA and if it doesn't crap out for a good long while. I'm glad I got the SquareTrade warranty, so I can hopefully upgrade to something more robust, but I will miss the cool little features of this home theater immensely (binding post speaker outputs, insane number of inputs, network connectivity, front-panel connection for an ipod, multiple surround modes, etc. etc. etc.).

review_title: An elegant and superb device.  It changes everything.  KISS.
review_text: OK, let's be clear.  The Pixel is something special. It is a work of art, an engineering triumph, and a game changer.  You really have to experience it to fully understand it.  I have been using Chromebooks for a couple of years, the first Acer model, then the Samsung 5 550 model.  Both decent for what they cost, but with limitations as far as quality and performance.  Samsung performed better, Acer actually had the nicer display.  So I use them and I understand ChromeOS and the experience it delivers.  I also understand the virtues it brings and the trade-offs you make in exchange.  I have some excellent Windows Notebooks accumulated over the years, a tablet and other similar devices.  So I know the gear, the OS, and what to expect.I read probably every review of the Google Pixel online and all the comments.  Thankfully, there were some good reviews in all the chaff.  But...you really have to see, touch, and use the Pixel to know.  That said, I ordered mine sight unseen...a man of faith.  ;)I have always felt the physical limits of the low cost devices were a mixed blessing.  Yes, cheap is good and has it's attractions.  But if you spend untold hours online as I do, you begin to long for a nice keyboard and, especially, a nice display for tired eyes.  Also, as someone who enjoys art, photography and videography as hobbies, a good display is something I require.  I appreciate the value of having a good one and am willing to pay for it.  Life is too short to endure the crappy displays so prevalent these last many years.  Thankfully, that's now changing.So...to me, the Google Pixel, while expensive, was something of which I could understand the value proposition on offer.  The minute I got mine, I knew.  This was what I had been looking for, not just in a Chromebook, but as my primary computing device.  Yes, damn expensive (even though I got a very good deal on mine), but worth every penny to me.Incredible display, gloriously clear text and beautiful colors and images.  Excellent keyboard, one of the best I have used on a notebook.  And absolutely the best trackpad/touchpad I have ever used in my life.  What a joy!  I feel no need for an external mouse at all and that's exceptional, because I feel that way about no other notebook.  Perfect right out of the box.  No false taps or errors.  It simply works.  (For those who have experienced the truly abysmal touchpads on many recent highend notebooks, this will catch your attention and I hear your sigh of relief!)An "intelligent" back-lit keyboard...best I've used (in a thin ultra-portable size device).  Fabulous tactile feel and response.  And the perfect size and shape!  The Pixel is exactly the right size.  That is no small thing.  And the screen is exactly the right size - and the perfect ratio (3:2), same as my photographic images.  At working distance, the width is correct for your eyes and the height as well.  I can live with wide displays and even prefer them for certain things.  But the 16:10 and 3:2 ratios have always seemed the best to me for general use.The quality of the display and the appearance of text reminds me of the very expensive typesetting machines I used many years back when I worked in publishing.  They had very expensive high resolution monitors for displaying fonts with precision...just as the Pixel.  My eyes are loving this.The build quality.  The elegance of the design.  If you have to work long hours online and then you are crazy enough to also want to play longs hours online...well, then you might rejoice at using such a finely crafted rig, one where you enjoy it every time you open the lid, or feel the solid mass and quality as you pick it up.  I value good gear highly, so this is a natural pleasure for me.The speakers are also outstanding.  The stereo separation is excellent.  The tonal qualities are very good for a small unit such as this.  Music is very pleasant.  Good clarity, plenty of volume.  The tonal range seems very good, bass is meager, of course, but overall the sound is very good and you can get by without headphones or speakers (though, of course, either will improve the sound).  Sound while watching videos/movies/Netflix/Amazon Instant Video and so on is also fine.  Never did I feel I had to go looking for my bluetooth speakers.  Perfectly acceptable sound for a portable device.It is nice to use something where everything feels right, works well, and you never think...oh, I wish it had a better screen, or keyboard, or whatever.  That is worth a little extra in my book.  Watching movies is fantastic.  Great contrast, black levels, detail, color...and it was weird at first.  I am so used to having to adjust the screen for the best image...here the image quality is constant...no need to adjust the display angle...move left or right, stand up, sit down...the image still looks great.  Amazing.  Good image quality and a good video/movie experience are a hard requirement for me and the Pixel delivers.The free terabyte of cloud storage is nothing to sneeze at, either.  It's free for three years.  At the end of three years, you get to keep everything you have stored there indefinitely, but must pay if you wish to add more.  Google Drive as it's called is well integrated with the File Manager and is very easy to use and quite convenient.  It's worth $1800 if you bought it outright, so a nice bonus.  (If you are a small business, this is something to consider.  A terabyte of Google managed storage at your disposal and an excellent high-end notebook...hmmmm.)The Pixel comes in a nice box with a magnetic latch (mirroring that of the Pixel display).  There is no manual, per se, but there are extensive 'getting started' items in an included app of that name and plenty of info online and on the unit itself.  And, of course, if you've already used a Chromebook, as I have, then you're all set.  There are a bunch of useful apps preloaded, such as the main offline apps you might want (Gmail offline is very nice), and it automatically syncs up with your apps, bookmarks, and other content as ChromeOS is designed to do.  So, whichever of my chromebooks I use, I can access everything and it will always be up to date.  Sweet!At about 8.75 x 11.75 inches (slightly larger than a sheet of paper) it's very portable and easy to handle.  And the solid feel and heft are a pleasure in use.  This rig is about as close to perfect as you can get as far as design and build.  It really is that good.  Really.The ChromeOS which elicits so much comment and sometimes scorn is, in my view, an equally great asset.  I have been in IT nearly all my life and have been living and breathing computers and tech since I was a child.  I have owned and used an incredible variety of units, from the Commodore, Apple, Amiga days til now, and worked with Linux in the late 80's and 90's, back when only a few hundred people had ever heard of it.  I have spent countless hours installing and maintaining both hardware and software.  I know the nitty, gritty details quite well.  I have power-user rigs at hand.  Maybe that's why I understand and value what Chromebooks are all about.  First of all, the security.  For daily use, nothing beats a Chromebook for security. Reliability.  Synchronization across all of your chrome devices.  Ability to easily wipe the unit clean and start fresh -- without losing anything, without having to constantly backup and manage disk, without having endless updates, viruses, and other annoying problems popping up.  The Chromebook is the most stable, reliable, secure computing environment I have ever used.  The hardware and OS are designed for security from the ground up.  Back in my UNIX Sys V days I championed thin clients and I still appreciate their virtues.Chromebooks are the perfect notebook for 80% of the people who just want to do the common things like read email, surf the web, post their photos, watch streaming video, listen to music, and so on.  Very few people actually edit video or photos at any level that requires Sony Vegas or Photoshop.  Having spent many hours helping friends and colleagues with computer and software issues, I know how happy they'd be with a Chromebook if they made the switch.  But, though it's popularity is growing fast, it's still a small part of the overall market.  That may well change.  The Pixel stands as a beacon as to what is possible.I just use it.  It works.  I enjoy what I'm doing and can focus on what I am doing and not the tool I am using to do it.  Though, as a techie, I do stop now and then to admire the elegance of the Pixel.  For me, it is well worth the price I paid.Pros:Very fast web surfing, faster than any of my windows notebooks. Web pages look great, easy to scroll and zoom.Gorgeous 2560x1700 Display has beautiful colors, contrast, and detail. Everything looks good.Solid aluminum body looks great, feels great. Top quality build.Keyboard is one the best I've seen.  Intelligent back-lighting works very well. Use Alt-BackSpace for DELETE. ;)Touchpad/Trackpad might be the best in existence.  Works exceptionally well.Elegant design means a pleasure to use, everything just works and well.  Ultra-portable.Chromebooks are very secure, data syncs automatically across devices, very stable and reliable.Includes a Terabyte of Google managed online storage (an $1800 value) - probably the best quality cloud storage on offer.Has a touch screen that works well.Cons:Expensive.  (But you get what you pay for.)ChromeOS wifi connect can be flaky sometimes (a known software issue which hopefully will be fixed by an update). [Update: this has stabilized over time with further updates and I now have no more issues in this area.]Keyboard missing keys like Delete, Home, End, Page Up/Down, etc. (There are equivalents, like Alt-BackSpace for DELETE)ChromeOS still maturing.  An occasional minor quirk here and there.Battery life is only 5 hours or so, could be better.  Mitigated a bit by the nearly instant on/off cycle of the Pixel. [Update: has not been a real issue, Pixel charges quickly, has an accurate battery gauge, and since you can instantly sleep/wake by just closing and opening the lid, easy to save power during the day.  I can get a full day, usually, with no problems.]Display is glossy and reflections can be an issue in some lighting situations, but very bright screen means mostly a minor issue.

I have three retractable clotheslines installed on the T poles I erected in the backyard.  The clotheslines are similar in design but represent three different brands, Butts (in the rear),  Sunline, and the Crawford-Lehigh RC40 40-Foot Retractable Clothesline. All are retractable 40-foot lines, but the Lehigh design differs from most other retractable lines I've seen or used, and I've gone through many of these things. The mounting bracket for the Lehigh is metal and swivels smoothly, a feature handy during installation and tightening of the line. I think that the Lehigh has a sturdier design because the body of the durable plastic case extends to give firm support for the mounting bracket. On other clotheslines only two thin pieces of plastic support the mounting bracket. Also note when choosing a retractable clothesline that the Lehigh uses a two pronged hook on which to fasten and anchor the line. Other models use a larger circular attachment on which to wrap and anchor the clothesline. I prefer the hook design.To get a nice, taut clothesline, pull the clothesline tight with one hand while holding onto a short segment of line pulled out from the line reel. Wrap the taut rope one or two turns around the anchor hook. Then pull slightly on the other end of the line. Let go and it will retract tightly into its protective case.Finally:Of the three clothesline mounted on our clothesline pole, we like the Lehigh best of all. It maintains its tautness during and after use, is easy to install, and is fairly simple to tighten.In less than a month the metal rivets at the pivoting points of the hinge are beginning to rust. Buyers may want to coat those points with spray oil, clear nail polish or a sealer.

I wish it would just light up and perform the action I've requested by pressing the button (I know that is not technically a screen issue, but it has to do with how the display operates when it is in sleep mode).Third, the display is so small that, once again, you almost have to place your eyes right up to the unit to view the information on the display.  The most important to me is the title and artist of the song currently playing, and less so the settings displays when I press the menu button.  This tiny screen just can't handle all the information displayed - all the important information gets lost in this myriad jumble of data contained on the screen.The unit is small enough to go most any place I would want to take it when I need music - traveling, in my car, at a party, etc.  It is only about 6 inches long and very thin, maybe 1 1/4 inches.If they could only fix the screen issue, and provide better directions, I might give these SimplyVibe speakers a higher rating, but as it is, the excellent sound doesn't make up for the flaws in the screen, and the button interaction with the screen.

review_title: Great surge protector with one major flaw
review_text: It's a wire jungle underneath my desk and I was previously using two power strips to power my little tech haven. I purchased this about a year ago on sale here on Amazon to minimize the clutter and organize the mess under the desk.I've now owned this surge protector for over a year, and it's been a tremendous help in reducing clutter. It's sturdy, stays flat due to its heft, has a sufficiently long cord and the plug is flat which is great for plugging it into an outlet behind the couch.This surge protector was so close to being perfect, but there's one major design flaw I'm surprised got past Belkin's engineers. The big gray power switch is like a hair trigger. You just need to depress it a couple millimeters and it turns off. Since this sits under my desk, my feet sometimes end up pressing and pushing against random objects. On three occasions now, all my devices powered off because I accidentally brushed against the power switch with my toes. The proper way to make the switch would've been to power it off once the button is fully depressed and snaps into the off position.Since then, I've learned to keep my feet to myself like I learned in kindergarden. If you buy this product, make sure to keep the power switch well out of reach of anything that might accidentally touch it.

review_title: Excellent standard zoom lens for APS-C cameras
review_text: Please don't take the Amazon star rating too serious - every lens has its pros and cons that I wouldn't want to squeeze into a single one-dimensional figure...A quick note about me: I have been into SLR cameras and lenses for more than 20 years - as a hobby in the beginning and professionally later. Maybe because of my technical background I started testing my own lenses quite a while ago. I have a (no longer so) little test lab of my own where I do 6 different image quality tests (after taking a lens out for a while).The EF-S 15-85mm f/3.5-5.6 IS USM is one of quite a few Canon standard zoom lenses for APS-C cameras. "Standard" of course refers to the focal range of this lens rather than its build and image quality which is certainly above standard. Made from high-end plastics and featuring a metal lens mount the EF-S 15-85mm f/3.5-5.6 IS USM does have a very solid feel. The ultra sound focus motor is very fast and acurate and even more impressive is the modern image stabilizer that compensates 4 exposure values.While the resolution of the EF-S 15-85mm f/3.5-5.6 IS USM is really good and rivals some L series lenses other image quality factors are not as good. Distortion is a serious issue at the wide end of the focal range but well under control for longer focal lengths. Color errors ("chromatic abberrations") are quite intense but only in focused areas of the image ("transverse CA"). Out-of-focus areas fortunately do not have color fringes ("axial CA") and the bokeh is very even as well. There is also some curvature of the focal plane ("field curvature") and a still healthy amount of corner shadow ("vignetting").Overall the EF-S 15-85mm f/3.5-5.6 IS USM is certainly one of Canon's high-end offerings and has its price tag for a good reason. Some might prefer theEF-S 17-55mm f/2.8 IS USMover this lens for its better maximum aperture and image quality. But of course that lens is bigger, heavier and has a much narrower focal range which limits one thing that's very important for a general purpose standard zoom lens: versatility. I have taken the EF-S 15-85mm f/3.5-5.6 IS USM on many trips with no regret...A much more detailed review of this lens together with all test shots, sample images and technical data is available on my website LensTests_com.

review_title: Good Set of Surround HDMI Headphones
review_text: I did buy this set from Amazon in June, but for some reasons the product page has been lost, so I am going to post this review under this new page and new reduced pricing. These are a very good set of headphones. Actually, the only one so far that use HDMI inputs, and can process lossless audio. The other models from Sony or other brands, all use the optical cable. A quick search on the internet will show you that optical and SPDIF versions cannot handle higher bandwidths. Unfortunately, these headphones are not available for the US market, and I had to buy them directly from Japan. Good news is, they ship pretty quickly. I received mine in 5 days, but I waited a little to write this review to be able to provide some information other than the operation and sound quality.Setup:Setup is easy. You just connect the adapter, charge the headphone, and plug the HDMI in and out cables, and you are ready to go. However, I had network interference between my Linksys E-4200 router and my network media player for streaming videos.These do work on the 2GHz channels, and their signal is strong. In fact, it is too strong that caused enough complications for my network player that I no longer could stream and watch x264 movies. My Sony BDP player kept restarting and giving error messages even on XviD files. Fortunately, there is a switch on the left side of the base receiver unit and you can change the transmission channel.  This switch has two separate sides. One side controls the functionality and can be set to either of "Auto" or "Manual," and the other side controls channels in manual mode in three positions: 1, 2, and 3. I had some luck with Manual and 1st channel. Other switches on the side are a Control HDMI that can be set to "Off," "Mode 1," or "Mode 2," and Display switch which only has "On," and "Off."Operation:Once you place the headphones on your head, it automatically turns itself and the base unit on. You have several controls right from your headphones cans under your fingertips. On the left side, there is only the power button, and charging socket. On the right side however, you can change the volume, input source, loudness, center channel volume, and DSP effects. You don't have to leave your seat to change these settings, and you can do it very conveniently.Sound Quality:I never had any 7.1 headphones before, but I have a good set of Nocs headphones for iPod. Compared to those, the sound is really good. I can't say they are as good as being in the theater room, or as good as Paradigm Signature series home setups, but for what they do, they are completely adequate. You can actually feel some of the lower frequencies and subwoofer effects on these. The maximum volume however, is not going to damage your ears' drums, but it is satisfactory.Shortcomings:1- The automatic HDMI switch acts weird. It does not work with Apple TV 3 at all. With my Blu-ray player, if I just want to watch a movie without the headphones, I have to go either to the base, turn the headphone base on, and change the input channel to HDMI 2 manually, and then turn it off again, or I should do the same process by putting the headphones on my head and pushing the buttons. It is a little inconvenient. I don't know why HDMI switch is not working all the time, maybe there is a glitch in their design or a uniform standard is not yet there.2- The size of the headphone is really big: My wife teases me of being a pilot when I have these on!3- No English operation manual! You have to figure everything yourself or translate from Japanese.Verdict:Do these worth about half a thousand of dollars? Same as everything else, it depends. If you watch too many TVs that your neighbors get angry all the time, it is probably the only way to go. There are cheaper optical versions like Sony DS6500 with half the price of these, but they are not as future proof as HDMI. If you are looking for a wireless headphones with good quality and bright future, then give these a try. If you do not need the wireless option, then you can also get theSony HMZ-T1 Wearable HDTV 2D/3Dfrom Sony. In that case, you better wait for the next version especially in Sony's world. Hope you got interesting information in this mini review.

review_title: Brilliant Sound & Mic Quality; Painfully Heavy
review_text: I have to admit being more than a little wary of buying such an expensive headset, but I'd been told time and time again that Sennheiser is the way to go for sound quality.  After reading countless reviews, both here and elsewhere, I decided to go ahead and take the plunge.The box itself was extraneously large and the packaging obtuse and unnecessary.  It's a waste of resources in my opinion, and probably an extra twenty to 40 dollars on to the cost as well.  Still, once I had them out of the box and realized just how huge the headset was, I was even more wary.  As a female gamer my head is smaller than the average PC gaming headset will comfortably fit.  I was really worried I'd be in for some serious ear-aches and neck strain, but they felt so light in hand that I gave them a go anyway.(Edit on 10.11.09:  I've had to replace the headset; the weight is giving me significant neck strain if I wear it for longer than two or so hours at a time.  A real shame; the quality otherwise is amazing.  I docked a "star" in my review because of the painful weight.)They come with no drivers to install, which is a definite plus, and as soon as I was on Vent my husband and friends all made note of the quality of my voice.  They certainly sounded much clearer as well, and so I was already feeling better about my purchase.  As soon as I launched WoW, though, I was immediately blown away.  I was hearing music and effect in the login screen that I'd _never_ heard before on my previous cheap USB headset, and I couldn't help but sit there, stunned, and listen.Actually playing with the headset on is going to take some getting used to -- it does hurt my ears, as the sides of my head are engulfed by the earpieces -- but I certainly can't hear anything around me, either!The amazing quality continued when I hopped to Left4Dead, and even on to Team Fortress 2 and other games I regularly play.  This is definitely an amazing headset, but my rating will remain at 4 of 5 until a smaller choice is made available for those of us who have smaller noggins.  I'll be buying a portable headphone set for listening to music on the go as well, and they'll definitely be from Sennheiser.

If you're looking for a USB 3.0 hub, this device is easy to use and performs as claimed.A USB 3.0 hub requires external power. The A/C adapter IS large and heavy, but at least it is a good 3 feet away from the power plug. I hate large A/C adapters that take up half the wall outlet! There is a nice long power cord to this hub, in fact; in addition from the 3 foot length from the power plug to the A/C adapter, I counted another 5 feet from the A/C adapter to the hub. Even though the hub comes with a 4 foot USB 3.0 cable, its power cord is so long that I had no issue stretching it from the wall outlet to my laptop, with plenty of cord length to spare.The USB 3.0 connector on the hub is B male. The hub itself consists of 7 USB 3.0 ports and 1 charging port. They are clearly marked. I ran several benchmarking tests on the hub, testing transfer rates on my various USB 3.0 external hard drives and flash drives. Even though I had 3 devices connected at one point, I noticed no drop in transfer speeds as I copied large files from my laptop via the hub to an external drive. The speeds were consistent, and in line with the rates I would get had I connected the USB 3.0 device directly to my computer: my rates ranged from 75-110mb/s. All my devices were recognized instantly by Windows 8 and assigned drive letters when plugged into the hub. I have also been able to select "safely remove" the USB drives, which is also a concern when using a hub. In the past, with other hubs I'd have to go into Device Manager to safely remove the hardware. I found that with this Anker USB 3.0 hub, it took about 10-15 seconds but the devices did for the most part eject successfully.The charging port on the hub also offers the 2 amp current at 5 volts for high speed charging, as advertised. Many newer devices, such as smartphones, have a higher demand for current than USB typically provides. USB 3.0 only gives 900mA output for charging when a device is plugged into the computer. USB 2.0's output is at 500mA; furthermore, this amount of current may have to be shared over more than one USB port. The result is a VERY slow charge rate when a device is plugged straight into your computer. Thus, the dedicated 2A rapid charging port on this Anker hub is a big added bonus, for example, if you don't have your phone charger with you, don't have the power outlet space, or are using this hub for a cleaner workspace. My Android phone charged quickly when connected to this port, at a comparable rate to the 2A wall charger I normally plug it into. As Anker notes, this port is NOT meant for data transfer; you'd have to connect your device to one of the other ports for that function. Now, the only drawback to this charging port is that this hub may not provide the wattage that your device needs, even at 2A and 5V. Wattage is calculated at V x A = W. I know that some Android tablets are higher wattage than 10W, such as the Asus Transformer line at 18W (due to its direct current voltage requirements). These devices may charge, albeit much more slowly than with their stock chargers. I tried my iPad 2 on this Anker charging port, and noticed that the charging indicator did appear on the iPad screen, but it charged VERY slowly; it took several hours longer to charge than with the iPad charger, comparable to the USB 2.0 (500mA) rate. The stock charger is 5V at 2A for 10W, same as this Anker charging port, which initially confused me. But I also remembered reading that Apple's USB charging standard for some of its devices actually varies from the universal standards for other USB devices. That's why there are chargers on the market with Apple and Non-Apple ports; these devices have different charging behaviors even at similar currents. I am not sure that at least at the time of this review that the circuit is designed for both iOS and non-iOS devices.

review_title: The Seagate expansion is a great little drive and I got it to work on the Mac!
review_text: The Seagate Expansion Drive is small, about 4 by 3 by 3/4 inches in dimension. Since the size of this device is so small, I think that it would be very useful for an owner of a laptop who is always on the go. Although this drive is advertised to work only on Windows, it will in fact work on the Mac (as I can personally attest to, having formatted it to work on my mac). As I found out on the web, after attaching your drive to the computer via the included USB cable, all you need to do is go to Applications/Utilities/Disk Utility, launch the Disk Utility program, click on the Seagate Expansion text + icon (on the left) and then select "partition" in the tab menu to the right. Next, choose, as your format, Mac OS Extended (Journaled) and then in the options button below and to the left of the partition tab window,  choose "GUID partition table" and then click Apply. Note: make sure you have not saved anything on the disk already, as anything on the Seagate Expansion will be erased! This approach worked fine with me. I definitely recommend this drive to anyone who either has a small amount of space on their desk or to anyone who is on the go a lot and needs a light external drive for travel whether you are a Windows user or an OS X user.

review_title: Fast, Loaded, but Check Your Display for Yellow
review_text: I anxiously awaited this summer 2010 update to the iMac line.iMacs offer a better value than one might think, and the space saving they offer compared to having many components spread out on a desk, make them an attractive offering from Apple.My current iMac was an aging model, summer 2007. The first iMac with aluminum enclosure. Honestly, however, it is not far off the machines of today particularly notebook models. The iMacs are aging nicely, and I'm sure this new model will too. iMacs tend to offer a better value than notebooks and because they aren't carried around, can have better reliability / longevity too.When I opened this new computer, I loved the widescreen display. This display is 16x9 similar to a television, whereas conventional widescreen computer monitors were 16x10 (including my old iMac). The extra width gives you more room to fit documents across your desktop (screen) while working. I like that.Furthermore, don't let anyone suggest that this is not a fast computer. Its 3.06 GHZ i3 processor includes hyper threading to give you up to four "virtual," cores. Some argue that this feature isn't useful, or that not enough applications utilize hyper threading. However, I was able to look at CPU usage and see video encoding software on my computer using the multiple threads. It was fast.I chose the 21.5 inch model because my desk is simply too small to house the 27-inch model. The 27 is absolutely staggering in size. I would choose it, if I had the room, but the 21.5 is far from being a slouch and is somewhat more sensible looking.It features standard 4GB of memory, which can be easily upgraded to 8GB by buying two additional 2GB sticks. A 500 GB hard drive being standard on this model will be plenty for all but the hard drive pack rats out there. While optical media is less popular today, do not forget this iMac can play DVDs and burn DVDs. Burning DVDs can also be useful to backup important data such as your family photographs. The speed of the drive is satisfactory, and it is the cool slot loading variety.A SD card slot is located under the DVD drive, to easily load pictures onto your computer direct from your camera's SD card.Why choose this 1199 model over the 1499 21.5 inch? Both are actually competent machines. The 1499 model gives you a larger hard drive (1 TB over 500 GB, so twice the size), and it has a faster graphics processor, which is useful when gaming and in other graphic intensive applications. While I chose the 1499 model, the 1199 doesn't lack much, if that final ten tenths of graphic performance and extra hard drive space is not something you believe you will need.The $1199 model is the RIGHT choice, unless you "know," you need the specific benefits of the 1499 model (larger hard drive and faster graphics processor).  Truly, this $1199 model is one of the best values of any Mac right now.The iMacs are great values over notebooks, if you don't need portability. You get more performance, more storage, and a massive display by comparison of a MacBook Pro. All at an attractive price.One of my favorite features? iMacs have included for the past year bluetooth keyboards and mice standard! That means when you take the iMac out of the box, if you have wireless internet, you can be up and running by simply plugging in the power cord. The Magic Mouse and keyboard are both wireless and work flawlessly. They are easier on batteries than you might think too, though they take easy to acquire AAs.Included software? The latest operating system Mac OS X Snow Leopard is included, plus iLife 09. iLife includes great and useful applications such as iPhoto, iMovie, and Garage Band.Someone new to Mac might consider picking up the Student/Teacher/Home edition of Microsoft Office for Mac. It runs beautifully and has a Mac feel to it, despite being a Microsoft product.My final verdict? I absolutely adored the machine. It was the fastest Mac I had ever used and a solid upgrade over my previous iMac. However, a week into ownership I discovered that the bottom and right side of my screen had a yellow tinge/appearance to it. A white background window, such as Amazon.com page, looked beautiful and white in the top left, but on the rest of the display, it turned yellowish. I had invested so much time transferring my data from my old iMac to my new one. I had to transfer everything back and securely erase the new one before returning it. I didn't want to go through that entire process again, during my busy time of the year, so I just returned it for a refund. Once I have some spare time to go through all the trouble, I will try again. Just be sure to check your display when it arrives because I have read some others having a similar display issue on the Mac Rumors forums.Overall, this iMac was an impressive update. It features the latest processors, plenty of storage, and offers one of the best Mac values. The display is a great size and aspect ratio, but be sure to check it for the yellowish color when it arrives.

Rather than simply repeat what others have said, I prefer to list the areas in which the Zen Micro, in my opinion, surpasses its chief competitor the IPOD...(I own both), and the areas in which I give the edge to the IPOD.First, let me say that, in general, I (very slighly) prefer the Zen Micro.Areas in which the Zen Micro outclasses the IPOD:User replaceable batteryBattery Life..realistically about 8-9 hours compared to about 5 with the IPODSound is somewhat better..definitely more bassThe Zen, in addition to having configurations for Classical, Jazz, etc, also has a five frequency graphic equalizer that can be customized, i.e. each frequency range can be strengthened or weakened as necessary. The IPOD's controls are very smooth.MusicSource and Itunes....I find this is a toss-up. The only disadvantage of Itunes is that you do not want to touch it if you own any other MP3 players..It is really proprietary in nature...Music Source is much more flexible with other equipment (such as pocket MP3 players of other maufacturers)Why do I then slightly prefer the ZEN....Sound, sound, sound....

review_title: Decent brick-powered hard drive —if it came with a working OEM cable
review_text: Normally out-of-the-box hard drives from big name brand manufactures work just fine. Mine didn't quite work. Sure it plugs in and runs but I wanted details. On both Mac and Windows, the drive reported 480 Mbps maximum speed —wait, that's USB 2.0! The supplied cord has a blue tip which indicates USB 3.0 but the speed wasn't there. Using Blackmagic Disk Speed Test, my suspicions were correct: The drive was severely underperforming. After switching the cable out with another USB 3.0 cable from a Transcend portable drive, both systems reported the Seagate connected at 5 Gbps. Sure enough the hard drive was now reading and writing about 197–205 MB/sec with a different USB 3.0 cable. I'm not totally irritated…at least the hard drive is okay but I'll have to spend a tiny bit extra for the advertised speed. Seagate, come on —how could you skimp on quality OEM cables?

Others have reviewed the player's capabilities, I have little to add there, most importantly, the player will produce full 1080 output over an HDMI link, and has Dolby 5.1/DTS it will output on optical, coaxial or HDMI ports provided HDMI is connected, same as Blu-Ray DRM requires.What is important is this: when you first set up the unit, it won't talk to your newer high resolution display, because that has an electronic signature that did not exist in 2006, when this player was built. If you simply connect this player out of the box using ONLY the yellow RCA video jack, most flat panel displays have one, you will see it come up in setup mode in a couple of minutes. Have patience, it will get there, just make sure you don't have anything else connected but the yellow RCA video jack and the Ethernet internet connection. If it gives you nothing after 3 to 5 minutes, use the V.OUTPUT and RESOLUTION buttons on the remote to make sure there is no entry on the LCD panel for V.OUTPUT, and 480i for RESOLUTION. If you get no response, it is still starting up, the first time startup takes forever. Have patience, it will get better.I know many reviewers have gotten update disks from RCA - there is no need for this, the unit will update fine over the internet. Once you have done the update, it will talk to any HDMI port equipped HD screen in the market today.Once you have a startup or signature screen on your monitor using the RCA video connection, push SETUP on the remote if the unit did not go into setup by itself. Make sure your Ethernet is connected to your cable, FIOS or DSL router. I keep a 100 ft Ethernet cable (too long for permanent use!) around for setting up the odd piece of equipment that wants to see an internet connection while it configures. This is one. Now go into the "Ethernet" section of the setup menu, into the DHCP option, and turn DHCP and DNS on. Confirm, and exit that menu section. Set the NTP server on, and the network speed to T1. Your player will now establish a connection with its manufacturers - wonderfully, after all these years, RCA and Toshiba have made sure the site the player needs is still up and running.Now go into the "General" section of the Setup menu, and go into Maintenance. Once there, go to Update, enter that, and confirm you accept the T&Cs.; The player will now begin to update over the internet. This can take anywhere from 15 minutes to half an hour, the player will turn off BY ITSELF after it is done. YOU NEED TO DO THIS at least TWICE, or as many times until the player returns an error, when it can no longer find an update to install.You will know you are successful when, once you've done the updates, the player turns on and no longer identifies itself on the screen with "RCA" but instead says "HD DVD" and "Toshiba". When you see the "No Disk" screen, you can connect your HDMI connector to your HD screen, use the V.OUTPUT and RESOLUTION buttons on the remote to change output to HDMI and 1080i, and you will have signal on your HDMI input (turn the unit on and off if you don't see anything on your HDMI input screen). Do any other setup you need to (my Dolby decoder is connected to the player using the optical port, so I set it up that way) and you are all set to enjoy your HD-DVD movies. There is no need to worry about 1080i versus 1080p, the player outputs 1080i, and all modern HD displays show that to you in 1080p, you won't notice any difference.

review_title: Outstanding consumer receiver for a media room
review_text: I am extremely happy with this product, and I'm very glad I didn't buy the Onkyo or HK I'd also considered. I wish I'd found this one, and all the positive reviews (and negatives on the others) sooner, as I spent far too much time researching and making sure I had the right one! This is the right one for us (and for most folks, I suspect). My prior receiver was an HK that cost 3x more, weighed 2-3x more, and didn't sound nearly as good. The surround on my prior-gen HK AVR635 was muddy compared to this Pioneer VSX-919AH-K. A few years back I'd also had a previous generation Pioneer Elite that cost a lot, and this new (and inexpensive!) toy is far more useful due to advances in technology.  For the first time, surround actually works well enough for me to use it.  I'm a bit of an audiophile, and I have a stereo-only rig for that; I actually got the VSX919AH-K for a media room for my wife. She loves TV and movies and has a pretty discerning ear, so it's a tough test to pass. She loves this thing. Once it was set up and she heard it she became very enthusiastic about the sound quality, how clearly she can hear dialog on both TV and movies, and all the convenience features (2nd room, etc.).  Happy wife means happy me, so that's a win!  I used the manual set up, which was quick and painless.  Reviewers are right; the manual is very nearly useless.  Fortunately, the default settings on most things work entirely adequately (you do need to do the speaker set up, either manually or auto), although there are so many features one could play with it for ages if one were so inclined.  For TV, movies, and FM it's outstanding even with just minimal set up and the rest on default settings. The remote is a bit confusing, with so many modes and buttons, but I think it is better suited to a "power user" who has learned many of the functions. Kids could easily change some of the not-so-obvious settings with this remote, leaving the system in a suboptimal configuration that might not be noticed but which was less than pleasing.  A universal remote, without all the rarely used buttons of the unit's dedicated remote, may be a good complement if that's an issue for you.  I found the VSX919 a better value than the VSX1019 (which has a fourth digital input and somewhat better video upconversion).  Reviews indicate you can get much better video upconversion in a good new Blu-ray player, so it's really not important in the receiver.  Blu-Ray players, and upconverting capabilities in general, are still evolving so fast that spending more on the 1019 to get capabilities that are already marginal just didn't make sense to me.  OK, on to sound quality! Stereo sound is good for the price, but a finicky user with high end tastes and fancy speakers and sources won't mistake it for anything but a good consumer unit. The sound tends more towards clarity than warmth or smoothness to my ears, but that's normal for mass-market solid state gear. I think this is a pretty good example of that, and a great value at the price. More than that, if you're in need of a home theater style receiver with a range of inputs, a ton of functions, and good surround...well, you'd be hard pressed at this price to do better than the VSX919AH-K.

review_title: old web camera video quality (in daylight), rubbish audio quality
review_text: I have been using this dash camera for about two weeks now. For what it is and how cheap it is, it is good. I can't complain for something that is only $21 dollars. It automatically records when the car is started (as long as the power is plugged in), deletes old recordings as new videos are shot, automatically shuts off when power is cut, and is fairly small and unobtrusive and comes with it's own window mount.The video quality is actually quite poor by today's standards but it's a dash camera and doesn't need to be amazing. It's okay in daylight. Pretty much just black if you're driving at night without street lights on the road. Barely registers my own vehicles' headlamps unless they are shining on something other than the road. It's better if there are street lights and other traffic during night footage.The audio quality is just terrible. I don't know if there is a problem with mine or not, but when i was testing it out in the house when I first got it, it constantly records a very annoying loud noise that doesn't exist. Subsequently, audio while driving has to be louder than the imaginary noise to register on the videos. I'm always blaring my radio so you can hear that, but being quiet or speaking soft around it just sounds like loud noise.There is also a constant defect or something that shows up in the audio on the videos every few seconds. Almost like a split second of radio static every few seconds.The camera has a full-size sd slot. I purchased a 16 GB card for it. It fills up pretty quickly. I do maybe three or four hours of driving a week, commuting and a few other minor trips here and there. It currently has only a week and a half of footage on the camera and it's full. But as I mention earlier, it automatically deletes old footage for storage of the new. If you want more of a buffer, however, I recommend you get the largest capacity this camera will support (32 GB). I personally find the 16 GB works just fine.This camera claims to have a 270 degree fish-eye lens. I am not entirely convinced but I have no way of proving it does or not. I have footage, but I have no idea how to submit it for reference with this review. It's mounted at the top of my truck's window, and it can't see both corners of the hood.The mount functions great. Very similar to any gps or phone suction cup window mount, but just with a camera screw mount point for the dash camera.For something so cheap, I think it functions great. I believe that for its intended purpose the quality is decent. Enough to show things moving around and if it's a clear day and sunny, you can get a few good details if you're close enough.

Of course, they are kind of expensive, when compared with the usual power strips and surge protectors, but you get what you pay for.  The cost of replacing/repairing motherboards or losing critical work in progress shouldn't be discounted.  Having seen them deliver results in a black-out situation, I would never use a computer for important work without them.I thought about getting one of the larger versions (1000, 1350) but didn't see the point.  There are so many things you can't plug into these units - space heaters, printers, copiers, etc. - that they're basically just for computers and monitors.  It seems like the small 850 model handles my robust Intel i5 systems with 23" and 24" IPS monitors and various external disks and whatnot, with ease and lots of extra headroom.  Each system is using (according to the LED display on the CP850) about 125 watts, while the unit is rated for 510 watts.  Even if you wanted 50 % headroom, you'd still be able to plug in a whole separate computer system and not hit a 255 watt limit.

review_title: Night vision for this price?!  A must have!...however...
review_text: I am going to describe my experiences (good and bad).The good:  It is absolutely amazing that I can have night vision for this price!  The slide switch to initiate IR/nonIR mode is really easy to reach and use.  Night vision videos are great!  They're not blurry at all and the range of the IR lamps on the camera reach at least 30 feet.  Such an awesome device!The bad:  This is quite possibly the worst regular (nonIR) camera I've ever seen.  Even though it is a 12MP camera, the images are horrible if you move slightly.  If you hold the camera perfectly still (which is necessary to do any time after 4pm due to the lighting), your pictures will come out fine.  If you are standing on a sidewalk ,it can be 7pm (during May - so still bright out), and take a picture of people walking, the people (which happened to be men and women with walkers) will be blurry.  The lack of a focus half-press shutter button irritates me.  To take a picture you just click the shutter button. It focuses on whatever it wants to focus then it takes the sub-par picture.The camera is extremely light.  Usually that is a good thing, however, it gives it more of a "don't drop this or it will break easily" vibe.  The buttons on the back next to the LCD screen are very awkwardly placed.  If you are using night vision in pitch black, there's obviously no light...therefore, you can't see what buttons to push.  You have to memorize the buttons by feel and association prior to going into the night to take pictures.  If you cup your hand over the screen to redirect some of the light from the screen, you can see the buttons.Night vision pictures are very blurry if you are not holding the camera completely still for more than 2 seconds (or until the picture appears on the LCD to view it).The flash on this camera is decent at best.  It takes at least 8 seconds (I've counted to 15 seconds on a new battery) for the flash to recharge before taking the next picture.  (Like I said, worst non-IR camera I've ever dealt with).To sum up everything:In regular (non-IR mode), horrible and blurry if you or the subject isn't standing completely still even during the day.  The FLASH is sub-par.  The time it takes to recharge between pictures is a huge issue.  This camera feels like it is ready to break (fragile) at any time.  It feels almost hollow.  The lack of features and selecting buttons in the menu bothers me.  Some buttons share functions  - which makes selecting and navigating a pain.  Also, the lack of a focus half-press shutter button irritates me.  To take a picture you just click the shutter button. It focuses on whatever it wants to focus then it takes the sub-par picture.In IR mode, awesome video.  It's not blurry.  Very awesome to have whether it is to ghost hunt or make your own home videos.  Pictures are not so great unless you hold perfectly still for a couple seconds until you KNOW the picture has been taken.  Hard to find the button you want when it's dark.  The buttons aren't illuminated by any light on/behind the button.  You have to learn the buttons perfectly to know which you want to press.Overall it's awesome to be able to take great videos in pitch black and photos if you hold still.  Horrible regular camera.  They shouldn't even have the regular camera as an option.  It's an insult to real/legit 12MP cameras.  IR photos/videos completely outweighs the 99 problems it does have.

review_title: Stay away - proprietary software nightmare kills PC performance
review_text: I wanted a simple external add on hard drive for my PC, what I got was an unwanted custom back up software solution that killed the performance on my PC.Buyer beware.  If you buy this device, thinking that you will get simple USB external mount hard drive, you are not buying the right machine.  The WD installation process drives you to install WD Smartware that is a custom back up solution that installs into root of your operating system.  It automatically tracks all changes you make on your PC in order to decide what it wants to back up (you have no choice in what files are backed up).  Over time, the performance of this software will gradually degrade your PC performance as it stores more and more back up data.The WD drives contain the WD Smartware on the drive, you can not kill this software off of the drive without a special program that is located somewhere on in WD tech support pages.  Once installed, you can not get rid of the Smartware software as even administration privileges are not sufficient to run the uninstall program.  I have yet to find an uninstall link on the tech support pages at Western Digital that is not broken or moved.  I had to resort to just deleting the directories from my machine.Some users may find the simple interface and back up process to be to their liking.  If you are buying this as an external drive and not as a simple, brain dead back up solution, then this drive is useless.

I have owned this Fuji F-480 camera for about three weeks now. The F-480 is small, has a wide angle Fujinon lens (28mm-112mm), a 4.00x optical zoom and provides a higher resolution (8.2 MP) than my Fuji Z-3.  This new Fuji f-480 camera seems to be a durable little package that should withstand a few bumps along the way.Those things and the comparatively low price gave me reason to make the purchase.  Admittedly, the differences between this camera and my Z-3 are not large, but significant to me since I use my cameras to take landscape pictures while traveling and I have been looking for another small format camera with a wide angle lens.  The wide angle lens on the F-480 is just what I needed for my landscape shots.They refer to ultra-compact cameras like this one as "entry level" which implies they are somewhat toy-like, but that couldn't be farther from the truth in my opinion.  The capacity of these tiny compact cameras is amazing to me having used 35mm film equipment extensively over the years.I have gone through the entire instruction booklet trying out each attribute found in the F-480 camera.  Everything works as it should, but don't expect perfectly exposed pictures when using a number of the AUTO settings.  It takes a bit of experimentation to determine how some of them behave.This is a Japanese camera made in China, but the quality is very good.  The price on the camera represents an excellent value for what it provides in photographic choices and performance.  I paid about $180 for mine, but fully expect to see that price drop a few Dollars in the near future.  The camera is new to the market and represents one of the latest additions to the F-series Fuji FinePix line.  It is the next edition of the F-470, but is (in many ways) an entirely different camera.The menu of settings is extensive yet easily understood and used.  The only complaint I have is with the highly touted anti-shake (picture stabilization) setting.  It can be set from the mode dial on the back of the camera, but when it is activated many other shooting options are apparently unavailable.  I can set my older Fuji Z-3 on `anti-shake' from a dedicated button on the back and the other shooting options remain accessible.  Not so with the F-480.  I see that as a shortcoming.  I shake all of the time (taking pictures at the beach, under fluorescent light or in the snow) and would like my cameras to compensate for my twitching no matter what shooting options I choose.The F-480 accommodates both x-D and SD memory cards, but not at the same time.  I suppose that attribute advances the versatility of the camera.  However, the feature is not particularly important to me personally.  The large 2.7-inch anti-glare LCD display is clear, crisp and provides a good idea of color balance prior to shooting a picture.  There is no eyeball view finder on this camera, but I don't miss it.  Not many of these modern mini-digitals have a separate view finder anyhow.The only real measure of this camera is in the photos it is capable of producing.  This is not a big cumbersome high end professional camera with a super fast shutter and a high powered lens, but is just great for family photos or getting that quick shot while traveling.  I am satisfied with the passable quality of the pictures I have shot so far and believe the camera will give me the photographic versatility and image quality I require as I begin using it on my next trip abroad.

I picked up a laptop recently, and I've been hauling it, it's power cord, and mouse here and there in a shoulder messenger bag.  That was working just OK, but when I had a chance to check out this backpack I jumped at the chance.I have an Acer Aspire 5560 Series laptop.  It's 15" x 10" x 1.25" and it's a perfect fit for the designated laptop sleeve built into this backpack.  The laptop compartment has thick foam protection on both the front and back.  Oh, if you have a laptop any bigger than this (length x width) this back will be too small.  Frankly, there aren't many laptops out there that I've seen lately that are much bigger, though there are 17" units around.  They won't fit in this pack.OK, what else?Likes:1) It has a comfortable air-flow design so air can flow along your back while you have it on.  There are padded sections by each shoulder blade and the small of your back.2) The straps are wide, nicely padded, and fully adjustable.  If you've ever been frustrated because the snap-straps between the shoulder straps in the front are on the wrong place, this is a pack for you.  The snapping cross strap traverses up and down most of the distance of the straps.  There are also neat little velcro straps that allow you to secure the ends of straps that extend below the bottom of the shoulder straps - so this is a real plus if you don't like dangling straps.3) There is a webbed coat-hook loop at the top of the pack AND a large padded handle.  Yeah!4) Laptop/tablet zipper compartment is, as mentioned above, large enough to accommodate a 15.6" screen laptop.  There is also a sleeve in there that is large enough to accommodate a full sized iPad or similar sized tablet.5) Main zipper compartment: This is large, but padded only on the side facing the laptop compartment.  Anything in here is fully exposed to bumps and bangs.  It's good for books, binders, etc.  There is also a mesh zipper pouch (good for things you want to see at a glance when you look in this compartment.  There's also a slip-in compartment - no zipper.  This could be good for papers, folders, etc.  Oh, I like that this compartment has two zipper pulls.  Cha-ching!6) There is a second, smaller front zipper compartment.  It's also large enough for papers, pens, calculator, etc.  It's got mesh and non-mech slip pockets for the little stuff.7) There's kind of a stealth zipper pocket with a side zipper. This pocket is big enough for a modest-sized lunch bag.8) There is a second stealth zipper pocket that opens a thin pouch on the back of the pack under the padded lumbar support.9) There is also a small, plush-lined pouch at the top of the pack.  This is obviously for personal electronic devices - cell phones, ipod, etc.10) There's a second handle on the bottom front of the pack.  What a great idea!  This would come in handy while stowing or retrieving this from airplane overhead bins, etc.11) I like the rubberized zipper pulls.  They are comfortable, and all zippers operate smoothly.Dislikes1) There is only one zipper pull for the laptop compartment.  I'd prefer two.2) The small slip pockets in the second outer pocket won't hold things in place if the pack gets inverted.3) I wish the small plush zipper pocket were crush resistant like you find on theThule EnRoute Escort Daypack for 17-Inch MacBook Pro and 10-Inch Tablets - Black (TEED-117).  That would make it more useful for storing things like sunglasses and increased protection of personal electronics.4) There are two small zipper pockets on the sides of the pack, but, well, I guess you could put your keys in there, there's a plastic loop you could clip them to, and the other one has an opening to accommodate a speaker cord.Wrapping things up...my laptop is already home...5 stars, with only a few minor shortcomings...it looks like a real winner!

review_title: Not perfect, but a good entry-level 3D platform
review_text: Talk about a modern feature set. Whether or not firmware will upgrade HDMI 1.3 or not on your existing system, choosing a system with an HDMI 1.4 repeater for all inputs is a good idea and this unit certainly has the skill to do so. Let's jump right into the pros and cons of the unit because it certainly isn't perfect. As a long-time user of Pioneer/Sony ES/Denon receivers, I think Denon's done a fair number of things pretty well.Pros:- HDMI on-screen Audyssey eq and assignment functions. This helps a lot because the small screen on the unit won't suffice. Using the same technology as the Alpine imprint system (which works great in the car), you can tune to your environment. Not unique, but well done all the same- HDMI repeater for all inputs. This is a pro and con, read more to find out why.- HDMI 1.4 for future 3D capability. Plan for that future 3D screen (Especially good if you already own a PS3)- Denon reputation and audio quality compared to similar priced Pioneer/Sony units- Price, very reasonable for the feature setCons:- Power rated at 6 ohms, which, as you might expect means that it doesn't have quite the juice of its rivals (70w/channel at 8ohm). I definitely notice the lack of power with many inputs more than my previous Sony unit- HDMI repeater is not particularly good with component inputs. Using the component inputs on the Wii, direct connection to the TV is vastly superior visually to the HDMI conversion the Denon performs- Relatively steep learning curve. You will find a little frustration with some of the advanced functions as the manual is a bit tedious. This is par for the course though, so nothing specific to Denon.

I bought these to replace a simple pair of Sony SS-B1000 bookshelf speakers.  Unfortunately, the Sony's blow these away.  I bought them for a small office and use them for music and NPR on a simple Sherwood RX-5502 receiver.  At the same volume and settings, these speakers were terrible.  I could not even hear the full range of speech of the people talking.  I had to increase the volume another 50% to get the same out of these speakers, yet even then there was so much less depth to the sound.  With music, the sound was only from the mid range, with no bass to speak of and very little at the top range.  I like to listen to music as I work, so I keep them at a moderately low volume.  Wiht the Sony's, I get the full range of the music even at lower volume.  With these, it seemed that the more quiet, delecate notes simply were not enough to get the speakers to make a sound.  I thought maybe they needed to be broken in so I left my stereo on a local pop station over a 4 day weekend, which gave the speakers more than 80 hours of continuous play at moderate volume.  Some improvement but still such a limited range.  I have decided to return these.  Maybe of you play them at a much louder volume they will be better, but they were not good for my use.  I don't love the Sony's but they are good enough.  If you have the shelf space, the BIC DV62si speakers are $115 and are just wonderful for their size.  They are just a little too big for my shelf space (have a pair at home).

review_text: I got this having used, actually still using, the original o!play. I liked the simplicity of the original and was looking to expand my recorded tv and archived movie viewing to another tv. Naturally, I went right to Asus and picked up the oplay mini. I looked at the ports, but it didn't have Ethernet. Not a huge deal I have a wireless n access point about 10ft from where I was planning on placing the mini. So, I ordered the mini. It wasn't until I received the device and tried to add it to my network that I discovered that it doesn't have any form of network connectivity.I had to return it. I wish I didn't. The o!play is by far my favorite device. I'm not looking to stream from Netflix or Hulu or vudu or Pandora. Nor am I looking to play angry birds or post on Facebook. The o!play was the perfect device. If only the mini has some form of network connectivity.Now, I don't see a huge market for this device. Who keeps their entire video collection on a portable hard or USB drive? The option to have the ability to play video from removable devices is nice, but the ability to stream content from another computer, NAS or DLNA device is virtually mandatory among this segment. So for that reason I'm giving it 3 stars. It will still play virtually everything you throw at it, more than the WDTV Live which could only play a subset of the files the o!play handled successfully.

I actually purchased this drive in an effort to beat the encryption.  I thought if the drive was stolen by somebody they could reset the drive and use a data recovery program to recover the data.  I was wrong.  When reset, the data remains forever encrypted and unaccessible (when you reset the drive, nothing is visible on the drive).  Most crooks would be too stupid to think of this anyway.  I had a large external hard drive hanging around on the floor near my computer, the kind that required a power chord.  I realized that any crook who broke into my apartment would have easy access to my data if they stole my drive.  So I put all that data onto this Padlock drive and placed the old hard drive [as backup] in my safe.  Now I just leave this drive, which to a crook might just look like a Keyboard Keypad or calculator, lying around.  If it gets stolen- I'm out the $100 I spent on it, but I don't have to worry about them accessing my data.  Also, I can bring all my data to work now and access all my files all the time.  Even though this thing is USB powered, there really isn't any noticeable difference in speed between that any my 7200 rpm external hard drive.  I love how small and convenient this thing is.  I would highly recommend it.  Just make sure to have a good password.

review_title: TV will keep you happy until 4K is perfected & prices lowered
review_text: *Updated after 9 months*Overall: I have had this TV series for about 9 months now.  I am VERY pleased with the purchase.  Glad I went to the 60".  The previous ES8000 model was plagued with cloudiness, banding--both gone in F series(55/60" tested).  Flashlighting is minimal on this set and improved over the ES series.  I needed a LED TV upgrade and was on a budget ($2500 OTD/with tax) that didn't place me in the local array dimming technology zone(I believe to be the best type of TV right now).  Plasma's are too reflective for my environment and the extra heat is unwanted (check out theSamsung PN51F8500though, sounds like it is well liked).Right away I noticed how solid the TV itself felt.  IF I had to do it over again, I would definitely recommend the 55" OR 60" F8000 for others to buy over the ES8000.  Just ensure you get the best deal for it as the MSRP is way overpriced.  For ES8000 owners...I wouldn't upgrade.  No way.  This TV will hold me over until 4K's are on the market for awhile, helping companies perfect the tech and lower the price.Be wary of some of these random 1 star reviews, as many users do not even own the F series TV!  Or they had an issue because they didn't have the right settings configured.  If you read the comments, under those reviews you will see they fixed their issue.  I feel this TV rates 5 stars as I believe this tech is at it's "ceiling" and there is minimal room for improvement using edge lit tech.For those who wish the short and simple, thats it!  Keep reading for indepth review.Current FIXABLE problems with firmware 11.16:-3D setting "light control" settins on "high" resets to "low"-Netflix, Vudu, Amazon Prime, DLNA video's all have cinema black disabled(supposedly this can be fixed in app updates but its remained off)Picture Quality: The picture quality on this TV is fantastic especially after a few color tweaks (posted below).  The blacks are so DEEP compared to my last tv(direct lit led).  There is a SMALL amount of flash lighting in all four corners(more noticable on 60" when in PC mode); I believe this is a fault for ALL edge lit tv's as that is how the image functions.  I can only notice flashlighting in all black lighting with something like movie title in middle of screen and black on rest of screen, or if in PC mode with a most black screen.  Unless you are really looking for it in a black screen and concentrated on a corner you will not notice flashlighting.  Also when testing it, please play a movie or something, as when the menu is up or the TV states "check source HDMI not connected" flashlighting is more evident and nobody uses their TV to watch a blank screen.Viewing Angle:  Fairly limited until it begins to wash out(ALL edge-lit tech will have this issue).  You will notice the farther off center you will notice more of a degradation in picture quality.  This doesn't bother me as my "seat" is always right in front.  Most end users are not as particular or picky as me when it comes to picture quality, many will not even care or notice a difference until a more extreme angle(an angle you can't reach in the room my TV is in).  I sit about 14 feet away and if I go 4 feet to either side, I cannot notice the picture washing out.Price:  MSRP is overpriced.  Ensure you get a good deal and get a store to pricematch to best price you can find.  The 55" should be around $1730 and 60" $1945.  I attempted to get Amazon to price match a store that was not on their official authorized list and they refused (attempted multiple times, through different numbers and chat).  It was a $500 difference.  When I was looking I found the 60" as low as $2400 at the time. I ended up having the local Best Buy price match this tv for me.  I bought my last flagship Samsung TV in 2008/9.  The A850 model(now in bedroom, this TV still satisfies me and looks better than many lower model new Samsung TV's on market today).Stand:  I hated the TV stand.  To feng shui for me.  My wife loved it though.  It actually fit our TV stand, be warned if you have a small TV stand it will not fit...this stand is very wide.  This helps the tv to appear to "float".  It even came with some sort of oversized plastic screws and rope that ensured a child couldn't pull the TV down (smart).  I planned on mounting this TV though like my last TV, so the stand doesn't matter much to me.Wall Mount:  I opted for a low profile wall mount from Monoprice.  The one I picked was $14 and the product ID number is 5918 from monoprice's website.  I linked the same mount below through amazon but it is $8 more here.  This places the TV pretty much ON the wall with this mount.  It's about 19mm off of the actual wall.  I was able to run the power cord and a Redmere technology HDMI thin cord(10ft for $17 over at Monoprice..same cord is cheaper on Amazon)Monoprice 10-Feet HDMI Cable with RedMere Technology.  It came with all the necessary bolts and spacers for the F8000 (1 small/1 large on top bolts and 2 smalls on bottom bolts).Monoprice Ultra-Slim Low Profile Wall Mount BracketHeat: Had the TV on for 12 hours and couldn't find any hot spots or to much heat to make me worried with how close the TV was to the wall.  Was an issue on certain ES8000 sets last year causing a V spot of cloudiness.Remote: The remote is solid and touch part feels just like a laptop.  It's not a gimmick at all and actually works great.  I find it easy to type with there on screen keyboard.  Came with crappy batteries so I opted for some standard spare ones I had in the house. I bought this to replace an older, now broken JBL OnStage that I used on my desk and carried around in my briefcase. I also considered the Bose SoundLink and Jabra Jambox, which were much more expensive.Pro:1. Looks good - nice quality plastic, cloth-covered speakers, no sharp edges from manufacturing molds. Textured top panel with the docking connector and volume buttons.2. Decent sound for its size. I've used quite a bit of Yamaha stuff over the years and have always been impressed. A nice remote control is included that mimics iPod functions when your iPod or iPhone is in the charging cradle on top. Works great and I got at least 20 feet or range from it.Con:1. It's plastic. We'll see how durable it turns out to be from frequent moving around.2. No battery option, but I knew that and don't really want to carry extras around. I always have AC available so that's a non-issue for me.3. Bulkier than the newer units like the SoundLink and Jambox. On the other hand, the stereo separation should be better because of that.Summary:A lot of wireless, Bluetooth/Airplay speakers have come on the market recently. I went more basic (no compressed, wireless streaming to degrade the sound), saved a bundle and am getting better sound than I expected. Unless you really need/want battery power or wireless, this unit is a good choice.

review_title: Excellent product for it's size and price
review_text: This unit was designed specifically to work with iPods. It comes with universal docks and inserts to fit popular docking iPod models. It worked perfectly with my 32GB iPod touch, my hard drive based 80GB iPod, and with my nano model. It will also work with non-iPod players using an auxillary input.This dock is very light and would be very easy to take with you on a trip. In fact, holding it in one hand and my 80GB iPod in the other, they seem to weigh about the same.It is very easy to set up and to use. The instructions are well written; always a big plus! Setting the clock could not possibly be easier. There is a button on the back that automatically sets the clock to whatever time the iPod connected to it is set to when pressed. The alarm feature is really easy to use and I like the way it works. When the alarm's wakeup time is reached it turns on the iPod and gradually increases the volume to whatever volume was last set. I like the fact it doesn't startle you.For such a small and light device, the sound is very good! Don't expect to be able to get really loud rock music. Expect reasonable volume for the size and price and you'll be pleased. One recommendation that I would make, in order to get the most out of it's sound, is to place it in a corner with the 2 speakers facing the walls (about 1 to 2 inches from each wall)  so that the sound reflects off the walls. This will give it a sound that seems larger and more spacious than simply setting it in an open area like a table top.It is powered using 4 AA batteries or with the AC adapter that comes with it. It also comes with a round watch-type battery that stores the settings so that you can move it from one location to another without losing the stored settings. As long as all the batteries are good, this unit will work even if the AC power was lost for some reason.There is a dimmer with 4 settings. The dimmer button also serves as a snooze button which will silence the alarm for 9 minutes and then come on again... There is a sleep timer with four settings: 90, 60, 30, or 15 minutes.Overall, I am very pleased with this product and can definately recommend it. It is very well designed, easy to use, and all the features work as described.

The Zoom X7N is the same price as the Actiontec GT701D (which I also have), but you get more for your money with the Zoom.  A router/bridge for less than 50 bucks.  What more can you ask?Not that it will be useful for most shoppers, but I have to make Linux comments.  Reference is Xubuntu 12.10, 64-bit.  One slightly frustrating lesson was that the X7N does not appear compatible with the Xfce Network Manager.  It is not necessary to uninstall the mgr though, just deselect 'enable networking,' and uncheck the autostart of the service in 'session and startup' in Xfce settings mgr.But first download and install wicd and the gtk front-end.  For me, no settings in wicd-gtk required changing.  It autoloads, but can also seek on restart.  No dropped connections so far.Somehow the rom in the X7N has to be written with the ADSL provider details.  Communication with the configuration mgr is via an ordinary web browser, where usrname+password information is provided.  That's all.  The configuration mgr can snoop out everything else. However, I had trouble accessing the Zoom config mgr in Linux (ditto with the Actiontec), but I think Xfce network mgr was still alive and interfering at that point.  Anyway, I took the easy way out and set it up in winXP.  Since personal info and environment details (telephonically speaking) for win and lin are the same, it worked super slick at the next Linux reboot.The X7N broadcasts WiFi automatically each time it is connected.  A good strong signal which my Galaxy Note reports as 65 Mb, though my true ADSL is a puny 1.5 Mb.  Knowing the WiFi is always there is a nice feeling.Zoom also has email support, which is quick if not too insightful.ADSL ethernet bridge solutions for Linux are few, especially ones which are cheap.  The Zoom and the Actiontec are two.  Nothing against the Actiontec, but I think the Zoom is a better deal.

review_title: Where are the high pass caps?
review_text: These speakers sound great (for being budget marine speakers). The sizing is bizarre and has been addressed in other reviews. My main complaint is that there is no high-pass capacitors to cut the low end. If these are rated for 80Hz there should be a cap to prevent block out anything lower. I run these off of a head unit as I'm sure many people do. There is no crossover but it desperately needs it to prevent your speakers from distorting with your bass. I used two 470uF 35V bi-polarized caps (ECE-A1VN471U) which are close enough to decrease the deep lows. Immediately I noticed I could turn the stereo up without the sound of the speaker dying out on me. For under $1 a piece I highly recommend doing your own research for your setup and determine what value you need.All things considered I'd give the speakers four stars with the proper high pass setup because they are a great value. Also the rigid plastic grill is a nice touch as far as durability goes.
