review_title: Shure SE215 vs Klipsch Image S4
review_text: Let me start off saying that for price on Amazon, the Klipsch headphones are a great buy. I have owned them for about 6 months before they started shorting out. Im not sure if it was the headphones themselves but I tend to run through earbuds rather quickly. That let start the direct comparison.Comfort:I would have to give a slight edge to the Klipsch headphones over the Shures here. The Klipsch soft ear sleeves just slide in but there is a pro and con to everything. The Shure's use a foam tip that expands in your ear. It creates a much better seal and therefore has better noise-isolation then the S4's. My ear sometimes feels a little discomfort after wearing them for a while but i may just need to switch the smaller sleeves they provide.Secure Fit:The SE215 has the clear advantage hear. The headphones are tricky to learn to get in but once you do the very nature of how the sit in the ear makes them much more secure. The headphone cord comes forward then loops over and behind the ear. Tugging on the cord rarely budges these things. Meanwhile, I have had problems with the S4's coming out, especially if I'm working out.Ease of use:The S4's have the edge here. You simply push them in. The SE215's require to roll the foam tips before you put them in to get the best seal and to loop the cord over your ear. that can be annoying if they fall out while running. That said they much less likely to fall out. The S4's have alternate of putting them in that involves looping the cord as well but i found it to be uncomfortable.Noise-isolation:Advantage goes the SE215s for the reasons mentioned before, the foam tips.Construction:Both seem well constructed. The SE215 feels more substantial and the cord is much thicker. It seems less prone to tangling.Performance:As i wrote this I listened to the same song once with each pair with the same EQ and volume settings. The SE215 were louder and sounded cleaner for the same songs and settings. The bass was deep and the highs were clear. The S4's are no slouch either. They outperform most other sub-$100 earbuds out there.Bottom line:Both are a great set of the headphones. The SE215's are $100 and the S4's are $60. Do the Shure's justify the extra $40? yes. but its all personal preference. The S4's are a steal for $60. That said I really appreciate the superior performance, fit, and noise-isolation.

If you computer lacks a CD drive, you can download and run the driver package from the Edimax website.  I had my adapter installed and ready to use after a couple minutes. I didn't expect perfect speeds, but I was blow away at what I experienced under such difficult connectivity conditions.Overall, theEdimax AC600 Wireless Dual-Band Mini USB Adaptercan help if you have an inadequate internal wireless card, or if you are looking to improve connectivity already provided by your internal wireless card. The feeling of each key is very adequate and the comfy feeling of the palm rest is really nice.  It has an LCD display showing key statuses like "Num Lock" and the battery level.  With the combination of an 'Fn' key you see on the notebook keyboard, you can launch Microsoft Word and Excel easily.  And the convenience of the wireless keyboard is always nice. I use this key a lot to do calculations.The mouse, MX620 is a rather plain mouse from Logitech.  I am already using their top of the line MX revolution and the MX1100, so the MX620 did not make impress me.  Specifically, to toggle between hyper fast scrolling and clicky wheel, you must adjust the switch located on the bottom of the mouse.  As a matter of fact, for a few weeks, I naturally thought that this mouse did not support a hyper fast scrolling feature.  I do not read the manual for a mouse anymore.  I bet there are some people out there who still do not know that this mouse supports a smooth scrolling action.The package box says the battery of the keyboard lasts for three years, and the mouse for 12 months.  I have been using them for only a month so I cannot verify that information yet.Other than the cramped keyboard, the keyboard and mouse are OK.  The soft feeling of the palm rest is still very good. review_title: Works great with Snow Leopard / Macbook Pro !
review_text: This drive is perfect for the minimalist with only a notebook. It's small, lightweight, and is completely USB powered. At that point, Blu-Ray disks were recognized perfectly, appearing instantly right on my desktop!  There were none of the issues that Windows users complained about.Pros: Excellent Mac compatibility, small, lightweight, portable, actually a bright white plastic - not the dingy gray in the picture - that well complements Mac hardware.Cons:  Only a 2x BD reader = 9MB/sec.  So it takes a few hours.Caveat Emptor:  As everyone knows, Apple does not officially sanction viewing BluRay movies on the Mac.  Using the standard software out there did allow me to play the movie, but it was not a first class experience.  You end up with a single track: no chapter marks or menu accessible special features, although you can manually watch the special features. And my 2007 MBP is a little anemic - it can't keep 100% up with showing BluRay movies - there's a little slowing of frames.  It's a little annoying, but minor enough to be usable.But the video quality is SO MUCH BETTER -> compare the quality a 22GB movie (Blu-Ray) vs a 5GB movie (DVD) vs a 1.5 GB movie (iTunes HD.)  So if you have an HD screen, for me, it is well worth the inconvenience.

review_title: Sound quality is good, battery life is fine, lag is unacceptable with video
review_text: Overall, I'm happy with the milage I've gotten out of my Jambox so far. The battery life on this thing is pretty unbelievable. I used it for about 10 or so hours at full volume over Bluetooth before it started complaining about low battery.Getting started:* I unboxed and was surprised to find that the product was completely dead. I paid Amazon to overnight it, and I couldn't believe that it didn't have any charge. Luckily, it worked with my cigarette lighter USB adapter so I was able to charge on the drive up to my vacation spot.* The software update was quick (had to create an account and download some software) and worked without problems. Make sure you pick all the software/voice packs/etc you want first before syncing (each change takes about 5 minutes to complete).* Pairing with my iPhone 5 was easy and took about a minuteUse:* Overall, I'm impressed with how loud this thing gets. It's definitely not as loud as some other full-size docks, but I didn't expect that.* The bluetooth works pretty well (I could usually get about 30 or so feet from the Jambox before it starts to cut out). One of my biggest complaints is that you definitely cannot use this as a Netflix speaker. The lag over bluetooth gets the audio out-of-sync to the point where I couldn't watch Netflix wirelessly. Plugging it in using the provided speaker cable got rid of the lag, but it sucks to have to use a cable with a wireless device.* LiveAudio is pretty nice, it produces a noticeable difference in the sounds fullness. It does, however, reduce the maximum volume, so if you're looking to pump your music, make sure it's off.I'm pretty pleased with this product so far, and it got a ton of use in my first few days of owning it. I have yet to run into any of the problems other customers are reporting (if I do, I'll update the review). The only thing keeping this from getting 5 stars is the lag with video (which, honestly, is probably an issue with Bluetooth audio in general, not with the Jambox in particular). If you can snag this at the $119 price point, I think it's definitely worth it. I don't think I would have paid the full $200 for this product.

review_title: More than one year's worth of review
review_text: I am a professional photographer, and was looking or something to put on my desk to show a continuous slideshow of my work. After holding off on buying a digital frame for years, I thought the EX1011 would be just what I was looking for.Unfortunately, it feels like a product that is not quite done. The WiFi transfer only works with Mac OS X if you buy a $39 3rd party app called TwonkyMedia (more on this later) and you can configure the unit to go online to retrieve photos off Kodak's EasyShare gallery which works OK. The image quality is fair, but disappointing for something from Kodak. The only adjustment is "Brightness" control which normally means white point, but in this case using this adjustment distorts the image. I had to put a color test pattern on a CF card and use this to calibrate the image which is WAY too much work, and there aren't enough controls to allow for a real calibration anyway:The web-based EasyShare feature is kinda neat, and actually works pretty well. You'll need to go to Kodak's web site and download a firmware update otherwise you'll see that the images lose some resolution, somehow, going from upload to download, plus the photos end up being shrunk in size by about 15%. In other words, you upload a 800x480 image, and it ends up being 680x408 on the screen, and the colors undergo one more level of distortion and decrease in color depth. This was fixed with firmware update 2007.7.06.Also, when the unit starts up, there is no way to have the unit default to the online gallery. The manual talks about setting an online gallery as My Slide Show, but having talked to Kodak customer support (don't ask how long THIS took to successfully accomplish) this feature was never implemented, so you can only use the default directory to function as My Slide Show (which is what the unit uses as a "Screen Saver"). You need to replace the photos in this default folder with your own. Be advised, when the unit shuts down and restarts (for whatever reason, including if you use the frame's auto timer), it will restart by going to a slide show in this default folder. Unless you want to watch Kodak's sample images all the time, you need to go in and change these photos to your own.Plus plus: when you update the online gallery, the frame doesn't know this, even though it's connected to the online site. You need to shut the unit down then return to the online gallery in order to have the display update.The unit is WAY too dependent on the remote control, and sooner or later the remote WILL be lost since it's really, really tiny. Sure, Kodak provides a little compartment for you to install on the back of the frame, but how many people are going to use this?  Plus, if you hang the unit on the wall, you can't install the remote control storage compartment - it goes in the same holes used for wall mounting.The way to get the unit to work with the WiFi file sharing is to download a program called TwonkyMedia (I'd include the link to the software but Amazon won't allow this - do a Google search and you'll find it), pay $39 to register, then open up ports TCP 9000 and UDP 1030, 1900, 9080 on the Mac's firewall. In addition, you need to find the Twonky configuration screen (an HTML file hidden in the Applications folder) to set up which folders you want to share with the frame. All in all, a pain in the rear, even for an Engineer like me. Once I worked through all this, though, I have to admit it's a cool feature, and one I have found myself using frequently. Also, THIS is what separates this frame from the others on the market, which is why I stuck it out until I got it to work.The improve how the images look on the frame, save them in the highest resolution you can (> 200 dpi if possible) and crop them to a 16:9 aspect ratio. I also wrote a PhotoShop action that optimizes the appearance on the frame, including some sharpening, contrast and levels adjustments, and now they look much better.All in all, though, it took a LOT of work to get this thing to work as it should have right out of the box. Admittedly, I'm a perfectionist, but just to get the online file sharing to work right requires a firmware update, and to get the WiFi sharing to work require s 3rd party app, then more finagling. Honestly, how many people are gonna go through all this, especially if buying the frame for someone else, who may be less technically adept?Update 11/15/07: Just upgraded firmware to the 2007.10.09 version. Changed some of the user interface items, and gives a few more options than before (like auto-notice of firmware update availability) but the frame still doesn't recognize ANY video formats I use (and I've tried almost every possible configuration of Quicktime, .avi, .wmv, etc.). Also, still no wireless support for Mac, so you still have to use the glitch-filled TwonkyMedia 3rd party app.I've noticed several WiFi capable frames come on the market in the past couple months in preparation for the Holiday season, so if I were you, and WiFi were important to me (especially if you're a Mac user), I would again advise you to look elsewhere for your digital picture frame. This unit is STILL not finished.FINAL UPDATE 9/26/08: After just over a year of use, this produce simply stopped working. Admittedly, I had it on the internal timer to come on every morning and go off every night, but now it turns on and stays on for about 5 seconds then shuts itself off.When I finally contacted Kodak (after they hung up on me twice), I found out the standard cost of repair exceeded the clearance price my local Costco is charging for this frame by $10.Amazing. Makes me not want to buy another Kodak product ever again. In fact, makes me want to revise my review to be 1 star, but Amazon won't allow this.In this day and age, you expect a modern product to last more the ONE YEAR, don't you?

review_title: Good Basic Functionality, A Few Flaws
review_text: Overall, this is a nice partial replacement for, in the words of Corel on the product page, "the leading PDF solution."  (I got a kick out of that one - I wonder what product they could possibly be referring to?)  If you want to print to PDF, assemble multiple PDFs into a single PDF, play around with bookmarks, edit and save PDFs, and a lot of the other lovely things Acrobat Reader won't let you do, this is a good option.However, saying it has "all the power of the leading PDF solution" is a bit of an overstatement.  The most annoying thing I've come across is that certain secured forms - forms that can even be edited and saved in the free Acrobat Reader - simply don't work in Corel PDF Fusion.  Legal forms, for example.  They'll open, but the "save this form" and "clear this form" buttons at the bottom, which work perfectly in Acrobat Reader, seem to be interpreted as useless images by Corel PDF Fusion.  Text entry boxes just aren't recognized at all.  That's a pretty big flaw, and hopefully Corel finds a way to remedy it in an update.Conversion from PDF to other formats is also not so hot.  It could do all the conversions I tried, but it lost or moved text or graphics in each instance.Also, opening big PDF files sometimes locks up my system for 10 or 15 seconds.  The Corel screen pops open, but all the pages in the PDF are blank, and all signs point to "crashed" - frozen screen, mouse won't move, keyboard is nonfunctional.  Then, abruptly, the pages load, and the machine is functioning again.As I said above, overall, it was fine, and I'm continuing to use it for the time being on my home computer where I don't have full Acrobat.  However, I wish it could do more, and I wish I didn't have to plan for a pause in everything I'm doing whenever I open a big PDF.

review_title: Apple's USB 3.0 is unreliable with this and other USB 3.0 hubs
review_text: 130402 • Posting to Amazon for 10-Port Uspeed HubAfter unreliable operation with the 7-Port Uspeed hubs it was hoped that this would be a better performer as a newer model. I had to return it for a refund. I gave this hub a 3-star rating because I suspect the problem is with my Mac and not the hub. My friend uses a Uspeed 7 port hub with a Windows 7 PC and says it performs "like a dream". I'd bet that if I had a PC it would work well. I hate to say it, but as indicated below I wish I'd avoided Apple and their USB 3.0 until they'd identified and corrected the bugs. I still have the problems, although this vendor, and Sunnie in support, has been very cooperative in trying to find a solution.My experience since June 2012 with my MacBook Pro Retina and a 7-Port Uspeed hub was terrible. Then I ordered a variety of other brands and all exhibited similar behavior. This was a good indicator to me that the problem was with Apple and my MacBook Pro Retina's USB 3.0.Although my USB 3.0 drives (x5) work fine if plugged directly into the Mac. Apple says that's the end of their responsibility. The hubs are unreliable when connected to a hub so they pass-the-buck and say it's the hub manufacturers that are at fault.I can't say this hub is bad because the other hubs exhibited  similar behavior. My belief is that the Mac is unable to communicate effectively with the hub causing the erratic behavior.The problems that I experience are: 1) Drives fail to mount. 2) Drives spontaneously dismount individually or all together. Sometimes they will spontaneously remount and often not. 3) The hub will, at times, connect the drives as USB 2.0 or USB 1.1 and their corresponding slower speeds. (That's right, System Report says that my expensive MacBook Pro Retina has mounted these drives as USB 1.1 (and up to 12 Mb/sec) instead of 5 Gb/sec.)Another consideration is that my current Uspeed hub was tested at the Apple Store using 3 drives on a 2013 MacBook Pro 15" Retina and on a 27" iMac. We didn't have time to wait for the other errors to appear, but we did find that drives connected through this hub on new Macs had the same problem with failing to mount drives when connected, or on a restart.This was documented by Apple.If you review the poor ratings on any of the USB 3.0 hubs that identify the platform they are used on I expect you'll find in most cases that it's the Apple computers since Mid-2012 that exhibit this problem. There appears to be a bug in the OS, hardware, or firmware that remains unfixed by Apple.(I'm running the current OS X Mountain Lion version 10.8.3 so that's not the problem. Nor is my MacBook Pro Retina as Apple has replaced it on warranty and they both operate with the same problems with USB 3.0.)I love USB 3.0, but not what Apple has not done with it.

review_title: Great item / Showed Amazon's no-hassle service, too
review_text: This was purchased to replace an older 400 GB drive inside my Mac Pro. When it arrived, physical installation was a breeze. A 2 TB drive takes a long time to write all zeros into (Apple's method tracks any under-performing sectors and isolates them from later use) so I wasn't surprised when that took about a day. A trillion here, a trillion there, pretty soon we're talking about some real time.But then it would NOT perform. It was a rare example of a Western Digital drive that was DOA. I have a number of WD drives in my system, and this was a first. Oh, well, best to have it fail on day one than on day 200!I contacted Amazon and this is what they did:Instantly, they sent me a new drive. Also, they sent a return authorization and shipping label that would get the drive back to them after I was satisfied the new one had worked. They even credited me with return postage.When the new one arrived, installation went fine. Now all is well, and the new drive is noticeably faster (and five times bigger) than the old one. The new WD20EARS is not today's fastest drive, but it is way ahead of the older Hitachi Deskstar 400 GB from March, 2005.This transaction demonstrated to me two things:* The newer tech, even though less than today's top echelon, is better/faster/sweeter than the tech it replaced.* And Amazon is doing things right.If I had purchased it locally, sure, I would have been able to cycle the return quicker. And it would have cost me around $30 more from a local supplier, plus gas, plus a nice long stand in line to do it.But in the Amazon transaction it was far easier, less expensive and less hassel, and that made it more satisfying.I'm BuzzMega, and I approved this review.

review_title: Simply the finest camera strap I have ever used
review_text: I used the Joby strap for the first time this past week on my trip to Europe. While I was a little skeptical about how the design would work with a mirrorless DSLR (read, a smaller camera...Sony A6000), I was delightfully surprised. Mind you, I needn't have been. Everything worked exactly as the demonstration video on their website indicates. Basically, the Joby UltraFit sling strap is remarkable.For the past few decades, I've walked around with a dual mounted (via d-clip) over the neck strap that I'd occasionally try and sling across one shoulder. The problem with wearing the strap over the neck is that the weight eventually digs in and causes noticeable discomfort after about 30-60 minutes. This is especially the case when I used larger full-frame DSLRs and remains the case with my smaller mirrorless cameras now. Then, it becomes a game of shifting it from one shoulder to the next, over the next, over the shoulder, around the head, etc. It's never really comfortable and if it's only hanging off of one shoulder, it's not particularly stable. If it's looped criss-cross over the shoulder, then it's impossible to raise it fast enough to get a quick photo. Net net, over-the-neck mounts have never really worked for me.Enter the Joby sling strap. Let me first address the mount since there have been some (one?) concerns here about it working loose. When I first got it, I was a bit leery of the tripod mount coming loose because of a couple of reviews here. However, I really don't know how they had difficulties. The mount screws in VERY securely and seems to offer some cushioned give via a flexible washer to allow the mount to screw down even 'tighter'. Moreover, the mount itself doesn't spin; the harness is attached via a free spinning mechanism so that the screw won't come loose. Nevertheless, because of a prior reviewer's experience with the mount coming loose, I also opted to buy Joby's camera tether. It's basically a locking carabiner that attaches to the camera's d-ring and the sling strap itself so that even if the camera would work loose, it wouldn't fall to the ground. While the tether is very nicely made and unobtrusive, in my one week of using the strap, the strap mount via tripod mount NEVER loosened a bit. In fact, because of the 'flexible washer', it actually seemed to 'tighten' up even more. Moreover, I never felt the need to take it off after the first day because the strap use became instinctive. Last, some have argued that its one minor flaw is the hassle of taking the mount off if one wishes to shoot on tripod. I would suggest buying their quick-release tripod mount (I think it's called an ultra-plate) and your issue is solved.Anyway, continuing to the strap itself: it is very well made. All the materials seem extraordinarily well made and I had no frayed threads nor any evidence of shoddy manufacturing. It just looks top-notch. From the very solidly designed and built mount (discussed above) to the soft but supportive strap, it's smells of quality. The real key to the strap is the design itself. Most straps are one fixed length (after adjustment) of the harness that crosses the shoulder and that the camera then moves along for a shot. The problem with this implementation is that the strap is too short for shooting if it fits comfortably when not in use (at your side) OR it fits comfortably for shooting (enough play) then it's too long when you then want to let it rest by your side when not in use. Joby solved this via their speedcinch. Basically, you pull up on the circular ring on the strap at the front of your check and it tightens the strap down for camera 'storage' by your side when not in use. Then, simply click the locking lever and it stays there OUT of the way. Then, when an ideal photo op comes along, you simply unclick the lock and just pull the camera to your eye. You do not need to touch the strap to lengthen it at all; it happens automatically. Genius.What this results in is an across the chest (over the shoulder) strap that is extraordinarily comfortable to walk around with all day. While some may contend that the strap doesn't have a lot of padding or neoprene (presumably so it can adjust/slide very smoothly), I didn't have an issue at all. The strap is made of 'high-performance webbing' and because it's a little wider than smaller over the neck efforts, it distributes the weight nicely. And candidly, it actually feels MORE comfortable with heavier lenses because they automatically position themselves aiming 'down' so that you can quickly grab the camera body handle when ready to shoot. That, my friends, is bonus.I hate to come across as an evangelist for this strap, but man, it's just a fantastic product. It makes walking around with the camera an absolute joy...any camera. It 'hides' discreetly under my arm when not in use but then pulls up rapidly (after unclicking the locking tab) whenever I want a shot. I can't recommend it more. Five stars.

review_title: Comfy, but perhaps a bit on the small side.
review_text: I've been wearing this bag for a couple of weeks now and feel I can give an informed opinion about it.  Bearing in mind the price, I think this is an excellent bag.If I was on Amazon, wondering if I should add this to my cart, I'd want to know about its durability.  When I first took this out of the box, I realized one of the straps had some loose threads on the stitching.  It gave me a very negative opinion of its build quality, but I removed them (burned them) and after some very rough use, the bag looks fine.  I'm quite rough with this kind of thing, throwing in the bed of my pickup, riding it on a crowded bus, and filling it with a heavy laptop and heavy books.  The bag is holding up.I'd also want to know how much stuff this bag holds:  not a whole lot.  That's not necessarily good or bad... it's just not a very large backpack.  It's nice and trim.  I can only put two large textbooks in, with a laptop in its compartment, leaving very little room for food.  However, this is the perfect size for people who aren't carrying huge textbooks and want a medium to small footprint for their bag.I guess you already know what it looks like, but I think pictures don't quite do it justice.  The little orange marks across the bag look almost like a ninja sliced it.  It's a great look, with a little flair, without losing a good conservative basic look.  This is appropriate for work, school, and most settings that aren't quite formal.The straps are super comfortable as long as you don't overload it (which you basically can't do because of its size).  There is a nice strap across the shoulder straps that acts as a handle, instead of sewing on on top.  This is extremely smart design.  It's durable and provides a cleaner look.  The zippers are well made and plastic (they don't rattle like my metal zippered backpack).I also found that I can wear a larger camelback hydration bag under the backpack, thanks to the way the straps work.  This is a super-cool surprise.

The MOTOACTV is a fun little device.  Set up is very simple.  Thedevice walks you through all the steps.  The screen is very responsiveand despite its small size, I was able to easily enter all myinformation and sync it with the MOTOACTV website.First, I loaded a bunch of music onto the device, which was simple.It syncs with either iTunes or Windows Media Player.  The soundquality also seems great (although, I'm not an audio snob).  You canuse the buttons on the MOTOACTV to control the player - pause, play,skip, and repeat songs.  I looked for an equalizer and couldn't findone.  It would be nice if one was added in a firmware update.So far, I have used it mostly while I'm on the stair stepper or takinglong walks.  The walk stats seem to be very accurate.  The GPS takes acouple minutes to get a lock on the satellites, but you can begin yourworkout before it gets a lock.  In downtown Chicago, I was able tolock on the satellites, which actually surprised me since my car's GPSoften gets confused in the downtown area.  After walking, it plotsyour course on a map you can view on the device.  It also shows the distance traveled andestimated calories burned.The MOTOACTV website is also fantastic for people who like keeping track of their workouts in minute detail.  I'm actually surprised at home much detail is available.  Viewing my most recent walk, I can see exactly where I walked, how many calories burned at different points in the walk, and my walking speed, among other details.  It even keeps track of which songs I listened to during my walk and can create play lists based on calories burned.I have a couple minor quibbles.  First, the little plastic cover for the headphone jack isn't tethered to the device, so it's easily lost.  One suggestion I saw in the comments was to secure it to the wrist band.  I prefer to use the clip instead of the wrist band, so that suggestion doesn't help me.  My other quibble is the band itself.  It's large and rather garish.  As a woman, I would have preferred a more feminine option (even though I'm not a girly type girl).Overall, I love using the MOACTV. I especially recommend it for those into the "quantified self" fad as it allows users to track many different variables of their exercise routine.  I also find that using a cool tech toy encourages the geek in me to exercise more.

review_title: Great Accessory, but Best with a Good Headphone Amp
review_text: I am using the L3 Line Out Dock (LOD) cable with an iPod Touch 4th Gen. I had previously purchased the FIIO L1 LOD cable but the L1 was cheaply made. The L3 is more durable, made using better conducting material and has the lock-in feature that keeps it securely attached to the LOD on your iPod. A noticeable and welcome improvement from the L1.The FIIO L3 LOD is a great addition to my music gear because iPod headphone jack is made from low quality materials which produces low quality sound. The L3 LOD cable bypasses these materials and reduces the noise you will hear on your headphones. This is important because the iPod LOD is a better quality connector than the 3.5mm (1/8-inch) headphone jack. So by using the L3, you are connecting a better quality adapter to a better quality jack on your iPod.The iPod really isn't the best music player for audio quality on the market, but the L3 improves the audio significantly by taking the audio directly from the LOD (I would use another music player, but the iPod is just so useful for so many other things that I live with the sound quality for now).SOMETHING YOU SHOULD KNOW ABOUT USING THE L3 ADAPTER!Something to know about using the L3 adapter is that when you plug it into your iPod dock jack, your volume function on the iPod disappears, both from the side of the iPod and the touch interface. When you use the L3 you will need another method of adjusting the volume. NOTE: It IS POSSIBLE to adapt the L3 for headphones using a female to female 3.5mm adapterC2G / Cables to Go - 03170 - 3.5mm Stereo Coupler F/F, but you will have no volume control. That's where a good headphone amplifier is needed. I use a FIIO E7FiiO E7 USB DAC and Portable Headphone Amplifier (Black). (I am not trying to sell FIIO products, it's just what I have)I connect the L3 adapter to the 3.5mm input on a FIIO E7 Headphone Amplifier & Digital to Analog Converter (DAC). The FIIO E7 amplifies the input audio for headphones that require power to drive them. The E7 has 2 headphone jacks to share your music (and the amp boosts the signal to power headphones that require power for the incredible sound quality of which studio quality headphones are capable - here's an example:Audio-Technica ATH-M50 Professional Studio Monitor Headphones), but any amplifier with an 3.5mm input with volume control will work. I am able to adjust the volume of the music from my iPod using the E7 AMP/DAC. Other options are an iPod dock with volume control or any other amplifier with volume control. I just happen to have a FIIO AMP/DAC.The L3 LOD helps you get the best sound you are going to get out of your iPod/iPhone and is also helpful if your iPod headphone jack is broken, just remember that you need a method to adjust volume and may consider adding some quality headphones to your music rig to hear the improvement of the depth and quality the L3 can help bring to your ears.Enjoy!

I was skeptical of this working very well, and I am happy to say that I was surprised by the quality and function of the pen. I have major issues with the included software, but the hardware is pretty impressive.You get the Smartpen, a USB cradle for the pen, earbuds, ink refills, and a specially printed notebook in a nice box with fairly good instructions.I followed the tests and demos included in the pen, and was amazed at the computing power that can fit into something the size of a healthy fountain pen. It was a real trip to write words in English on the special pages and have the pen instantly translate into Chinese, Spanish, Swedish, and Arabic. Wild! (Okay, it does have a limited vocabulary, but hey, it read my handwriting and translated what it could!) It was also a trip to tap sections of text and have the pen play back audio synced to the text (or diagram).This is an exciting concept and the hardware is well designed and executed. The software, however, is another story. I installed the software on a computer I borrowed for the test, as it requires Windows XP or Vista ONLY. (Major error.) Although I was able to install the software, I was not able to use it, as it requires online registration and locks you into only ONE computer per pen! (Pretty lame idea for an item as portable as a pen, IMHO.) As I didn't intend to leave the software on the test machine, I didn't do the registration, hence the software would not perform for me. I really hate that in a product. Way too Nazi for my taste.In this day and age, to lock a person to using a single computer for a portable device is extremely shortsighted, if not downright counterproductive. To tie users to an outdated, glitchy OS like Windows is unwise, particularly with Linux rapidly on the rise. It struck me as being like building a nice, new starship and installing a governor on the warp drive to hold it to sublight speeds. The hardware is such a great leap forward - why hinder it with such software limitations. Anyone not writing software to be portable across multiple OSs is not paying attention to the trends or the desires of customers. The flak Asus got from other laptop vendors over the Eee PC idea shows just how blind many vendors are to customer needs.Also, there are no serious options for exporting content from this package. Why bother recording the text if you cannot use it in another application or on another computer?One other, lesser, complaint is the high cost of the specially printed notebooks for use with the pen. $20 seems a bit high for 100 pages in a spiral notebook, again IMHO. I could be wrong, as they don't really give one much information about the process involved. I get the feeling that the marketing/financial types had way too much to say in the development of this product.That said, I think it is a great idea, especially for creative types or people who design or work in teams that brainstorm on paper. I can see a musician composing on the pages while humming or singing along while the pen records it all. People designing anything could draw designs and make audio recordings of the discussion as the process goes on. While the primary target market seems to be note-taking  college students, I think that is quite shortsighted.If you can live with the drawbacks of the software, and work in an environment where easily capturing rapidly evolving ideas on paper and audio would be helpful, then I can recommend this Smartpen. If being tied to a single Windows computer cramps your style as much as it does mine, I think you will be disappointed with that limitation.I would like to see the manufacturer port their software to a platform agnostic language and loosen up on the use of the pen on multiple machines. I would normally give an item with such issues a 3 or less, but it is such a great idea and the hardware is so well done, I have to give it a (conditional) 4.

****To start with, the specs are accurate in the sense that the Acer Aspire V5-571P-6642 15.6-Inch Touch Screen Laptop (Silky Silver) really does sport an i5 processor and a 500-Gb hard drive and 6 Gbs of RAM and so on.  Now, let's turn to five particular subjects, those being the screen, the keyboard, form factors, Windows 8 and battery life.**** ScreenAt 15.6 inches the screen is plenty big enough for my vision, but my vision is excellent since I wear glasses. I will now swicht to weeearing a pair of mitteens to test how ell the keeyboradd workss.  Well;. as you cxan see, the answer id NOT VEERY QWELL.  Mittrns off.  And one star off for this.Now that I think about it, I'm not sure I should take one star off for the reason that this laptop doesn't work well while wearing mittens.  (I mean while I am wearing the mittens, not the laptop.  That would be silly.)  I have now tried wearing mittens while using other products' keyboards and, sure enough, the result is pretty much the same goobleddygrok, so I hereby add back that star.**** Form factorsThe Aspire V5 is thin and plastic.  The thin part is awesome and stuff because it looks so cool and sleek and silvery but I wasn't so sure about the plastic part, so, as will not come as a surprise to readers of my other Amazon reviews, I decided to test its durability unusually.  Here's how to conduct the test, if you want to add your data points to the database I'm maintaining on this very question.Step 1. Acquire one undamaged Acer Aspire V5-571P-6642 15.6-Inch Touch Screen Laptop (Silky Silver) and one undamaged laptop with a metal case.Step 2. Place either laptop on a concrete floor or driveway and drop the other laptop onto it from a height of 1 meter.Step 3. Test both units for any sign of brokenness.  If only one is broken, the other one wins.  If both are broken return to Step 1.  If neither is broken return to Step 2.In my testing, which turned out to be a LOT more expensive than I had originally foreseen, after three trials the Aspire V5 broke and the metal-cased one didn't, so I add one star to my review of that other one.**** Windows 8The product under review comes fresh from the birth canal with a spanking new version of Windows, that being version 8.  Whether you like version 8 compared to Windows 7 Home Premium, or Windows 95 for that matter, depends on how much you decide to allow yourself to be annoyed by how long it takes to get used to.  Change for the mere sake of change is, pretty much by definition, undesirable, but I'm sure the wizards at Microsoft have somethings more justifiable in mind with version 8, although so far I haven't yet discovered what they are by using the laptop under review so far as of yet.  I neither add nor subtract any stars for this product's being born with Windows 8, as opposed to Windows 7 with an optional upgrade to 8, because I figure anyones who mistakenly think this product doesn't come with Windows 8 deserve to be surprised, and perhaps initially disappointed, by that fact.**** Battery lifeMany previous reviewers, both here on Amazon and elsewhere, have expressed opinions ranging from great certainty to more or less a great deal less certainty as far as the V5's battery life.  Goes.  Surely some of those opinions are more valid than others, just as just as surely some are better-researched and more well-backed-up than others.  To be honest, after much actual experience and mental cogitation I actually personally happen to agree.Here's the thing, as I see it.  If you know you're going to be away from any appropriate source of electricity for so long that the battery on the Aspire V5 is going to become depleted, whether that takes three hours of hard use or six hours of less hard use, you should charge up that battery to its absolutely full maximum (it's lithium ion, which is good) before you leave for wherever you're going to go that has no appropriate source of electricity or get a laptop with a battery that lasts longer to begin with.**** ConclusionIf this product cost a lot more I'd reduce it to three stars, but it doesn't.  If you don't mind the extra cost of the touch-screen feature and the choice of Windows 8, you would give this a five-star rating.

I'd had my eye on the Samsung LN-R**8W series for quite some time after starting to see them in various places used as monitors for PCs and as televisions hooked up to XBox 360s. Every time I saw one of these sets (the demo models were invariably the 23" version), I had to stop and stare. Usually the game playing was "Call of Duty 2", but it looked positively stunning. Finally I watched some high-def programming at a store on the 26" model and I was sold. Having read not a single on-line review and without doing any research whatsoever, I was sold by my eyes alone. The only 'research' I did was comparing this set to other brands, and this was the clear winner.The 3000:1 contrast ratio is misleading. They used 'dynamic' contrast ratio to come up with that figure. I've since learned the actual contrast ratio as used by most other manufacturers is around 800:1, which is still among the best of the current crop. The next generation will undoubtedly beat this figure. But for my purposes, this set is just fantastic. The blacks are black, and all shades of gray seem to come through as intended. To judge this, I'm replaying "Deus Ex", a PC game from back in 2000 (which runs fine in WinXP and supports 1360 x 768). This game takes place entirely at night, so there are a lot of dark areas along with many shades of gray. This game looks amazing, as does FarCry (2004) with its beautiful vivid tropical colors and water. Those are the only two games I've tried thus far. And I imagine games that natively support 1360 x 768 will naturally fare better on this set. For instance, a game that only supports 1024 x 768 will probably look kinda crappy because of scaling problems, a problem all LCD monitors share when not running in their native resolution.I'm using it primarily as a huge monitor for my PC. I had to think hard about this, because using this set as a PC monitor, your screen resolution will max out at 1360 x 768, which is great for television, but hardly cutting-edge for a computer monitor. However, to find a PC monitor this BIG with ultra-high resolution would have set me back about double the dollars. And since my rig (An Athlon 2600+ with an NVidia 6600GT video card) isn't capable of playing games at ultra-high res anyway, I'm happy with this. Also, I've since learned that this series of sets is the easiest to configure for computer use. It's got a VGA port on the back, so just buy a VGA cable, hook it to your PC, and it's Plug-And-Play. Just remember before unhooking your old monitor to resize the screen in Windows to 1360 x 768 so it boots to the correct size after you hook this up.Picture quality is excellent. The best I've ever seen in an LCD. They're all pretty decent these days, but this one stands out as brighter, sharper, crisper, clearer, at least to my eyes. Before buying anything this expensive though, I'd make sure you actually see various brands in action at various stores before you buy.I don't have high-def service at home yet, so the only HD I've viewed on this has been at the store, but it looked awesome to me.Picture-in-picture is really only useful if you're surfing the net and want to watch TV at the same time. For that, it's great, though you'll have to manually use the remote to activate sound in PIP each time. An annoyance. The speakers sound clear and crisp. Not huge, but nice-sounding.And now, the only flaw I've found: Out of the box, the reds can be oversaturated when contrasted with black. I've only noticed this with text; graphics are fine. I might be able to adjust this in the set's menu, but haven't tried it yet, because otherwise it looks just absolutely perfect and I hate to mess with it.

This review will confirm and expand on the unhappy review by Jon Robert. The PN-60 is best suited for someone with extensive prior experience with GPS or who can get tutoring on the device. As a novice user of handheld GPS, I may have thrown the $239 price down the toilet, as I've not been able to do much useful with it so far.The PN-60 appears quite powerful and cleverly designed. However, it is complex, and the manual describes the GPS as a collection of screens that one can invoke -- it scrupulously avoids saying how to accomplish any high-level task (such as finding your way) one might want to use a GPS for. After reading the entire manual (!!!!), I am scarcely less in the dark about using this thing than I was before. Why DeLorme never thought of writing a task-oriented user's manual is a puzzle.The supplied Topo software is also quite powerful and also poorly documented. However, I have not yet waded through all its documentation. The GPS manual, by the way, says almost nothing about the Topo software, although it is required to use the GPS most fruitfully.(I should mention that I am not a stranger to technical things. I have a PhD in a scientific field; I have used computers since 1966; I have written software used widely in my field; I have a large and growing collection of gadgets that I CAN use effectively.)In conclusion, The PN-60 is a well-built device with great promise but incredibly, frustratingly, bad documentation. The unit is highly complex, the related software is also complex, and you are pretty much on your own in figuring how to use them. (The online Wiki has bits of the manual only, and is no help.) If you have a LOT of time on your hands and like to solve difficult puzzles, this would be a great GPS for you. Or if you have extensive previous experience with GPS, you may not have the frustrating experience I did. The PN-60 is NOT RECOMMENDED for beginning GPS users.

It works well at night in headlight or limited streetlight light., it even picks up some infer red light “BUT” the auto light level setting gets confused, sometimes it  “blooms”, more often you see lines/streaks degrading the pix quality. review_title: Nice, Works Well, Except for Local Media Streaming
review_text: Very tidy (small) box. Basic setup is simple (no need to use the manual) - just plug it into your TV and off you go. Connecting to Netflix was straightforward - it gives you an activation (device) code and the URL on Netflix to use - and almost instantaneously the Roku box sees your instant queue. Nice quality (I didn't checkout surround sound as I have a very simple setup in my workout room which is the location of the Roku - I know it's heresy, but right now I'm just using the builtin TV speakers).Not so nice is the "local media" streaming. This is done via chaneru. You get a 30 day trial, but it is only a 1 time charge of $10. You set up a chaneru server application (they call it a client???), configure the server so it knows where your media is, and off you go. It doesn't know how to "autostart" so you get to screw around getting it to do this (you will also need the command line switch "-s") but once done it seems to work well enough. However, I have not figured out the data path and suspect it goes via the cloud. While I was messing around with the autostart setup, I closed and deleted the server exe but the TV continued to play the movie for many minutes afterwards (after 30 seconds I checked the task manager to make sure the exe was not running), which all makes me thing that chaneru streams to the roku from your server to their server to the roku box. It does play MP4 but not avi(divx). Says it can handle itunes library but I didn't experiment.Everything runs via "channels" so chaneru is a channel. You get to pick channels and add them to your line up. Fairly wide choice of media including Pandora and other internet radio stations (eulive gives me radio stations from all over Europe). And of course there are a bunch of subscription channels.

I have been using a Logitech wireless keyboard and mouse for several years, and although it served me well I decided it was time for a new one.  I got this MK300 and couldn't be happier.  Super easy to install/set-up, more compact than my old keyboard, and more programmable too.  It has some nice options for a low-priced basic unit.INSTALL/SET-UP:I use this unit with my Acer desktop - because I like wireless.  I plugged the receiver (smaller than a deck of cards) into a USB port, and the keyboard and mouse worked instantly (they came with batteries - nice!)... no downloading or installing needed.  If you want to program some of the keys on the keyboard, you do need to put in the included CD ROM (so this may not be a good option for a netbook that lacks an optical drive) and install the software.  It's very simple, with an extremely idiot-proof user interface; I didn't need to look in the manual at all, it was very self-explanatory.PROGRAMMABLE FEATURES:The keyboard comes with 'hot keys' already set up.  These include an 'Internet Zone' (keys for email, browser, search engine, messenger), a "Multimedia Zone" (controls your media player - like iTunes), a "Volume Zone" (including a mute button), and a "Convenience Zone" (calculator and battery status check).  With the software, you can over-ride any of these pre-sets and program what you want.You are also able to customize your "F" keys.  F1 - F4 launch your applications for documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and calendar.  F5 - F8 are programmable to launch your favorite application, game, or folder. F9 - F12 are shortcuts for saving files, undoing, redoing, and opening your CD tray.The mouse is also programmable to a degree.  Via the software, you can set speed, enable game options, and assign tasks to the buttons/scroll wheels.THE HARDWARE PER SE:The keyboard is more compact than my previous Logitech wireless keyboard, which makes it easier to move about my desk.  The keys are "low profile".  At first I didn't like them - they are a little bit old school.  But I got used to them in a few hours and now I like their quiet sound and the firm 'feel' they have which lets me know that I have actually pressed a key.  The mouse is standard - nothing fancy or ergonomic, no extra keys - it does fit nicely in my hand.  The receiver only plugs into a USB port, which is nice - my previous set's receiver plugged in in 2 places.BOTTOM LINE:Easy set-up, compact design, and a nice array of programmable features for such an affordable product.

The Maxboost Electron 15000 mAH battery pack offers alot for a single device.  For one it is about the size of a portable hard drive but 15000 mAH capacity.  This is good engough to fully recharge your iPad.  If you haven't tried a power bank yet then let me tell you they are ultra convient and this one has a multitude of features.There are a couple of things that stand out:This particular power bank has a LCD that displays the amount of charge that is left on the device from 100% down to 1%.  This is a great feature to have that not all powerbanks have.  The usual norm is a couple of LED's which doesn't allow for an accurate picture of the amount of charge left.The power bank does have some weight to it but then again it is 15000 mAh so this is expected.  I wouldn't carry this around for everyday trips to the office but more so for trips that last atleast a couple or more hours or leaving it in the car for emergencies.The power bank includes two USB ports (2.1A and 1A) for charging devices simulatenously.  The 2.1A port is great as it allows for normal recharge times for tablets which usually recharge at 2.1A versus 1A. Not to mention the Maxboost Electron has a built-in flashlight.  The flashlight is just an included feature that doesn't really get much use due to the size of the power bank.The design is also sleek and attractive.  The case has a smooth finish and feels like it will hold up well to being dropped.Recharging of the power bank took a about 7 to 8 hours.  Which if you think about it is pretty fast for 15000 mAh.Accessories that are included: Carrying Pouch, USB cable, mini usb connector, micro usb connector and Apple 30 pin connector.The one con I have about this item is that it doesn't include a wall charger.  Although this seems to be the norm of devices that are rechargeable via USB port.Device Battery Capacity Information:IE rough estimates, the 4800 mAh power bank can recharge a iPhone 4 about 3 to 4 times (4800 device power bank battery / 1420 iPhone 4 Battery = 4 recharges) before the RavPower RP-WCN11 battery depletes* iPhone 4 Battery (1420 mAh)* iPhone 4S Battery (1432 mAh)* iPhone 5 Battery (1434 mAH)* iPad 2 Battery (6944 mAh)* iPad 3 Battery (11560 mAh)* iPad 4 Battery (11486 mAH)* iPad Mini Battery (4490 mAH)* Kindle Fire Battery (4400 mAh)* Kindle Keyboard Battery (1750 mAh)* PlayStation Portable 3000 Battery (1500 mAh)* BlackBerry Torch 2 9810 Battery (1270 mAh)* Nintendo 3DS Battery (1300mAh)Overall, this is a great device, simple to use and cheap compared to competitors for the battery capacity.  If you are in the market for a power bank I would give this one a serious thought.I was supplied a sample product in order to provide a fair and unbaised review.

I recently received my Ape Case ACPRO2000 backpack and I'm absolutely in love with this thing. I wasn't sure what to expect for a sub $100 dollar DSLR pack, and was going back and forth between this and a Tamrac Evolution (at $60 more) before I finally bit the bullet and hit the order button. I was still concerned that it wouldn't fit all of my gear as I have quite a few accessories beyond lenses and filters, but, when I opened up the box, any fears I had were laid to rest as the Ape Case Pro2000 is ENORMOUS.First thing's first; I'm NOT a hiker by any means, but I was looking for an upgrade over my Canon 200DG, which I'd outgrown a few months back. I wanted something I could house all of my gear in for "shoots" (I'm an amateur working toward professional gigs by doing some freebie shoots for bands, friends, etc), as well as something I could take on long trips where I never know what I may find and always fear I'll leave behind something I could have used! LOLThere are a host of external and internal pockets to house all of your filters, memory cards, guides and manuals, and virtually anything else photography related. There are even a pair of large zippered compartments that fit my reflectors and Rogue Flashbenders nicely (one is actually meant for a 15" laptop. I have a 17" laptop, however, and it doesn't fit, but I already have a nice bag for that)!Once you work your way through all of the other compartments, you come upon the massive removable "main" compartment which can easily store a couple of camera bodies and several lenses. I really liked the dividers in this backpack, as they're very firm and of high quality, not floppy "stuffed" jobs like other cases I've seen. Currently, in the main compartment alone, I've got my camera body (Canon 600D/t3i) w/ grip, five lenses (Canon EF 50 mm f/1.8, Canon EF 85mm f/1.8, Canon EF-S 15-85mm f/3.5-5.6, Canon EF 70-300mm f/4-5.6, and a Sigma 10-20mm f/4-5.6) a pair of speedlites (a 320EX and 420EX), a Rogue Grid, two AAA chargers, a dual LPE8 battery charger,stock Canon charger, and a couple of filter cases and still have room to spare. The other pockets hold my manuals, Lowepro memory card sleeve, the aforementioned reflectors and Flashbenders, and a variety of other doo-dads.The construction on this backpack is superb, with quality stitching and zippers, super rugged materials. There's also a built-in tripod holder (a pocket folds out of one of the side compartments, and a pair of lashings holds it in place) as well as a protective weatherproof cover! Now, make no mistake; if you fill this thing up, it's HEAVY, but weight distribution and comfort is excellent thanks to the amply padded shoulder straps and thick waist belt.If you're looking for a backpack or just a larger case to lug around all of your gear in, look no further. The Ape Case Pro2000 is an absolute steal at $99 bucks!

It also has 3 USB ports, bluetooth, 802.11b/g/n wireless LAN, memory card reader and best of all 10.5hours of battery life, that you cannot beat.Overall, for the cost and value plus the things you get from this machine, it is definately worth the purchase in my opinion.You might be wondering why I gave it 4 stars after all the praise. And while the machine perfoms well for a netbook, dont expect to be doing lots of task at once. When you are use to fast desktop PCs it can be hard to take a step backwards.

This review should probably apply to all sound isolation earphones.  That is, phones that require you to insert them into your ear canal, much (very much) like ear plugs.First off, a word about fit.  The E2Cs come with seven types of buds to provide the best fit to your ears.  It is absolutely necessary to find the right fit.  Apparently I have very narrow ear canals, since the only ones that fit were the smallest buds, and I still have to work to get them in.  The main reason I wanted to try these headphones is because normal ear bud phones simply do not fit my ears - the slightest head shake and they fall out.  The E2Cs provide a decent fit.  I could not go jogging with these (wouldn't want to - see below), but normal walking around is fine.  The first few days were sort of uncomfortable, after a while my ears would ache a bit.  But you DO get used to it.  Give it at least a week before you decide if these are for you.Important!  Buy from the Shure Website.  It will link you back to Amazon.  The reason for this is to make sure you get Shure's 30-day money back guarantee.  These phones are not for everyone and you can't try them out before you buy.  Even if you find a local store, it is unlikely that they will open the package and let you stick them into your ear canal to test them.  And some stores will not accept returns on ear bud head phones.  Wherever you buy them, ask about their return policy first.Now to the sound.  These little guys sound great.  Clear and accurate, I am hearing things in the music that I didn't know was there.  They completely isolate what you are hearing, blocking off 95% of external sound.  Whether you are listening to hard rock, or something acoustic, you can be in a subway and it's like you are in a movie with a soundtrack - no noise but what you are listening to.  Quite simply, this type of headphone gives you much better sound than any other portable system.It is these earphones greatest strength that is their greatest limitation.  Imagine going through life with ear plugs and you may get my point.  Sometimes it is important to hear stuff and with these all you hear is the music.  Things you can't do with sound isolation ear bud phones:1. Jog - too dangerous.  Unless you are in a deserted area, it is not a good idea to totally isolate yourself.  Even hiking can be chancy.2. Walk in crowded areas.  After just a week, I lost count the number of times I have bumped into people or almost got run over.  You don't realize how much you unconsciously rely on you hearing to get through your day until you lose it.3. Eat.  Try eating with a set of those foam ear plugs in your ears.  Every body movement (especially chewing) is magnified.  It just feels weird.  This applies to running/exercise as well - the sound of your feet striking the ground is deafening.4. Have any kind of conversation.  You can't hear them, and you find yourself shouting.  Can't do it.Try spending a day wearing ear plugs and you should get an idea of the limitations.What you can do is sit in a train/plane/car (as passenger, duh) and ignore everything else.  I am using on the DC metro and it is great.  No stress with crowds, just find a seat, close your eyes and try not to miss your stop.  If you have a job that lets you tune out your co-workers, the phone and any fire alarms, these are great as well.I have not yet decided if I am going to keep these.  For around $100, they are very limited in their use.  They simply cannot be your only set of head phones since you WILL need another set when in situations requiring at least some hearing.  But the sound can't be beat by any basic ear bud or behind the head ear phones out there.  If you are into the sound, get them and give them a good two week trial to see if they work for you.

review_title: Fast, Easy to Install but Larger Capacities are Needed
review_text: Historically, I have purchased the best hardware available in an effort to improve my productivity.  So, I when I transitioned from a desktop with a 15k rpm nine years ago to a notebook with a 5,400 rpm drive, the performance hit was a real disappointment.  Hence, I was more than happy to spring for a an Intel X25-M to make my HP Elitebook Mobile workstation even faster. Generally, I have been happy with the performance of X25-M but not astounded like other users.The principle reason I have spent so much on hardware is to improve the performance of one particularly disk- and processor-intensive application -- X1, which is a real-time, fast-as-you-type indexing application.  Over the years, it has felt like an arms race: I get better and better hardware but the volume of indexable documents keeps increasing, slowing down X1 and overall operation of the computer. Meanwhile, Microsoft chooses to make increasingly bloated software necessitating ever faster hardware.  My latest notebook is an HP Elitebook mobile workstation with x9100 3.06 GHZ dual core processor, 4 GB of RAM, and a 7200 rpm drive running on Windows Utimate 64 bit.  Out of the box, it seemed oddly sluggish on occasions due to either X1 or some application that HP installed.  Given the specs and the cost of the notebook, I was a bit surprised it wasn't faster. Wanting to avoid the hassle of purchasing another extremely expensive notebook, I decided the simplest approach to improving overall performance would to purchase the X25-M.My two major reasons for hesitating to purchase the X25-M were the meager 160 GB capacity and unpleasant memories of upgrading drives in the past.  Remarkably, the installation was painless using Acronis true image using only my HP notebook.  Moreover, Acronis offers a fully functional free demo that worked without a hitch.  I did need to purchase an external USB/eSata enclosure (Acomdata Tango) to connect to my existing notebook to complete the process, however. This too worked without a problem.  In total, I was pleasantly surprised at how easy the process given that no second computer was used.While I haven't precisely timed various operations, the X25-M is clearly faster than the previous 7200 rpm drive.  However, I haven't been overwhelmed by the performance like other users. There is still some hesitation when opening large files. Also, Windows 7 Ultimate takes a significant amount of time to load even though it is faster than with the 7200 rpm drive. Note this is even with disabling many services and startup applications.  Truthfully, I have to wonder if it has something to do with software HP installed or just the bloated operating system.There are some noticeable improvements. Most Office documents open much faster (2-3x).  Critical for my particular situation is that X1 ties up the computer much less frequently.  The initial indexing and optimizing (275k documents and 126k email messages) is significantly faster, perhaps as much as 3x. Opening 100 MB Filemaker databases is easily 3x faster.  Creation of new records in Filemaker is similarly as fast.My overall opinion is that the X25-M is an excellent SSD albeit at significant expense and with less than ideal capacity.  If cost isn't a problem but space is, I would suggest relocating files to an external drive to free up some space.  The cost/space/performance tradeoffs make the investment worthwhile.ProsVery fast, uniquely fast for certain applicationsEasy installationShock resistantNo defragmentation necessaryCons160 GB too small enoughExpensiveCould be even fasterSystemHP Elitebook Mobile Workstation 8530wX9100 Dual Core Processor @ 3.06 GHz4 GB RAM7200 RPM drive upgraded to 160 GB X25-MWindows Ultimate 64 Bit

review_title: Great Product, but an Extended Warranty is a Must!
review_text: About six months after giving this product a two star rating, I have re-gained my faith in the iPod as a great piece of technology for listening to music. You could literally store an entire music collection on it and keep it in your pocket. With iTunes, updating song lists is a snap..especially if you like downloading tunes, but choose not to burn a new cd-r every time you get a few new songs. The iPod also works as a really handy external hard drive. The one flaw in this is if you format your iPod for a mac, it cannot be used with a pc unless you format it again. If you only use one format, this little unit makes a flash drive obsolete. Please protect yourself when buying this product and get an extended warranty, however. I had problems ranging from battery failure to long hesitations between songs after using mine for a few months. At that point I had to choose between paying $30 to ship the product in for repair or $59 for an extended warranty. After buying the extended warranty, they replaced my iPod with a new one. From what I've seen, the lemon rate for this product is very high. While I recommend this product, I warn you to be prepared to pay for repairs. Being a relatively new technology, I suggest you buy a less expensive iPod and plan to upgrade after a couple years. Many of the kinks should be worked out by then.

review_title: Worked great on my TV/Cable Box Connection...for a while...poor connection on PS3
review_text: I bought this HDMI cable to connect my Playstation 3 to my 32" LCD TV.  It seemed to work great for a while, but I later found that is made a poor connection in the back of my PS3.  I would be playing a game, and the screen would go black.  It would return if I pressed or wiggled the cord in the back of the PS3.  I thought there was something wrong with my Playstation, but I decided to switch cords with the one I had going to my cable box (Dynex cord from Best Buy).  I have not had the problem with my Playstation since.  The Amazon cable seems to work great with my cable box though, so I can't call it all bad!I'm not sure if I got a bad one, or if they just aren't meant for the PS3, but I had bad luck with it.  If you're getting it for a cable box or probably even a blu-ray player, it seems to work great.  If I only had used it on my cable box, I would have given it 4 or 5 stars for sure.**Update**This cable DID work great on my cable box.  I was experiencing blips with my TV picture from time to time.  I began to suspect the HDMI cable.  Finally, tonight, I turned on the TV and there was no sound.  I switched it to my PS3, and the sound was great.  I switched back to TV, then reached behind and wiggled the HDMI cable in the back of my cable box.  Sound!  If I kept wiggling, the sound would cut in and out, and the picture would skip.I put an end to this cable.  I switched my other HDMI cable back to my cable box and just ordered a new cable for my PS3.  This knocked my review down to 1 star.  At least it wasn't an expensive mistake!

But every time I use this lens it just amazes me.  It's really sharp, even usefully sharp wide open and stopped down it looks like a stopped down prime lens. No need to set up a tripod.  I can also get away with shutter speeds at least two stops below what I can hand hold with a non-IS lens. review_title: Now I use my computer instead of the other way around!
review_text: I've been told by my irritated PC using friends that I'm a walking switch ad, but you know what?  I don't care.  I'd had computers going waaaay back to 1981 with a TRS-80 model 3 with cassette tape drive.  I knew about computers, but they never seemed to deliver on their promise of improving our lives.  I lived with PC's up 'til last year and finally threw in the towel.Last year, I realized that I'd spent more time trying to get the various hardware and software to "play nice" with one another than actually doing anything useful.Fast forward to the recent past.  I pay the rather hefty sum (yikes!) and I take my sexy new iMac home.  I uncrate this thing and within ten minutes of power up I'm already burning a CD to iTunes.  Cool!  I didn't like the mouse that was supplied, so I plugged in my Microsoft (gasp!) optical mouse and away I went.  Now, you need to realize that I plugged the mouse in while the computer was running and it just worked!  If I tried that with one of my PC's, best case it'd just crash.  Often as not, it'd necessitate a trip to the grocery store for Doritos, etc.One thing that my PC buddies like to remind me about (other than cost) is that my iMac isn't the last word in gaming performance.  To that I say...  so?  If you're a hardcore gamer, the Mac platform isn't for you.  For EVERY OTHER application, my little iMac can go toe to toe with a PC and usually come out on top.I use it for photoshop, I've used it to master my LP records and language tapes to CD and MP3.  These are things that I dreamed of doing with my PC's but was never able to.  I now have an iPod and I absolutely love it.  I use my computer every day and don't regret the investment even the slightest bit.  I play games (Warcraft III, Diablo II and Everquest) once in a while.  I watch movies on the widescreen monitor, and on and on...Yes it's expensive, it's not for members of the upgrade of the month club, but if you want a computer that behaves like a reliable appliance and allows you to do the things you want to do without an IT certification,BUY A FREAKIN' MAC!Oh, and another thing.  In several months, the computer has not crashed.  Not once.  Ever.

I just recently purchased this tripod for an upcoming trip. I really don't have room to take my Velbon tripod (which is an excellent tripod) but it's just a little too big and cumbersome for long trips, especially when air travel is involved. The MeFoto seems like it will be just the ticket. It is much smaller and easier to pack than a standard tripod. Also this thing is definitely heavier than I expected but that is due to the quality this thing has. For it's size it is pretty darn sturdy. If you scope out the last section of the legs they are a little thin but still they remain steady. I'm not a real tall person so I typically get away without having to use the last section. The ball head is great and it does an excellent job supporting my Nikon D7000 and believe me, my camera is not light with all the extra junk I have one it, battery grip, tele-lens, etc. The head just stays put. Also the movement is so smooth and fluid when you pan left and right. The design of the mounting plate took me a little getting used to but I like it. It has the Arca Swiss style mounting system which was new for me. Just keep a good grip on  your camera until you have the plate secured in the holder and you will be fine. It also comes with a very nice carrying case which hidden inside you'll find a set of spiked feet along with a hex wrench tool should you need to make any adjustments. Oh, and before I forget. One of the legs converts into a monopod so you really get a two in one deal so that you don't have to pack one separate .Last of all and one of the big things I have heard some minor complaints over is the twist lock system on the legs. I have heard a lot of people say that it is rather time consuming to set up and secure each section. Honestly, in my opinion once you do it a couple of times the setup is just as easy and quick as the lever lock system. I set it up in just about the same amount of time it would have taken me for any other tripod. If anything we are only talking a few seconds difference so I really don't see what the big deal is. Plus I think the twist locks feel more secure.In all I don't think this tripod will disappoint. It is much better made than I ever expected it to be for it's size and I think it would be perfect for anyone's travel need. It was just what I was looking for.

review_title: Amazingly Good Value for a Nikon TTL Flash
review_text: I shoot a lot of weddings and interior/outdoor shots needing flash or some fill flash.  I have two Nikon bodies (7000,7100) and a Nikon SB700, but, only carried a manual non-TTL/sensor type backup flash  (Vivitar 285!). I wanted something in TTL that would typically stay in my photo bag for emergency use only and yet, be low in price and do the job in a pinch as back-up.Having tested this flash in about 100+ shots under a variety of conditions, including low/very subdued light and for fill-flash (outdoors) using TTL and the auto-zoom feature, I'm really delighted over-all on how well this inexpensive TTL flash performs. Exposures were all accurate and nothing was burned out nor under-exposed. My test images were all "usable" and in the "sweet-spot" for easy editing as needed in PS/CS.My only gripe and a minimal one (since this flash will not see a lot of use unless my primary flash dies in the middle of a shoot) is that due to using only 2 AA batteries, the time for the flash to zoom to match the lens focal length being used, is rather slow.I feel this is partly due to the total voltage for this flash (2 X 1.5V, 2 AAs) which is 1/2 of what many other flashes typically use (4  X 1.5V, 4 AAs).That means in a situation where you are zooming a lot and firing away with several shot bursts close together, the flash head zoom might not be quite at the light angle distribution angle it wants to be to match your lens focal length at the moment of image capture.The good news when I tested this for the slow zooming speed is that, the light uniformity across the image frame wasn't that bad in shots where I tried extremes of the zoom range and took two to three shots one after the other while the poor flash zoom mechanism was trying to keep up with me. (I think I heard it panting at least twice :) )If you use a light diffuser (with closer shots, ..ie: portraits or in a fill-flash situation) I think this flash will be forgiving along with TTL managing the right exposure given it's sluggish zoom performance as it tries to match the focal length of your lens (and within it's specs for the focal length range, to be fair). Visually, the series of shots where I purposely zoomed fast and shot images this way to keep the zoom moving during exposure, would be keepers and work out fine.No complaints on this flash. It's accurate for TTL, has a nice small profile, certainly seems stingy on battery life and has decent recycle in the close to mid range. Even my SB700 has to fully recharge the capacitor on those long shots (fully depletes it like other flashes at long+ range) so I'm not going to be critical at all for any flashes performance at extreme distances.The focus aid illumination is less bright then my SB700, but, hey, this flash is a fraction of the cost of my SB700. If you use a lens in the close to mid range, I'm guessing auto-focus using this flash will work well even with those of smaller apertures. Even with my SB700, I've gotten into some very low light situations (wedding dance floor, very low lighting, you can hardly see everyone) and simply focused manually using a higher ISO and flash and lens fully cooperated! Don't be afraid to crank up ISO where needed in very low light to help both flash and lens get that image that otherwise might be missed. Go with manual focus too!Be sure to follow the label warning that's right on the flash to turn the flash on only AFTER mounting it on your camera and turning on the camera first and then the flash AFTER!Failure to do so will cause the camera and flash not to communicate at all, the flash won;t know it's on the camera nor will the flash even fire off.Just switching the flash off and back on resolves this instantly if it was off and on the camera (powered on). A bit odd, but, easy to resolve correctly once you know the symptom and correct procedure to resolve.Bottom line is this is a superb little TTL flash for the price. Not a lot of bells and whistles on this flash as other reviewers pointed out, but, the fundamental features and performance of the Sunpak PZ40X all work perfectly. It'd stable and consistent. Excellent Guide Number too for it's supported zoom range. Not bad at all from just TWO AA batteries!This is absolutely a keeper for my photo bag and will be a backup as needed that I know I can count on.Highly Recommended!
