review_title: Consider Me A Convert--The Ipod Rocks!
review_text: Ever since the Ipod first came out, I was determined not to buy one.  Why?  Well, the main reason was that it didn't come with a replaceable battery.  I didn't want to be charged $50 just to replace it, when in other MP3 players, I could buy an extra one for half the price and do it myself.Well, after a dismal experience with the Archos 504 (Note to people:  stay away from anything with that brand name, trust me on this.) I received the Ipod as an early Xmas present.  Though I was disappointed in having to downgrade (My Archos 504 was 160 GB), I was glad to have an MP3 player again.  At that point, the Archos had been in RMA land for about three months (2nd time in a year it went to that magical place).  And though I was anti-Ipod in the past, I decided to give this device a try.  Let's say I was EXTREMELY impressed--so impressed that when the Archos returned from it's RMA vacation, I didn't touch it again.Even though the Ipod has about as much disk drive space as most laptop computers, it is extremely small and slim.  It's about half the size and width of the Archos 504.  It can easily fit into just about any pants or shirt pocket.  I didn't realize just how clunky my Archos was until I got the Ipod.  Also, there seems to be no issues with overheating or static with the hard drive.  I've heard it's not a traditional hard drive, but a 'solid state' one.  Well, anyway, I don't care what it is, all I know is that it's fabulous.  It's great not having to worry if the hard drive is going to freeze up on you any second now.I wasn't sure about having one wheel and one button for all the controls.  It didn't seem intuitive to me, but actually I got the hang of it in about ten minutes.  It is very easy to figure out how to navigate through the player.  It doesn't really come with a manual (though it should) but you can access the manual on the Apple.com website.  I only had to look at it once.About the battery, which is the main reason I didn't buy an Ipod in the first place--you can't change it, but for the most part, you don't need to.  I use it everyday (mostly to play music) with the backlight on for 2 seconds and I only have to charge it every 7-9 days.  Also, when I charge with the AC adapter, it takes only about an hour.  In this aspect, the Ipod blows Archos away when it comes to battery life (FIVE of my Archos batteries together lasted about the same amount of time as the Ipod battery and took about three hours to charge EACH.)You can only sync music using Itunes.  I prefer to sync directly with the computer but the Itunes program is fairly easy to use and it's very easy to organize your music (once in a while the songs ID3 tags will be messed up in Itunes, but it's a very easy to fix them.)Another fantastic thing with Ipod is that it plays standard formats without having to pay extra for 'plug-ins' (UH-HMMM, I'm talking to you, Archos.  All songs on Itunes come in AAC format and video in m4v but Ipod also supports MP3 and MP4 and a variety of other formats right out of the box.  About playing videos, movies, etc.  the screen is a little small in my opinion for watching a full length movie (though I know people who have done it and say it's not bad) but for watching music videos it's awesome.  The screen is crystal clear--it's like having a tiny HDTV in the palm of your hand.  The Ipod also has various extras, like games, a clock, a stopwatch, etc.  I've tried all of these and they're all pretty cool little toys.There are only a few things that I wish the Ipod had--one is more hard drive space (I don't know why they discontinued the 160 GB--I would have bought that one if I had gotten the Ipod myself) and two, is that the sound quality could be better.  It's not bad, most people would think it was pretty good, but being an audiophile, this area could use some improvement.  I noticed that on the songs that have a booming bass, the Ipod distorts the bass so much that the song is almost unlistenable.  The Ipod has various settings like most mp3 players have 'pop' 'electronic' etc., but I wish you could manual adjust the bass, treble & midline manually like you can on the computer or on a regular stereo.  Also, I have my music organized in separate A-Z files and unlike in my last two MP3 players, you can't actually see them, though they're there.  So, if I want to listen to a song in file W and I'm in file B, I have to scroll through all the songs to get to file W.  Also, you can't scroll backward from the first song to the last song--if you're in File B and want to go to File W, you have to flip through C,D, etc.  and not the shorter way A, Z, Y,.  In both of my old Mp3 players you could do that.  Sometimes if I scroll fast enough, the player will start 'flipping' through the files but this is hard to do.  Perhaps there is an easier way to do this, but I haven't figured it out yet.  Also, in shuffle mode, I'd love to have a preview of what song was up next on the list.  The Archos, and the Creative Zen Nomad Xtra from Eons ago both were able to do this.  I'm not sure why the Ipod doesn't have this feature.  Other than those minor things, the Ipod is incredible and I would highly recommend it to anyone who wants an MP3 player that works reliably.So, to those afraid of the dark side, there's no need to be.  The dark side is your friend!October 2011:  This Ipod still works perfect.  So far, it hasn't caused me any problems, and now it has a sibling, a 160GB Ipod!  Yes, I DO need two Ipods, believe it or not!  If you can't afford a new one, I highly recommend getting an older or refurbed model.

review_title: Western Digital Passport 250 GB - Nice Looking Portable External HD
review_text: WD Passport Portable Hard Drive 250 GB/GoOut of the passport lineup, this is the fourth one I've bought and I couldn't be more happy with them.  Passport hard drives also have a new and slightly thicker essentials version.  I own both, which other than the slightly different form factor are very similar in terms of performance.  Both are great for mobile backups of data, but both are also slower to copy large backups than their A/C powered MyBook big-brothers.There's also a newer version that isn't out on Amazon yet and an Elite version.The LooksThe drive has the shiny exterior sported by most passport drives as well as the new MyBooks.  The body has an offset shape with a blue activity light.  The white version may appeal a little more to Mac users, but the black version is the same in every other way.The case does scratch in transit and the surface also attracts fingerprints and dust.  But the look is still nice and you can easily purchase a case or holder for the drive if it bothers you.  Most versions don't ship with the included case, but you can pick it up for $10.The FeaturesTransfer speeds are ok but definitely slower than it's A/C powered big-brothers.  This guy is still limited by the 480 Mps connection speed of USB 2.0, but performs somewhat slower than this when performing large backups.  The USB2.0 speed rating can not really be achieved in production and you will get a fraction of that.  But it's a trade-off that's worth it since it's USB-powered.The software utilities included with this device will be most useful for beginners.  I tested the backup software in particular but found it to be slow and impractical.  It works, but cutting and pasting worked better.  Take my advice: don't use this utilities and just do cut and paste backups and saves to this drive.I've had no problem connecting this drive to any computer, including Windows XP, Vista and Mac OS X.ReliabilityI've had good luck with the passport line of drives.  They seem to have lower failure rates than many MyBook drives, though I also own those and haven't had issues their either.  I hope it stays that way.  Maybe my gentle care has helped me to get lucky with these guys so far.  Maybe it's because these drives are generally off when in transit.  Regardless, these guys have held up fine.Pros+ Nice portable form factor that easily connects via USB+ USB powered, no A/C required, which is great for portability+ Works well on Windows Vista, XP and Mac OS X+ Easy to set up disk encryption for security and privacy+ Nice looks, in my opinion better looking than the new essentials version+ Turns on and off with your computer or easily ejected via system tray+ Easy plug-and-play installation+ Integrates nicely with my growing stable of WD MyBook drives+ Included software may be useful for some novices+ 250 GB capacity is just about right for most users+ At this price, a better value than the 320GB passportCons- Somewhat slow file transfer speeds for larger backups- Included software not useful for power users- Shiny body attracts scratch, fingerprints and dust- Have to spend your cash to get a case that should have been included- Larger sizes availableConclusionThis drive is great or those who want a portable drive for backups on the run.  You can get this 250GB version for around $100, versus the $150 charged for the 320 GBWestern Digital 320 GB Passport 2.5" USB 2.0 Hard Drive.  That makes the price ($ per GB) better and this 250 GB unit a better value than the higher capacity 320 GB.  Other than price and capacity there is no real difference between them.  Get one soon!Enjoy!

review_title: A workable solution if you don't expect miracles
review_text: I've used two of the older 2.4 GHZ units for more than three years.  Service has been consistently good, and it has met my expectations.  I have one unit feeding from a standard-def satellite receiver to a CRT-TV in my garage; it works well over a transmission distance of about 40 feet going through two walls and a garage roof.  The other feeds the signal from an HD satellite receiver to a small flat-screen TV in my kitchen through two interior walls. The result is not HD on the kitchen set, but to my eyes it's cleaner than an average SD feed. In neither case was it practical to run cables, and in both cases the signal received is clean and viewable. (And I'm a broadcast/video producer, so I don't watch terrible signals.)It's important to read the directions and set up carefully, then experiment with antenna placement.  If you have large metal objects (like a big CRT-TV) sitting next to the transmitter and positioned between the transmitter and the receiver, you're going to have trouble sending the signal through them.  Move the transmitter to a spot where it's not blocked by a large electronic device and you will get better reception.The 2.4 GHZ model X10 receiver does experience interference from our powerful kitchen microwave about 10 feet away, and it also has occasional bursts of static.  That's an artifact of the bandwidth, so if you run a microwave all the time and want the X10 receiver hear it, make sure to get the newest model. You may also notice some interference if you run a laptop computer using Wi-Fi very close to the receiver, but it's not constant. Aside from these rather predictable interference points, our reception is clean and nicely viewable 98% of the time.  Since I avoided thousands of dollars in remodeling which would have been required to run cables to the locations in question, I consider this an excellent trade-off.These are inexpensive units which provide a great deal of convenience and give you a nice clean signal with occasional static problems which are more due to the band they operate on than the devices themselves. If you want to send an HD signal across the house to a 55-inch flat screen, this is NOT the way you want to go.  But if you want to send a signal to a smaller TV that's in a spot like a kitchen or work room, they can do a very nice job for you.  I rated it four stars because it does exactly what it's designed to do, and although it's not perfect, it does the job and saves you both remodeling and expense.

review_title: Now any stereo system is Bluetooth compatible
review_text: I'm quite excited after using this product and here is why.I have a mini stereo system on my desk in the room. So when I'm in bed, I'm not able to listen to music stored in my phone through the stereo, and phone's built in speaker doesn't really cut it. I was thinking about buying a docking speaker for the night stand, but a good one costs quite a bit.Here is where this bluetooth adapter comes into play. Its outside has a mirror finish, casing is nicely fit together, have a quality feeling holding in hand. Anker logo is printed on top, on the bottom, there is the 3.5mm audio port and a USB output port rated for 1A. On its back, a tiny blue LED is located in the center to indicate operational status. Once you find Anker on your device, simply click on it and you're set. Takes 10 seconds to do.Specification says it can pair with 8 devices, I've only tested with 5, including iphone 3G, 3GS, Galaxy S3, S2 and Nexus 7. All paired successfully.Audio quality is solid, within range, it's just as good as using a audio cable. Max range spec is 33ft according to manufacture.One big added bonus is the USB charging port. With 1A output current, it can easily charge most smart phones and some tablets. I'm able to charge up all my phones as fast as their stock chargers and my Nexus 7 tablet, a little slower than stock 1.3A charger.Over all, considering its function, price, build quality, ease of use, I think it's an excellent buy for anyone that needs a bluetooth adapter.

review_title: Perfect answer for my audio books needs
review_text: I'm on the road...a LOT (150-250 miles a day).  I love listening to audiobooks while I travel from one appointment to the next.  For the past two years, I've been using my Samsung tablet for listening to those audiobooks and it does a very respectable job as far as it goes.  The only problem with the tablet is that it's big and clunky and very distracting (read dangerous) to deal with while driving.  I was looking for a decent alternative; something that was smaller and easier to control, but something that could still hold all of my audiobooks and that had decent sound quality.  So...I looked and read many reviews.  Money really wasn't that big an issue with me; I was willing to pay for the best if that's what it took.  Bottom line is that it came down to either the Apple iPod Touch (4th or 5th generation) or the Sansa Clip Zip.  So I figured, what do I really have to lose by choosing the Clip Zip since it was $250 cheaper than the iPod Touch?So I bought the 4GB model along with a 16GB microSD card and gave it a try.  I am blown away!  I went to Audible and downloaded all of my books, ran a cord between the ClipZip and the Aux input of my van and away we went.  Okay, so the controls are a little less than ideal, but they work and aren't so distracting that I feel as if I'm in danger if I have to pause it in order to answer the phone.  So the screen isn't the latest retina scan whatever; what it has it works just fine.  You can easily move between your downloaded music and radio and books and stop watch and even control what you see on the screen. I haven't used the Stop Watch nor do I expect to anytime soon and I could choose not to see it on screen by simply going to the Settings Menu and instructing the ClipZip not to show it.  But I've left it on there for now just because.When I get home, I simply plug the ClipZip directly into my home stereo to continue listening to my audio books or to the FM radio. Let me talk about the FM radio for a minute.  It's wonderful!  My home system isn't able to pick up on one of the Houston stations that I like, but the ClipZip is able to pull it in perfectly.  That's just frosting on the cake for me (I was ready to go out and invest in a new home stereo system; now I don't have to).If you've read any other reviews about the ClipZip, you've probably already read a couple of hundred times about the lousy headphones that come with it. Ditto. It isn't that the sound quality is that bad; it isn't unless you're some kind of audiophile in which case you shouldn't even EXPECT them not to suck. But the FIRST time I went to unplug them, they pulled apart at the plug even though I was pulling on the part of the plug that directly connects to the unit.  I refuse to take off a star based on that, however, because the ClipZip itself is such a great little unit.  Just as a side comment, I read one of the so-called "professional" reviews going on about the "build quality" of the ClipZip being something less than sterling.  Listen, I'm here to tell you that I am very tough on electronic gadgets and I've already put this thing through it's paces.  It's built like a little tank.  I've already dropped it and banged it around in my van; I've gone to sleep with it pinned to my shirt and rolled over on it.  I'm quite certain that it will hold up well for those of you who are into exercising.  The clip on it seems to be very sturdy.  I mean, I don't know what these other guys are expecting, but for crying out loud, the build quality for an MP3 player under $50 is AMAZING!  One reviewer made the old, tired, typical comment: "You get what you pay for.."  I completely disagree.  You get a whole helluva lot MORE than what you pay for with this little thing. For UNDER $50, I got a very decent 20GB MP3 player!  That is a bargain and a best buy in my bookOne final thing:  I've read a couple of Amazon reviews griping about the fact that you can't play audiobooks on the ClipZip.  Perhaps that was once true.  I don't know.  But those gripes are no longer relevant, so you might as well completely disregard those ratings.  In fact, those comments almost prevented me from buying this since that was what my own personal focus was about to begin with.  Fortunately, in the course of my research I discovered others who put that concern to bed.  So, for any of you audiobookaphiles out there, I highly recommend this little guy.  And for anyone who wants something to listen to while jogging or working out, this would be perfect (except for the lousy headphones, of course; there are plenty of nice replacements out there and you'll still barely have to top $50).So there you go.  Highly recommended.

Bought by G-Box Midnight MX2 Android TV device for one purpose, to view placeshifted TV content off of my Dishnetwork receivers at my home in Florida.  This was to avoid having to pay for cable (in Florida) and Dish (in Arizona) at two houses when I can only be at one home at a time.Here is my setup.  I have a VIP722k Dishnetwork HD receiver which I hooked up a Sling Adapter ($50.00 from Dishnetwork) and a my other receiver is a VIP612 in which I run a Slingbox 350 (can't use a Sling Adapter on this device).To test the viability of placeshifting using Sling on the G-Box, I installed Dish Anywhere Android App from Google Play.  I also installed Sling Player for Tablet also from Google Play (this costs $14.99 and Dish Anywhere is free).Both Apps work fine on this device.  Only issue is you need to have HIGH upload bandwidth (I have 19 mbs).  I will provide a review on the Sling devices at a later time.  There is a delay in using the user interface and when I response takes place on the screen but it is acceptable as this is a reality of network latency.Okay, so the G-Box does what I wanted it to do.  What else can I do with it?So, I buy a UKB-500-RF mini keyboard with airmouse.  Works nicely but Android is better suited for a touch pad.  I am not satisfied with this (and tried another wireless keyboard from Favi) but it is all I can find right now.  I also installed DroidMote which allows you to use your Android phone as a remote to the G-Box.  It works a bit better but still not the perfect solution.  Bear this in mind when getting the G-Box.  The remote that comes with it is not sufficient to control the applications efficiently.Okay, let's talk XBMC.  This is the open source capability installed on the G-Box that allows you to configure various applications that can stream content from the web.  It's kind of an open source Roku.  Very flexible but there are issues.  First, the navigation is different than the Android.  Bothers me as I like a more unified approach.  Also, content is vast but I still haven't found any content that really interests me.  The Amazon Video Streaming app doesn't work so bear that in mind.  As a matter of fact, you can't play Amazaon Streaming content at all on an Android device.  As I explore XBMC more, I will comment on this.The G-Box has great sound and video quality and it's dual core processor gives it plenty of capability of streaming HD 1080p content.  No issues or lag of any sort.The User Community on the Matricom forum is robust and very helpful.  If you have an issue, you can find your answer pretty quick.This device is not 100% idiot proof but it has great potential.  I like it and recommend it to any device geek.  Don't buy it if you want an out of the box solution and are not fairly technical.  I found this device to be easy to configure and use, but I have been working in technology for decades.You can run virtually any Android application that works on your phone.  For me, the G-Box does what I want it to do.  It will save me a lot of money for my particular application.  I am also finding all kinds of things it can do as well.  It works very well for streaming videos off of your media server, it can also act as a media server using Upnp.Some apps are not as robust at the G-Box can handle (the Android Netflix app from Google Play does not support HD).  You can find alternatives but I do think that the market will start to get out more powerful apps to match the more powerful hardware like the G-Box.Thank you.

At this point, my advice, is to avoid integrated Cable Modem-Routers. (Avoid--run, do not walk away from them. Do not buy if it can be avoided.)Instead, think about getting a separate Cable Modem and a separate Router.  The integrated units do provide a lot of functionality for the price. If they work for you, that could be great. But, a very big issue is that you can't apply needed firmware updates. And even if they work now, this issue can "byte" you in the future, when your needs change. With a separate router, you can, at least, upgrade the firmware in your router independently of the cable modem.The new Motorola SBG6580, integrated Cable Modem-Router with wireless N support looks like a nice enough package and a good value for the price. However, we quickly discovered an issue that Motorola's web site indicated was now fixed in a later firmware.The bad news is that Motorola's interpretation of DOCSIS is that it prevents them from making firmware updates available. "Motorola is not allowed to control the upgrades of DOCSIS devices, per the standards specification.  Any firmware or software changes must be implemented via the cable network. "[...]The Widipedia page on DOCSIS seems to agree with Motorola's interpretation. "the cable operator (or Multiple Service Operators - MSO) exercises full control over the cable modem's configuration"[...]My understanding is, that in the earlier days of cable modem service, that some crackers loaded their cable modems with "tweaked" firmware to get bandwidth and other features in excess of what the cable companies wanted them to have. (Or at least wanted them to have at the rates they were paying.) As a result, the newer standards prevent user initiated firmware updates.So if you need a firmware update to fix something, you need the cable company to do it for you. And our experience with two different, both very large, cable companies is they won't do it and don't care. Check the blog comments and you will see our experience is not unique.

My wife and I purchased this TV as a Christmas gift for each other. This is our first "large" screen flat panel TV (compared with our old 27 inch CRT TV). We got the 37 inch because we felt that the 42 inch size would crowd the space near our room's doorway. The picture is exceptional, and we really appreciate the wide viewing angle with our room set-up. The contrast is great. It looks good both in daylight and at night. While we do not watch in a dark room, we do not have the light leakage problem mentioned elsewhere. If you look into the heat vents in the back, you can see some light, but it does not radiate from the unit. I really like the LED backlighting, and the fact that the set uses only about 40 Watts when operating. The sound is decent, not theatrical, but probably what you would expect from built-in speakers. It is good enough that I have no plans to add speakers. This model has only digital (optical) audio out. It turns out that our audio receiver, purchased only several years ago, does not have this. Happily we do not need it. The TV is "internet ready" if you have hardwire ethernet or a Roku or Apple TV box. Wi-Fi "ready" means that it is ready for you to purchase a Wi-Fi USB dongle. I did purchase the Panasonic DY-WL10 wireless LAN adapter, which runs 802.11n at 2.4 or 5 GHz. We have relatively slow 3.3 Mbps DSL service, the best that is available to us. (That's 3.3 Mbps, not 33 Mbps - not a typo). I thought that 802.11n at 5 GHz could handle anything that 3.3 Mbps DSL could offer. However, I was disappointed by constant rebuffering and interruptions to movies using the built-in Netflix application. Finally, I strung a Cat 5e ethernet cable from our DSL modem/router to the TV and the problem went away. I broke down and snaked ethernet cable through the walls and basement and up to the TV, and I have had no problems since. Your experience may differ, especially if you have broadband internet, but I really think the limiting factor is the USB Wi-Fi dongle. Pros: great picture, wide viewing angle. Cons: needed a hardwire LAN for Netfilx streaming (at least for me). Overall, I really like this TV.

review_title: Finally, some decent tunes in my old Chevy Truck!
review_text: I have an old plain-Jane 1984 Chevy C10 pickup truck.  It is a work-truck, and nothing fancy.  It came out with a old two-knob AM radio, which had later been replaced by a aftermarket AM-FM Cassette two-knob radio.  I bought the truck second-hand, and for as long as I've owned it, I have suffered without music.  The old radio worked, but getting a single station tuned in and made to sound remotely like music, was simply more hassle than it was worth.  I bought a Sony CDXGT540UI Stereo here on Amazon.  I paired that up with a Jensen Marine MGH300 gimbel mount stereo enclosure that I learned about through Amazon, but bought directly from the manufacturer (who happens to sell through Amazon anyway).  Add to that, four 5 1/4 inch JVC dual-cone 150W speakers, a new fender-mount antenna and some speaker baffles from a certain auction site, and I was set.  The Sony CDXGT540UI stereo arrived quickly, and I waited for the rest to arrive.  To mount the stereo in the dash would have meant cutting up the steel and plastic of the dash, and even then would not be an ideal looking finish.  When the Jensen Marine gimbel mount arrived, I removed the smoky door on the front, disassembled it, and painted all the white plastic with flat black paint.  I reassembled it, and mounted the Sony stereo inside, and mounted that under my dash.  I just tonight finished all my wiring, and tested out the stereo.  I LOVE IT!  Hitting seek on the radio instantly and clearly brought in 50 or so FM stations.  For a pickup truck, the sound levels were excellent.  With the Sony mounted in that Jensen Marine enclosure, it sits down low, under the dash, and being dark flat black, it isn't easily seen, and behind that smoky front door, it doesn't scream out to thieves "I'm a stereo, steal me!"  The Sony stereo blue lights shine though the smoky door of the enclosure enough to read, and the Sony remote communicates through the smoky door so you don't have to keep opening and closing the door.  I'd bought a Transcend 32 G flash memory drive from Amazon, and when I plug it into the Sony with my music collection onboard, the Sony reads in the contents and plays very nicely.  All in all, I am one very happy Chevy Truck owner now!  Thanks Amazon, Sony, Jensen and JVC!

Furthermore, the new Logitech USB "Unified Receiver" holds the promise for simplifying connectivity of multiple (Logitech-only, no doubt) wireless devices (keyboards, mice, and who knows what else!) through one single USB tranceiver that's small enough to leave plugged in. (The glossy black finish tends to accentuate the slightest fingerprint, but Logitech's renowned industrial design masters may know something I do not in this area.)In short, a perfect keyboard would mate the diNovo's layout and tactility with the K340's excellent connectivity. When it arrives, I'll replace my K340.

review_title: Easy to install, easy to use. A winner.
review_text: For years, Bose has been making an all-in-one amplifier/receiver/media player package with an array of the iconic cube speakers. Now Sony has a similar model. Everything you need (minus the TV and an HDMI cable) is in the box, all the way down to the speaker cables. I can see the appeal of such a system to those who are not technologically proficient. Since that is the intended consumer, I will attempt to make this review as free from jargon as possible.1) SetupThe installation was quite simple. All the cables are labeled and color-coded so that virtually anyone can install this without hassle. The front channels, center speaker, and subwoofer plug into the back while the "wireless" rear channels plug into an external amplifier that you position in the back of your room.Once the proper connections are made, you just follow the on-screen directions to configure everything else. This amounts to making a network connection through either the built-in wifi or through an ethernet connection and calibrating the speaker levels. Interestingly, Sony includes a microphone with a long cable that plugs into the back of the unit and stretches to wherever your optimum listening position happens to be. In my case, my room layout doesn't allow me to sit in a position equidistant from the two surround channels, so the Sony unit automatically detected this and attenuated the volume on one of the rear channels to compensate for me sitting closer to it. It's actually pretty cool.Once I went through the basic setup, there were a few software and firmware updates to install. These took about ten minutes to run, all in all. After that, I tested out the system with a Blu-ray disc and discovered that the dialogue emerging from the center channel was a bit low. Happily, this was an easy thing to adjust. Sony includes a nice menu system with good graphics to help you pick the speaker that is too quiet and change its output level. Overall, I am very pleased with the menu system. It's about as good as you'll find for a company that isn't necessarily in the business of designing stunning graphical user interfaces.A word about the "wireless" speakers. I have no idea why companies describe speakers as "wireless." Unless you have a battery-powered speaker, it WILL need power and that means speaker cable. The only benefit here is that you don't have to run long strands of speaker cable from the front of your room to the back. Otherwise, both rear channels are 100% wired, plus you have the external amplifier that needs to be near a wall outlet. If I seem to be harping on this point, it's because people like my mother (a confirmed cable hater) always see systems advertised as having "wireless" speakers and she always thinks that, somehow, there are no cables at all.2) The Receiver/Blu-ray PlayerI must give Sony recognition for designing a nice looking unit. The touch screen is cool and the solid top slides across the top to reveal a top-loading Blu-ray spindle. It looks cool, but how does it function?In a word, flawlessly. I read that the Blu-ray player allows you to "begin watching your movies in seconds," and I was skeptical. Any Blu-ray player I've ever encountered takes anywhere from five to ten minutes to go from disc startup to main menu. It's so annoying. There are FBI warnings, anti-piracy warnings, trailers that you can't chapter-skip, advertisements, and all sorts of other crap. It's infuriating and makes me hate the Blu-ray format. HOWEVER, this unit allows you to skip all that! It's amazing; utterly amazing. I tried six different Blu-ray discs and all but one allowed me to skip everything--even the FBI warning. "Inception" wouldn't let me skip right to the main menu, but I could chapter-skip through the previews and warnings. This is reason enough to justify a five-star review.The various network functions worked flawlessly as well. Bluetooth allowed me to stream music through the system via my smartphone, Amazon's video service worked well, YouTube was fine, and I even tried the Internet browser. It's idiotic to try to navigate the web through your TV using a conventional remote, but hey - you can do it. Netflix was great. The Sony interface for Netflix is very nice and provides a good mix of information with a clean layout. It's essentially the same as the second generation Roku box, but a bit sleeker. I still prefer the way my AppleTV handles Netflix, but this is a close second.The YouTube interface isn't quite as good as the Netflix interface. It's a bit clunky and it uses a keyboard layout that is nonsensical. If you have to use a standard remote to enter in words, it makes a lot more sense to have the letters in a grid rather than a long horizontal line. It's not horrible, but it could be better. On that same note, every interface has a different keyboard layout. It's not a huge deal, but it would be nice if the onscreen keyboard always looked the same.Finally, my one complaint. Yes, this system is designed to be simple and fool-proof, but the only available inputs are HDMI inputs. That means if you have some sort of archaic device like a Wii, you have no way to use it with this system. Sony does provide a couple of HDMI inputs, but some devices still need to make an RCA connection.3) The SpeakersThe speakers are decent. They have plastic bodies, so they feel a bit like over-sized computer speakers. Build quality aside, they do sound bigger than one would imagine. The system can play quite loud, and when you're watching certain kinds of movies, loudness is actually a pretty important factor.The sound is more suited for movies than music, as one would expect. There is a lot of treble and a lot of bass so that everything sounds very bright and loud. This makes movie soundtracks pop, but when listening to music (especially acoustic music like jazz and Classical/Romantic/Baroque/whatever), the midrange is underwhelming and makes the music sound cheap. There are some built-in EQ functions so that you can get use a flatter frequency response curve, which sounds much better for music.You can get a much more balanced sound using the Energy 5.1 Take Classic. That speaker system is superior in every category (e.g., build quality, neutrality of sound, size, usability for music) and it typically costs about half what the Sony system costs (although you'll need your own receiver and Blu-ray player, which will ultimately make it slightly more expensive). The downside is that if you're uncomfortable around technology, the Sony system is slightly easier to manage when you consider set up and the purchase of a separate receiver and Blu-ray player. Basically, if you're okay making a few simple speaker connections, I highly recommend the Energy Take Classic. Otherwise, the Sony is a reasonable substitute, provided you're using the system mainly for movies instead of music.4) Ease of UseAs I mentioned above, the system is very easy to set up, and the onscreen menus are well organized and easy to navigate. Because you only need to make a few cable connections (most of which are color coded), installation ought to be approachable to virtually anyone who can handle a minimal amount of reading and follow the largely pictorial setup instructions.The real test though was having my mother navigate the menu system and try out the various functions. My parents stream Netflix through their Blu-ray player and the menu system is confusing enough that she can't really get from the startup screen to the Netflix menu on her own. Yeah, it's not that hard, but she's utterly befuddled by technology. Interestingly, Sony includes a special "Netflix" button on the remote that allows you to jump straight there. With that helpful feature, I watched my own mother power up the Sony unit, open up Netflix, select a title, and start watching. I'm sure some of you will identify with this either as technophobes or as children of technophobes. It really is a well-designed system. In fact, my parents ended up liking it so much, they bought one for themselves, which allowed them to remove a big stack of audio equipment and a tangled mess of cables.5) OverallI highly recommend the Sony BDV-N7100W system. It's simple, but not simplistic. It works well, it has a nice array of useful features, the speakers are decent, and it's easy to set up and use. And most of all, the fact that the Blu-ray player allows you to skip to the main menu (or at least chapter skip) really lessens the usual aggravation that accompanies Blu-ray discs. This is an excellent product all around.

review_title: Nearly useless for Macs (pre-2012 and post-2012), regardless of OS version
review_text: Don't bother with this drive if you have a Mac - regardless of hardware age, make or version of OS X you're running.When this drive works, it works fine - it's very fast and nicely quiet. The trick is *when* it works - and that is hardly ever.  Most of the time, the drive refuses to mount or spin up when you connect it to a computer, requiring you to power down the drive, and power it back up to try again.  And even that fails to work much of the time.I've tried this drive with:* pre-2010 Mac Core 2 Duo (USB2) - Leopard (OS X 10.5)* 2011 MacBook Pro (Core i5 / USB2) - Snow Leopard (OS X 10.6), Lion (OS X 10.7)* 2012 Retina MacBook Pro (Core i7 / USB3) - Mountain Lion (OS X 10.8)and it fails to work reliably with any of them.  I've tried a variety of tricks that I've found across the web (patches, firmware updates, Seagate software and removal, etc), and nothing has made a difference.  The only step I've read about that supposedly "fixes" the issue is to call up Seagate and get them to send you a USB2 base for the drive (for which they  often try and make you pay) - but I want the USB3 speeds for my current mac (Retina MBP), so that solution doesn't fit me.My recommendation for Mac users: Save your money - buy another brand drive for your backup solution.

review_title: Great sound and comfort, but still made of plastic...
review_text: This is the best headphone for sound and comfort that I, and everyone that I've shown it to, have heard or felt.  It plays very well without an amp, even on a little nano sized mp3 player.  I have a used it with and without my NuForce Icon uDAC2 headphone DAC/AMP.  It sounds good either way.  The DAC/amp was a small improvement over my computers sound card (Asus Xonar DX) and a large improvement over my net-books built in sound card.  I have only tested with loss-less (FLAC/computer) or high bit rate compressed music (ipod).  I have owned the HD595 for about 10 months and have used it nearly everyday since I bought it.Pros/some things to consider:1. It's under $200 and I felt it was a much better value than the HD650.  The money (~$150) saved would buy a nice USB DAC/AMP.  The uDAC2 is a very nice 24bit 96kHz DAC/AMP that could be bought with the money saved.Side note: For those who wonder if 24bit equipment is just marketing, it's not.  The 24 bits allows volume control without causing the loss of data/clipping on 16bit CD music.  It also allows more accuracy during digital processing, for example a software equalizer.  It allows all the math to happen at 24 bits so rounding errors don't effect the final output as much.2. The cord is not removable, but on the plus side it's a very good cord.  It's thick, strong and long (10').  It comes with a 1/4" to 1/8" adapter so it can plug into computer equipment.  I have not noticed any noise leaking into the cord from other AC devices (computer/lights/etc).3. I can listen all day and neither my head nor my ears get tired.4. The sound is, of course, perfect.  It's an open headphone so sound leaks in and out.  This is both good and bad depending on you and your environment at the time of usage.  All open headphones leak sound because they were designed to allow air to move freely and sound travels through the air.  By allowing the air to move freely you get a better quality sound. I hate it when people buy a product and then give it a bad review because it does what it was designed to do.  As a general rule, if you don't want sound to leak in/out you should buy closed headphones and if you want better quality sound you should buy open headphones.  Open headphones lets you talk to and hear someone as long as the music volume isn't too high.  With the music off I can hear perfectly even with the headphones on my head.Cons:1. The only negative I have noticed is that the plastic used is too week where the ear pads slide.  I have small 1/4"-3/8" (about 1-1.5cm) cracks on the top/outside of the ear pads developing (growing with time).  The ear pads are going to break off at some point in time.  It's only been about 10 months since I bought the HD595 and I would hope that a high end headphone set would last more than a year.  I'm going to attempt to RMA the headphones as they have a 2 year warranty.  They should have used metal on such a stress point as each time the headphones are put on/off, all the pressure pulls at this point causing stress cracks.  If they didn't want to use metal they should have reinforced the area by making it thicker than the rest of the headphone body.  I will update this review (if I remember it) with the outcome of the RMA request.  In fairness, I have nearly 300 days of usage on this headphone.  You should keep that in mind.  If I had used it for only 1 days a week it would be equal to nearly 6 years of usage and it's still going.Final thoughts:Would I buy them again?  My first thought is yes; I like them so much for sound and comfort that I may risk it even if I don't get new pair from the RMA.  My second thought on the subject is that depending on when they actually break (1,2,3 years) and become unusable I may try another model/brand.  I would rather pay more and get a quality product that will last.  There is no reason why a good headphone set shouldn't last for several decades.

I bought this card for my Nikon FinePix Camera. I plugged it in and immediately got card not initialized. I'm writing this review to inform other of what to do in this case.If you get this card and use it in a camera and get this error message, the reason is because your camera cannot handle the NTFS/exFAT file system this card comes formatted in. Odds are the SD card that you used before this one was formatted in FAT32, and that's what your camera needs.The problem that arises from this is that Windows (at least 8.1) was incapable of converting this card over to FAT32 natively. I'm going to go out on a limb and say that, due to the size of the card, it can't change it to a lower standard than NTFS/exFAT. I could get into the differences of the filesystems; but that's not what you people want. My suggestion; if you have a camera that cannot handle NTFS or exFAT filesystems and want to use this (ridiculously) large sized card, use a Third Party Software. A single DDG search [...] gives you a number of options. Obviously, you should ALWAYS exercise caution when using 3rd party software (Mainly NEVER choose the Quick install...choose custom and remove any toolbars or extra software).Once i got this all figured out My camera recognized it and it works wonderfully. I didn't benchmark the speed; but i noticed that on the HIGHEST & SIZE my camera said it could take 12,000+ Pictures. I'd say that was well worth the work and price.

review_title: The Fit, The Battery, and The Software
review_text: The Fit, The Battery, and SoftwareTHE FITThe Logitech Wireless Headset H760 is not snug enough for average heads like ours.  Rather, the unit is loose and noticeably uncomfortable to wear for extended periods of time.  The headset would've been much with an adjustable design for a wider consumer base, instead of a one-size-fits some.  However, the sound quality is good for voice transmission, and fairly average for regular music listening.THE BATTERYIn the technology age of 2010, the battery doesn't hold much charge for frequent use; and standby time is similar to smart mobile phones depending on how much use occurred before the standby period.The battery and charging system could use improvement, as it's also unclear whether or not the device is fully charged because the LED light appears part red and green. If left unplugged, the power drains and there is no clear indicator to denote the current charge status.  Furthermore, we haven't found any data to indicate exactly how much talk time is available with this headset.THE SOFTWAREAlthough this device is slightly better than others in its class and price range, what's seriously missing, and most limiting is the lack of software to control user experience.  For example, if you want to use the headset for internet communication (e.g. VOIP - phone calls, chat, etc), and still have standard external speakers to transmit audio, there is no way to direct the headset to ONLY work with calls.  This product takes full control over all sounds, so the USB must be unplugged, which sometimes may require a computer system reset or restart due to the change in audio driver allocation.Overall, the Logitech headset is decent, but could use much better improvement in this day and age.

review_title: If only the battery could charge quickly...
review_text: (updated 2x, at bottom)I got a refurbished version through a recent Woot! and I'm impressed with the speed, functionality, quality, usability.  The only sensor it is missing is barometric pressure, but the GPS (using GLONASS and QZSS) has no problems.It has one major flaw.  My last and sometimes current tablet is a Toshiba Thrive.  While watching an HD stream it will charge in an hour, but it has a laptop style charger - it also has swappable batteries.The Samsung can only charge at 2.1a, which means over 4 hours to get the 8Ah back to full WHEN IT IS OFF.  When it is running, e.g. using Google Maps to navigate with other things in the background, it will at best breakeven or slowly go down.  This is without "powersave", but even with it on, charging is glacial.There were some very pleasant surprises.  First is a hard app/home button, and offscreen menu and back buttons (which I accidentally press when holding it at times, aargh, but I think I can get used to it).  On my Thrive and other devices where this is "soft", when things bog down, whatever system that reads the screen/touch needs to do its thing to detect it.  The home hard button always works.The digitizer pen is nice.  Even things like typing just work better.  At least for me, touch will never be precise, so it is nice to have this when I need it.  The place where it is absolutely vital is selecting text for cut-paste.  I have never been able to move the cursors - they always disappear or select the wrong thing.  With the pen, no problem at all.I'm annoyed that to use a bluetooth keyboard, I have to switch back to the Samsung keyboard (I prefer Hacker's keyboard).The Browser works and manages to get a zoom-to-select right.  I wish it had more junk filters though (maybe a local privoxy type app?).I haven't tried all the facial recognition scrolling, pausing, etc. but may explore that, and some of the more advanced apps later.The brightness can be made both bright - and as importantly dark enough for any time of day or night.There's more but I will need to continue exploring.  Again, my only real complaint is the charge rate, especially when I'm using the tablet.Update: Pleasant surprise - it uses bluetooth headsets (my EtyBlu2 or BlueParrot noise cancelling)!  So I can Skype or GrooveIP (Google Voice) or use SIP phones.  Unpleasant surprise: it won't use a bluetooth keyboard unless the original samsung onscreen keyboard is selected (so I have to keep resetting to Hacker's keyboard).  Still having problems charging - they need two USB connectors, or a special dock, or a laptop/netbook high current plugin.Update 2: - Another very, very, pleasant surprise, USB OTG works, and works well.  I'm typing this from a logitech wireless keyboard (and the mouse works too).  An ethernet adapter worked (the one I use for the Raspberry PI or Toshiba Thrive), as well as USB flash drive sticks.  One of the reasons I liked the Toshiba Thrive so much was the full USB support.  I think this is beyond OTG (On the Go), and it seems like a full USB.  I regret moving my Thrive farther back in mu toolbox, but it has been a few years.  Also, I got an Anker smart charger, and although it still can't overcome the sippy straw pipe that is USB charging (The Thrive has removable battery, but also goes from dead to 85% in one hour).  It at least manages to do some charging when I'm in worst case - navigation so all sensors active, in the sun with a bright screen, and talking directions - it still manages to charge.  GSam battery monitor shows charge/discharge.
My original laptop hard drive went out, this was a good affordable replacement. I would recommend this drive to anyone.

review_title: Adequate for some applications but not a replacement for LAN
review_text: The RCA DHP50 is a great product in theory. Converting your existing home wiring into an Ethernet connection is a marvelous idea, one that if executed well, could potentially be a game changer in certain circumstances. In locations where running LAN cable isn't realistic (through brick walls, in an apartment, etc.) it could make having a wired home a reality. And for the most part, the DHP50 does just that--with some major limitations.I manage a fairly complex network at my workplace that includes several layers of routers, switches, access points, etc. At home I have a less complex but robust home network (wired and wireless). I have been creating and maintaining networks for around 12 years, so I know a bit about the process. I wanted to see how the DHP50 stacked up against a true LAN network. Would the connection speeds be similar to actual CAT5 cables?The DHP50 is marketed with the fairly ambiguous statement "full 1080p support." 1080p is a resolution for a television or computer monitor, NOT a network transfer speed. There is no standard on how large a 1080p file might be--an uncompressed BlueRay might be 25 or even 50gb of data, while a 1080p recorded TV show is about 4gb an hour. So 'full 1080p support' communicates nothing really.I wanted to see if this device could support streaming of HD content, and in particular 1080p .MKV blueray rips as well as bluerays played through Windows Media Center 11 and streamed to an extender.My test set-up consisted of my current home network vs. the DHP50. My home network supports steaming Blue-rays throughout my home from my WMC media center. I can also steam to several WD TV Live media players in bedrooms, even large 8gb .MKV files. All of this is without hiccups or stuttering, over gigabit LAN or wireless N-band (300mb) signals.Getting the RCA HDP50 setup is very easy. Connect your LAN cable, plug into the wall, connect the receiver into another outlet, and you're pretty much ready to go.I tested out the network speed using Windows 7 and found that the transfer speed was around 600-800k a second. That's substantially lower than even 10/100 LAN. I can't say I was surprised, but it certainly wasn't close to the speed you would need to stream 1080p content around your home. I think that the marketing in this case is highly misleading--you may find that your mileage varies depending on your set-up, but for my purposes, this device would fail miserably.That said, is the HDP50 worthless? Absolutely not! 600-800k transfer speed is more than sufficient to surf the net, stream internet radio, connect a VOIP phone system, or connect a networked security camera, and many, many other applications. In certain circumstances it is a remarkably useful tool. Getting internet to that hard to reach room in your home that wireless just won't reach, or adding an LAN jack to your garage or third story bedroom, are just some potential uses. I am currently using it to connect my basement to my network for streaming internet radio. It's working perfect for that purpose.Just don't expect this to allow you to stream HD content reliably. It probably won't. Again, your mileage will vary greatly depending on the distance between the two devices, the type of wiring in your home, interference, and a whole range of other factors. If you really need a highspeed connection for HD content, there is no substitute for a dedicated LAN wiring or a 5Ghz N-band wifi set-up.Ease of set-up: 5 StarsUsefulness: 4 StarsStreaming HD Content: 1 StarForm factor: 3 StarsFinal Grade: 3.5 starsConclusions: Get it if you don't have other options, but don't expect lighting fast file transfers or the ability to stream 1080p content.

[11/23/2011 - UPDATE] -- I wanted to mention that the right speaker (the passive speaker) stopped working for about a day. I've replaced the speaker wire with one of better quality, and it seems to have fixed the problem. I'd likely suggest spending a couple of bucks to replace the thin wires that the speakers ship with. [11/23/2011 - UPDATE]I bought this set of speakers to replace a 2.1 Logitech speaker set that I really wasn't satisfied with. For less than $150 this is an amazing pair of speakers for the value, with only a couple small caveats to speak of. For starters these aren't really studio monitors, at least not by standards. There is an amp built into the left speaker and a volume pot located in the front. These are more like fancy PC speakers (in terms of sound, as well as design) than anything else - and that is totally fine - if that's what you're looking for. I would be hesitant to recommend them to buyers looking for a pair of authentic monitors for recording, or for critical listening. Their sound is a bit too colored (more so in the lower frequencies) to be considered neutral. They are fantastic however, if you just want to enjoy your music with higher sound quality.The build quality of these speakers is very high. They were packaged nicely and the units themselves feel very sturdy and solid. As noted in other reviews the left speaker runs a little hot in the back due to the amp being located there. But it really isn't hot enough to worry about, and you'd only notice it if you put your hand close to the back of the speaker. The sound quality is very good - with the highs being crystal clear and the mids well represented. The bass is a mixed bag depending on what you expect. I'm not really a bass fanatic, and most of my listening revolves around instrumental, classical, and ambient types of music. That said, the bass is probably a touch strong for my liking but it isn't anything unbearable either. There appears to be a bump in the 130 - 140 hz region of the mid-bass. On some recordings this is more obvious than with others. The rest of the bass is very tight and clean where it needs to be. -- Quick update on this note; after moving the speakers around and testing the audio from different locations in the room, the effect seems to be more likely the cause of the acoustics of the room. Amplified bass frequencies seem to be common in smaller rooms with less than optimal monitor positioning. -- As you may have noticed from some of the other reviews, there appears to be some conflicting opinions over the quantity of these lower frequencies (IE - the bass is too loud, the bass is not enough! etc..) The truth is that while these certainly do not lack bass, they will not rattle your room or shake your jaw around either. Your preferences on this matter will likely depend on what types of music you listen to, and what you expect from a speaker. The bass does seems to settle a bit, and the over-all sound improves as well, after some burn in. These speakers will probably require about to 20 to 30 hours of burn-in to sound their best.I recommend elevating these speakers to ear level for the best clarity, or finding some kind of stand to place them on. The Audioengine A2 speaker stands work really well, and they are a cheap and easy solution for getting the sound to point towards you. Overall I'd like to give these speakers 4 1/2 stars out of 5 (but Amazon doesn't seem to let you rate in halves). They are a great bargain for the price and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend them for anybody looking for better sound from their PC. They will sound even better with a good soundcard or an external DAC. And don't forget to use at least 320 kbps mp3 files, or flac/lossless if you can.And lastly, I also wanted to comment on the 'popping' sound some users have said to experience when switching the speakers off. Turning the volume all the way down on the volume pot and leaving it there for a minute or two seems to alleviate this problem. After doing so you should then be able to switch them off without the speakers making any sound. Perhaps doing this helps to discharge some power in the unit, I'm not sure - but it seems to work just fine.

3 wireless speakers that you can place around your house without wires? it sounds too good to be true. But it really works!The Bem HL200A Speaker Trio is very flexible. You can stream music to it using bluetooth, or if you don't want to be fancy, just plug your computer or iPad (or MP3 player, Walkman, whatever) into the charging station using the included 1/8" cable and you are up and running. Both methods seem to have the same sound quality so it's more a matter of preference.The speakers last a long time and have decent range. Depending on the type of house you have and how much interference from other devices, you can get a good 30-50 feet of range, with walls in the way. Line of sight is probably even farther (for example, if you have a very large living room and want to spread out the speakers). In my smaller house, I was able to put a speaker in the bedroom, one in the bathroom, and one in the living room with no problems at all. This is an amazing speaker system if you have a party and just want to spread music around your home without blasting your primary hi-fi speakers.The sound quality is ok. It isn't as good as a bluetooth speaker like the Jawbone Jambox, but it is good, especially if you just want background music in your home.I did run into some issues when I tried to get fancy. I have a lot of electronics in my home and I am always trying different combinations to see what happens. For example, I have Apple Airport Express base stations throughout my house attached to different powered speakers. I wanted to add the Bem speakers to one of the base stations to further expand my home sound system. But because of interference, it wouldn't work. I think the wifi signals are somehow clashing with the signals that the Bem speakers use. It may be an isolated situation so I wouldn't worry about this unless you plan to add these speakers to a similar system.Another thing I noticed is that the reception improves if you don't move the speaker too much. Almost like it needs to stabilize. Not sure how this could be a problem for someone. Maybe if they had it floating in their pool on a little raft or something (definitely not recommended). These speakers will work outside, by the way, but they need to be fairly close to the walls of your house because the signal seems to have trouble once it passes your outer wall.Finally, I have run into the problem of the speakers not being in sync. Not a super big deal. I found that if i turned the out of sync speaker off and on again, it fixes the problem.Overall, the speaker system is easy to set up and use. I did put it through some fairly tough tests, but the average person who just wants to stick this in their living room and stream to it from their phone will have no problem doing so. It's really fun having sound spread all over your home and consider what this speaker system does and how well it works, it's a bargain.The design of the speaker system is very modern and clean, with a rubberized finish. The speakers blend in with most decor, so you can place them anywhere without them looking weird.I originally was going to give this item 4 stars, but after writing this review and thinking about it some more, I think it deserves 5 stars for the innovation factor alone. It's not perfect, but it looks and works great, sounds decent and is a pleasure to use. That's worth 5 stars to me.

The one you're looking at now is pre-formatted for use with Macs.Most Macs, except Macbook Airs, have firewire ports, and this drive is a great choice for firewire users.Seagate makes a less expensive version of this same drive that comes with USB 3.0 but not firewire:Seagate Backup Plus 2 TB USB 3.0 Desktop External Hard Drive STCA2000100It is the same drive, but with a different interface.  It has the same capacity (2TB) and is backwards-compatible with USB 2.0, and costs less than the firewire version.  It's not pre-formatted for use with Macs.  But it's easy to use with a Mac, either by installing the included driver on your Mac, or by reformatting the drive yourself.  (Reformatting a drive is very easy, even if you're not tech-savvy.)If you now own or expect to purchase one of the new Macbook Airs, the USB 3.0 version of the Backup+ is a better option than the firewire version, as the new Airs have USB 3.0 but no firewire.If you now own or expect to purchase one of the Macbook Pros introduced in 2012, you'll have USB 3.0 and firewire ports, so you might consider the USB 3.0 version of the Backup+ to save some money, or you can stick with the firewire version to keep your USB ports free for other peripherals.

review_title: Great HD camera, excellent video quality and features, battery life could be better
review_text: This is my 7th Canon digital video camcorder, having owned a ZR30MC, ZR50MC, ZR90, Optura 20, Elura 100, and FS100 before this one. My main objective for purchasing this HD flash-memory based camcorder was to upgrade from my standard definition FS100.  Even though I really liked the size and design of the FS100, I couldn't push myself to accept the grainy images and picture ghosting/artifact in low light (i.e. indoors).  Outdoor footage on the FS100 was much better however picture ghosting was still present at times.  I still wanted the convenience of flash-memory, but I wanted a Canon camera with a larger image sensor (for better low-light performance) and overall higher picture resolution.  The HF200 fit the bill, and I purchased it from a major electronics retailer with free financing.I am not "high-definition ready" at the moment, meaning I still watch TV and DVD's in standard definition, however, I'll be ready to upgrade to at least a HDTV in the upcoming months.  So after reading the reviews for the HF200/HF20, I decided on the HF200 since I had already a few SDHC memory cards I had used with the former FS100.  I also like the fact (after reading the reviews) that my spare BP-808 battery from the FS100 would work with this model.  I also have the CG-800 external battery charger.Right out of the box after charging the BP-809 battery, the unit starts up very quickly, just as fast as the FS100 model.  My first impression of image quality was "wow", as compared to the FS100.  In the same room with both cameras side-by-side, the HF200 image was so much sharper with much improved light sensitivity.  The instant focus is just that, even over the full optical zoom range.  The optical image stabilizer is perfect even at 15X zoom, as compared to the FS100 electronic stabilization.  The menu hierarchy of the HF200 is different than the FS100 menu system, but I like the HF200 system much better.  Still, I am disappointed that you have to activate the fader again after you start recording, as has been the case of all Canon models I have owned.  The unit's mic will pick up that pressing of the button to activate the fader!Now for the video quality, it is true the video is somewhat grainy and noisy in low-light settings, but it still is such an improvement over the FS100 image in the same environment.  I also do feel the single LED video light works very well to help out in low-light situations.  I am very satisfied with this unit's image quality, even when played back on my 55" TV through the composite video output (remember I don't have component or HDMI inputs yet).  Because I don't have true HD equipment, I choose to film at XP+ (12 Mbps) data rate to allow longer recording times.  Once I get an HDTV, I will try out the MXP and FXP modes.  Oh I forgot to mention, I use both Transcend Class 6 and Kingston Class 4 16GB SDHC memory cards, and both work flawlessly.  I also purchased a 6-ft mini-HDMI to HDMI cable to use when I do get an HDTV (I am going to try this out on the in-laws' HDTV this weekend).Battery life of the supplied BP-809 battery is about 70 minutes with normal camera usage, and I agree that is very poor battery life.  Like I mentioned above, I already had a spare BP-808 battery to use, but I chose to shell out the $85 for the BP-819 model.  I haven't used it yet, but about 3 hours, 10 minutes is available at full charge.  The BP-819 does stick out of the camera, and it is a little more difficult to hit the record button, but it does serve as a nice thumb rest, and most importantly, it gives you the time you need to capture that special footage!Still photo quality is much, much, much improved on this model (as compared to experience on previous models), and this is the first camcorder I have owned that has its own independent flash.  It does work well even though resolution is 3.3 MP.  Finally, with Dual Shot, I am also able to take pictures while filming, something I hadn't been able to do since my mini-DV years!I use iMovie '09 on a 1st generation black Macbook and the software has no problem recognizing the files.  I don't like the fact you have to use AC power to transfer your files/photos to your computer, but I bought the USB card reader to get around this.  I also have the latest version of VLC video player for Mac (which recognizes the native .mts files), but my computer is not powerful enough to handle the playback without difficulty.If I have to describe any problematic function of this camcorder, I would have to cautiously complain about the file size and import times required for transfer into iMovie.  Now I know that AVCHD is a different animal altogether, and I like the fact iMovie gives the option to import at 960x540 resolution (half of true HD) to reduce file size (good for me now since I am not HD-ready), but import times are long and file size is even larger than importing older mini-DV footage (about 1GB for 4 minutes of footage imported at 960x540, God knows how much space full size would take).  This is in no way leading me to give this camera a lousy review, I just have to realize multiple 1-2TB external HD's will be required to store future footage, and I have to learn patience that will be required for import times of some of the larger clips.  This is the only characteristic from my FS100 that I miss, the ability to edit and import footage without much difficulty or wait.In summary, the unit is very light and easy to hold, very responsive to start recording in about a second, and the electronic lens cap is a nice little feature. Here are my PROs and CONs:PROs:- Sleek, lightweight unit that is easy to hold and the major user features to operate it are well placed- Focus and image stabilization is excellent and very responsive even in low light settings- Very bright LED video light that helps in low-light recordings- EXCELLENT video quality in very well-lit surroundings, and audio is great with no motor noise!- Excellent menu hierarchy with quick, easy playback of your scenes- Flash memory is great and very reliable, but pick up extra cards (16GB Class 4 or higher) especially with the good prices here at Amazon.com. I recommend Transcend and Kingston from experience with this unit, but I also hear Sandisk is great too (and recommended by Canon).- Many manual controls I have not yet explored- Quick start standby mode is great and really helps to conserve battery power.- Intelligent battery meter a great addition to help you gauge remaining battery lifeCONS (none are a showstopper):- Optical zoom is only 15X as compared to the 48X of my former FS100 model.- You have to use the joystick to activate faders and digital effects during your recordings, so expect to hear the button-pushing on your video footage.- File size is large after importing into computer, and import times are long in iMovie as the software converts AVCHD into something that usable in the program (WAH, WAH).- Have to plug in the unit to AC power to transfer video/photos to your computer.So as you can see the PROs outweigh the CONs and I am extremely happy with this unit in overall performance and value for its price.  This camera is a definite keeper for me, even though Canon has just announced a plethora of new HD models, including ones that will convert HD footage to SD on the fly, for easier editing and sharing of movies.A super job by the Canon engineers on this HF200 model!UPDATE 2/23/12:I've been HDTV-ready for almost two years now, and I have to say that watching footage recorded at the highest bit rate (MXP 24mbps) is just absolutely phenomenal when using the HDMI output.  I've been experimenting with different memory cards, and while my trusty Transcend 32GB Class 6 card works well with the camera, it has recently given me numerous input errors on iMovie 11.  I think the card is becoming faulty, so I recently purchased a 32GB Class 6 Sandisk card here for $34.  I chose Sandisk because Canon recommends Sandisk and Panasonic cards for their cameras.  I have yet to test it out but was happy with the price/GB (just over $1).

review_title: Better by far than the knockoffs. . .but a little room to improve
review_text: 2013-07-15 UPDATE: The only issue I really ran into with the Celestron after some use was that the stand didn't seem to quite have a secure grip on the unit. Note that the stand overall was a far better piece of design and execution that the junk knock-off I first purchased and returned. I mentioned the problem to Celestron Customer Service even offering to buy a new stand to try out. I got a prompt response that a replacement stand had been ordered and would be shipped shortly. Several days later the replacement stand arrived and it works perfectly in all ways including the secure locking grip on the microscope unit itself. Now if I could just find a way to turn off or dim the LEDs it would get all 5 stars!PRIOR REVIEW:This comparison review is of the Celestron 44302-A model I recently received. Note the "-A" suffix. I bought the Celestron after returning the knock-off (and not much cheaper) microscope that I first bought thru Amazon:IMAGE 400X USB 2MP Digital Microscope with Handsfree Stand for Education Industrial BiologicalI wanted this for some serious close-up views and documentation. It has areas for improvement in design BUT compared with the glut of crappy knock-offs on Amazon, this appears to do a far superior job. The cost is also VERY reasonable for my needs. The software seems to be better than the more generic WebCam application used by the knock-offs and has an extra and useful measurement feature. (You might also want to checkout the YAWCAM application for unique motion detection features that work with this unit.)Compared with the knock-off I bought and returned:GOOD things:* The first important thing is that the stand is FAR superior. That is important because any USB microscope is virtually useless when hand held. The Celestron stand clips much more securely to the microscope, can be easily adjusted, doesn't fall apart, AND holds its position! All things a "stand" should do but the other I had could do NONE of those things. Sheesh!* The Celestron microscope holds focus. The knock-off I had drifted severely and continuously.* The Celestron microscope DOES NOT OOZE gooey silicon lubricant like the knock-off unit I bought and returned. It was in the stand for most of a day and goo had oozed out from around the lens and was forming a drop on the end! Yes, the knock-off appeared to have a runny nose. Snot my idea of a quality product :-) If the Celestron does the same later on I will update this review.* Because the stand is more solid I can actually use the snapshot button on the end of the microscope. It is on the very end of the microscope which results in far less camera shake that the side mounted button on the knock-off unit.* The software has more features and accuracy than the generic WebCam software with the knock-off version.* The transparent ring around the front can be removed for extreme close work and magnification. (IMPORTANT: When you go to put it back on note that there are three slots in the ring that need to align with three ridges on the microscope to fully seat.)* The measurement capability with the Celestron software on the CD works well, but you are unlikely to figure it out thanks to missing info in the manual. I believe the problem is in the MANUAL/documentation. I had no luck with measuring until I thought about the check box for LOW or HIGH magnification.After some playing it appears, although I found NO mention in my new manual, that the magnification is ONLY accurate with the clear ring properly seating on the front of the unit AND with the front of that ring resting on the object being measured AND with the target object in focus at either the high or low magnification point. Then you need to check the appropriate magnification option in the software before setting the Pins. When I followed my "unwritten rules" the measurement was "spot on" at BOTH the LOW and the HIGH magnification. Truly amazing accuracy within a couple 1/100's of a mm. I was measuring a precision engraved metal engineers/die makers rule. Note that if the object under the 'scope sticks up a bit, like chips on a circuit board, that shift in distance will likely invalidate the accuracy. Now if I could only get the saved image to include the distance pins without having to resort to a screen shot (Alt+PrintScreen).* I discovered that the Celestron 44302-A works as a webcam that will focus to infinity. (Actually "To Infinity and Beyond" for Buzz Lightyear fans :-) Point it at a distant object and continue to move the focus past the 10X position. If it is in the stand the view will be upside down, but you can go into the properties for the unit in some software and FLIP the image both Horizontally and Vertically and Viola. That could be really useful with the motion detecting software like that in the free "YAWCAM" application. Of course the "always on" LEDs make it less useful in security surveillance.ROOM for IMPROVEMENT:* The LEDs cannot be turned off, let alone adjusted. I would like to see both features.* Add the ability to capture the measurement pins and distance notation in the saved image. (Unless I missed a setting somewhere.)If I find any issues with the Celestron after more use I will update this review.

review_title: So nice, I bought them twice!
review_text: I have a pretty strict set of rules when it comes to my headphones. They have to fit comfortably, they have to sound good, and they have to be affordable. I know, I'm so demanding, right?FIT: In the interest of full disclosure, I'm not a fan of the earbud. They've come a long way, it's true, but I just don't like them for me. I also don't think much of over-the-head headphones - they look and feel like I'm back in high school. So, behind-the-head headphones are generally my best choice, but there are many that don't fit well. They either hurt the ears or the back of the neck, or both.The Philips SHN5500 fits very nicely, with an adjustable, firm but flexible band around the neck and a good fit around the ears. Once you get them adjusted, they fit snugly and comfortably and don't move around much, if at all. Since I wear them while riding my bicycle, they have to stay in place without me needing to futz with them, and these do the job admirably.SOUND: I like it loud. Probably too loud, and in a few years I may regret that, but for now I like to hear every thump, every sustained note, and every inflection of voice.Again, the Philips SHN5500 do well in the sound department. The highs are crisp and clear, the lows are deep and rich. You can get a lot of sound flowing through these and it's still distinct, not muddy. There is a noise-canceling feature which can be turned on and off with the flip of a switch, but I rarely have cause to use it. It does help on windy days or in noisy areas, but for the most part the normal setting does fine.I purchased two of these because I wanted one for work and one for play (mostly biking). At work I shoot and edit videos, so I need something that gives me a full range of sound and a good stereo mix. For biking and other play, I like lots of good, loud music. These headphones work well for either use.One criticism here, which is pretty common for most of the Philips headphones I've owned: the sound "bleeds" out of the headphones pretty badly. I've been told that people sitting two or three seats away can tell what I'm listening to, and I have heard for myself that even when they're being worn, you don't have to be very close to the person wearing them to hear at least some of what's coming through the speakers. It's an annoyance, but I just have to remember to keep it down in crowded spaces. I hate keeping it down, though.PRICE: When I bought the Philips SHN5500's (both of them), they were around $15 per pair. I'd pay a little more, up to $20. More than that and I'd probably start looking elsewhere. $15 is a great deal for these, $20 is a fair price. At the time of this review, the cheapest price Amazon has for these is just over $25, which is more than I'd pay.EXTRAS: I've already mentioned the noise-canceling feature. This comes in the form of a toggle switch attached to the headphone cord, which also has an external volume control. When the switch is on, a red light indicates that noise-canceling is active. This requires a AAA battery, also housed in the same compartment as the switch and volume control. This extra piece includes a hook to fasten it onto a shirt, belt, or pocket. I rarely use the noise-canceling, the volume control works independently of the battery and is sometimes handy.Overall, the noise-canceling is something I find mostly unnecessary, but here it is done without getting in the way of the other, more important functions, and it's optional. It works for me.Which brings us back to this: The Philips SHN5500 headphones feel great, sound great, and for $15 to $20 it would be hard to do much better. I liked them so much the first time I went back for seconds.
