I was very please at first, until I noticed that the platter was warped, and caused the tone arm to move up and down with each revolution. I checked it very carefully, but it was the platter that was defective, obviously it came from the factory like this. I decided that I might be able to live with this, but after a few weeks of light use, the deck threw me another "surprise." The speed control would be set slightly faster than normal, as is often the case when playing techno records. However, the speed would suddenly decrease significantly with no reason at all, when the control had not been touched in any way. Obviously this is completely unacceptable! When I contacted Amazon I was dismayed to find out that they will be charging me for the return shipping. Therefore, I must recommend anyone to THINK TWICE before choosing this deck, as you are taking a gamble with your money. I would recommend going to a merchant who will stand behind their product, or buy from a more reputable manufacturer. Remember, if it's too good or cheap to be true, then it probably is!

EDIT: 2012: This become unusable at work when I got stuck in a 4-up cube. Just too much interference.I brought this home and gave it to my son - who insists on having his study desk next to the home theater. I can't blame him per-se - but he's been on the edge of eviction to his own room due to two-way noise conflicts.He hooked these up put them on and wouldn't let me touch them. He gets good noise isolation (almost too much - doesn't hear the intercom) and it's got the quietness and good range as advertised.So I recommend these - just with the caveat that they may not work well in a work cube type environment.Original follows:This is for RS120 and RS130 - and I eventually bought the RS130.I work for a computer company and bought this for my cube. A key characteristic is lots of RF noise - nearly every adjacent cube has a laptop and a deskside (or two if doubled up).Essentially all reviews were for home use. I was fortunate to borrow an RS-120 and an RS-130 at work - same floor even) I used the RS-120 for half hour and the RS-130 all day.From overall performance, I found RS-120 and RS-130 comparable as far as susceptibility to interference. I preferred the around the ear of the RS-130 over the RS-120 and my colleage with the RS-120 indicated his ears need a break from the RS-120 after several hours.The surround sound and auto tuning of the RS-130 were plusses but I bought the RS-130 mostly for the around the ear comfort and fit.Overall I really like these - but I do have some comments - and those tie back to other comments - "the hiss in the background".Some posters commented on "the hiss in the background". My RS-130s (and the one I borrowed) had this - but as Bruce Campbell said "it's a trick - get an axe".OK, they're not tricking you - but there is a workaround.The hiss seems to come from their on-headphone amplifier. You can make that go away by1) setting the on-headphone volume very low. Essentially dial it down until the hiss just goes away. Or a little more if you want to adjust volume more from headphone than computer.2) Crank up the drive to the base unit. I've got my computer Wave and Volume controls set very much higher than I used with my corded headphones. And now I get great volume out of the headphones. And I get it without any perceptible clipping or degradation.The bottom line - the base unit likes and is fine with driving it relatively hard - and by doing that not using much of the headset amp you sill not have a hiss problem.My last point is interference. In this very noise (ambient RF) environment at work I occasionally have a "pfft" as I turn my head or move about. Occasionally. Even with base 3 feet away. But so far, I've found no headset better and these are otherwise really sweet. [I otherwise can't say how these do with 900mhz phones]Overall - 4 stars and in particular prime for office use.

I wasn't sure how to rate these earbuds. I've used and loved Koss headphones since the mid 80's and was really impressed with the sound of the Porta Pro series of lightweight phones. The bass is always very tight and the highs are crisp and clear and I was originally pleased that I got the same sound from these earbuds. One thing I don't like is that the cord for the left ear is only 5 inches long and the right ear is 22 inches long. I've seen other buds that are made this way and don't know why. Maybe some people like it, but I find it annoying. There is also a slide volume control on the cord which is handy but the slider only moves about 1/4 inch so it's a bit tricky to adjust it.  I've had these for about 7 months now and recently the right speaker just died. I've been careful not to pull or stretch the cable so I don't think it's the wire but more likely the transducer itself. I don't listen to them at high volume so it's unlikely that was the cause.  The good news is that I can send them back to Koss and they will fix them for free, no questions asked. Turnaround time is usually very quick. Their website states they will send replacement or repair and return within 72 hrs so you can't gripe about their customer service, which is excellent. They require $9.00 for shipping and handling. Plugged into my TV, and was pretty much painless to setup with an Android smartphone.* Getting the device to play YouTube videos and Play Music audio is straightforward and pretty simple to figure out.The bad (condemnations):* YouTube playback is awful.  Not only that, it's *inconistently* awful.  It's one thing when every single video experiences stuttering, but in this case, it seems like some videos play great and others - for no explicable reason whatsoever - mysteriously start stuttering.  It doesn't help that there's no easy way to install YouTube Center (or some equivalent) on this thing to disable YouTube's poorly-implemented DASH functionality; thus, it's not possible to pause the video and wait for it to buffer.  Thanks, Google!*** As an addendum to the above, VEVO's ads play without any issue whatsoever.  Y'all know that meme image that shows a massive datacenter for YouTube ads and an old 80386 desktop for the YouTube videos?  Yeah, the truth in that joke is more prevalent than anyone could possibly imagine...* When using the Play Music app, playback works fine when connecting to the Chromecast first, *then* playing a song.  Switch this around, and the Play Music app crashes upon trying to connect to the Chromecast.  This is probably a limitation of the Play Music app, however.The ugly (nitpicks):* The reconfiguration portion of the Chromecast app (i.e. for changing network details / device name, viewing license info, etc.) doesn't respond to touches half the time, making it a nightmare to reconfigure the device.* Zero Firefox support is lame, but at least I went in expecting this.  At least it's not too hard to launch a Chrome session if I want to send web pages to the thing.* Zero ability to change the backgrounds on the "Ready to Cast" screen.  Not *that* big of a deal, but I hope Google implements this in the future; I'd much prefer to have some of my own photos on there.* Zero ability to stream arbitrary files/streams, i.e. from one's local device.  I suppose I'll have to wait for a suitable app (and hope that said app doesn't get removed.  Thanks, Google!).The conclusion:* You get what you pay for.  If you want something more capable, I reckon you'd be better off with one of those full-Android plug computers.* My four-year-old niece could probably throw together a more competently-designed ARM-based Linux and stick it onto a Raspberry Pi, and it would only cost $20 or so more to do, SD card / HDMI cable / USB cable / USB-to-mains adapter inclusive.  The hardware's great, but Google really dropped the ball on the software - which somehow doesn't surprise me, come to think of it, now that I recall the various services that have gone to crap lately (*coughcough*YouTube*cough*).* Given that the majority of the issues I've been running into are software-based, I hope to someday be able to edit this review and bump up the number of stars.  Until then, the 3-star rating is generous.

I have never really used radar detectors - once the speed limit on interstates were raised to above 55mph I rarely go much above the posted limit. However, the inner technology geek in me found the idea and concept of the Cobra iRad to be fascinating. The Cobra iRad integrated the functionality of a multi-band radar detector with crowd sourcing data in the app. What is not to like?Notes -- The app uses crowd sourcing data across all of the iRad in use to piece together a map of potential radars, red light cameras, and areas of heavy traffic. The key to outstanding functionality is having enough users to reach a critical mass of data. A limited number of users means that the data pool is to spotty or inconsistent to be fully trusted.- The radar detector seems to work ok - although I have gotten a lot of false positives (especially around banks and jewelry stores). I have also passed six or seven police officers where the detector did not go off. Now it is possible, and maybe probable, that none of them had their radar on.- The "Find my Car" functionality is a nice concept, but again in use it could use some tweaking.- The dashboard feature isn't overly cool, but useful as it shows you your speed- The bluetooth pairing is ok, but it did take a bit of effort. Make sure that you have the iRad set correctly between ios and android devices.- The power plug has a USB plug for charging devices, which is very nice since the app seems to really pull down the battery on my iPhone.Final Verdict - I am a fan of the app, and with a few tweaks it has the potential to be very useful for anyone who spends significant time driving. The radar detector seems ok, but I certainly got a lot of false positives.4 Stars

The antenna is supposed to be pointed directly at my kitchen (according to antennaweb.org) which is filled with appliances and a huge metal counter. review_title: Sony BDP-N460: Easy, Convenient with Stunning Visuals at a Value
review_text: This is without a doubt the most user-friendly and easiest home electronic that I have ever had the pleasure of using and owning. It literally took 20 seconds.Be sure to check out the 6 pics of my Sony BDP-N460 and remote that I posted. Each pic is labeled; I hope they are of some help to you if you're considering buying this item.The video and sound clarity is second to none. I have never experienced a movie so crystal-clear and vibrant and vivid until I watched my first blu-ray.The Internet streaming is an added bonus that I really appreciate because Comcast's on-demand is getting worse and worse and there never seems to be anything on Home Box. Besides Amazon and Netflix (I suppose those are the most popular), it includes: You Tube-this is 100% free, Michael Jackson music videos-100% free, Style, Concierge, Blip TV and lots of other channels that I haven't even gotten to yet, such as Daily Podcasts. There is even a search engine built in to search the entire network for a specific channel.When the blu-ray discs are inserted (simply press the right-hand silver button on the BDP) it loads in milliseconds. This is not a DVD player.Speaking of DVD's this WILL play all of your old(er) media discs. And it plays all formats wonderfully.The unit is small, sleek-looking and compact. It's a shiny black. I have spent a lot of time in recording studios fiddling around with microphones and audio interfaces and sound editing software trying to get a decent recording. The Zoom H4n almost matches the quality of recording that I can get with a couple of Shure mics, an audio interface, and my laptop.  The advantage to the Zoom is that it is insanely easy to use.  Out of the box it was able to produce excellent recordings without any tweaking or set-up.  This makes quick and easy on-the-go recording almost feel like cheating.  In fact, it is so easy and so good that I don't pull out my pro gear anymore unless I absolutely must.  As an added bonus, it has two jacks that allow me to plug in up to two more microphones, so I can actually have true 4 channel recording pretty much anywhere so I can ditch the laptop most of the time.  The main recording device is quite good as long as you use a fast SD card.  Using slower SD cards WILL result in clipping and popping noises in your recording because cheap SD cards simply don't have a high enough read/write speed to handle this device.  Do yourself a favor and buy a good SD card.I mostly use the Zoom's stereo recording capability, but I also have played with the USB audio interface functions as well.  The device interface is easy, intuitive, and responsive.  My only complaint is that the scroll-wheel used to select menu items is also a button used to confirm choices and actions. Nothing exceptional but very functional.The tripod that came with this package is a piece of junk you could buy at a dollar store.The remote is nice and functional, but it feels cheaply made.  If you step on it once, it's a goner.The SD Card as part of the package was OK, but I upgraded to a card with 30MB transfer speeds instead just to make sure I wouldn't have any problems.The case that comes with this package is excellent and very, very durable.  I wouldn't suggest driving your car over it, but you could easily drop this down a flight or two of stairs and probably have nothing to worry about.With this package deal, you are basically getting a Zoom recorder, the remote, a totally decent pair of headphones, and an excellent case.  The rest of the stuff is just cheap fluff.  All in all, a great combo package and I highly recommend buying it.

I had to refresh my browser window several times before it connected.I can't really review the performance, because I have it connected to my old TiVo, which does not need a lot of bandwidth. review_title: Great price and performance. Remember to buy two!
review_text: With memory, the main variable is reliability, and obviously one reviewer alone cannot vouch for that with any statistical significant. However, cast my vote for this memory being a great deal. If enough of us give this a good review, and it appears we have, then you can be pretty sure this memory is solid. I can't add much more than that, as this is otherwise a commodity product, but in an attempt to be useful, let me add the following advice for those that aren't familiar with how modern memory works:You need to buy at least two to get the full performance! You PC or laptop invariably will have at least two memory slots. You MUST fill both in order to get the full memory performance, as the machine will use both RAM modules in parallel. Thus, if you are buying just one of these in order to get 2 GB of RAM, you're making a mistake. Either find 1 GB SODIMMS and buy two, or go ahead and splurge on the extra $12 and get another one of these. I highly recommend the latter option. If you think you need 2 GB then it's highly likely that you actually need 4 GB. And if you don't know, you probably will later. Nobody ever regrets getting more RAM or disk space. It's one of those things that you always use up if you have it.

review_title: A Chromebook for the mature crowd.
review_text: A review for the mature crowd, on using the Chromebook as your go to computer.  It actually is a 5 star but I gave it 4 because the size leaves just a little on the "wanting/needs" list.I've been using computers since 1979 and now at 72 I’m using a Samsung 11.3” Chromebook and the whole Google Chrome OS experience.  At 250 bucks it’s a great deal for what it does because it does it flawlessly, with minor exceptions.  The Chromebook size is almost perfect as a convenient door into the internet.  At about the size of a pad of paper it has all you need.  All the positive marketing points of the machine and Google Chrome OS system are true. For the majority of the population it fills our needs and is as simple as it gets.  If you use MS Internet Explorer the first thing you will notice is Google Chrome has eliminated every annoying attribute MS-IE ever invented.  Be honest with yourself and think about what you really do on your personal home computer.  If you feel the need for a Microsoft OS along with all the annoying security and daily updates in addition to the same for MS Office on a 1500 buck desktop maybe you should consider incorporating your family and hiring an IT guy too.  Personally I feel Google is the future of internet computing for the world.As to the negative aspects of using the Chromebook as my “go to” computer.  After three weeks of using the Samsung 11.3" Chromebook the screen is still difficult to see and hard on my eyes.  Adjustments have been made for larger fonts and color changes have been made on some reading materials.  Could be because this reviewer wears bifocal eye glasses but it’s more than that.  There just isn’t much real estate to move things around especially when it comes to photos.  The clarity of the screen just doesn't pop out at you as would be the case in the Chromebook Pixel (I’m assuming).  However more to the point is the color or contrast on some web pages.  An example is Google Calendar,  the type just doesn't have good contrast.. One major problem on some web pages is the page does not fit on the screen.  I’m not a web designer so  I’m not sure where the problem is, the web, the Chromebook or Google. An example: I was on the Delta Airline reservations site and I could not use it to make my reservations because some of the page was overlaid and jumbled.  Same problems happened on many other sites where you have selection options in ordering things.Again, for the 250 bucks delivered into your house it is a steal.  It is really the perfect “recliner” companion for wireless surfing the web and general research/entertainment needs. Plus Google has so many “apps” you could spend the rest of your life just setting those up for “whatever”.

I primarily use my Kindle Fire as a media consumption and basic communication device (so Skype, Amzon videos, book reader, podcasts, email, grocery lists, calendar, etc), and my review will focus on the pros and cons as it relates to these activities.Summary: The reason I took a star off is because Amazon has a little way to go in terms of usability improvements and features. Just a little bit of extra effort in the design would take it all the way (for my usage scenario) - specifically user accounts, email, and camera/photo capabilities.Pros:1) Stunning screen. The screen of the Fire is lovely. It isn't too bad in full sunlight either (though if you use it like this frequently, you might want to get a matte-screen protector)2) Exceptional Audio: This is where the Fire truly shines - the audio quality is much better than anything I have found on other tablets.3) Carousel: This is definitely a controversial design choice: most people seem to dislike it. I actually find it quite nice. I pin apps that I want frequently to favorites, while the Carousel lets me quickly flick through and find what I need in case it isn't pinned (like books, music, apps, etc). In any case, I can go into the subcategory and just pick out what item I want in case I don't want to scroll across the entire carousel.* What would be nice was if the carousel was like a loop, so I could start scrolling in reverse.4) Amazon ecosystem: I have a Kindle HD, and have access to a large reading list (especially from my public library). When I sign in, I can see all the apps, books, music, and movies I bought.5) Email: The email supports Exchange, GMail, and Yahoo all in one app. That is much more convenient that on my android phone's stock email client.6) Content: Amazon (with Prime Lending Library) has a great selection of books, movies, and music. Coupled with my public library and the access to Zinio (a magazine service) they provide, I have a lot of reading material at very good rates (a lot of it free).7) Swype: This is one reason why I wouldn't use an iPad/iPhone as a primary tablet - I just couldn't do without Swype for emails, searching, taking notes, etc.Cons:1) User account - while Freetime does give a certain amount of account-like capabilities, I'd like full fledged account setup capabilities, where I can control access to individual books, videos, and music.2) Camera: While I don't want a rear-facing camera (I have both a phone and high end camera for taking pictures), the Fire camera doesn't perform well in low light conditions. Still, it is more than adequte for my needs3) Cloud-sync: This is one area I am really disappointed in the Fire OS - Cloud Sync. I expect Amazon to have pushed the Cloud-Sync feature into a lot of its native apps. However, pictures I have on the fire (either from the camera or downloaded from the web) cannot be directly put into the Amazon cloud. In fact, it is easier to upload pictures onto Facebook, or email it, that it is to push it to the Amazon cloud in one step. The photo app does not even allow selecting multiple pictures at once (to delete them).4) Email client: The email client lacks fundamental features like "Select all" - this makes it difficult to delete lots of emails.Modifications: I think just making a few modifications or improvements would make Fire perfect for me:1) Improved email client2) Native RSS reader - while I like Feedly, a good reader that can save/sync content onto the Amazon cloud storage would be great - so that I can continue reading articles on my Kindle reader, or save items for long term.3) Better cloud sync - this is something I consider crucial. I'd like a lot of app settings and content backed up to the Amazon cloud so I can easily access it wherever I am. Photo gallery and app settings comes to mind - if I later use the Amazon app store to load apps onto my phone, it should take the settings from Fire (if applicable) and use it.So while I am happy with my Kindle Fire, it just isn't good enough to warrant a five-star review. In this always-connected age, I'd love to be able to have my tablets and phones in sync and data stored online, so that I can use my computer as a real work-horse, and my mobile devices exclusively for content consumption. The Fire is very good, but just not there yet - I still need to go back to my desktop computer/laptop to do things that should be easily handled on the tablet.

review_title: Affordable digital camera; nothing more, nothing less
review_text: This is a pretty standard digital camera; for those of you who want something simple and easy to use, without many advanced/special features, this is a good camera for you.Pros:-Easy to use; the buttons are pretty much right in front of you.-6 different modes; an auto for general use, one for objects in motion, one for dark scenes, one for landscapes, and one for close-ups. It also has a video option.-It's not incredibly small, but it'll fit in your pocket.-If you turn the live view off (where you see the image on the screen before taking the photo), the battery life is pretty good (just don't take many videos). A few days ago, I took about 60 pictures and about 10 videos that were about 20 seconds each.Cons:-It can't take pictures in the dark. Or, for that matter, anything without a big, visible light source. When in auto mode, the pictures become waay to dark and undefined, but the shutter speed for the night mode is ridiculously long, so no matter how still your subject/hand is, it'll be too blurry.-The batteries fall out easily. Twice during concerts, I've lost batteries because I rubbed against the bottom of the camera.-The zoom isn't terrific. In fact, it doesn't really 'zoom in' at all; the closest you can get on any mode except for close-up is the same as you'd see through your naked eye. But that's where the close-up feature comes in handy. (It's only if you want great detail on objects near you, such as flowers; any further and it's just a big blur)-Without a tripod and a still subject, it's hard to get clear photos on the night and close-up mode.You can get decent photos with this camera under the right conditions, but this is just a simple camera for unprofessional images. Probably good if you're on a family vacation to Disneyland, or on an outing with friends. In broad daylight, that is. It's not necessarily a bad camera, but it was insufficient for my needs. And yes, this is a horrible camera to take to concerts.

review_title: These little speakers pack some serious sound - I'm impressed!
review_text: I've tried a lot of different Bluetooth speakers and was pleasantly surprised by how well these compare.The sound is loud and the bass is powerful. I can use these to fill up a room with serious sound - my only worry is that when the bass is loud they bounce a little bit, I had them sitting on my book shelf playing some Fatboy Slim and one of the speakers was nudging dangerously close to the edge... It didn't fall, but it made me think that maybe these were too light.Still, their size means easy portability. The top opens up for deeper sound, and collapses for convenience. As far as form goes, these are a lot like theX-Mini MAXspeaker pair, but the AYL set is less expensive, sounds better, has deeper bass and a more expansive sound, and has the Bluetooth compatibility I was wishing for when I used those.You have to pair the speakers together via a micro-USB cable that comes with this, and that also connects to a standard USB plug for charging. You can play from them wired - with a standard 13mm stereo plug that will connect to a computer, tablet or MP3 player. What's really special about this set is the quality of the Bluetooth connection it delivers. Many of the Bluetooth speakers and headphones I've tried have a bit of a choppy connection - especially when they're far away from your device. With this one, even across the room you get a bold and clear sound. It connects directly, and works nicely.It comes with two (left and right) speakers, a charging and connecting cable, a direct input cable, and a handy bag for storage and transport.I was given this test unit by the manufacturer for the purpose of testing and review. Having tried lots of other, similar products, I was prepared to be disappointed, but I was pleasantly surprised to like these as much as I do.

I splurged and bought a pair of these after demoing them at a local retailer.  I compared them side-by-side with Sennheiser's Momentum over ear headphones and chose the P7 over them for a number of reasons.The B&W; P7 needs to be seen, touched, and worn to be truly appreciated.  This is a lot of money for a pair of headphones, but the luxurious feel of these headphones is really, really top-notch.  Except for the cable, it is constructed completely of steel, aluminum, and leather.  The entire headband and earpads are luxurious leather.  Even the trim around the earcups is trimmed in leather!  You won't find even a scrap of plastic on this headphone.  And it is still not too heavy.In addition to being beautiful made and designed, these headphones do sound good.  They have a weighty, yet detailed presentation that sort of complements their luxuriousness.  The whole experience of listening to music through these is like smoking a Cuban cigar and drinking a top notch Scotch whiskey in a five star, modern hotel suite.  It is a guilty pleasure.To be honest, there are headphones that also sound very good that cost a lot less.  I'd say that the Audio Technica ATH-M50 and Grado SR-80i (with L-cush pad upgrade) are incredible values in headphones that have comparable sound quality.  But they feel and look cheap in comparison to the P7.  The ATH-M50 is very close to the P7 in fidelity, and I wouldn't be surprised if it actually measured flatter in frequency response.  The P7 has a bit more prominent high frequencies and weighter bass presentation, making it sound a bit more dynamic than the ATH-M50.  The Grado SR-80i has a very detailed high frequency response, but the bass weight can't compare to the other two headphones.The P7 is a comfortable headphone, but isn't as lightweight and breathable as the SR-80i, which is open-backed.  It comes sumptuously packed with a quilted carry case that looks like a purse, and two cables that are removable.  Each is about a meter long and one has remote controls and a microphone for use with Apple products.  These cups of these headphones do fold upward towards the headband, but even folded they are fairly decent sized.Finally, I chose these over the Sennheiser Momentum over-ear because I was looking for a nice headphone with genuine leather earpads.  This is surprisingly hard to find.  The Momentums get great reviews and seem to sound pretty good, but I would argue that they are overpriced considering the basic build quality and the fact that they are very small for so-called "over hear" headphones.  To me, the P7 was easily worth the extra money because they are much more substantial, larger, and exhibit such incredibly sumptuous materials and build quality.  They cost twice as much as B&W;'s P3, but they are easily worth three times as much.  The P3, while a neat product, doesn't have the quality and it really doesn't sound nearly as good due to the rolled off treble response.The B&W; is a beautiful product.  Owning these is a splurge, but anyone who appreciates the finer things in life will appreciate these headphones.

I use them in almost any event requiring louder noise than what the conventional laptop can provide, and the best part is that the sound quality doesn't get fuzzy at high levels of sound. I also use it as a bluetooth speaker for my cellphone and that has served my rather well too. The battery levels are really decent and I rarely have to keep on charging the device, making it very convenient for me to use and carry around.
It's hit-and-miss when I plug it in. It will often work for me - sometimes it won't. The range is adequate. You shouldn't get this if it's going to be your primary access to the internet.

review_title: Great Receiver and Easy to Setup
review_text: First off, let me tell you my setup.  I have this AV Receiver, a pair of Dual 8" speakers (100 watt peak), 2 pairs of Pyle 3" speakers (100 watt peak, only using 3 of them), Optical Out from TV.Front Speakers (left and right): Dual 8" (100 watt peak)Center Speaker: Pyle 3" (100 watt peak)Rear Speakers (left and right): Pyle 3" (100 watt peak)This is 165 watts per channel (each speaker can handle 165 watts).  I am just using 100 watt speakers since they are cheaper and my room is a normal size living room and these are more than capable of providing theater quality sounds for my room (20x15 feet)These speakers were relatively cheap and sound great with this system.When I first got this I tried using the HDMI cable passthrough, I liked the on screen information and menus (the AV Receiver shows what it is set to and menu windows over the screen).  It was nice, but the fact that I had to leave the the Surround Sound system on all the time and leave this AV Receiver on all the time (I either leave it on 24/7 or have to use another remote to start TV and all).  I hate wasting electricity (and based on the heat this puts off it would be a waste).  I decided to switch to Optical Out from my TV (plus one cable provides audio for all my devices plugged into the TV).  I could not tell a difference in the audio quality, and I still had support for DTS and Dolby, just no onscreen menus).I got the speakers connected with some cheap speaker wire (this system is just push in and so are the aforementioned speakers).  I ran the Optical Out from the TV to the AV Receiver using an Amazon Basic Fiber Optical Cable.  And booted it up.  I had the volume at 10 (not wanting it to start up and blow me away), but I did not hear anything...  I kept playing with it and could not figure it out.  I finally turned the volume way up and finally heard it (I guess with the speakers I am using (since they are only 100 watt peak and not 165 watt) I could not hear low volume settings.  I turned it up to about 50 and had a great sounding system for general use and around 70-80 for Movies.  The DTS and Dolby sounded great and the TV put out both (just not virtual, so also try changing the Surround type if you do not hear anything).  I listened to all the Surround types and DTS and Multi Channel Stereo are my favorite, DTS and Dolby have a lot of independent noises and have that immersive effect, but Multi Channel seems to give me that in your face action sound.Also, the system also includes a front 3.5mm jack for hooking an iPhone or other MP3 device to it and a front HDMI input for hooking a camera or newer model phone (like BlackBerry z10) that HDMI out.  However, since I am using Optical, I cannot use the front HDMI and see the picture, I would only hear the sound, but I can hook it to my TV and the Optical Out will send the appropriate setup (DTS/Dolby/Multi Channel Stereo) to the AV Receiver.  It also has a headphone jack, but it uses that large jack (like in musical instruments), so you will need those type of headphones or an adapter to use 3.5mm.I ran the sound setup on the TV, PS3 and Roku and all changed their supported settings to match what the TV could passthrough.  The sound is amazing and you feel immersed in the sound, the remote is easy to use and you can setup independent settings for each input (I also have the Roku hooked using RCA Audio cables for Pandora without leaving the TV on).  The settings are easy to understand and for the most part it works great out of the box, their are just a few settings that you want to change to optimize for your setup (Surround, Speaker sizes/distances...).  I also like the FM Tuner (a little antenna is included), I finally found a sweet spot and can listen to my local FM radio on this (I found I had to aim the tip toward the window).  You can save Channels to memory and scroll through your favorite channels using the channel button.The physical look of this is gorgeous, like most AV Receivers it is large and takes up room, it also gets pretty hot.  The top grates also can come off easily (pop off) so you can upgrade or fix internal problems (if you do not know what you are doing, I highly recommend not opening it; also make sure to unplug it first).  I am limited on room, so I planned on putting the PS3 on top of this, but I know because of the heat that would not be good, so I have a laptop holder (one of those that hold the laptop 5 inches off the ground and have an open area under it for keeping stuff cool), and have the PS3 on that so that the vents on top of this are open and the PS3 has plenty of room to breath and stay cool.  The remote is also easy to use and you has a button for nearly every input (great for easily changing inputs, you can also hit a input while it is off and it will start straight to that).  --Another thing to mention, you can set it to either start the volume at a certain level or start where you had it last, that is a nice feature!In the end this is a nice AV Receiver.  It works great and is easy to setup.  I was able to buy relatively cheap speakers that with this provide great sound and provide that theater sound in my living room.  If you plan to use this for watching everything, than you will love the HDMI passthrough, otherwise you can use alternative connections (this has a lot of options).  It does not come with Speaker wire or HDMI cables, so remember you will need speaker wire (very cheap) and an HDMI cable for the passthrough (one for each device and than one for the final connection from this to the TV; also HDMI cables are cheap, I have always gotten the cheapest ones and have never had an issue).  I really like this and it is a great improvement to my sound system (originally a sound bar).  I do not think I could ever go back to using any other type of sound system for my home theater!  I will always have to use AV Receivers in the future!  I really love this and highly recommend it!!!

review_title: Very pleased with my new TOM TOM VIA
review_text: I am very impressed with the new Tom Tom VIA gps portable unit.  The street accuracy and the GPS accuracy is really great!  I was impressed that it has several voices that you can choose from for the directions voice.  It is also customizable so that you can change the symbol for your vehicle ( a wide choice of various types of autos, SUVS, etc), and the unit allows you to choose between aerial birdseye (90 degree straight down) view and a rotated angular view.  It also allows you to choose to have the displayed map rotate so that the map is oriented the same direction you are going (rather than being oriented so that north is up all the time).The screen is bright, clear and the touch screen features seem sensitive enough for use while driving.  The base suction cup works great and it comes with a flat plastic round piece with an adhesive to attach to the dashboard, in case your dashboard is one with dimples or some kind of odd texture (like mine).  The screen display flips as the entire unit is rotated, so that it could be used mounted on the dash or rotated 180 degrees and hung from the top of the windshield.The unit itself seems sturdy but the unit is thin, very thin, takes up little space when you remove it and tuck it away inside the console when you park your car. The interface cable works well, the interface and download of maps from Tom Tom online worked great for me, got all the info in maybe 3 minutes with no problems.The maps with street names are so accurate, I am learning a lot of street names just by looking at the display as I approach them on the Tom Tom.The unit works both on a battery inside the unit, and also has a cigarette lighter plug that you can plug in for long trips, or to charge the battery inside the unit.Downsides for me: the voice recognition for me, doesn't seem to work very well.  I tried it with my voice and my wife also tried with her voice.  The instructions say NOT to enuciate the words...so we did that.  I tried maybe 15 times to get the unit to recognize an address of 2001 Loving, Ft. Worth Texas and it could not get even close....Granted I am from Texas and have a Texas accent (hill southern dialect) but this unit should be able to recognize voice commands.  That one thing has been my biggest disappointment with the new units.  Also the instruction book is a little short on information...should be more tips and instructions.The programming of "favorites" of locations is easy, and the unit remembers recent destinations and allows you to pick them for new trips...it also allows you to preprogram routes from say "daycare" to "church" or whatever locations you have.  I am still learning all the features of this many featured unit, which is a great little piece of technology, and a great GPS unit.  I highly recommend it!!

review_text: I tested this product extensively this evening on a number of devices. It's more effective on some than others:iPad3:Excellent results. I should have stopped there because other devices did not fair as well.iPhone 4S:Terrible. It's odd how effective it was on the iPad and how in effective it was on this screen.Macbook Air:Bad.  Perhaps it's because the Macbook Air doesn't have a glass surface like the iDevices do. It had zero impact on finger prints and gunk on the screeen.iPad 1:Marginal. It did an ok job getting some surface gunk off, but it did mostly what I found it doing on the iPhone: smearing stuff around as opposed to removing it.A cleaning kit might be a better option if you're looking for a clean screen. review_title: Final Thoughts - Great camera for what it's meant to do.  Good enough outside of the water.
review_text: ***Edit #2 - After using the camera a lot more, including in my pool, i've upgraded my rating to a 4 star.  The underwater capabilities of this camera are great.  Great photo quality (clearer the water, the better).  Survivability of camera is also great.  So far, 2 trips to the pool, approximately 30 min of consistent time under the water, including me jumping into the pool with the camera running - no significant issues so far.  Quality of pics are great.  Clear water provides great range.  You can see the other end of the pool from the opposite end clearly.  You will occasionally get bubbles that form on the lens and therefore, your image will contain this bubble, but, crap happens.  the bubbles did not stay on the camera and that's what's important.  I took a video of myslef jumping into the pool - no degradation in image quality nor issues with camera functionality.  Worked great.  No sound though for underwater movie mode - but it makes sense since otherwise, all you'd hear is water swooshing.  You're not buying this camera to listen to whales after all.***I've had this camera for a little over two weeks.  Bought it so that i can take underwater images when in Hawaii.  Haven't tried out the waterproof aspect yet, but can go ahead and give some insight into the quality of its normal pics.10 mp camera, but is limited to 3 mp images when shooting on some of the preset modes (scenes) - specifically candlelight images and other night-time image settings.  If you don't use the scene options, your images can be maxed at the 10 mp setting.  Night images using scene (candlelight) were pretty grainy, so i'd avoid using that setting.Normal daytime images were good.  Crisp and clear.  From power to first image - is really quick.  However, taking one image at 10 mp causes a delay before you can take the next image of ~2 seconds.  Unless you use the burst mode.  3-shot burst allows for 10 mp images, whereas the super 12 shot mode caps it again at 3 mp images.People have written that the lcd screen is easy to see in any light from any angle.  I discovered that this is not true.  Taking an image into the sun (i know this isn't recommended) while holding the camera up high (which people will use when at weddings to shoot over people's heads) leads to glare.  I had to guess what i was shooting at.  I'd say image visibility on the lcd was ~50% when doing this.Even given the above, i still like the camera a lot.  Looks nice.  Takes panoramic photos, battery lasts forever.  Used it on and off for 4 days before it finally warned me of being low.  Be careful b/c the battery indicator is deceiving.  It said full for most of the time and then jumped to warning quick on me.  Didn't even notice any intermediate indication position.I give it a 3 for now until i go and try out the underwater capability.Edit #1: Forgot to mention that the menus are pretty easy to use.  Scrolling wheel menu cycles between the different options.  One touch photo preview.  Icons are easy to understand.I've tried using the macro and super macro - works really well.  Good detail on the close images.One other con though - could not for the life of me figure out how to get the face detection to work.  I swear that it'll sometimes follow a face and sometimes it'll target a random cup. I don't yet see an option in any of the menus that allows me to force it to do face rec every shot.  Not a huge issue - but it's a spec that is being advertised, therefore i expect it to work.

review_title: Attractive, lightweight, and reliable, but rather slow and noisy.
review_text: I bought the ASUS USB 2.0 8x DVD Writer External Optical Drive SDRW-08D1S to accompany my ASUS Eee PC Seashell 1201N netbook. There was no software installation necessary for me to run the optical drive on my system. I simply plugged in the two USB cords that connect and power the drive unit and it was ready to go. Since they are from the same company, the Y cord on the USB cable was the perfect length to span between the two USB ports on my netbook. When using this drive with a larger system or one from another manufacturer, you may need a USB cable extender to make a dual connection. (The cable between the two USB heads is approximately 4 inches.)The first thing I used this optical drive to do was install the entire Adobe Design Premium CS4 software package. This 2 disk process involved well over an hour of continuous drive use and this drive matched the challenge well. It is not a quiet drive, but is not the loudest I have ever used. It seemed to thrash a few times during the installation, but recovered without crashing the process. It also makes that weird little electronic access sound (sort of a "*grind*-chee-dibby-dibby-dibby") when reading discs. This was a standard sound in the olden days of optical drives, but not one I had heard in a long time. The noise didn't bother me really, but I wouldn't recommend using this drive in an environment that requires minimally intrusive sound.I gave it 4 stars because it fit the needs that I have that rank portability (light carrying weight, small size, and no need for an electrical outlet) far over speed. If top speed and quiet operation are your key needs, this is not the external drive for you. If you want a drive you can quickly tuck into an already jam-packed bag along with your netbook or ultralight, you should be as satisfied with this drive as I am. If you own an ASUS netbook or laptop you should also find that this drive is designed to work with your system both functionally and esthetically.It lost a star to the sounds it makes, the relatively slow read/write functions, limited installation documentation, and the lack of some fairly standard codecs. It also does not come with a carry case/sleeve and is a "fingerprint magnet."

This review is not about who should buy and who should not. I am assuming that you have already done your homework on what the box is capable of and what features would be useful for you.These are just my findings after I used it for about an hour or two and would like to share it with everybody.First i'd like to jot down the connection details:1. Comcast HD Cable Box2. NSZGT1 Google TV Box - HDMI In from (1)3. Onkyo HT-S3300 AV Receiver - HDMI In from (2)4. Samsung LN46B530 - HDMI In from (3)1. The setup was very simple, but a bit long and with a few glitches.When I tried to connect the wifi, the setup hung and did not come back for at least 10 mins. Granted that it could be a one in a thousand cases, and then I restarted my box. Was entering my wifi password in this second try, and the screen hung and did not let me enter the password. Luckily, the box is next to my router, so I plugged in an ethernet cable and it connected successfully. Then it downloaded the 3.1 update, and I found that it asked me to maximize the screen again. All in all, a 15-25 min setup, if you have a good internet connection. (BTW, I set my box up to start instantly)2. Syncing my TV, AV Receiver and Comcast box was a breeze. Follow the steps and all should be good.3. The first thing I checked was the TV and movie app. This app is awesome!! Lets you search the current showing programs, based on categories like Movies, Comedy, Drama, Family, Animation etc..In my opinion, Comcast TV guide and the useless remote that comes with the set top box are the worst of all designs ever. I have the basic TV subscription from comcast, so most of the channels are blocked, so I never bother changing channels much, hence I did not know what all channels I am subscribed to. This app resolves all this for me, and I came to know that I have channels like LNM, Syfy and Hallmark. Was really happy with the output and the way the programs are categorized and showed on screen.Tip: I do not subscribe to the HBO package from comcast, but I use an HBO Go account separately on my PC to see HBO's online content. If you do the same as I do, and want "TV & Movies" app to search HBOGo for content you types in, click "Yes" when the setup asks you if you receive HBO, Starz etc. This will let the box know that you subscribe to HBO, so you already have a HBOGo account. review_title: okay. but odd routing, and no mac support
review_text: So this is a midrange gps navigator that has a large (thankfully non-reflective) display, it has a good response time, and is encased in a somewhat cheap case.The GoodIt tells you which side of the road your destination is (unlike TomTom which shows you a tiny arrow if you have a magnifying glass).The voice and the bell right before a turn are amazing, not annoying and the bell grabs your attention at the exact right time. Perfect.Turns on instantly.One Touch menu is just brilliant. One screen that has all your favorites etc.Has unique hidden features like if you slow down too much on a freeway, it assumes you are stuck in traffic and calculates alternate routes.The BadIt wants to route me through the streets with the most stop signs for some reason? It's extremely stubborn about the routes it pics and will nag you to take u-turns or anything to get you back where it wants to route you initially regardless if it's the quickest path or not. It's as good as how well it routes. That is its primary purpose and it does a mediocre job.It always overestimates the arrival time.Doesn't display speed limits (if it's based on navteq maps so it should have that data).When you don't have a destination in, it tells you what road you are on. Well, I know what road I'm on I would like to see what the next road I'm crossing is (Garmin does this).When you look for gas stations along the way, it doesn't tell you which direction they are, just the distance. Great, there is a gas station 4 miles away but I have no way to tell if that is behind me...Can't update maps with a Mac. Normally I don't have a problem with this as I would just avoid it, but nowhere on the Amazon page does it mention this. Another reviewer mentions this and it seems like fans of this navigator are attacking him... Now according to Apple, ~20% of new computers in the US are Macs, why would Magellan ignore that market share. I have Macs, many variants of Linux and other OSs but not a single Windows machine and I'm not going to get one just for this navigator. Both TomTom and Garmin support Macs. (my star rating does not take Mac compatibility into account)If your region has no traffic data you get a constant red x in the display. And if you are in an area that has traffic, you have to manually intervene to reroute making it more dangerous.Possibly a bug: if you go to map options and then click on map view, you will permanently go to different 2D modes and the only way to get back to 3D mode is to restore default settings.ConclusionThe ultimate test: Would I replace it with the same model if it gets lost?No. For this price range (while not that expensive), I expect a more polished product (actually for any price).EDIT (Feb 2011): I contacted Amazon and told them about the Microsoft Windows requirement and they have since changed the description to include this.

review_title: Inconsistent Performance Flaws Device in Urban Areas
review_text: I really wanted to like this device (because you have unlimited choices of stations to tune to, and it is powered from the iPod itself) -- but ultimately, it just doesn't work well when used in a car in an urban area.  It MAY work well in a rural area that has lots of blank radio stations on the dial, but here in San Francisco, every station on the FM band is used, or the few that aren't still receive bleed-through from adjacent or far-away stations.I've been using the iTrip for a month, trying many different stations, and driving between San Francisco and Sacramento -- and I consistently get some degree of static -- often a LOT of static.  The only time the iTrip works well is when you 1) can find a totally clean station to tune into, AND 2), you're not moving (e.g. driving around in your car).  The only thing I will use my iTrip for is for playing my iPod through a stationary home stereo -- where reception and conditions are fixed.In fairness to the iTrip, it is POSSIBLE that the difficulties I have with my car stereo are unique to my particular car radio.  For the record, this is a VW stock Monsoon-brand stereo in a 2004 VW GTI.  This car has the radio antenna at the rear (roof) of the car, possibly affecting reception.(As a side-note, I am not too impressed with Griffin Technologies on-line tech support -- they are VERY slow to respond to tech support inquires via e-mail.)What has wound up working for me for playing my iPod through my car stereo is a cassette adaptor.  I highly recommend the Sony CPA-9C, $16.  I tried the much-less-expensive ($5) Radio Shack cassette adaptor first, but it was awful.  The Sony version works flawlessly -- the sound is beautiful.

No Core Duo in sight. Despite that, I did not bother correcting them, as I don't want to go through the hassle of sending this current one back in exchange. It has been a month and the computer continues to work at acceptable speed for me and my family. I have turned Windows Aero off, which hogs a lot of processing power.I recommend everyone here go look at their own dxdiag and see what processor they have. I have a feeling many people have been duped because they do not do this and don't know any better.I've upped the review to 4 stars, because I've come to appreciate it. It's small (and quiet as long as you're not doing anything intensive, in which is chugs still, but I've gotten used to it.)JUST BE AWARE OF WHAT YOU'RE BUYING. IF YOU'RE COUNTING ON DUAL CORE 3.4GHz, AND INTENDING TO USE THIS COMPUTER FOR HEAVY DEMANDING TASKS, DO NOT BUY.Other things worth mentioning:DOES NOT COME WITH A DVD BURNER/WRITER. This was and still is a huge con for me to not be able to burn movies, and a downgrade from my last computer. I'm thinking about putting the old burner into this computer, but I do not know if it will fit. We'll see.Headphone jack works.Had a lot of windows updates to install on the first boot--around 100 I think. Also make sure you download some Driver Update software (I use SlimDrivers) , which will automatically update all your drivers for you. In this case, many of my drivers needed an update. Once they're updated you will notice a preformance boost.No issues concerning internet, just plugged in the ol' ethernet cable and everything worked right away. NOTE, does NOT include WiFi card. The little plastic paper I got with this had a wifi logo on it, so maybe that's why I assumed it was WiFi-capable. Recommend buying a WiFi USB adapter if you want wireless internet.The OS that came with this is x32, not x64. I believe you can however switch to x64 somehow, but I am not skilled in this area so I've left it as is. x64 would be more beneficial to anyone that wants to get full use of the 4GB ram.**Things you should do right away: Get some good anti-virus (I am running free Avira and Microsoft Security Essentials currently). Install Firefox or Chrome, and get CCleaner which will help speed it up a little. Also consider getting the K-Lite codec pack which will let you play any audio and video files and avoid errors in WMP. While you're at it, VLC media player is much better than WMP.Computer comes with basic Wordpad. As a writer, I found this sufficient enough, but many would probably want to pick up the latest edition of Microsoft Word.***In the Windows Experience Index, the lowest subscore is 3.3 for gaming graphics. I've been looking into buying a new graphics card. The computer has 1 PCI slot and 1 PCIe slot, and a 275w PSU, and will most likely need a low-profile card. The Radeon HD 6570 and 6450 seem like good choices.All in all, it has its issues, but for 230 dollars it's still a steal.******************UPDATE 2014:Since been a year and there's been some new developments and I'd thought I'd inform everyone of what's happened.Since the last update I purchased that graphics card I mentioned, the Radeon HD 6570 LP and it worked fantastic. I've upgraded to the 7750, AND a new cpu, the core 2 duo e6600 2.4ghz. Besides going quad core, getting an SDD and more RAM, I believe I've sufficiently maxed this baby out. I get 60FPS on the Sims 3 with expansions and the settings maxed, 60FPS on Bioshock, I play the Mass Effect series, Assassin's Creed, all on high settings and it's very smooth.But I've had a lot of problems the last year.Soon after my last update Windows 7 decided randomly that it was no longer genuine after it had been working great for a few months. I tried to reactivate it with the authentication code I got with the computer, which worked until it didn't. I believe this was a counterfeit version of windows, and that assumption is buoyed by the fact that I didn't receive a restore disk. I continuously got a black desktop with the "windows is not genuine" error, 15 days left to activate, blah blah blah.So I spent 150 bucks on a brand new Windows 7 64-bit copy. Problem solved. Unfortunate it had to come to that, and bittersweet because I lost important files.A few months after that cunundrum the hard drive failed. Remember that chugging noise I mentioned? It was coming from the hard drive!! POS. This company is freaking lucky I saved the HDD from my last computer to put into this one. now the computer is finally running blissfully quiet. What a difference. Still, all data was lost in the switch, had to start from scratch AGAIN.At that point it hadn't even been a year yet and I had more problems in that time than my last computer which I had for six years.Just don't bother with refurbished computers, is my recommendation. This is the definition of "too good to be true." The money you'll spend upgrading and fixing it would be better spent on a brand new computer.  You want "ultra fast", you want to use Windows Aero, stream youtube, photoshop, games, be prepared to drop some money on this thing for new CPU, GPU, HDD, and probably a new OS because the one you get with it's counterfeit.Don't expect a powerhouse out of the box. Don't expect it keep running like a dream.It's too much of a freaking hassle. Save your money up for a nice, brand new PC, or a Mac. You don't want to be stuck with this thing.Was:4gb Ram3.5" 1TB Hitachi Ultrastar HDDIntel Intergrated gma 3000 graphicsIntel Pentium e2160 dual core ~1.80ghzWindows 7 32-bitMy build now:4gb Ram (came with)3.5" 350GB Seagate HDDRadeon HD 7750 Low-profileIntel Core 2 Duo E6600 ~2.4ghzWindows 7 64-bitWindows Experience Index now:Overall: 5.9Ram: 5.9Gaming Graphics: 7.4System Graphics: 7.4Hard Disk: 5.9Processor: 5.9

review_title: Great for the price, just be careful about a couple of things...
review_text: First, I won't attempt to give as comprehensize of a review as  Eduardo gave.  I pretty much agree with EVERYTHING he said.  This system is really awesome, esp considering the price tag.  I'm REALLY impressed with the performance, sound clarity, features, functionality (HDMI, etc) at this price point.  I'm almost certain that you can't do better for under $300.  On that basis alone, this is easily worth 5 stars.However I need to echo something Eduardo mentioned briefly, and expand on it a bit.  First, digital amplification sounds  little different that what you're probably used to hearing from analog amps.  Some folks hate digital, others love it.  But all opinions aside, you'd be wise to test this out with your speakers and the rest of your home theater system before you decide to buy (or be ready to send back to amazon if you don't like it).  For sure, this system doesn't sound that good when you pair it with certain speakers.I have a pair of Cerwin Vega VS120s, which are AWESOME speakers, but this amp just can't drive them properly.  The sound is just terrible.  So I put my VS120s back on my older stereo amp (120W/ch) and hooked up the rest of my home theater speakers to the Panny.  The rest of my speakers are lower power Cerwin Vegas (5" fronts, 4" surrounds/rears, 5" center, 100W subwoofer) and they sound just GRAND.I decided the best solution for me was to use the Panny for watching movies (on my lower power speakers) and use my old stereo amp for my higher power VS120s.I'm sure other folks will notice that this amp is overall an AWESOME value and a fantastic performer for $299, but you should also be ready to make sure you're not putting it into a home theater setup that it's just not well-suited to.Otherwise, I'd recommend dropping the $299 on this, it's really an exceptional piece of equipment.  When did Panny learn to make good audio equipment, anyway?  ;)

review_title: Great for Video and Photo Enthusiasts
review_text: Compared to Similar Drives:I've owned the drive for about 8 months, and must say that I've loved it from day one.  Similar Raid drives that I've had experience with have either burned out or have noisy fans.  I also use the Lacie Rugged portable drive.  With my MacBook Pro, I've used both intensely with great results.  I've had experience with many other Raid and portable drives.Cooling and Noise:Since the hard drives are mounted next to eachother by the skinny side, and not by the fat side like most Raids, they do not generate so much heat for eachother.  The drive stays very cool, even after intense hours of running during massive video encoding or batch picture processing.  This is also helped since the stress is spread across drives.  As mentioned, most Raid's are like a 747 with noise and still stay very hot.  This drive is calm, stable, and quite, no matter what you do to it.Speed:Even when daisy-chaining two other HD's and a scanner, this thing is still blazing.  With a 100gb transfer of pictures, I clocked it at around 80-100 mb/s.  When copying and pasting, it makes a light noise, rather than a loud chug chug clack clack from one side of the HD to the other.Travel and Wear:As a transient college student, I have traveled many time with this drive with no problems.  Its been subjected to cheep air conditioners and heaters, along with very humid dorm rooms.  No problems, always ran without a hitch.  Even though the drive is thin, it still stays very stable with its heavy metal stand.Quality:This thing is a beauty and looks its price.  The case and vertical stand are made of solid metal, and you can feel its weight and quality.  Its connections are tight and well located.  The cooling system is quiet and worked fanastically.Other Reviews:Unfortunately with high-end HD's, who are mostly bought by busy professionals, buyers seem to only take the time to review if they've had a bad experience.  Would you write your congressmen to tell him you were happy?  If you look at reviews of other Raid drives, such as Western Digital, you'll see similar bad reviews, people saying they switched to Lacie.  Those drives are genuinely noisy and have other concerns, however.  You don't know if people are throwing things on top of them or knocking them around all of the time, or tearrying them out while there processing data.  Overall, a great product product.

review_title: This Time It's Too Good And It's True
review_text: Pros:Has all of the sound decoding choices that you can possibly need for a very long time to come. It has four HDMI inputs.  Can be fully operated with or without the remote control...all buttons are on the front of the receiver.  You don't even need to turn on the TV to view the internal menu.  It can be viewed through the display panel window on the front of the receiver.  Just press receiver button and then set up button.  This receiver delivers incredibly big, clean, beautiful full sound.  Smart, easy, intuitive remote control.  Beautifully, well thought out menu.  Thoughtful back panel that makes putting in speaker wires way less painful.  Un-selfish, non-proprietary inner-workings that allow you to play well with the other components that you are using. Has function to take max volume off internally (in menu) and thus gives you plenty of sound while you are still in the negative volume numbers. Let's you start your receiver with a low volume of your choice so that you won't blow your speakers.  Sweet.  I can use receiver with the TV on or off.  That's just real smart.Other Thoughts:I hope that you don't mind me sharing the benefits of my experience with the receiver and I hope that it will be a great help to you.This is my second Onkyo receiver.  I had the TX-SR606 a little under a year but sold it so that I could get the extra ten watts that the 706 receiver affords.  I have JBL speakers from a previous 5.1 system that are 100 watts so I always wanted This 100 watt receiver but couldn't afford it at the time.  My point is that the previous receiver, the 606, had the same abilities (Except THX and the extra 10 watts) but I couldn't get the benefits of it until I had the PROPER blue ray player to compliment it.  These receivers were tremendously built to supply you with the very latest that technology has to offer.I just purchased two back speakers (enery speakers sold at New Egg) and the new Play Station3 Slim SPECIFICALLY to compliment THIS receiver.  I also have the original Play Station 3 but the new PS3 SLIM is the one that sells for 300.00 and has the new chipset that decodes the DTS HD Master Audio and True HD sounds.  I'm mentioning the PS3 so that all are who are reading this understands just how to get all that this receiver has to offer and understand how it all works together.So, here are the mistakes that I made and the things that I learned.The Onkyo technicians stepped me through the following settings and helped me to understand why and how everything worked (various components with one another) and all of the things needed to get the most out of the receiver.  So here goes.No matter what anyone tells you, you won't see your receiver flash across the words DTS Master HD or True HD without a blue ray player that has a chipset in it that plays Master HD or True HD. Also remember that DTS is not the same as DTS Master Audio.  DTS Master Audio is the one that will allow you to hear sounds through all seven speakers and some sounds are only available using an HDMI connection so just play it safe and always use HDMI.I hope that you can appreciate what it means to have a 1080P TV, the Play Station 3 that puts out every music and movie sound (DTS HD Master audio, True HD, and many others) and then to have this receiver that allows it all to play through it's circuitry.I put in a movie called "The Punisher" and saw the receiver display say MASTER HD. You see, the movie must have an audio track that says 7.1 DTS Master Audio on it before your receiver can decode that particular sound.  This movie has such an audio track (always check the back of the box on all blue ray discs to see what the audio will be.  It sounded so incredible that I wanted to cry.It's important to understand this because I looked for this on my Onkyo 606 front panel display window for all of that time without the knowledge that my play station 3 had not, at the time, have these decoding and, therefore, my receiver couldn't play it. I thought that there was something wrong with the receiver. The music sounds so wonderful on this receiver that I've become an audiofile.Regarding various sound decoding, you MUST let your blue ray player select the various decoding settings, DTS, True HD, etc.  You do this by going into the BLUE RAY player's menu and choosing them.  Only then, can the 706 receiver play those great sounds. By choosing bit stream instead of linear in the blue ray player settings, the Onkyo 706 will play all of the sounds.  You will never want to go to a movie again. Onkyo was very helpful in helping me understand how these things work and I feel very much like an expert.Now I'll comment on the topic of up scaling.  I don't upscale.  I don't like a picture to appear stretched.  Be sure to make sure that your cable box is properly formatted.  I just spent the last month thinking that there was something wrong with the 706 receiver.  I called Onkyo at least four times and the cable company even more than that.  For whatever reason, even thought my cable settings read as if it was formatted, it wasn't and caused me to think that the "pass through" function on the receiver wasn't functioning properly.  Once again, there was nothing wrong with the receiver.  Instead, the cable box was frozen internally.  I took it back and got a new one and now I'm in seventh heaven.Also, be sure to unplug the receiver each and every time you want to make any changes to the wires or cables.  The receiver protects itself so that you CAN'T blow it out.  Be very sure to go into the menu and make sure that the Zone 2 setting is set to "Not Act" if you are not using the receiver in 2 different rooms.  Again, if you have all 7 speakers set up but you are using them all in one room, zone 2 should NOT be active.  If you see the red indicator light on and then right under that light, you see the green light on, and you are not using the system in 2 rooms, you need to press the zone 2 button on FRONT OF THE RECEIVER to "off ".  A lot of folks think that the receiver isn't working but it's fine. Heck, more then fine.  Just unplug the receiver, wait a bit, and try again.  You can also use the display panel on the front of the receiver to manually go to the set up menu and get to whatever part of the menu that you need to in order to make any changes that you need to. These new Hi-Def receivers have different rules.All of the new receivers get hot.  Let it breathe.  It's normal.  It is supposed to make a clicking sound when you switch from CD to DVD or Cable.  It's called switching and it's a beautiful sound.  The click let's you know that it switched.  I think that I am an expert now and have helped at least two other people set their systems up.  I'm just a grandmother that was forced to learn how to work this stuff just because I couldn't hear my TV dialog well.

I had (have) a JVC UX-LP5 shelf system that I absolutely hate - supposedly it plays MP3 CDs but it doesn't.  Well it does but only if written in a specific format.  But then that may make my MP3 CDs incompatible with my other players.  So I decided to sell it after having it less than a year.  Looking at a local retailer I found this Panasonic unit.  OK it is a somewhat pricy boombox, but a pretty good one a that.  It plays my MP3 CDs just great.  All my CDs.  Radio reception is excellent.  Granted the display is small, and although it will read MP3 ID Tags the view space is limited.  And it does have a clock, but as another viewer stated maybe not the best for an alarm.  My JVC had an alarm clock function too, but I never would have used it as such as it had no battery backup - as in when power goes out so does your clock.  So I use an alarm clock for my alarm. Sounds good, a full size remote not one of those tiny cheap ones, and IPOD functionality (which I have no use for.When looking at this unit I saw a TEAC unit also. Reason I picked the Panasonic was because it had integrated speakers versus separate, and it has a weighted base with rubber feet so when you put in a CD or push a button it won't go sliding all over the place.  With the TEAC unit I saw you couldn't even take out the CD unless you held the unit with one hand and took the CD out with the other.  I feel that Panasonic took into account some good design considerations when making this unit.I rate it 4 stars rather then 5 only because it would be nice to have a better display, but if all you really care about is compatibility and playing tunes that sound good, this is a great unit.  Also I wish it could read standard (non MP3) CD text.

I've used these headphones in a professional setting for about three years now and I am very impressed with how they've held up.A few things I like:Comfort. These headphones feel great on your noggin. They have no pressure points like other headphones I've used over the years.These have a VERY flat EQ curve. If you are in the professional audio business, you know about the importance of having flat EQ monitoring. Whether you are mixing audio in a studio or trying to obtain the best monitor mix on stage for a live band, these give you a true sound.Clearly labeled Left and Right sides. This is another simple but important attribute of these headphones. Obviously if you are doing anything in stereo, you want to hear which side you're mixing to. I hate when headphones have tiny, unreadable L and R labels. I spend time fumbling and holding them up to the light trying to see which way to put them on. Good job Sony.Nice long cable and comes with an 1/8 to 1/4 inch adapter and a leather pouch! You might be rolling around the studio or need to step back from the sound board and having a nice long cable is great. Also if you need to listen to something on the iPad or other device you just pop off the adapter and plug into your mobile device. Some headphones come with a cheap plastic pouch or none at all, but this pair comes with a very soft leather drawstring pouch. I think it's a nice touch.What I don't like:Like others have said, the pads wear out. This is the main reason I have to take away a star. I'm not sure if this is a way Sony makes continuous profit on a pair of headphones that lasts for years? Not a good way to make profit on their customers... They should just fix this problem already.Another annoyance is the long cable that I like gets tangled VERY easily. Also if it does get tangled, certain spots lose their "spring" winding and it looks funny. Not sure how Sony can fix this but it is a small annoyance.

These filters are a STEAL. They aren't perfect but they did introduce me to some of the challenges of macro photography that I now face with the real macro lens and to some of the things you can accomplish with macro photography.One reason I picked up the macro lens instead of continuing to use the filters was there was a substantial amount of ghosting and slight loss of quality. review_title: All Things Considered, A Solid Pair of Earbuds
review_text: Full disclosure: I generally dislike most earbuds. They're often fragile (with connections that break, sometimes with relatively new earbuds even), they get tangled ultra-easily, I find them uncomfortable, and the fidelity they provide is often lacking.That said, this pair of Belkin earbuds is definitely above average - especially given the moderate price. The only thing I can't say, since they're new, is how long they'll last (and how much average handling they can sustain without the connections breaking). But in terms of comfort, that was the first plus I noticed upon initially using them. There are extra silicone tips for the ear buds - different sizes in order for the user to achieve a better fit. The stock tips that were already attached worked best for me and these are among the most comfortable earbuds I've ever used. I usually experience irritation/discomfort with prolonged earbud usage but not so with these.They're great for plugging into the cell phone, leaving one bud in, and speaking on the built-in microphone. I've had zero problems hearing calls or with callers hearing me via the mic. I happen to not have bluetooth and was accustomed to just putting the phone on speaker when driving in order for it to be 'hands free.' This solves all the fidelity problems associated with that. The mic is attached under the left bud, so that's the preferable one to have in while driving.Music sounds surprisingly strong through these as well. I was very pleasantly surprised to hear a relatively full range through these, including a decent low end (often the Achilles heel of ear buds). I couldn't care less about the color, I happen to snag the blue ones but it's not something I gave any thought to. The only thing I am indifferent (or maybe slightly negative) about is the multi-function remote. I can use it to active the mute on my phone... Otherwise it's kind of puzzling (for me, anyway) what this button on the mic is supposed to be for. There's no instructions with this either. Oh well, I just ignore that part of it.
