I should say right from the outset, the most important factor in buying a digital camera for me is the camera's zoom capability.  Several years ago, I began my digital camera collection with a cheap Samsung (S630), followed the year after with the Panasonic Lumix DMC FZ-8 (432mm zoom)  and the next year with the FZ-18 (504mm).It seems each year, camera companies try to outdo one another with the biggest zoom for the buck.  Several weeks ago, I bought this camera with a mind-numbing 840mm zoom.  Don't be surprised if the 1000 mm zoom comes out next year.  Surprisingly, for a camera with this kind of capability, it is light as a feather and differtentiates itself from the other ultrazooms out there by eliminating the Electronic View Finder completely in favor of a 3" screen monitor (I suspect this omission may cost them sales).  The instruction manual can be downloaded from the Olympus web site.  The camera's software can be downloaded by connecting the camera to your computer (make sure your memory card has been removed to download software)What also differentiates it from the others out there is that you can edit the still pictures you have taken using the special effects function from reducing red eye, shadow adjustment, adding/reducting color saturation, and cropping.  Some of these functions were available in my Samsung S630, but in none of the more expensive Lumix models.  With most digitals, if you want to edit your pictures, you would have to download them to your computer and use the camera's editing software or Photoshop.By using Panorama function you can take up to 3 shots manually or automatically  and the camera's computer "stitches" them together into one panoramic wide angle shot. quite a technological achievement.Also differentiating this camera from its main competitor, the Fuji HS 10, a rather affordable price tag of $349 vs. $499 for the Fuji.  The HS10 also has a smaller manual 720mm zoom and uses 4 AA batteries as its power source, which I consider a disadvantage in taking motion pictures.  The SP 800uz has the capability of adjusting the focal distance during film recording in some modes, not always available in cameras of this class.  Unlike the Lumix cameras, there is no hood lens included to take shots in bright sunlight, a slight disadvantage.  There is no thread on the barrel for attaching wide angle or telephoto lenses, but with an 840 mm telephoto lens, why would you need one?The camera comes with cables to connect to your computer and your HDTV to playback still and movie pictures in 720i high definition.  A rechargeable lithium battery pack is offered instead of the Alkaline or NiMH rechargeable batteries in Olympus' previous models.  If you take a lot of motion pictures, alkaline or rechargeable NiMH batteries must be replaced or recharged at more frequent intervals than most Lithium battery packs, or you could continue to invest in 12 packs of disposable alkaline cells.The rating for the included standard Lithium battery pack is 900 mAh.  Imported batteries with a rating of 1400 mAh are available from 3rd party suppliers.  A higher Mah rating means you get more usage between charges since the battery has a higher storage capacity, similar to having a larger gas tank on your car.  Battery capacity is important if you use your camera frequently or take motion pictures which drains the battery...and your memory card.Another factor to consider is the camera's 2GB internal memory, making it possible to store many pictures without the use of a memory card.  The camera has an app to transfer the pictures taken from the camera's internal memory to the memory card.  The camera accepts SDHC cards up to 8GB, an important consideration if you take a lot of motion pictures.There are several shooting modes available and the camera has a small user-friendly internal manual to explain each mode and what flash, ISO, aperture, white balance settings are available for each mode, making taking pictures almost foolproof. There is a manual pop up flash for low light conditions.  For shots taken with the digital zoom you should use a tripod to avoid camera shake at the far ranges, a problem endemic to a lot of ultrazoom models, not just this particular model or manufacturer.This is a great camera if you take sports pictures from the nosebleed seats, go on whale watches frequently, or want to take unobtrusive shots of your subjects from a distance.  With an impressive ISO of up to 3200 sensitivity (unfortunately, the higher the ISO, the higher the distortion and graininess when enlarged for prints) you can also take excellent shots of moving subjects.I rate this camera highly.

Before I opened the box containing my new iPod Touch 5th Gen, I decided that I wanted to protect the screen from the start. Other Amazon reviews of this, and competitive, products seemed to point at this screen protector being the best. Of the four alternative screen protectors offered by Tech Armor (HD Clear, Anti-Glare, Tru Touch, and Anti-Fingerprint), I opted for the HD Clear primarily because 1) I did not want the protector to be noticeable when installed, and 2) I did not want to risk degrading the image quality of the Retina display on the Touch. The Tech Armor HD Clear exceeded my expectations on all counts.The package in which the screen protector comes contains: a sheet of detailed installation instructions, a "thank you" sheet with contact information for Tech Armor Support, a lint-free cloth for cleaning the iPod's screen prior to installing a screen protector, a sheet of dust-removal tape, a squeegee made of plastic-coated cardboard for removing bubbles between the iPod screen and the screen protector, and three die-cut screen protectors. Each screen protector, which has die-cut holes for the iPod's "home" button and front-facing camera, was itself sandwiched between two thin, tabbed sheets of plastic to protect the protector. It was clear that the Tech Armor people thought about what their customers might need, and addressed those needs. I should mention, too, that this particular screen protector is designed specifically for the 5th generation iPod Touch, which has screen dimensions different from all previous iPod Touch generations.The instructions encourage the customer to view a short, narrated video on the Tech Armor website prior to installing the screen protector on their own iPod -- something that I would recommend doing. After viewing the video and reading the instructions, I was ready to install a screen protector on my own iPod. After cleaning and polishing the screen with the supplied lint-free cloth, I partially peeled back one of the two thin, tabbed sheets of protective plastic, aligned the protector with the bottom edge of my iPod, and slowly allowed the screen protector to lay itself against the iPod screen. Two bubbles were easily removed using the cardboard squeegee. It was at that point that I noticed a tiny piece of dust, between the protector and screen, that I had failed to remove. I lifted the edge of the screen protector, used the supplied dust-removal tape to remove the speck of dust, and let the protector lay against the screen once again. Unfortunately, I had inadvertently touched the underside of the protector with my fingertip during the partial removal, and a tiny semi-circular edge of the protector would no longer stick the the screen. I removed the first protector from the iPod and prepared for a second attempt.The second installation attempt went perfectly. Circular cutouts in the protector aligned perfectly with the iPod's "home" button and front-facing camera, and the edges of the protector aligned perfectly with the edges of the iPod, covering its entire screen without overlap or skewing. At this point, I removed the top, thin, protective sheet of plastic from the protector and installation was complete.The screen protector is so clear, so glossy, and so perfectly cut that it is difficult to tell that the screen protector is installed. Touch sensitivity of the iPod's screen is not impaired, and the Retina display is just as clear and bright with the screen protector as without. Wiping fingerprints off the protector with a cloth or (in my case) a tissue leaves no streaks, scratches, or other marks. I have to admit that I was expecting something to be deficient about this product, but there wasn't. It exceeded all of my expectations.

I run them at a constant 34% and even under load by Benchmark programs the fans never need to run faster than 40% and it stays quiet. I highly recommend this card for anyone wanting to run an overclock system without having to really overclock the card yourself. Sure you can, but I didn't need to with this card like I have had to do with other cards in the past. MSI knows how to push the edge of technology and provide a robust and powerful, yet stable setup. review_title: Cheap, Good For Windows, Not For Linux
review_text: It's really cheap and looks like it's probably a Chinese generic product complete with improper English on mine (which doesn't match the picture). To be honest, I bought this from another page under the name of GTMax Flexible 5.0 or something like that, but the colors on mine actually match this one, and besides they look almost exactly the same, so I'm guessing they're just different batches of the exact same product. It has worked flawlessly for many months now on Windows. The only downside is it gets extremely annoying because for my girlfriend to get a good front view of me when we video chat, I have to put it right in front of my face between me and the monitor, and then I can barely see a thing, but clearly this camera wasn't designed with that in mind, and I wanted a self-standing thing which many of the smaller webcams are too short and inflexible for.The major bummer for me is it doesn't work on Linux (tested on Mint 13 / 14). Another review said it does, so perhaps the chipset varies in production, or maybe my distro is loading the wrong module. It loads the uvcvideo driver just fine at first, but as soon as any application accesses it for about a second, it completely stops working. I've tried reloading the module and it doesn't work. The funny thing is even restarting doesn't work until about an hour later. It's almost like the camera shuts itself off internally with a timer, and after some delay it will work again but have the same problem as soon as applications try to access it again. I'm planning on buying a replacement soon so I can finally get rid of Windows once and for all (gave up gaming which was holding me back, woohoo!). review_title: Some Great Features-Some Not So Great
review_text: This is the first 3rd party mouse I've ever bought. I always used Apple's mice and generally been happy with them. I dislike the Apple Mighty Mouse however and think it's little scroll ball is cheap and flimsy and way too easy to click unintentionally. This Logitech Mouse has much to admire and a few irritations as well. The absolute best feature is the central scroll wheel; this invention is on par with Apple's magnetic power cable connector on their laptops, pure genius. It can be spun freely or set to click line by line. When spun freely it scrolls down a long web page or text doc faster than any other method short of grabbing the elevator and dragging to the bottom. It is very sensitive and I don't know how I ever lived without this feature. On the 'con' side of this feature is that this scroll wheel cannot scroll horizontally like the Apple scroll ball can. I don't use this horizontal scrolling feature much anyway so it's not a big deal to me. Another little annoyance is that whenever you wake your Mac up from sleep and the mouse comes to life again (with an audible 'chunk'), it always resets the scroll wheel setting back to 'line by line" ratchet mode, instead of the smooth free spinning mode that I almost always use. Then, you must click down on the scroll wheel to change the mode again.The thumb wheel is marginally useful and feels like it's in the way at times. The Cmd-Tab method seems a bit more intuitive. I have not yet explored redefining in the driver software what that thumb wheel does but I hope I can change it to something that I would use more.It's nice to have separate right and left buttons since the Apple Mighty Mouse always feels like you're not quite sure which side of the mouse you are really clicking with.I have large hands and this mouse feel a bit too small for me although I am getting used to it. I agree with other criticisms that the shape of the mouse necessitates that you wrap your hand fully around it but my hand is big enough to manage with a somewhat lighter touch. The mouse doesn't feel too heavy in contrast to some criticisms I've read.All in all, I am happy with this mouse and feel it adds to my productivity. I wish it were just bit larger though and my hand wouldn't work as hard to use it.

review_title: A minimalist's dream home theater setup.
review_text: We used to have only a pair of front shelf speakers with our HDTV, a temporary setup when my wife decided to rearrange the furniture for the umpteenth time.  This was very annoying as we can't hear the spoken voice clearly, not having a center channel.  We used to have a 5.1 home theater set of speakers connected to a 7.1 channel receiver, but reconfiguring it every time we relocate the TV is a pain.  So, for many months, I was planning to convert our system as simple as possible - a soundbar would be an excellent solution.I got mine a refurb.  It has built-in amplifier which means I can get rid of my receiver.  This soundbar is not heavy at all and you can install it on the wall or just lay it on top of the TV stand;  We chose the later. It has only three inputs, an optical,  2 pairs of red and white RCAs and an output for a subwoofer if you choose to add one.I heard a lot of problems on the remote. Ours works just fine, but you have to aim it where the sensor is located which is the lower right of the speaker.Currently, all my devices (low profile Dell Zinio PC, Xbox, Wii, WDTV) are connected to my HDTV (old 42" LCD Vizio), then from the optical output of the TV to the optical input of the soundbar.  I also have a powered subwoofer connected to it.  No more multi-wired complex speaker layout and no need for a stereo receiver.  This is a very simple setup but at the same time provides a very good home theater experience.  Soundbars tout that you will hear 5.1. Not so true.  It still makes a difference to have a physical satellite speakers behind your ears.  But for everything we were considering, we are more than satisfied with the result.  The sound from the VSD200 is loud and clear, big and crisp.Why not 5 stars?  I heard some slightly better sounding soundbars from Yamaha, etc., but for twice or triple the price.  For the value, the Vizio VSD200 easily worth 5 stars.

review_text: I bought the Almond model, the one with the color touch screen. I had trouble keeping my Ipads connected to it, and returned it. It might look nice, but the touch screen only added to the cost, and did not make it any better for me.  The Amped model was easy to configure via a computer ,and once it was set, it worked, and has been working for a few months now. I have not needed to reset it, or do any other troubleshooting with it, it works.  It puts out a powerful signal and I like it very much.You can configure it to be a repeater, where it will catch a signal from another wireless internet router, even a neighbors, and retransmit it on another channel.  So if you have a friendly neighbor who will let you share their internet connection, go for it.  Just don’t talk about it because your ISP won’t like it.The Amped product will also work as a standalone Wi-Fi wireless internet router.  Keep in mind that all of these devices that call themselves routers, and range extenders, only provide the basic minimum of firewall function. That function is called NAT , otherwise known as Network Address Translation, this simply is the function of all routers, and firewalls, and it just means that your computers in your home have an IP address  that is different from the IP address that it has out on the internet.  Many people do not need a hardware firewall, they simply rely on having no firewall, or they activate their Windows firewall.Take it from a person who knows, you are only as safe as your actions on the internet.  If you invite trouble in, it can come in, no matter what firewall you have. It’s like inviting a criminal into your home, the locks don’t do anything to stop them because you invited them in. This is what you are doing when you install a lot of free software. Nothing is truly free, the cost is not always easy to see.

review_title: The Best In Sound Quality By Far!
review_text: This soundbar from Harman is the same company that produced Harman Kardon and JBL speakers, so you know its high quality.  The soundbar itself is extremely attractive and looks great either below or above your flat screen television.  The sound is beyond anything I have heard in home theater sound in the past.  It is simply astounding.  I replaced my excellent Definition speakers (left, front and center) with this Harman Soundbar with great results.  The dual midrange and tweeters have a sound range that brings out music I didn't even hear on my definition speakers.  Specifically, guitar chords, strings, horn highs, bass/cello lows and various ambient sounds are crystal clear.  Even when I move around the room, the sound is there, unlike my former speakers on stands that gave specific sounds from that corner of the room (unless I cranked the music up).  For example, there are songs I've played with multiple guitars that can be individually heard, when in the past all I could hear was a 'harmony' of strumming.You can read all the specifications above and how the speakers are exceptionally strong, with the speaker cones being 200 times stronger than regular polypropylene or that they are three times stronger than titanium (watch all the videos).  However, the resonance and overall tone is truly remarkable.  A lot of this is due to the construction of the main enclosure as well, preventing vibrations.  Keep in mind that the soundbar is 15 pounds, but comes with wall brackets and a  base for shelf placement.  I've placed mine just below my flat screen.I've never understood how people can spend thousands on a great flat screen television and seem content with the average speakers that are attached.  It just doesn't make sense.  With this soundbar you are halfway to a completely surround 5.1 or 7.1 sound system.  Also, the price is very competitive when you look at surround systems in general.  To truly get a full range of sound, I'd suggest also buying a subwoofer like theSony SA-W3000 Performance Line 12" 180-Watt Subwoofer (each, black)or theYamaha YST-SW216BL Advanced YST II Front-Firing Active Subwoofer(which I have) to get that true theater experience.  I also compared the sound quality/output to myDefinitive Technology ProMonitor 1000 Bookshelf Speaker (Single, Black);Definitive Technology ProCenter 1000 Compact Center Speaker (Single, Black)and they sound almost the same. review_title: 65Watt unit is working as it should at a good price... check how much wattage your computer needs before you order
review_text: I always depend on owner reviews with an item like this as you will find some are junk and some are just fine...  Many reviews for this item said it worked just fine and it does for us also.Seems to be a wide variety of quality out there these days.The one we bought charges the battery pack and runs the Dell Inspiron 1501 without problem.THIS notebook has the optional extended capacity battery pack from Dell also.Will this replacement power adapter last as long as the original Dell AC adapter?  Won't know until it quits, but will report back when it does to let everyone know.  Although the original Dell that came with the notebook didn't last very long IMO, around two years I guess.Everything breaks sooner or later, its value depends on what you paid and how long it worked, at this price, even a year would be ahead of the original Dell unit.Maybe even 6 months would be good, going by the price of the replacement direct from Dell.We shall see how it goes, but I've already ordered a second one to use at the office, at these prices might as well not carry an AC adapter back and forth IMO.All volts,watts & amps on the label matched the original unit, computer side plug matched and fit well and has the positive on the center post.Note that SOME electronics use the reverse on the DC side (notebook end) and have the positive pole on the outside, so be sure you are ordering the right one on the computer end.  Reversed polarity is a sure way to blow more than the new AC adapter out.It does not have the rubber belt to hold cord around adapter like Dell, but I think that is bad idea on the original adapter as it bends the DC side connection too hard, this replacement adapter also has a third wire grounded AC line unlike the Dell unit which is always good.Be careful which one you order through Amazon, there are several 3rd party suppliers and not all of them give the same details but still use the same photo.  The one from "Super Deal" lists the input/output numbers and that it fit my notebook, some don't... some have BAD reviews, this one has pretty good reviews and they all look the same at first sight, read the details and specs firstCord length is 18 inches less than Dell unit.Both of the replacements have a total cord length of 92 inches not counting the adapter box, 46 inches of cord on both AC and DC sides.Original Dell has total cord length of 110 inches not counting the adapter box, 36 inches on the AC side and 74 inches on the AC side.  Not really a problem as I plug them into a power strip that makes up for this and has it's own circuit breaker.Power plug on the DC end (computer end);Dell unit measures 9/32" outside diameter with 7/32" inside diameter (negative pole)THIS replacement measures 9/32" outside diameter with 7/32" inside diameter (negative pole) and does not fall out.It would seem that Dell uses two sizes of plug that goes into the computer, if you get the smaller size and needed the larger it will keep falling out as many have had happen.Please NOTE, I'm talking about using this on a two year old Dell Inspiron 1501, they might have changed the plug size needed on other notebook models AND might even change sizes within the same model over time.  Be sure to check the size of yours and IF possible the size of the replacement you are going to order."Super Deal" page on Amazon also lists a 12 month warranty... good/bad hard to say, but it is given.No doubt price of warranty shipping each way would buy a new unit outright anyway.My order was filled by "Super Deal" and they got the order out very fast and was delivered ahead of time given.I've seen some reviews that just sound like horrible results and have to wonder if some of these people had other things, like their battery packs go bad without knowing it and tried to fix the situation with this adapter only to find out it gets hot and quits trying to power through a shorted battery pack that was the real problem in the first place.Of course, BOTH could be bad at the same time so just be sure this is the whole fix for your power/charging problem first.One big item to consider is something I found while searching the problem on the Internet;Some Dell notebooks are programmed to detect when a non-Dell power adapter is used, and will restrict the ability of third-party adapters to charge the battery but still supply power to keep it running.  There may very well be various combinations of trouble if Dell has tried to defeat owners when they try to bypass Dells high prices.Can be the same with replacement battery packs also, Dell uses "Smart" packs that have their own electronics in them in order to try and keep all sales in house.  Mixed results from people who try to buy and use outside sources.Try not to drop your adapter, that COULD also lead to some problems you are reading in many reviews... knock out one little component and you stop electrical output.Keep your power adapter as cool as you can.  Do not pile things on top of it, or let it slip under furniture etc.  Also, realize that if you have it on a rug or carpet, it can not cool as well as it would on the desk or bare floor.Do know though that even the expensive power adapters can and will get hot to the touch when they are working to full output, so some of the cheaper made units with lower end materials used for the case and cords could get too hot and fail. If it's the cable or plug, it will short out after it melts enough to let the wires make contact with each other.I can only wonder how many reported problems are because of cord/wire failures rather than the power converter itself.  Would be interesting to know how many of the problem units always get their cords wrapped around them for transport or storage.  I for one do not wrap the cords as that can weaken them where they attach to the unit.Too bad that reviewers don't always say which seller they bought from when they say "junk" or "great item" at least there would be a chance to weed out the worst units from same suppliers and come up with some kind of list of best place and unit to buy.If you are worried, you could try one in the next higher priced adapter/chargers which is about three to four times this price... but still much less than OEM from the notebook Mfg.For example;OEM Dell Ac Adapter Laptop Charger for Dell INSPIRON ,Dell XPS ,Dell Studio, Dell Latitude ,Dell Vostro, P/N PA-10 PA10 90w 90 watt Genuine/Original/OEM Portable Charger for Laptop Notebook Computer Battery Charger Power Supply Cord PlugAfter that, you can still step up to a more expensive universal adapter like the one from Targus for example;Targus Premium Laptop Charger (AC/DC) APM69US (Piano Black)CAUTION: Be sure and check the actual wattage needed for your computer, many can require as much as 120w or more, a 65 or 90w adapter will get hot and die trying to keep up with the demand if it is higher than output!

review_title: Cramped but solid; cool enough for a fine HTPC
review_text: I've been using this case for an HTPC for about four years.  I use it almost exclusively for watching high-definition video---mostly terrestrial broadcasts recorded on a PC.  With that in mind I bought a low-power Sempron 140 designed to use only 45W, and an Nvidia GeForce 210 low-profile, fanless GPU with a maximum draw of 30W.  (Were I building the same system today I could undoubtedly get motherboard graphics that could handle MPEG-2 and H.264 video.)The case ships with an 80mm fan controlled by a switch with High, Medium, and Low speeds.  With the fan set on Low it is quiet, but everything stays cool.  CPU temp runs around 26C.  The hard drive runs around 41C at idle, up to 48C when in heavy use (e.g., OS upgrade).  I don't have software installed to measure GPU temperature.The inside of the case makes for a cramped build, and depending on the position of cables in the motherboard may be tricky.  It would be easier with a modern all-SATA motherboard; the PATA cable for the optical drive is a little hard to manage.  Also, it took be a little while to get the hang of the inverted drive cage. But everything fits, and the drive cage does not wiggle or buzz.Finally, as noted by other reviewers, the case is very solid and the body looks good.  (In my opinion the front panel does not look as nice as the rest, but I'm still happy.)Summary: nice-looking case; build is no harder than you'd expect from a uATX in a system with a small form factor; and with suitable components inside you can build a superb HTPC that will stay cool and quiet even under load.

review_title: High on convenience (no cables!); low on power.
review_text: After finding an answer to charging my wife's iPhone and my Touch 5 in the portable "lip-stick shaped" unit made by Skiva (Skiva Apple Certified External Battery Pack with built-in Lightning and microUSB Connectors for Apple and Android Devices (Powervault Lightning A2600)), I realized that most of my Apple devices used the 30-pin dock connector preceding the new Lightning connector that debuted in late 2012. So now my search was on for another portable charger, one that would service my old iPods (I never trade or sell them--instead I dedicate each to a different audience, artist, or style of music).I'm admittedly less impressed by the Travel Battery Pack made by Kensington than I am by the Skiva.  To be sure, it will charge Apple purchases made prior to late 2012 (including iPod Classic, Nano and Shuffle) conveniently and quite effectively. The unit is shaped like an over-sized cigarette lighter but is smaller and lighter than the aforementioned Skiva. The top lid flips open to expose the dock connector.  Hidden on the bottom is a USB connector, which is easily extracted for charging the Battery Pack.  Unlike the Skiva device, no extra cable is included.  It's probably not needed for the USB connector, which will plug directly into most computers and AC adaptors.  The lid on top, however, may not open wide enough to accommodate some extra-wide devices (the first iPad?) requiring Apple's 30-pin dock connector. If your device needs it, a cable with male connector on one end and female on the other will ensure a good connection:Patuoxun 30 Pin Dock Extender Extension Cable for iPhone 3GS 4 4S iPod Touch iPad 1 2 3 (Data Sync Charge Cable, Support Audio/S-Video Transfer).Like the Skiva, the Kensington unit uses individual lights to indicate remaining power. (Simply depress the large button on one side of the device.) The Kensington, as might be expected due to its smaller size and lighter weight, did not charge a dead iPod Touch 4 battery as quickly or completely as the Skiva brought a dead iPod Touch 5 fully back to life.  Also, with the Skiva I was constantly aware of remaining power as the lights stayed illuminated throughout the charging process.  The Kensington lights, on the other hand, illuminate for 2 seconds in response to the user depressing a button on the side of the unit. As a result, I found myself constantly pushing that button to determine remaining power.  After 30 minutes I disconnected the unit and, upon depressing the button, saw 3 illuminated lights, indicating the charger was about 40% exhausted. To my dismay, upon disconnecting the charger I noted that my iPod Touch 4 showed only half a charge.. Worse, as I was about to reconnect the Kensington unit to my iPod to finish the job, not a single LED became illuminated. The battery was completely drained.  Warning: don't place too much faith in the Kensington's 4 charging lights.The packaging and instructions for the Kensington are more elaborate and complete than those accompanying the Skiva Lightning charger. Curiously, the instructions indicate that the charger must be attached to a USB power source in order to read the remaining charge. An extra step--but my experience would suggest it's a necessary one. The price has been reduced, possibly reflecting the charger's application only to discontinued (prior to late 2012) Apple iPhones, iPods, etc.Just one additional caveat: Kensington, IMO, risks misleading the buyer by calling the unit a "Travel Battery Pack AND Charger."  Even though the charger may be the best value for use with devices employing 30-pin dock-connector receptacles, it gets a low score in simple math by representing the product as 2 rather than 1 thing--a Charger AND a Travel Pack!  But however you choose to name it, 1 thing remains 1 and not 2 things. I even put the preceding theorem to the test and, try as hard as I might, could not locate the 2nd component, whether it be the Battery Pack or the Charger.  In this case, the company's endeavor to "double" the purchaser's good fortune is at best a needless distraction; at worst, it's reason for the consumer to register a complaint, or at least an inquiry, like: "Where's this 'pack' that you promised to include with my charger?"In short, my experience suggests this device will revitalize a partially discharged iPod, enabling it to last the duration of a cross-country flight. But the absence of technical specifications and the less-than-stellar performance I observed while using this highly portable and lightweight charger (designed, above all, for "convenience") should lead those who can afford it, to look instead to one of the high-power, universal, back-up batteries made by Anker, Great Shield or Energizer (be sure to throw in a few extra dollars for the cable(s) and adapters matching your particular device).

review_title: Expectations Restored! -- Should be 4 stars! (see addendum)
review_text: First off, let me say I'm a huge Plantronics fan.  I use theirPlantronics Foldable USB Stereo Headset (Optimized for Laptop Use) (Audio 470 USB)regularly with Dragon Naturally Speaking, and it works better for voice recognition than any other microphone I've tried, and it's a great bargain:  I gave it a 4-star review, and I recommend it highly.This Plantronics .Audio 995 I cannot heartily recommend other than to wired Ethernet users.Installation is a snap, as with all Plantronics products I've tried, but the ensuing results for me were dismal.  I'm trying to use this "wireless" (here's the "tricksy" part) on a desktop Dell XPS Gen 3, P4 3.4GHz, 3GB RAM, XP SP3 computer using a Wireless-G Network adapter.Sound quality on these headphones, when they work, is surprisingly good, and I had no problems with the remote volume and track controls on the outside of the headset.  However, with even minimal movement while listening to a CD or mp3 via my computer, sound distorts terribly.  Sounds like a bad "flanger" act from a '70s retro-band, and this occurs within 10 feet of the USB antenna, sometimes even within 2 feet if I simply tilt my head.  Appalling.I'd hoped to upgrade to these so that I could do some "pacing," or walking around during dictation with DNS, but that's simply impossible. Even sitting perfectly still within 2 feet of the USB antenna, the signal-to-noise ratio in DNS for these either equals or slightly underperforms when compared with my wired Plantronics headset.  Moving at all is simply not an option, so I might as well use the corded headset.Here's where things get murky, and, while I can't confirm that the following is the cause of the problem, this is what I think is happening.  These "wireless" headphones are apparently NOT a Bluetooth emanation, though they have similar range characteristics and use "pairing."  They appear to be a proprietary system, details undisclosed, that uses the same frequency spectrum as Bluetooth but are NOT Bluetooth.Interestingly, as they do use the 2.4GHz spectrum, when I turn on the headset, my Wireless-G adapter often crashes and loses contact with the router.  As you probably know, Wireless-G uses this same band, as do some cordless phones (and microwave ovens).  I have a 2.4 GHz band phone handset within 3 feet of my computer.  Hmmmmm.Either there's an interference issue with this headset's proprietary transmission technology, or I received a defective headset.  I am told that I will be receiving a replacement headset shortly to re-evaluate.In short, if the problem is interference, this is a shame, because these are pretty decent headphones, and I suspect the mic is good as well.  Even if they worked, I wouldn't be trading in my Grados and AKGs, but for your standard .mp3 fare, they'd be quite acceptable.  I do wonder how they work with Skype.  Perhaps others will weigh in on that.I'll post an update when I receive the replacement set to clarify if the problem appears to be an interference-based issue or whether the first set I received was simply defective.....---Update June 17, 2009 -- Sadly, the "edit review" function here will not allow me to upgrade my initial rating.  Plantronics was kind enough to send me a replacement unit to test, and, clearly, the unit I was sent originally was defective.The replacement set hardly breaks up at all -- and if so, only rarely, and I suspect computer lag for that.  Bobbing and weaving my head does not produce the fragmented and distortion-filled sound that the first pair did.  Range is well within advertised norms, and I'm impressed.The signal-to-noise rating given byDragon NaturallySpeaking 9 Preferred [OLD VERSION]varies between 20-23, which out-performs my wired Plantronics headset mentioned above.  This should prove to be a very useful tool, allowing me to walk around as I dictate, which was what I was looking for when I decided to order them.  Very impressive.I'd like to upgrade this review to 4 stars if this forum would let me.  Sadly, I can't change that rating here.  The reason for dropping one star is that these do sound rather hollow when listening to music with much of a dynamic range and depth; however, as I wrote before, if I'm looking for top-notch performance, I won't be going wireless.For what these are designed for, they do a great job.  Thanks Plantronics for letting me give you another chance!

With the arrival of our third baby, we had to do some shuffling around.  Part of the shuffle included moving a PC from about 20 to about 80 feet away from D-Link 802.11b wireless router -- it's about as far away as it can in this house. Though the vendors claim their USB adapters work at much greater distances, I couldn't get a reliable connection until I got this unit from Hawking.I tried out a few other USB adapters, including two D-Link models (the DWL-120 and the DWL-G120), figuring that staying with a single vendor would help.  Nothing doing.  I couldn't get more than 10% signal strength with either D-Link model.With the Hawking, I get just about 50% signal strength and discovered that more of my neighbors have wireless routers than I thought -- at least 4 or 5 alternatives show up in the list of access points, and these detached single family homes are at least 100 feet away.I can listen to streaming audio from NPR and Real Rhapsody and can get just about 80-90% of the bandwidth delivered to the PC connected to one of my router's wired port.As a bonus, the USB adapter works great with Windows 98SE.  The product may look dorky (21st century rabbit ears, I guess) but it delivers reliability and speed at distance -- exactly what you want out of a USB adapter.Update: I had to switch my D-Link router for a Linksys router, and the Hawking didn't miss a beat.  The Linskys router puts out a better signal, so the link and signal strength are much improved.  I'm getting >65% signal strength where I was only getting 40% before.  Just wanted to add the note to highlight the seamless support for a different wireless router.

I operated a computer company for about 25 years and have grown with the computer industry. This tablet is simply amazing because it is simple, yet complicated, and very reliable. I purchased this unit for three features, it's a Samsung, the microUSB interface and the IR capability. I have a 3 year old Samsung Droid phone and I love it. I am a photographer and wanted the ability to preview images in the field. The microUSB port gives me that capability. If you want to use the microUSB capability, an accessory is required, the Samsung micro USB/USB Connector. I bought mine at Fry's Electronics for $20. One end is micro USB for the tablet and the other is standard USB for things like card readers and flash drives. Caution: I attempted uploading images through the connector using a USB card reader but it failed. Then I tried a USB connection directly with the camera and it worked. I also purchased a more expensive card reader, the Vivitar 50-1, and was able to upload images with that reader. In other words, you may have to try a couple readers to find one compatible with the tablet. I also tried interfacing a notebook hard drive through the USB port but there wasn't enough juice to get the drive spinning. The tablet also has a 64GB storage limit on the removable microSD card.I am embarrassed to say that I moved to this unit from a Nook. I won't make a comparison because there is no comparison. They are two different worlds. If you buy this Samsung, download the free, companion Kies software from the Samsung Web site. It will enable you to move files back and forth from your desktop or laptop. You can do the same thing using the file browser on your computer. I was really concerned about my contacts in Microsoft Outlook. I have been through the "moving contacts" nightmare countless times with different devices. The Kies software found my Outlook .pst file on my desktop hard drive and imported it flawlessly. The format for contacts on the tablet is very nice.Using the My Files app built into the tablet, you can view all the folders on the tablet internal drive and external memory card in a tree format. You can move files, copy files, rename files, delete files and make and delete folders. If you are a power user, these features will appeal to you.It comes with Polaris, an Android version of Microsoft Office that is compatible, file wise, with Office. I have only used it to view Word attachments that I have received in emails. The printer in my office is set up for sharing on the office network. When I wanted to print an email, the Samsung tablet immediately found the printer and printed the email pronto. Slick.Audio: Until now, my earbud purchases were for cheapies at any discount store. However I was unhappy with the audio volume on the tablet when playing music videos. I did some earbud research and found some good reviews on a set of Marley buds that have a rocker switch for up and down volume and a mic button in the middle. When you press the mic button, the display changes to a voice input screen, perfect for asking a question. Apparently the buds are designed for the iPad as the volume switch does nothing. No big deal, I adjust volume on the display. The big deal is that I get so MUCH volume from these buds that I can't keep the volume at the highest level without breaking my ear drums. Also the audio quality itself is incredible. Get yourself a set of quality buds. I found these $60 buds on sale at Radio Shack for $25. The tablet has another cool feature, Adapt Sound which is found in the settings menu. When you start Adapt Sound a series of beeps will be transmitted to your buds or earphones so the tablet can perfectly adjust the audio to your hearing. This feature makes a huge difference in the sound.It comes with a free 2 year, 50GB subscription to Dropbox, a cloud utility. I am going on vacation next week to the middle of nowhere. I will be able to take images, and upload them to Dropbox using the Hotspot feature on the Samsung phone in conjunction with the tablet.I watched a youtube.com review of this unit and the guy was unboxing the tablet complaining about the display resolution, although he had not yet looked at the display. This unit has a VERY impressive display. My pictures look AWESOME and I have uploaded some videos for the plane portion of my trip. They look AWESOME too. The unit has a new dual core Intel processor enabling the videos to play flawlessly. I watched another youtube.com video comparing this unit with the iPad 4. The reviewer was talking about how much better the specs are on the iPad, and they are. However there is something called the real world. I am sure the iPad display is somewhat better. However, as a photographer I can tell you that the Samsung display is awesome. This same reviewer also mentioned that the Samsung slowed down. When? When he was playing games and watching movies at the same time. What? Some of the conclusions in online reviews are simply idiotic.I purchased the white version and the unit itself is pleasing to the eye. I use the voice feature for creating and responding to emails and it works very well. I mentioned the IR, infa red feature. You can control your tv's, Directv set top box, stereo and a whole bunch of other IR home entertainment stuff. The Directv app is awesome as it has a much more comprehensive guide format than that found on your TV.I have experienced 2 glitches with the unit when starting it up after it had charged all night. The first time it hung up and then corrected itself. The second time I had to reboot. That does not concern me as the unit operates 99.9% of the time perfectly.If you're a computer savvy business person or a computer newbie, I think that you will find this unit to be very user friendly and functionally appealing.I wanted to post more of a hands on review and I hope that you find it helpful. Would I purchase this unit again? Absolutely. I now have my day to day life in this thing and take it everywhere with me. It's a great personal assistant.Update on 9/17/2013: Just got back from a week trip with the Samsung Galaxy Tab 3. Before I left for the trip, I rented 2 movies from my neighborhood movie store and converted them to MP4's using DVD Catalyst. Then I copied them to the 32GB chip I had in the tablet using the USB Connector that I mentioned earlier. I also did the same thing with 2 music DVD's. I had great entertainment on the 2 1/2 hour plane ride coming and going to my destination. I also ordered a 64GB chip but it didn't arrive before I left. A 32GB chip will give you plenty of room. I did discover a problem. Using the built in browser or Chrome, it is impossible to load Flash. I did find a simple solution and that is to purchase the app browser Puffin for $2.99 from the app store that is built into the tablet. It's a full-featured, super great browser and you'll have no issues with Flash. I'm thinking that a future firmware update will correct that issue but it is minor. I used the tablet for downloading images in my camera and it worked great. It downloads them into a folder, Imported Pictures, located in the internal memory of the tablet. I simply moved them to folders I had created in the microSD chip I had inserted into the tablet. While I was on my trip, a friend's wife became so excited about the tablet that we drove 100 miles to purchase one for her.

review_title: Cringe worthy. Get the iWatchz for $5 more, or just use the integrated clip on your clothes.
review_text: First, I received this through the vine program. I already own an iWatchz brand iPod nano watch case and I like it. The iWatchz has its drawbacks, but it actually makes the iPod nano a pretty nice digital watch.Keep in mind that no iPod nano watch case is great for listening to an iPod. IPod nano doesn't have bluetooth and having the headphones tethered to your wrist is not a great way to listen to music. If you plug a bluetooth transmitter into an iPod nano, the battery drains in less than 90 min so using wireless headphones is not much good. You carry the iPod nano on your wrist if you buy a watch case, you will need to move it to your collar, jacket, or shirt if you want to listen to it.This watch case is really really terrible. It does not fit snugly on the iPod, so it makes the iPod (and iPod watch) look huge. The iWatchz looks better than I expected. This product is so tacky and cheap-looking I would never leave the house wearing it.I don't understand the slap-on gimmick. I guess if bucking the strap on a normal watch is too much of a burden for you, this "slap on" method is a good thing.The only positive of this product vs the iWatchz is that this case provides slightly more splash protection.I honestly don't recommend buying any iPod nano watch accessory. The durable ones are very expensive ($60+). The affordable iWatchz line looks good but they are made from cheap plastic and losing your nano is a distinct possibility (iWatchz uses a plastic piece to attach the ipod, and the band is precariously connected to this cheap plastic with normal metal watch pins). All nano watch cases expose your device to splashing when you wash your hands, which is kind of a pain (nano is the worlds least waterproof watch). This has the cheap plastic feel of the iWatchz, only it is extra-ugly.This item seems like it is made for children, but no kid is going to wear it because of the size.This is manufactured garbage. Don't buy it. If you want a more-affordable nano watch case, get the iWatchz with the plastic band. I feel terrible for having requested it from the vine program because I am tossing it and have gotten absolutely zero use from it. What a waste of resources.

review_title: Fast, Cool and Quiet with horrible display issues.

You can see it when the display backlighting is off. It isn't a big deal and you cannot see it when the display is active.The build quality is great. The hinge is extremly stiff with no flex when using the computer. The keyboard is awesome. Of important note, and this is a rare feature on a notebook, it is a true full size keyboard. Meaning, you have a ten-key numeric pad. I was shocked when I saw it. The keyboard itself doesn't have backlighting, but there is a ring of light that is cool around the mousepad. Mine turns off on occassion, but it really doesn't serve a function so I don't care.As for the processor, it runs fast. I was very concerned about it since it is so new without a lot of reviews. The thing runs windows 7 like a champ, the lowest rating was 5.9 on the graphics card, which for Vista users, was the old max rating. The thing can do 1080p youtube adn HD netflix like it is a powerhouse. I was having software issues with bluray playback, so one might need to consider getting something better than powerDVD. As far as games are concerned, I've only tried star trek online. I couldn't play it on my dell with a core2duo and intergrated graphics, this one plays it on high. I've been lazy and haven't tried dirt 3, which came free with my purchase.I have one question for all those that own this... do you have plastic flex near the left side vent? when I push down or in on it, there is minor flex. It doesn't bother me too much, but for 700 dollars if no one else has that build quality issue I want a new one.UPDATEAfter owning the notebook for over a year, I absolutely hate it. I have had display issue after display issue. HP even did an out of warranty replacement for the display, which didn't help the issue. Stay HP negative and buy a different PC.

So I had no reason to prime myself with negative thinking towards this device. However, when it got here, it didn't waste any time making me a very unhappy customer. Splitting hairs with me over whether or not the HD7 is a "windows/microsoft product" or not is completely pointless, as the point is, it is a "windows phone", and it didn't work well with the "xbox earpiece". Do I have to be a comedian and say it in a funny voice for the levity of that to not fly right over your heads?Anyways, once paired, the piece performed horridly, I couldn't walk more than 3 feet from the phone, and I had to keep the side of my head upon which the piece was mounted facing the phone at all times, as apparently my thick skull was enough to interrupt the connection. review_title: Great until you pump it louder!
review_text: PORTABILITY: These are surprisingly light, making it easy to take around with you. Also, the handy carrying bag gives you a pair of draw strings to loop your hand through for easy of carrying.CORD LENGTH: At first I was concerned the cord was a little too short to have the mp3 player in my pocket while wearing the headphones, but it was just enough. If I needed a bit more length on the cord, they were nice enough to provide a 3-4ft extension cord. Nice!COMFORTABILITY: I have theSennheiser HD 558 Audiophile Headphones with an Internal Surround Reflectorwhich are fantastic headphones...and they better be for the price. What Sennheiser chooses to do is make the headphone opening large enough to encompass your ear with room to spare around it. Nothing is touching your ears for the most part. These Creative headphone sit on your ears, but are so well padded that they also very comfortable. With this style in having material actually touching your ears it gets hot and sweaty after a couple of hours, or sooner if the weather is warmer. Otherwise surprisingly comfortable.ACCESSORIES: You get the carrying bag, the cord extender I mentioned earlier and you get the adapter to plug into your stereo system. I really appreciated these inexpensive but necessary accessories already in the package!SOUND: When comparing them to the Sennheiser these headphones were surprisingly good for all types of music. It handled highs & lows well, and had a good handling of treble and bass sounds. My only complaint is when I cranked up the volume very loud (you know you do it too), the sound seemed to distort slightly and was in tones that were uncomfortable to listen too. At the same loud volume the Sennheiser handled the sound better...but they better since they are a more expensive unit.EXERCISING: Size does matter as they are smaller than the Sennheiser, but still too big for use while doing most cardio exercising. I still prefer the style of theSony MDR-J10 h.ear Headphones with Non-Slip Design (Black)when exercising as I can clip one ear on my collar if I need to hear things (such as traffic while riding my bike) or just knowing the clip style has less bounciness when running and other activities. Also if your headphone get wet from sweat the cheap stuff is okay if it gets ruined vs. a near $100 headphones like these.OVERALL:It's rare I'd pump the volume so loud that I'd distort the sound, but I do like listening to it super loud sometimes. The other 98% of the time these headphones performed admirably. The fact the price has already come down $10-$15 since I got mine a couple of weeks ago, is even nicer for new purchasers. I leave my Sennheiser at home and take these with me everywhere now. Great portable headphones.

review_title: A performance bump, but not a performance leap
review_text: I installed the SanDisk Extreme II 240GB as a boot drive in a four-year-old Lenovo workstation, replacing a two-year-old 120GB Intel 510 Series SSD. I knew not to expect the same kind of performance bump that I'd seen going from a platter-based drive to the Intel SSD, but I hoped that I might see just a bit of improvement. That's what I got--a little bit of an improvement in drive performance, but nothing really noticeable in day-to-day use. Still, that's not really a knock on the SanDisk drive, because it's not that realistic to expect huge gains going from one modern SSD to another one.I conducted a couple of before-and-after tests: reading 14GB of files (my Downloads folder, which I've set to reside on a three-drive RAID array in the workstation; most of these files are compressed), first to the Intel SSD and then, after cloning the Intel SSD and swapping drives, to the SanDisk SSD. The Intel drive completed the task in 1:50, and the SanDisk drive completed the task in 1:40, or about 9 percent more quickly. Nice, but just below the threshold of what would be noticeable. Typically 10 percent is a noticeable performance gain.I also tested writing my Adobe applications folder (approx. 4GB, mostly uncompressed) from each SSD to the RAID array. The Intel drive completed the task in 2:30; the SanDisk drive did it in 2:40, or about 7 percent more slowly. Understand that I conducted these tests only a single time; multiple passes would produce more reliable results (and you can find those elsewhere).The bootup on my workstation required the same amount of time to complete, of course; after it was done, getting from the Windows password prompt to ready to go was quick, but about as quick as the Intel drive.I also ran Windows 7's Performance Index with both SSDs; the drive score increased from 6.9 with the Intel 510 SSD to 7.4 with the SanDisk SSD. That's about a 7 percent improvement--again, below the threshold of what would be noticeable, but welcome nonetheless.The only thing I really curled my brow at was that the drive enclosure is plastic, unlike the Intel 510 Series drive's aluminum enclosure. Because SSDs don't generate heat--or at least, generate far less heat than platter-based drives--and they aren't as susceptible to heat as platter-based drives, this probably isn't a major issue. I don't keep irreplaceable data on the drive, as I'm using it as a boot drive, and I back everything up faithfully, so my main need for this drive is performance. I'd just rather the drive be contained in something as solid as possible.So the point is, it's a good drive, and if you'll be using it to replace a platter-based drive, prepare to be astounded. If you'll be using it to replace another SSD, prepare to be pleased, but don't get your expectations too far out of whack.

review_title: Not as good as iPhone5, not as good as dedicated mp3 player
review_text: Because it's called an "iPod," people might think it's an mp3 player. Actually, it's a pretty mediocre mp3 players. For a lot less money, you can buy an mp3 player that's smaller and lighter and has physical pause and skip-song buttons. The lack of a pause button I find really annoying. OK, there's a trick that you can pull out the headphones and it pauses the music, but still, An MP3 PLAYER SHOULD HAVE A PAUSE BUTTON.But this is not really an mp3 player, this is probably more intended to be an iPhone that doesn't make phone calls or connect to a cellular network. An iPhone without the phone. And it's superior to the iPhone 5 because it's smaller and lighter.The real iPhone has two features I really like that are missing from or not as good on iPod Touch. (1) The iPhone has a light sensor so it automatically changes the screen brightness based on the surrounding light. (2) The iPhone has a MUCH BETTER CAMERA. Trust me on the camera part. I took my iPod Touch 5G and iPhone 5 and took the exact same picture, so I could compare. The iPhone obviously has a much better sensor, the picture from the iPhone had much less noise, and was sharper because there was less noise filtering applied. I also think the iPhone had better, more accurate colors.I really wish that Apple hadn't saddled the iPod with an inferior camera.The iPhone also has a more powerful microprocessor, but actually I don't notice any difference in speed of anything that I use these for. Maybe there's some game I'm not playing that runs a lot better on the iPhone. For reading the Wall Street Journal or ebooks, you don't need the extra microprocessor power of the iPhone.

review_title: Not Bad At This Price Point
review_text: I decided to purchase the 808 because of several reviews I had found online about how good they sounded at the $129 price point.  I went on Amazon and found them and was really happy to see they were on sale for $45.  I thought what the heck, not very much money, and if by some chance they didn't meet my expectations I could give them to one of my children. You can definitely tell they were going for the Beats by Dre and Soul by Ludacris crowd by their design.  I own numerous pairs of headphones, but, since these are targeting the Beats by Dre Market I will compare them to my Beats by Dre Studio and Solo HD, which is probably a better comparison since the 808 does not offer noise cancellation.I am a huge fan of Beats by Dre and I know some people are and some people are not, sound can be very subjective.  The 808 comes in a very nice box, but not quite as elegant as the Beats, but at such a low price point, I didn't expect them to.  The 808 comes with a carrying case, made of a cloth material while the Beats come with a hard case which will offer better protection for your headphones, but also adds a lot more bulk.  I wouldn't advise throwing the 808 in the carrying case in a book bag or luggage with anything other than clothes to help keep them from getting damaged.  They have a nice fold able design and comes with a DJ cable and a nice flat cable that I was surprised to find out that it could be used to control my Samsung Galaxy S3.  The box states it can control Android devices as well as iPhones.  Nice to see the flat cable so you do not have to worry about the cord getting tangled, and at this price point it can be difficult to find a pair of headphones where you can detach the cable because that is usually the first thing to go on a pair of headphones.The 808 do resemble the Beats, but I do not think anyone would get them confused.  They say 808 on the headphones where the logo of the b for Beats by Dre would be and are actually made pretty good.  They are not as comfortable to wear for long periods of time, but provides some decent padding on the ears and on the head and on the headband, they look pretty nice and they do cover the whole ear which is nice where the Solo HD are on ear headphones and not as comfortable, especially for people who wear glasses.The reason people buy headphones are for the way they sound, but I also want something that looks nice.  I mainly listen to music on my Samsung Galaxy S3 and I listened to everything from Rock, Pop, Rap, and RnB and I found the sound to be very flat, and not very engulfing, and it felt tiny compared to my Beats, and I was a little disappointed because of some of the excellent reviews I had read before purchasing.  I then preceeded to full around with the EQ and wow, did the sound really come alive.  It got 100% better.  The bass is still muffled, and not as tight as it should be, especially compared to the Beats Pro and Beats Solo HD, but, not super bad either, but the mids and highs were very good and the music didn't over power the singing like some headphones do.I can recommend these headphones to people who have a eq on their listening devices or for parents who kids want the Beats look, but you don't want to pay the beats price, and at less than $50 I can tell you that you will not be disappointed.  If they were the origianl $100 to $140 price I would say stay away especially since the Soul by Ludacris headphones are so reasonably priced right now on Amazon for around $150 for the SL300 which is a 5 star product and the SL150 for around $120 which is 4 star product for on ear headphones.

review_title: Great Camera for a Photography Newbie
review_text: Before I had this camera, I had a point and shoot compact - the Hewlett-Packard R607.  After time, I noticed that I desired more of my photos.  My photos lacked depth of field, vibrance, resolution, and detail.  I started reading about photography and associated terms such as aperture value, shutter speed, ISO, exposure, white balance, and metering.  I quickly learned the basics of photography by visiting a few websites and determined that the camera I had wouldn't hack it for me anymore.I researched a number of cameras and landed at a review site that previewed this camera.  I compared it with some of the competition, noting that the Sony DSC-HX1 has some amazing features such as the hand-held twilight mode, anti-motion blur, sweep panorama mode, 10fps continuous shooting, and rechargeable batteries (would you believe some of the competitors use AA's).  After a lot of reading and debating, I decided on the DSC-HX1.In regards to the sweep-panorama mode: It works fantastically, both during the day and at night.The video is smooth and a high enough quality to please the eye.  This is, of course, an upgrade for me from 640 x 480 resolution video.  As I moved the camera in tight on subjects, zoom or not, I immediately noticed the Optical SteadyShot image stabalization working remarkably to make my video look steady and professional-like.  No tripod needed here.  I took the DSC-HX1 to a Killers concert where I was far enough away that I need 15-20x zoom if I wanted to get tight shots on the band members.  With proper camera holding posture (keeping it tight to my chest and using the digital viewfinder) and the SteadyShot, I was able to pull off some video that would not have been remotely possible with my limmited-zoom, no stability, HP camera.The image quality is what you would expect from a "bridge-camera."  The camera's CMOS sensor capture daylight pictures with remarkable vibrance and detail appropriate to this camera's market.  Night shots at ISO 100-200 given appropriate lighting look great.  Night shots and darker indoor shots at ISO 400-800 show a degree of noise that you would expect from a sensor of this size.  I have often found myself adjusting my aperture and shutter values to allow me to use ISO 400 vice ISO 800 if at all possible.  I have not had to use ISO 1600 or 3200 manually yet - so I can't vouch for them, but I would venture to say they should only be used if it is absolutely necessary.I have not yet tested the hand-held twilight mode or anti-motion blur modes yet.  When I do, I will edit this review.Battery life is stupendous.  It is far superior to my HP camera and I far prefer taking the battery out and plugging it into the wall.  The charger for the batter is small enough to fit into the small side pocket of my camera bag.  It beats having to carry around a charger.The articulating LCD screen is bright, clear, and reveals enough detail to make a good judgment of the composition of your photo.  Only under direct bright sunlight is it difficult to see.  If this is the case, simply switch to the digital viewfinder.The viewfinder is useful in high-light situations or when keeping the camera close to your chest to maximize your steady shot.  I can't say that it is as good as the viewfinder that you'll find in a DSLR and as a result, would submit that you only use it if you need to.  The good thing is, that you can correct the focus of the image in the viewfinder via an adjustment wheel on the housing.The burst shot mode is great.  At 10, 5, or 2 FPS, you can stop motion in time and catch those special moments.  Beware though, that after you've released the shutter button of you've captured 10 pictures, the camera must pause to write these files from buffer to the memory card.  This might be a show stopper for some who are not sure when precisely that special moment will occur.  You will have to allow time for the camera to catch up with writing the images to the memory card.The camera does, of course, weight more than your typical compact, but less than a DSLR.  It's portable enough and weighs little enough that it doesn't strain the neck when worn for prolonged amounts of time.  I've worn it for 3-4 hours and felt little discomfort if any.For the price, I feel it's a great camera.  There are a lot of compact cameras that cost nearly as much and have only half the power, speed, and capability.All things considered, I think this is a great camera for someone who wants great capability without the bulk and weight of a DSLR, and is willing to work within the confines of the camera itself with few customizing accessories available.

review_title: Very Good Sound, But A Few Issues
review_text: Headphones are a personal thing. One person's amazing set of ear buds is another's torture device.  So I'll give you a quick bit of information about my music background and needs list, then how these stack up.I started working as a recording engineer and producer in the 80's and worked in studios for almost two decades.  I value neutrality and balance in either headphones or speakers.  I listen to all types of music, from jazz to rock, singer/songwriter to alternative, punk to funk.  I've never found a set of ear buds I love, but really that's a function of what technology can do; I don't think it's possible to get some that sound consistently as good as, say AKG 240's or Sennheiser 580's (both big, old style, closed-ear design headphones).That said, most people don't walk around with that kind of headphones on, and most portable devices can't drive them efficiently anyway.  But then, life is about compromise, so most people choose one of two types of ear buds:  the kind that sit in your ear like stock iPod headphones, or the type that seal in your ear canal, providing additional bass but also isolating you from external sounds (um, you might not want to jog at night, in the street, with that kind).  The Altec Lansing UHP326's are in the latter category.  So how do I like them?The first thing that struck me was that it was really tough to see which was right and which was left.  They are marked, but with a black l or r on black plastic.  In the dark, or even dim light, that's not good.  They really should have put a colored dot on one or the other. They do come with four different sets of plastic covers to fit various size ears; very important because getting a poor seal will give you really awful sound, with no bass or lower midrange.But once I got them fitted, and in the correct ears, I was relatively happy.  The sound at the bottom end is full and accurate (assuming a good, tight seal), though I found the upper mids a bit harsh.  High end is clean.They do have one problem that also affects the Zune premium headphones: rubbing the headphone cord against your shirt, or in your hands, transmits that rubbing noise to the headphones themselves - it can be intrusive at times, particularly if you are listening to quiet classical music and moving around a lot.  However, this only happens when you make firm contact with the section of the cable between where the right/left cable split occurs and your ears.  The cable from the split to the music device does NOT transmit noise - a definite plus over the Zune premiums.So overall, I'd normally give them three stars or three and a half stars.  At suggested list price (does anyone pay that, anywhere?), I wouldn't personally buy them.  But at the 30 bucks amazon.com is currently charging for them, I think it'd be hard to find a better set of isolation-type, hence a final four star rating.

review_title: Well Built - Will Protect in a Monsoon (and the 300mm f2.8 monster lens fits)
review_text: The Kata elements camera cover is a well built strong cover for SLR cameras. The cover takes a little bit of practice to put on quickly. But once on, your camera is not going to get wet.This is a large cover. It's hard to tell from the product images, but the thick clear vinyl that covers the camera body is very large. It is so big, that I'm able to install my Canon 580EX II flash under the hood. Pop up flashes from the camera body will not work underneath this cover, they don't pop up high enough to clear the black lens cover. I have very large hands, and there's no problem slipping my hands in the hand accesses to the left and right of the camera. There's plenty of space to work the camera controls, front, top and rear of the body. Your hand can also slide up along the lens to turn the zoom or focus rings.My camera is a Canon EOS Rebel XTi with the standard short kit lens and a Tamron 75 - 300mm zoom. The long lens works the best, and should really be used with the lens hood installed.The one odd characteristic, if your lenses are front element rotating for zoom or focusing; you will need to take some care with how you attach the front lens covers (there's an inner soft, flexible cover with a pull string; and an outer very stiff plastic with Velcro that serves as a rain hood). If you pull either cover tight to the lens, when you focus or zoom, those covers will turn and twist. This isn't a problem if you are mostly shooting with the zoom at a fairly narrow range and there isn't a huge focus swing. If you aren't careful, you might over stress the focus motor twisting up the covers.Most consumer grade lenses have rotating front elements for both zoom and focus. The big pro level lenses all have fixed front elements and lens barrels.Overall, this is a super rugged, well thought out cover that will protect your camera from everything except horizontal rain (and then you probably shouldn't be outside anyway).Sept. 5, 2010 update: Guess what fits just exactly inside this hood? Yes, the Canon 300mm f2.8 IS monster telephoto. The inner liner just seals over the lens hood, and the great big velcro cover seals exactly right over the lens hood. It was a huge surprise.

review_title: Another thumbs up for the 10 inch Asus eee
review_text: I won't go into too much detail in my comments, as other reviewers have generously taken the time to provide a lot of specifics. If you're in the market for one of these, here are a couple of additional comments to aid in your decision-making.Size: I had the chance to see an Asus 1000 beside a 900 at a local Best Buy. In my opinion, the 9 inch version was just too small; it was surprising how much larger the screen seemed on the 10-inch version. This ruled out machines like the Dell Mini for me. This Asus 1000HA, while it is small, is still large enough for nice all purpose usage, while still being incredibly portable.Battery: I can confirm the general reports of 4-5 hours of battery life, depending on what you do with it. Netbooks like this one that use a 6-cell battery seem to have a distinct advantage over those that don't.Color: I got the white one. It really hardly shows fingerprints at all; the black one quickly looks very smudged.Quibbles: The touch screen is fantastic, with many cool features. However, the two finger scrolling doesn't work smoothly with Firefox unless you turn off the keyboard lock-out feature (which locks out the touchpad while you're typing). With that turned off, you have to really be careful not to touch the pad while you type or the cursor jumps all over the place. I'm hoping that Asus eventually provides a driver update to address this.Heat: the bottom of the unit gets warm sometimes, but not so much that I'd consider it a deciding factor in a purchase decision.Wireless range: Some users have reported concerns about the wireless range of this unit. I'm using this in a first floor room, and my wireless router is on the second floor at the opposite end of the house, and I've had perfect connections all the time. No issues here.I'm very happy with this computer. If this type of laptop is attractive to you, I think you would be too.
