If you are looking for a reliable, fast and large flash drive, it's hard to top this device.  When plugged into a USB 3.0 port, this thing is a rocket.  In fact, it's faster than most internal hard drives.  In fact, this device is nearly twice the speed of a typical 5400 RPM drive.  That's game changing.It manages to achieve this speed by using an 8-channel controller on board, which essentially compensates for the slower speeds of flash cells by splitting the task between channels... sort of like a RAID.  The great thing about this is that this means that even USB 2.0 ports will still get vastly better performance than low cost USB 2.0 flash drives.I'm not the typical USB Flash Drive user that just uses them to back up or transport data.  For nearly 10 years, I have made my USB drives my PRIMARY storage device for every document I work on.  This gives me the flexibility to go to any computer in the world and always have all my documents at my fingertips.In the early days, this meant I had to be selective about the files I could take with me... leaving me to leave some files stranded on my local drives, making it very difficult when I needed something that didn't fit while on another computer or while travelling to clients.Once USB drives got bigger, I finally could put everything on one drive, and virtually eliminate the need to bring my laptop to clients.  The trade-off at the time was the drives were a tad slower than my local drive.  Now that drives like this are not only large, but faster than most internal drives, there is no compromise.  If you decide to take the plunge and follow my model of using these as primary storage, my advice is to make sure you back them up regularly to your local drive or another flash drive.  Anything that is portable can be lost or damaged, so backups are important.  If privacy is a concern, consider a program that will encrypt the data or simply make sure you don't lose it.One thing... these drives come pre-formatted using FAT32.  I NEVER use FAT32 because although it's the most compatible format, it's not as reliable or fast as NTFS or in my case OSX, because there is no fault tolerance built in.Do yourself a favor, if you plan on putting important information on this, re-format the drive using NTFS (For Windows compatibility), or OSX for Mac.  I've done benchmarks using both and it performed much better when I re-formatted it.

review_title: Good adapter but will need to work around drivers for it
review_text: I bought this adapter because I upgraded my 128gb mSata SSD to a 256gb mSata SSD. I needed to clone my old mSata drive, so I bought the Apricorn USB 3.0 upgrade kit (basically a USB to SATA adapter cable and the cloning software). I've used the USB 2.0 Apricorn adapter kit previously to clone an SSD drive to both a SSD drive and a traditional hard drive and am very happy with the process of using the kit. So I placed the new 256gb mSata drive into the Syba adapter and then connected the Syba adapter into the Apricorn Sata connectors. I then connected the Apricorn USB connector into the USB 3.0 plug. In my past experience, I used the CD that came with the Apricorn kit to boot to as it was bootable and the USB 3.0 version was the same but when I booted to the Apricorn CD and ran the cloning software, I was getting messages that the Apricorn USB adapter could not be found. I unconnected everything and re-connected everything but was getting the same results. I want to boot to the Apricorn CD and run the cloning software directly from the CD instead of running the cloning software in Windows 7 to try to avoid any issues as I was cloning the main system hard drive.I had no choice but to boot to Windows 7, which was from my mSata drive that I was replacing and then running the Apricorn cloning software on the CD. The cloning software found the new mSata drive that was still connected to the Syba adapter, which was  connected to the Apricorn Sata to USB adapter because as soon as Windows 7 booted up, it found the Apricorn and Syba adapters and installed the correct drivers. I was able to successfully clone my old 128gb mSata (which the cloning software was running from) to my new 256gb mSata - I have to give kudos to Apricorn because their cloning software used a 'hot copy' method and I verified the clone was done with no errors and the entire mSata was clone to the new drive).The reason I was not able to clone from the CD and not Windows 7 was because when I booted from the Apricorn CD, the drivers for the Syba adapter was not loaded and thus the Syba adapter along with the mSata installed in it was not found also. In the end, I was able to accomplish what I need to do but the not by my first choice, which I considered the safest way to clone my mSata drive. Due my specific requirements, I am still giving the Syba adapter 5 stars because Windows 7 found the drivers and installed the drivers correctly and after booting into Windows 7, I had no issues with the Syba adapter. The Syba adapter did what is was suppose to do, the Apricorn upgrade kit also performed as specified, it was just my specific situation that I need to go to a plan B. I thing if you are going to install this adapter into a desktop Sata connector, you should have no issues.

Before I bought this camera, I had flirted with the possibility of doing so for about a year.Let me preface this review by saying that I am a slave to aesthetics, and this camera is absolutely no exception to that compulsion.This camera is replacing myPanasonic DMC-LX3 10.1MP Digital Camera with 24mm Wide Angle MEGA Optical Image Stabilized Zoom (Black)which was a bang-em up camera by all measures However, the sensor did get dirty and I also decided it was time to make the upgrade to a DSLR camera.Build Quality- Okay, so the first thing you notice about this camera is just how elegant and durable the camera looks. I've had the camera for a few weeks and I'm still taken back by how very solid and sleek the camera is. It also has a durable, weighty, well-built feel in the hands. Everything down to the battery door opens up with purpose and assertion- the hallmark of thoughtful, high-quality craftsmanship.Performance- What can I say? The camera does what I tell it to, when I tell it to, in the manner which I tell it to. The autofocus is very fast, and when you have to photograph something that's just too tricky for the camera to pick up on, the magnified autofocus assist is a lifesaver for those tricky macro shots. Combined with the f/1.7 lens, it does wonderful portrait shots. Some may be put off by the lack of zoom, but in my experience, a high zoom has seldom made for better pictures. Can you walk in to a dimly-lit bar and take one-handed, no-flash shots with it all willy-nilly? No. However, provided you can get some people to hold still for a few seconds and you know how to steady your hand, you should be able to take pictures in dimly-lit parties with not too much difficulty. For absolute low-light performance, look to upgrade to aVoigtlander Nokton 35mm f/1.4 Wide Angle Leica M Mount Lens - Black. However, if you're strapped for cash, you won't mind holding the camera steady. The menus go by very quickly with minimal lag in between photo deletion and navigation. I like that a great deal.Features- I've never used an SLR camera before, and as such I'm VERY used to setting up composition and gauging contrast using the LCD screen of point-and-shoots. I will say it- I don't like using the viewfinder in the least. To me, one of the hugest benefits of digital photography is the ability to immediately gauge and correct your settings. This camera more fully embraces that benefit by making an LCD-based autofocus quick, responsive and accurate. I enjoy it heavily, but not everyone will.Ultimately- I love this camera. It's beautiful, well-built, small, powerful and compatible with some great lenses if you don't mind shelling out the dough for them. I was intrigued by the way the camera looked, and sold by the pictures I saw people take with it on flickr (there's a very devoted following to this camera on the website if you're interested in seeing the kind of pictures it's capable of cranking out). If you're the kind of customer who cherishes the way a camera looks almost as much as the kind fo pictures it can take- this is definitely the camera for you. Click the "buy" button and don't look back. You'll be glad you did.

review_text: Overall I would say this unit has nice build quality and sounds better then others I have heard, such as the X-Mini and Brookstone Mobile Mini Speakers. I felt those sounded more like small cans with a speaker in them no real depth. I have not heard the 237 so I can't compare this to that one, but what I can say is this is pretty good for what it is. As long as you do not expect a lot of bottom end then I think you will be happy the clarity is excellent. It does have some mid-bass kick but not a lot. Overall the balance in sound is quite good.I am going to try and give others an idea of what to expect from this little speaker. All of my listening tests have been done with an Ipod 4G and MP3's encoded at 256. I have been testing this little speaker with well recorded Jazz instrumental as well as Rock and vocal. This way one can judge the speakers ability to reproduce instruments and vocals faithfully. I did not really see a review that went into detail so I will be the one to do that.The 228 speaker sounds very crisp with nice depth to vocals, they do not sound at all thin as with many others. I decided to do this test first with "Perfect Girl" by Sarah McLachlan, as it has very nicely recorded vocals. The vocals actually sound surprisingly strong and smooth with excellent presence and depth rather impressive for a 1.5" driver.Next test was with music by Kenny G, and Mindy Abair. This also sounded quite good, the orbit did a nice job producing the sax in her song "Right On", a lot better then you might expect, I was actually surprised.Kenny G's version of "Pick Up The Pieces" sounded really good, this is a superb recording, and so I felt a very good test. The song had solid punch to it, with nice open sounding sax.If the 228 sounds this good, I would really love to test and review the 237, as some say it is better. Unfortunately, I was not able to get one at a reasonable price, so I decided I would try the 228 in prep for the next possible storm outage, so I can listen without ear buds. Now I'm set./////////////////// UPDATE ///////////////////Ok here is an update to my review, the speaker is working fine no problem as of this writing, and I do like it overall. But heres the catch I wanted to reg the item and get the warranty in case I have a problem down the road. My 228 was brand new and came with a slip of paper saying give us 2 minutes and we will give you two years. Sounds good right? Wrong.I called Altec as the US website listed is not on line right now, they are apparently working on updating it.Anyway I got them on the phone and I was told that they would not warranty the product. I said it is brand new why can't I get the warranty? the woman on the phone told me because of some deal they made I told them I am not happy at all.I feel they should stand behind the item I purchased no questions asked. I also told her that I have a review up on amazon and I would be updating it with this info. Not sure how much she cared but she did give me an email addy to write to about my warranty.Complaint Filed with BBB today 12/03/12 for lack of response on Altec's part. Also note: they have an (F) rating with the BBB, this seems well deserved if this is the way they treat the end user. I will update this when and if I get a resolve.Well Going on several weeks now with no resolve. All they sent was a mostly canned response not really reading what my issue is with them, and still not honoring the 2yr warranty or even letting me reg the item, at this point they also did not get back to the BBB as Altec is not BBB accredited so all that can be done is a request for them to contact the BBB if they do not then its out of their hands, this is why they maintain the (F) status with the BBB.So at this point Altec has by far the worst customer support most likely because of who knows how many buy outs at this point, it's ashame to see a once great speaker company go by the waist side, and I guess they just do not care anymore.So my next step is consumer affairs maybe then we can achieve something.If Altec thinks this is acceptable, well they picked the wrong reviewer to play with. I suggest if anyone else has this same problem we all file a complaint with the BBB because in my opinion they need to stand behind this product no matter what deals they made with amazon or any others as nothing is said anywhere that Altec will not honor the 2 year warranty or reg the Orbit allowing for this extended warranty.Note: They did not put an expiration date on the slip.I hope Altec reads this.

Being that I am new to MP3 players and haven't set up an entire library using WMA format it is probably a little easier for me to be pleased with this player. Like so many others I spent several weeks looking over all the MP3 players and actually going to the stores and picking them up and looking at them before making a decision on one. Part of my decision came from price and size. I really didn't need anything over 1GB and I really was holding myself to around $150 or less. I am somewhat partial to Sony for most of my electronics have been from Sony and I am pleased with all of them. Here is what led me to the purchase of the NW-E507 listed in order of importance to me:Pros:(1) Price $149(2) The feel - It feels like a piece of electronics. It has a quality feel to it that you really can't grasp in the pictures. You have to hold it. It doesn't have the feel of plastic like so many others.(3) The Look - It has been described as looking like a cigarette lighter and maybe it does, but it looks classy especially with the OED display which in normal lighting you will have no problem seeing it.(4) The Sound - The sound is pretty good with the supplied earphones, but the sound is fantastic with better headphones. I am using the The Phillips Surround Sound "earbuds" which are very comfortable.(5) 1GB Storage - Which can be used for music and/or data. Sony clames that you can load up to 695 songs, which I believe is when you use their ATRAC3 format.(6) FM Player - This was a must for me. I have had this for over a week and the FM was easy to set up and the reception is great for such a small player.(7) Battery Life - Sony claims 50 hours. Haven't had it that long, but the several hours I have played it, hasn't made a dent in the batter life.Con:The only problem that has been mentioned several times was the OED display. It is hard to see when outside in direct sunlight, but the only time I really use it outside is on walks which I set up before going out and don't have a need to look at it again while walking.Summary: Overall I love this player. The software (which has been the major gripe to many reviewers) was no problem at all. Very easy to navigate and keep up with my library on it. Also, if you have Version 1.0 on your player you can upgrade it now to 2.0 at "[...]" , which adds another clock display and a couple more "cutsie" displays for your player. They also have Version 3.3 for SonicStage software at this same location. Downloaded both of them and no trouble installing them. One more application you can also download is the MP3 File Manager Application which lets you transfer MP3 files to the player without converting them to the ATRAC format. It is my understanding that you won't be able to get as many songs on it in WMA format, but if your songs are already in that format it might be beneficial to you. As you can tell I am very satisfied with this player.Update: Downloaded Sony's MP3 File Manager from the above site and had NO problem moving my MP3 files over to the player. I now have numerous albums in ATRAC format and an album in MP3 file. All play perfectly and can move the MP3 files in and out without any problem and the player recognizes them. Still love everything about this player. Totally satisfied.

Probably as good as any out there, which isn't really saying much.  It's obvious that this whole streaming/DLNA/etc paradigm is still a work in progress.Random observations after about 10 days:1.  WiFi works, but you definitely need a clear, strong signal - by that I mean 5 bars.  Otherwise, no connect.  You might want to invest in an extender, or else use ethernet exlusively.2.  Disc playback - trying to fast forward, the system gets confused.  You can only go about twice real-time speed without some temporary freezing.  Never gets up to anything close to full FF  speed.3.  Netflix app seems OK.  Good playback over WiFi.4.  Streaming video files (MP4) over ethernet is way better than WiFi, but same issue with fast forward as above.  Reliable connection, though.5.  For video media file playback, USB port off a thumb drive is absolutely the best.  Very smooth, and FF will go at top speed.6.  Random lockups, requires unplugging.  Not often, but happens.  No clear idea as to cause.7.  Have not tested other apps or add-ons.  There are a bunch.  Lack of Amazon seems to be a show-stopper for some, but I am not at that point yet.8.  Does not play AVI, but then again few of the new ones do, regardless of brand.  I am keeping my old player for that.9.  The included DLNA server Nero MediaHome on the CD seems flakey and unreliable.  Sometimes you can see the shares, sometimes not.  I removed it and downloaded the evaluation of the same product from Nero's website and it seems pretty solid.  I know it will expire after two weeks, but the actual file sharing capability might still remain, based on the nag screens it throws up.  I will know in a few days.  May actually buy it, but then again my router has a built-in DLNA app, so I may just forgo that.Overall, not great, but not too bad either.  Hope some of this is useful.Ed

review_title: Impressively-featured NAS fails at RAID recovery.
review_text: I had initially written a glowing review of this unit after loading it up with my data and setting my preferences. It was a great first impression, and many thing about the Synology NAS are wonderful; however only 2 months in I had my first disk failure and the recovery was anything but graceful.The first drive in my RAID-5 array became "invalid" and the array went into "degraded" status. I quickly popped in a new drive and clicked the repair button. The Synology then spent the entire day checking the consistency of the root volume and the swap drive, and announced it had been repaired; however, the data on the drives was corrupted beyond repair and a lot of it was unrecoverable from the drive, prompting a complete redo and recovery from backup drives.If you're diligent about your backup, and you want the features this NAS offers, it's a nice enough unit; however I honestly don't use 90% of the features and the failed recovery left me a bit disappointed. Despite all the packages available for this server, none of them handle data loss and recovery. Be aware that whatever data you put on this thing isn't nearly as safe as simply putting it on external drives formatted for your computer's file system.-------------------------------Original review:When I got tired of buying 3tb drives to keep up with my data needs, a friend recommended a Drobo. That was the third recommendation for a Drobo, so I starting looking into it seriously. What I found was a huge market of NAS devices, some that ran apps and services and I immediately felt flustered with all the options. Thankfully, after a few weeks of research, I began to learn about the quality of Synology units through online reviews, and I took a chance on the 5-bay NAS.I should have got the 8-bay. Don't get me wrong, the 5-bay NAS is amazing. It's so amazing, I just wish I had more of it! The web interface is simply astounding, blowing all other web sites and interfaces out of the water with functionality and stability; it's like a mix between Mac OS and Ubuntu -- in your web browser! The software applications you can add to it with a simple click are incredibly well-rounded, functionally impressive, and beautiful.So far I've made use of the Audio Streaming service (works great with my iPhone and is more reliable than iTunes Match), AFS (Apple File Sharing), the router configuration wizard (I can't believe it worked perfectly with my Buffalo router), the Synology DDNS service, and a few other settings. I haven't encountered a single bug or issue and I'm consistently surprised by the quality and depth of all of it. This thing is a better server than the variety I keep in a rack in the datacenter downtown.One small gripe: the iTunes Server, it's really poor. I'm glad they made an effort, but it doesn't handle album art very well, and it doesn't work with Apple TV at all since Apple has switched to "Home Sharing" using Apple IDs. It doesn't read meta data well or sort TV shows or anything of the like, so I still have to use my Mac Mini to manage the iTunes library and handle streaming video to my Apple TV units. The data all lives on the Synology, and I had to do some finagling in Mac OS with scheduled tasks and shell scripting to keep the Synology disks mounted and iTunes from freaking out and marking the data as missing. I half-expected this, but if you're hoping the iTunes streaming will replace your dedicated Mac, I'm sorry to say that it won't.Oh, and the DLNA: it's exceptional. I tried 6-7 DLNA servers for my Mac and the best one I could find had an obnoxious way of displaying files lists and couldn't play mkv files. The Synology DLNA server is near perfect, playing the lossless MKV files almost flawlessly, including the 1080i files I've had so much trouble with. My only gripe here is I have yet to figure out how to get the subtitles to work.One other note for Mac users, you cannot attach an HFS volume to the USB ports and mount it on the DiskStation for file transfers via USB.I will definitely be buying one or two 5-bay add-ons for this thing when it's financially appropriate to do so.

review_title: Great TV... IF You Get The Right Manufacture Date
review_text: Go for theSony BRAVIA XBR Series KDL-46XBR9 46-Inch 1080p 240Hz LCD HDTV, Black- I wish I would have.  The price difference is negligible  now compared to when I purchased my 46Z.  With the XBR9 you get better built in sound,  better backlight technology, and the speakers are hidden - taking an inch of the height of the bezel/TV.  Not to mention you might be less likely to get the flashlight effect and uneven backlight that I did.Luckily in this case I didn't purchase from Amazon; (1) I had a special deal and (2)having to return 2 units to - you know who: 'blue' - was a hassle but getting three shipped from Amazon would have been more frustrating.So here is my review for the 46" Z - the third one I tried.The Bravia LCD TV Z series are far superior to others in similar class and price range.  Sony has provided some fantastic features in this model; in fact, most of the specs are identical to the XBR9s!With the Bravia Engine 3 processor and Motionflow 240Hz refresh rate, fast panning and action scenes are rendered smooth and clean.  The exceptional contrast ratio and real time enhancer provide detail in the darkest shadows and deep blacks that rival plasma screens.  Coupled with the ambient light sensor which automatically adjusts the contrast and brightness levels to deliver a great picture in any lighting.The award-winning XROSS media bar is the easiest, most user-friendly menu navigation available on any TV.  For a unit with so many features the XROSS is essential for finding content and configurations with ease.  If you have ever used a PS3, the Bravia menus will be very familiar to you, If not, you needn't worry about navigating the TVs functions as XROSS is very intuitive and easy to master.Sony's Bravia link makes one button viewing a reality (when using compatible Sony components); want to watch a DVD or Blu-Ray?  Just insert the disc in a Sony player and the TV as well as A/V receiver will power on, tune to the correct input,  and adjust the audio and screen settings for optimal movie viewing.The included remote will automatically and seamlessly control all of your Bravia Link devices (Blu-Ray, DVD, Home theater surround, PS3, HD radio, and A/V receiver)The Bravia's ethernet port is your doorway to unlimited entertainment and painless firmware updates.  Provided with the Sony W, Z and XBR series is access to free and subscription based streaming content not available on other TVs.-Free, [...] streaming radio without interruptions.-Exclusive free Sony content including trailers, videos and music - currently featuring a collection of full length, high quality, classic music videos by Michael Jackson.-Amazon video on demand service in HD.  IMO much better than pay-per-view.-Netflix streaming HD video- although doesn't currently support  search and is limited to your "watch Instantly" queue.-Youtube, eHow.com, epicurious.com, and several other built in widgets to access online content and rss feeds.I have always been a Sony devotee, so I am a bit biased and stuck with this model (2 exchanges to get a defect free screen) when most buyers would have changed brands.I must admit that I was rather particular in my expectations for the video quality.  Most people would not even notice what I called defects in this model - I am a photographer and graphic designer so I have a trained eye for visual appearance and very picky about how a display performs.  The actual problem that I encountered has been documented in several Sony and Samsung models but is common to all LCD screens as far as I can tell.I spent a lot of time and energy unpacking, mounting, configuring, tweaking, contacting Sony support and ultimately repackaging 2 units for return/exchange.  I guess the adage, third times' a charm applied in my case.

Pros: Size(!), HD Video recording, Retina Display, Good battery life, and too much to list here..Cons: The rear camera is not the same as the one on the iPhone 4.There is really no need for yet another review so i am only going to compare it to the iPhone 4 here. I have had the iPhone 4 for a long time now, so when i held this iPod in my hand the very first i thought was - wow! this is THIN! The size and weight is almost unreal considering what this thing can do -- which is basically everything the iPhone can do (almost) and that's too much to write about.So, here's the short list of what it cannot do.- The camera is not the same, the pictures are lower resolution, there is no led flash, but the video is still 720p. For that reason, when you email several pictures at once, the iPod will not ask you to resize.- When taking pictures it will not focus or adjust light based on where you touch on the screen.- It has no GPS but it can still find your location info from the WiFi with pinpointed accuracy. It actually can even do that while traveling (my best bet is that it finds adjacent WiFi sources and although they may be locked, it can still tell where they are located. as such you get an approximate location based on the signal it receives, not where the ipod is - but that still works well). Another good point is that when tethered with the iPhone, the iPod DOES know where it is! So if you have both iPhone and iPod tethered in a car, you can use Google maps (and internet obviously) on both.- I didn't notice a big difference in battery life, but my guess is that it has a smaller battery than the iPhone 4 but they end up lasting the same amount of time since the iPod doesn't waste any on GPS, 3G, etc.- Using the front camera on apps like Skype we noticed no difference in quality and face time over WiFi works better than anything else i have tried (skype, qik, justintv, ustream, etc.) in terms of speed and quality.So, to sum it up, the basic differences are that it doesn't have GPS, no 3G obviously, and the low resolution rear camera. But the gain in size and cost are significant!If you already have an iPhone - Recommended: NoIf you don't have an iPhone and you don't want to get one - Recommended: HELL YES!(side note: i am not an appleseed or a fandroid, i like and use them both. the only reason i didn't make any comments or comparisons with the droids is that this an iPod review so people should keep it this way)

review_title: Excellent but Very Complex Micro 4/3 Camera and Lens, A Good Value Now
review_text: I wanted to give the OMD-EM5 a five star rating because of its quality construction, high image quality and the significant number of custom adjustments that pros will love. I have deducted 1 stars because I like the camera but don't love it for many reasons.  Why did I buy this camera? I am not a PRO but I do appreciate the feature set found on better cameras. This model has so many features and settings that it is a huge mountain to climb for the nonprofessional photographer. The more I use it the more I appreciate the great functionality. The camera has come down in price with the introduction of the M1 and M10 and it now is a great value for what it offers. I bought the Panasonic 14-140 M4/3 Lens which works perfectly and a great match with the M5.What's great about this camera?1. Very good image quality with the 12-50 mm kit lens. Perfect range 24-100 eq 35mm eq also weather proofed.2. Quality construction that is weather resistant and dust resistant3. Almost unlimited set of adjustments and custom settings4. Good quality EVF with display of lots of information. Works great indoors and outdoors.5. Custom image 5 axis stabilization with 3 settings work with any lens6. Two custom adjustment wheels on top. Terrific feature and works very well.7. Function buttons capable of many different settings8. Easy to hold and light weight compared to similar dSLR, some feel it needs added grip. It works for me as is.9. Very good image quality at higher ISO settings and lower noise that you might expect10. Easy to access reset control to reset to factory settings. Most used feature in the beginning11. Touch screen quick setting panel on OLED. This work superbly.12. Very Easy setting the focus point with the arrow keypad13. Ia setting works well and unlike other cameras has wide range of adjustments. More than some cameras with the P setting.14. Remote flash control possible with separate flash unit.15  Many other great features that you need to see to believe.What's not so great with the OMD EM51. Extremely complex camera to learn to use with a long and steep learning curve at least for me..2. ISO starts at 200 and will not calibrate with actual ISO, will not match real ISO. New V2 update starts at 1003. Higher start ISO at 200 makes some bright outdoor images require a ND filter4. Video missing avchd and limited video choices.  It's just  OK but does work well.5. Button feeling and placement not great. Small buttons have squishy feel. They work OK6. Battery life is limited and a typical day shoot requires a second battery. 300 plus images.7. No internal flash built-in, need to use small accessory flash supplied with camera. Inconvenient....M10 includes flash8. OLED is only slightly adjustable and difficult to see in daylight. Need to use the EVF outside.9. Limited OLED use when trying to view images taken through the EVF. Image appears in EVF Awkward setting.10. OLED cannot be turned around and covered.11. The complexity and wide range of information showed can interfere with viewing the image captured12. Some settings and adjustments seem counter intuitive13. Some settings which should come standard are buried deep in the menus.So who would most enjoy owning and using this camera?Answer:1 Former owners of Olympus film cameras or digital cameras.2 Professionals who love the ability to make custom settings and ultimately lots of setting adjustments.3 Photographers who mostly want images and a few videos. Pros who are tired of carrying their very heavy pro dSLR gear for  light shoots or travel.4 Anyone who has a large collection of older prime lens and wants to use them again. The image stabilization works will all lenses but require manual focus and manual aperture setting.  They do work with proper adaptors.Who should avoid buying this camera.1. Non-experts and anyone who mostly uses P or ia settings on their current camera.  The sheer complexity of this camera may interfere with your joy of Photography.2. Anyone who doesn't need weatherproofing.....new M10 is a better choice for you.I've owned many cameras and have taken thousands of images for many years and it wasn't until I bought this camera that I discovered just how little I knew about the complex issues involving the capture of truly great images.  This camera allows a huge range of adjustments that are not available in the typical consumer rebel like camera.  That is why this camera would appeal to the pro and advanced amateur. This camera is a world class camera for a pro and advanced amateur but a mistake for most of us who want an easy to use but customizable camera.  I do like the camera and I am warming up to it each time I use it but it will take a long time before I love it.

review_title: Best BT stereo headset!  Beats competitions hands down!
review_text: I've owned several high-end bluetooth stereo headsets and these Altec Lansing simply put are far and away the best of the lot.Pros: 1) Sound  2) Battery Life  3) Fit  4) Controls;1) Sound, sound, sound!  I've had other headphones with better specs on paper (higher db rating which usually translates to better and/or louder sound) but the Altec Lansing are loud!  Loud enough that I NEVER have them at full volume.  I used to turn my Jaybirds up all the way and still find them not loud enough on about half of my mp3 library.  The Altec Lansing have a lower db rating but in the real world the volume is unbelievable.  Volume without quality is basically worthless.  Not only are these headphones loud, they are also crystal clear.  The bass boost enhances some music but not all.  Overall the sound quality is in keeping with the Altec Lansing name.  That is to say outstanding.2) Battery life.  My Jaybird headset would last 4-5 hours no matter how I used it.  That was one reason after getting and liking the Jaybirds I kept looking for a better headset.  These Altec Lansing are rated at 7 hours continuous for music and/or talk, HOWEVER, (and this is a big however) they get repeatedly 10-13 hours depending on how I use them!  No matter how I've used my former stereo bluetooth headsets (including Jaybird, JVC and Blue Ant) I could never got more than 5 hours use out of any of them.  The Altec Lansing have NEVER gone for less than about 8 hours continuous and usually are good for 10-12 hours!  Simply amazing!  I attribute this to volume levels.  It must be 7 hours continuous at max volume, with lower volumes rendering longer battery life.  Again, these headphones are so loud that I never max out the volume and in many situations I'm somewhere in the lower to mid volume range for extended use, thus, giving me amazing battery life.  I'm tempted to wear my Altec Lansing to work as my primary bluetooth because they work so well.3) Fit.  This is a tricky one.  My previous favorites were my Jaybird JB200s, but in addition to insufficient battery life, fit was an ongoing issue.  (In fairness to Jaybird, fit is very personal and I'm sure for some the Jaybirds fit well.  For me, I was constantly fussing with mine while they popped out often or I'd just leave them out after getting tired of messing around with them.)  The Altec Lansing at first feel like they're not in properly, however, that is apparently part of their "open air" design.  They rest nicely on your ears/head and don't come off even with a vigorous headshake.  The reason they don't feel like they're on is the earbud design is NOT an INNER EAR bud but and outer ear bud.  The bud sits outside the ear canal leaving you exposed not only to the music but to ambient environment sounds as well.  Once you get used to this design and fit concept its super comfortable and secure.  I forget I have them on all the time.  Not only does the music sound great at all levels, you can also engage in conversations with people around you while wearing them and listening to music.  It's actually quite amazing.  The music sounds so good it's almost as if the music is being piped in over some quality loud speakers in every room you enter while you're free to converse with anyone and everyone around you.  The only aspect of the fit that I found difficult was the beefy behind the neck band connecting the two earpieces.  It is so beefy and oversized that when it hit my collar or I laid down, it would knock the headphones out of my ear.  I remedied this by twisting the band into a phone cord type coil behind my neck.  Once the band held the memory of the phone cord-like coil the problem was solved.  Not only did this solve the neckband problem , but it actually made the headphones fit superbly while also making them less noticeable while wearing.  (The do-it-yourself phone cord coil fix may void the warranty so do this at your own risk.  Being the uber-geek that I am, I'm willing to risk breaking something if it holds any promise of making it better.)4) Controls.  The controls of the Altec Lansing are simply outstanding.  They work so well and have so many features at your fingertips that your head becomes a walking remote for bluetooth calls and stereo mp3 playback.  You can take calls, end calls, mute calls, ignore calls, adjust volume, fast-forward, rewind, pause, play, standby, bass boost and even battery life check your way into oblivion with this headset.  The controls are well laid out and perfectly balanced so as to flawlessly execute all of the functions with little to no effort.  Listen to music loud and never miss a call.  Listen to music at mid to low levels while carrying on a conversation with those around you and never miss a call.  And so on.Cons: 1) Fit;1) Fit.  (I know I just listed this a "pro."  So obviously it's both.)  Fit takes some getting used to.  The beefy behind the neck band is a little on the long side, and a little on the thick side.  This makes for a fit that mimics the Motorola S9 behind the neck band vs. the stealthy behind the neck "wire" of the Jaybird JB200.  If I wore a t-shirt at the gym the beefy neckband wasn't a problem.  If I had any shirt with a collar or wanted to lay down while using the Altec Lansing, the neckband got in the way.  Once I got the idea that a phone cord-like coil setup might take up some slack and get the neckband closer to my head and off of my collar the problem was solved.  I now have a custom Altec Lansing Backbeat 906 with coiled (DIY) behind the neck neckband that hugs my head vs. hitting my collar.  It took a while to coil the neckband in such a way as to create some memory in the coil, but it was well worth it.  It fits more snugly on my head, is less noticeable wearing and never ever gets in the way of a shirt collar or pillow.  (Be careful if you try the DIY memory coil as it clearly could cause a short in the wiring if not done right or done carefully.)  All things considered, this "con" is no longer a problem.Summary:  The Altec Lansing Backbeat 906 is an absolutely amazing mix of sound performance with "sound" design.  I've stopped scouring the internet for the perfetct stereo bluetooth headset.  This one is darn near perfect and the pros seriously outweigh the minor cons (especially compared to other bluetooth headsets).

I had to fool around with the program for a while in order to get into the backedup files, but eventually made it.PRO:  It does what it claims to do - and I now have a new terabyte of handy networked storage that two computers can tap into.CON:  Backing up the files and then accessing them is slow compared to doing the same on an external NFTS firewire hard drive.  The application backs up data but NOT applications.  I still have to use my Acronis TrueImage 9 to backup applications, and when I started an Acronis image on the SC101, the program told me it would take 3 hours, as against 90 minutes on my external hard drive.OOPS!  WHEN IS A TERABYTE NOT A TERABYTE ... I just found out, much to my dismay, that the drives in the SC101 do not allow compression.  What this means is that a 324.7GB music file on my 400GB Seagate is 500GB on the SC101's 500GB Hitachi.  And it is going to take a very long time to move that 1TB on the SC101 back into my Seagates.  The Hitachis are going to have to go into external hard drive cases, otherwise I've lost 100GBs on each drive.  That's ridiculous!

review_text: My big issue with this AM/FM radio is tuning in radio stations, and signal reception. The tuning on mine is very coarse making fine adjustments difficult when trying to improve AM signal reception. Attempting to tune in and listen to weak distant AM & FM radio stations is difficult on the AM band and basically impossible for FM because the radio appears to filter/squelch out weak signals. For comparison on AM reception I placed my new Sony radio side-by-side next to an old General Electric AM only solid state radio and slowly advanced the tuning on both...and it was amazing how many more weak but good radio station broadcasts I could pull in using the older radio. Using a tunable AM loop antenna with the Sony improved both the reception and fine tuning issues for the AM band, but I can't see myself frequently carrying a loop antenna around wherever I might want to take a portable radio, and this provides no help with improving signal strength on the FM band. In conclusion, the Sony is a decent radio for listening to strong local radio signals, but I'd buy a better radio than this model if I lived far from the radio stations I wanted to listen to.

It just boost your cell phone signal in limited area in radius at least 30 feet from antennas.Here what I did. I had no idea where is the cell phone transceiver tower so I found most powerful spot with maximum signal bars with my cell phone near window, mounted cradle antenna with logo sign facing window, mounted cable from this antenna across the room to amplifier, connected "on board" antenna (cable about 4feet with desktop antenna) to the amplifier and moved away from amplifier as far as possible facing logo on this antenna in opposite side to first one (back to back). I got green light immediately and 6-7 bars instead 2-3.It works great if you are between antennas in direct sight. When I go to another room I have 3-4 bars and only one wall between cell phone and antennas.So did it solve my problem - yes for 90% but still there was not stable sound when I talked on the phone but much clear though. Did it boost in 15 times - no.It can help but not for 100%. So IMO the price should be adequate OR 100% result.PS It worked with AT@T, cell Nokia 5800

review_title: Great little router with great security
review_text: Originally I rated this REFURBISHED NetGear router 3 STARS (Original title: Probably good if you are router savvy).  When I purchased this refurbished router I erroneously thought that I'd get the whole package including installation disc.  The reason that I wanted this router is because I spoke with NetGear prior to buying and they suggested this particular router because I knew nothing about setting up a wireless router.  That was the single reason that I bought this particular model.  Ease of set up.  When I received the unit I discovered that the refurbished unit did not include an installation disc (and the serial number was eradicated, which is probably legally necessary). A note enclosed with the router indicated that the necessary downloads, etc were available from NetGear.  No they aren't.  I called NetGear tech support and discovered that to receive tech support for a refurbished piece of equipment I needed to buy the 6 month service for over $70.  You can install the router manually but the whole point for me was to have an installation disc that did the technical work for me.  So when you figure the cost of the refurbished router plus the tech support subscription you are better off just buying new.  (Originally 3 STARS because the description wasn't accurate.)UPDATE:  5 STARS.  Reviewing the router alone and not having previous experience with other routers I'd have to say that this is a great little machine.  First whether new or refurbished there is no installation disc.  The information provided with the REFURBISHED router was incomplete, misleading and in error.  I had a tech savvy friend drop by to beef up the security so that my router isn't visible to be compromised.  We changed the password which NetGear doesn't recommend (RECORD your PW, etc or you'll have to reset the router to default factory settings and start all over again.  He also set up the router so that it only recognizes my wireless equipment by entering the MAC number (recorded on the exterior of each potentially wireless peripheral).NetGear's NetGear Genie is really all you need to do this kind of security back-up and their 'help' is a big help also.  You may have to GOOGLE a few terms but all in all I, as well as my PC savvy buddy, think that the security set-up for this NetGear router is pretty solid.

The 615N cards have gotten a bad rap as being unreliable, although mine worked for about 2 years and finally died. The 620 is the upgraded model apparently to address the problems of the 615 and to provide for more seamless firmware upgrades for HP's more contemporary printers. The 620's are reputed to be well less prone to failure; however, I cannot comment on that personally since I just bought this module. Although the 4200 printer is a discontinued model, it was and still is a major workhorse in the industry and there are still millions of them out in active, reliable service and periodically needing network card replacements. The 615 module matches the 4200's beige color, while the 620 matches the gray color of HP's current line, but you never see it anyway at the rear of the printer, so who cares.Suffice it to say, it integrates seamlessly with the 4200, as I'm sure it would with any HP network-ready printer that doesn't have the network circuitry on board. I just configured the card in the on-board printer utility(I set my TCP/IP configuration to MANUAL which works best on my network setup), and I was up and printing within one minute from opening the package(and I'm NOT exaggerating!!!!). You don't have to reinstall the printer driver, unless somehow it was corrupted previously. The 620 is not faster than the 615, and I don't think you'll notice any difference regarding performance. There are no claims as such as far as I could find in the literature available, so there really is no reason to upgrade as long as your 615 is working properly.As I am a relatively light user, from other people's experience with the 620 card, I suspect this is the last Jet Direct replacement I'll ever need!I would also like to comment very favorably on Quick Buy 1, the merchant from whom I purchased this item. Amazingly, the order was shipped within 3 hours of my submission(notified thereof by Amazon), and although I didn't order expedited shipping, it arrived 4 days before the estimated time, I believe two days after the shipping notice. I also emailed them a couple of times about the product, and their responses were timely and informative. NO, I don't work for the company!!!The unit was exactly as advertised, brand new, sealed package, and a genuine HP product with their logo on it, and for about 25% of what you'd pay buying it from HP directly, which you can do. Whether it comes directly from HP, or from a bulk distributor, I'm sure they're all made by the same company, so it's not like a knockoff copy.Bottom line: first rate product and first rate merchant.

review_title: Superb TV for the price: Samsung UN EH5000
review_text: Well I always have been a LG fan - a 55 LW5600 doing the works in the living room (got a fantastic 1 K deal from Frys in California), but this Samsung UN EH5000 was a value star of sorts. Picked this up to do the duty in the bed room and had very little expectations from it. For a couple of hours of movie viewing at weekend or checking the news at night, wanted to spend as less as possible. Well Amazon to the rescue. After carefully lining up all the LG possible starters and a Toshiba TV found this gen for about $342 - that's correct for a 40 incher.Out of the box the TV had colors that need a lot of toning down. My LG had isf calibration and a THX mode I had unlocked which gave brilliant output but the only complain was a clouding with a black picture (that has detoriated a bit over the last 2 years - thanks to the IPS panels that LG used). The Samsung has no complaints till date - a S-PVA panel and after checking foe the UD04 version and system menu "40A6AF1D", which meant the higher end panel from Samsung.The right settings and pairing it with the Yamaha (YS101BL) the setup was amazing and just right for a bedroom.The sound from the TV is also decently acceptable but a soundbar does wonders.Biggest compliant was with Amazon shipping and packaging by both Amazon and Samsung. 4 blocks of styrofoam holds the TV in place in a thin cardboard package which was crushed and after taking delivery realizing it being sogging wet. Mid-west's amazing run of bad weather delayed prime shipment by a day and UPS ensured that even with a thin layer of plastic around the TV (courtesy Amazon I believe), the outer box was damaged. Had a word with Amazon CC (who are usually amazingly great) and cited my case. Though the TV is working for the last 3 days (put around 6 hrs) , I was concerned and insisted either sending it in for a replacement or getting a price match with Best Buy (Schaumburg) which had the same TV in store for a discounted 299 USD (only 1 item non open box). Amazon CC decided to give me 25 USD credit for my problems but all i got was a 5 USD promotion credit for my troubles. Come on Amazon you can do better than this.Will update on performance on the TV within a week or so. Did I say for the money this TV was brilliant.

this is a comparison of two products; one from HandHelditems, the other from am Case.Be sure to read the update at the bottom of this review. It definitely favors the HandHelditems protector.Both protectors were accurately cut.I had originally tried the HandHelditems protector and left negative seller feedback: no instructions included, and it left bubbles over lint.Their Customer Service contacted me soon afterward and offered me a free replacement. Meantime I had ordered a different protector for my Asus Eee Pad from amCase. It got delivered but I held on to it to await the handHelditems replacement.here is the result: the amCase protector now resides on my Eee Pad.I first tried the [instructions included] handHelditems replacement. This second one ended up with the same problems: lint, and bubbles. Within 5 minutes of discarding that one I successfully installed the amCase protector. Same environment---kitchen table. (And I have also successfully installed a protector on Wife's iPad.)The amCase has no bubbles whatsoever....it took about 10 minutes of work to get them out, but the lint was not there. The bubbles on the HandHelditems protector were not to be worked out. I believe the problem is with HandHelditems's lint remover cloth. First, it is way too small---about 1/5 the size of the amCase lint remover material. But the fundamental problem with the HandHelditems cloth is that it actually CREATES lint. I could shake it and watch lint come off. Perhaps it is due to the jagged scissors edge on it, probably made with a scissors? I could actually watch lint get attracted (static?) onto the screen within seconds of wiping with the cloth.The amCase "cloth" is more like a parchment material; straight edge, and it seems to create less static attraction.The performance comparison is this: the HandHelditems protector did have some glare reduction, the amCase one does not. My assessment of fingerprints is that they are about equal.11/9/2011 update:HandHelditems sent me a third protector sheet. I have applied it and it still has bubbles. To its credit it is definitely more of a matte finish and reduces glare so I have left it on in spite of 10 or so stubborn bubbles which do not seem to be associated with lint, but just air underneath. Wish List: wish someone would come up with a matte finish but which reduces bubbles by itself overnight. I cannot recall the brand name...we got it at Best Buy for wife's iPad.11/14/2011 update. As of yesterday all 10 or so of the bubbles had disappeared from the HandHelditems protector. Go figure.

I've finally found my bathroom speakers. ;)This is a neat little unit... it pairs very simply with your Bluetooth-enabled device and is small enough to take from room to room, like we all used to do with our boom boxes in the 80s (though this is smaller than a typical "boom box"-- it's slightly longer than my hand, and a little narrower). I love listening to Pandora, and this gives me the ability to do that in any room of my house without even using up an outlet. The next time you turn on the unit, it automatically tries to pair with the last device you paired it with, so you don't have to fiddle with the settings each time.The sound quality is not exceptional, but it's good, particularly for small speakers like this. I'm picky about bass levels, and this passes my inspection. The levels are not adjustable, though, so you'll have to be happy with the default.Voice commands work fine as long as you're speaking clearly into the unit. I liked being able to check the battery level just by saying, "Check battery level." (It was "high" even after listening to music for 3 hours.)You can use this both as a speaker for music/video, and as a speakerphone for your cell phone (for calls and for listening to voicemail).The packaging is sleek and upscale, and I disagree with the reviewer who mentioned the packaging as excessive-- I assume the reviewer was actually referring to the box Amazon sent it in, as opposed to the product packaging itself, which is not at all excessive. The company doesn't control Amazon's shipping choices. The product's box has a magnetic closure and looks nice for gifting.There are only three buttons on the device-- volume up, volume down, and a button for pairing. So even the techno-phobic can use this with ease.It doesn't show fingerprints, and has a rubberized bottom so it won't scratch your furniture.The grilles (or grills, if you're doing a search) run about $20 apiece here, which seems too expensive just to change the color of the front piece of the speakers. I'll stick to black, thanks!Neat toy for those who are into music and gadgets.

In the early 2000s I had a Motorola cable modem, and the best thing I could say about it was that it worked, which is certainly a very good thing but is probably a feature of most competing modems as well. My Motorola modem had really lousy human-factor design, however. There were two issues: it had a very prominent on/off button that made it almost impossible to touch the thing without turning it off. But most annoying was the fact that I always had to power the modem up and wait until it was fully initialized before turning on my router. If the router came on at any time before the modem was done initializing, the modem simply wouldn't talk to it. This ensured, among other things, that if we had a power failure the internet service in our house was guaranteed to fail to come up automatically after power was restored. Always there would have to be human intervention by someone who understood exactly what to do. I had to leave written instructions for my wife because otherwise she'd be helpless after a power failure in my absence.Well guess what? It's 10 years later and little has changed. This modem absolutely will not talk to my router (a Linksys WRT54G) unless the modem is fully initialized before the router is turned on. Sheesh. The easy-to-hit power button is gone from this design, thank goodness, but in its place is a blazing orange LED on the front panel. This is not a warning light that flashes, no, it's a constantly blinking LUNACY that is always flashing whenever you connect this modem to anything that's running at less than gigabit capacity. I could not stand the distraction of this thing and so devised a duct-tape-and-cardboard cover for this lamp but even that doesn't totally squelch the light. If I had this unit in my bedroom at night I'd simply have to throw the thing out.It is kind of sad that in the decade since I had my first cable modem the human factors design has, if anything, gotten worse. My suggestion for the management at Arris, the company that has bought the Motorola division that makes this thing: find the folks who are now on your staff who think it's OK to make a modem that can't possibly power up a home network without human intervention, and who believe that home consumer products should feature flashing orange LEDs during the normal course of operation, and FIRE THEM.

review_text: After reading Douglas Moran's incredible review with thermal measurements that he made from every known geometric angle on planet earth, it's hard to add much to that!But in a nutshell, the price of this unit is so good, it's almost cheaper to buy this compared to a bare drive! The design of this particular unit (2TB model) may not best-in-class for cooling but it isn't even close to the hottest external drive I've used in the past and I've owned more than a dozen. Douglas' measurements showed that it gets pretty warm but not in the freak-out zone and that's exactly what I found. For oustanding cooling you have to spend a lot more on units like the LaCie Quadra series (and some of THOSE models even run hot). With this you get a good basic fast drive with a ton of room. USB 3.0 runs fast, as you know; the actual Seagate drive inside has a decent reputation for reliability but there's no real way to review that unless I remember to return back to this in a year. The case is plastic, no surprise there, I just wish it had an easy way to open the case in the event I want to change drives due to failure, reconfig, etc.So right now I'm using this 2TB Seagate as my main backup drive for my 2TB internal RAID set that holds all of my video assets. Based on the build and the Seagate reputation I'm confident it'll hold up. If it doesn't, it gets chucked, but its features add up to what seems like a decent drive: not TOO hot, not too noisy, good company rep, fast USB 3.0, and a separate power supply (drives with wall warts seem to last longer that drives that suck power from USB).Best feature: the Price!Worst feature: cheesy case you can't easily open

review_title: Great sound, easy setup but some HDMI incompatibility
review_text: After research and mind changing I bought the AVR-2313CI. I selected it because it had more inputs than competing models and was discounted due to the release of its 2013 replacement, the AVR-3000. The 2313 and 3000 are nearly identical, so I saved a few benjamins with last year's model.The 2313 is compact and unassuming in appearance. From my couch the plastic faceplate is indistinguishable from the brushed aluminum of other components. The 2313 ain't eye candy, but blends in with the other gear. The two big control knobs harken back to receivers of yesteryear, but sans the silky knob action of a vintage Denon. There's a cluster of buttons on the front, a small subset of what's available on the remote.HOOKUP: The back panel has a handful of analog and digital inputs, a long row of HDMI ports and 7.2 speaker outputs. No preamp out (save for Zone-2 stereo out) or optical/coaxial out. Not the best choice if you have lots of legacy gear, but enough for Joe Average. If more analog ports are needed, similarly priced Marantz receivers are more endowed.My hookup was a bit complicated: Cisco cable box, Sharp Aquos TV (LC-C3742U), Sony BDP-S5100 Blu-Ray, Denon DN-600F CD, Marantz PMD 670 digital audio recorder, Teac audio cassette, Technics turntable, X-LPS Musical Fidelity phono preamp and 5.1 speaker system (5 JBL Control & Sunfire sub). The clearly labelled ports and terminals made hookup a breeze. Thirty minutes later I was ready to rock.I love the assignable inputs, labels and audio levels via the GUI. The only omission was the lack of optical/coaxial output for digital audio or CD recorders. Other than HDMI out, the 2313 only sports optical and coaxial in, not helpful if you want to record digital sources or use the DAC for converting tapes and LPs. So I used the "media player" analog in/out for the Marantz. There is no RIAA phono input so turntables require a phono preamp. I jacked my X-LPS Musical Fidelity phono preamp into the DVD analog inputs, relabeled it phono on the GUI, raised input 10db and it worked okay through the 2313.CONVERSION GOTCHA: Page 6 of the manual states, "this unit can not convert HDMI input signals to analog video signals." But it can convert analog video to digital output. So, if you have a mix of HDMI devices and component video devices, you may have kinks to work out. For example, a HDMI input signal from a cable box can only pass through the 2313 HDMI output. It cannot be converted to component video output (analog for old TVs). If you need conversion, consider theDenon AVR-1913instead. I suspect the lack of conversion is a cost cutting major. These "features" are explained in the PDF manual (Denon's website).SOUND QUALITY: I listen to jazz, rock and classical music and found the 2313 powerful, natural and detailed in stereo mode with digital sources. The clarity and position of instruments in the stereo field was vivid, making me feel like Steely Dan was in my living room. Not as warm as my old Harman Kardon AVR 85, but more revealing and edgy, but in a pleasant way. Analog sound sources are okay but not as rich as my old HK receiver. Denon cut corners on the analog input section since most people mainly use digital media.The 2313 spanked my old HK during playback of movie soundtracks. The processing of digital audio is amazing and has come a long way in 17 years! The ambient sounds of the rear speakers really woke up compared to my HK, albeit digital movie tracks sound more compressed. Voices through the center speaker were clear and balanced with the other speakers. I used the Audyssey setup mic to tweak speaker balance and it did a good job, although I touched them up manually. My Sunfire sub sounded best with the front speakers set to small with bass crossover at 80Hz.VIDEO QUALITY: I connected my Cisco cable box to the CBL/SAT HDMI input on the 2313 and ran the HDMI monitor output to a Sharp Aquos TV (circa, 2008). Denon HD video processing is excellent and image quality is noticeably better than plugging the TV directly into cable box HDMI. And the Denon user output tweaks are great for cleaning up noisy cable movies or DVDs. I was pleased with the clarity of Denon HDMI video performance when it worked.HDMI GOTCHA: For HDMI video to work: turn on video source first, TV second and the 2313 last (with source already selected). Any other way resulted in HDMI handshake problems detailed below. As long as I stuck to a single uninterrupted source, video from the 2313 was flawless. Any interruption--e.g., switching sources or turning off a component, cable burp--results in the TV flashing, stuck in a loop looking for the correct resolution. Obviously, there is a HDMI handshake problem between the 2313 and Sharp Aquos. The TV works perfect with HDMI directly from the cable box or Blu-Ray, but video is unreliable when passed through the 2313.After weeks of struggling I relented and hooked the cable box directly to the TV with component cables but kept the HDMI cables plugged into the 2313. It worked perfect! Unlike the 2313, the Cisco cable box outputs component video and HDMI simultaneously. So I can listen to digital surround sound from HDMI output and enjoy uninterrupted video through the TV. You're supposed to use optical/coaxial out on the cable box with component cables but, when I tried it, it played in stereo mode (no DTS, Dolby Pro, etc). So keeping the HDMI cable connected is the way to go for surround sound. Plus, when I have to use HDMI, e.g., for Blu-Ray, I merely have to flip inputs on the TV (and reboot everything...)REMOTE CONTROL: IR OR iOS?: The supplied IR remote works well for controlling the 2313 but lacks universal capabilities. So budget for a universal remote unless you don't mind wrangling a half dozen remotes. To use Denon's iOS app, I connected the 2313 to Apple Airport via ethernet. The connection was plug n' play and I was immediately informed of a firmware update. The Denon Remote app can trigger iTunes tracks via AirPlay and select sources. It often loses contact and contains a small subset of 2313 functions. If you want an iOS controller, the $4.99 DeRemote app is faster, has more GUI features and is reliable. Also, the TV doesn't need to be on to navigate options.LAST BLURB: I really like this receiver but it has a few zits: HDMI incompatibilities, mediocre analog inputs and no digital to analog conversion. But the good almost cancels out the bad: outstanding digital audio quality, small but powerful, a great GUI, endless user tweaks and enough inputs for most mortals. If some magical dance, chant or cable fixes the HDMI incompatibility, I'll come back and whip it another star. 02/11/2014 Update: No problems and still going strong 1 year out!

review_title: A great player. That being said, let me point out a few issues.
review_text: Let me start by saying I think this is one of the best blu-ray players on the market.  If not the best.  However, there are a few things that Sony *STILL* can't get right after several years.  This is my third Sony branded BDP-series player in five years.The long and short of it is the player does its basic functions - playback, internet connectivity, interactivity - all extremely well.However, Sony still continues to have weird proprietary issues, as they've had throughout all their history, which keeps this player from being basically perfect.To start:1. Controls are inconsistent throughout the internet apps.  Some (like Netflix) let you exit through the "return" button. Hulu requires you to hit the HOME button.  On-screen keyboards are different throughout every single app.  I know the individual service providers are often to blame for this, but Sony could have done a little about it. Other devices do. Having different onscreen keyboards is really frustrating.2. STILL, in 2014, onscreen keyboards are sluggish and difficult to use.3. Speaking of keyboards, one of the nice features of this player is that it supports a USB keyboard.  But good luck finding one it supports. The specs say it supports "101 keyboard" - that's all.. Which isn't even a thing.  I imagine they mean a 101 *key* keyboard, which is pretty much impossible to find anymore.  Several USB keyboards I tried didn't work.  The popular Logitech Unifying wireless keyboards, which work with everything else from my Stanton SCS-4DJ DJ console to my cable box, do not work with this player.  As a software engineeer, I can tell you this is just pure laziness. There is no reason they couldn't have simply written in support for the entire standard USB HID keyboard class, vs narrowing it down to a much tighter keyboard spec.  Much simpler and cheaper devices handle this just fine. Keyboards aren't exactly complex; they've been around a little while.  This could easily be fixed with a firmware update - lets hope Sony takes care of it.4. The Hulu app is strangely sluggish compared to others5. Despite a dedicated button for "SEN" (Sony Entertainment Network) on the remote, I repeatedly have tried but have not been able to get it to work. I simply get an "An Error Occured" screen. It works fine on my two PS3s and other Sony BDP. Makes no sense. I'll keep trying (EDIT: It eventually started working after about 3 hours. Mysterious.)6. Again, maybe I'm asking too much (since I own other players like an OPPO) - but WHY can't Sony integrate some simple support for formats that they (god forbid) don't own? Nobody ever wins in these stupid standards fights.  Why no FLAC disc support? Why SACD, but no HDCD or DVD-A? Of course I know the answers to these questions - especially when dealing with Sony - it's pure Not Invented Here Syndrome.  Sony has gotten better about that (fie, Memory Stick!) - but they still play this game for some reason.7. The pyramid shape, while cute, is really impractical.8. Lots of the included "100+ apps" (they are using some creative math here) and channels are really crufty and kitschy.  YuppTV? The Wiggles? Billabong? Red Bull TV? "CelebTV"? I have no idea what Opera is doing with the "Opera TV Store" which is completely analogous to the Sony Entertainment Network, just with fewer choices plus some games.  Trying to remain relevant, I guess, with yet another App/Movie/Game store. Yawn. How many of these icons will do nothing in 6-12 months? Most if not all.  It's starting to look like the old days of preloaded PC crapware. I'm all for choice, but some of this stuff is just garbage.9. FacebookTV. Automatically broadcasts to the world the title of what you're watching.  I'm not sure what kind of person this is for. I find it weird. Really weird. I can see no purpose for it existing other than for Facebook to grab metadata for targeted advertising. This trend disturbs me.  Before you know it, Coke cans will be wired and will broadcast to Facebook "Steve just enjoyed a Refreshing Coca-Cola (TM)!" Gah.10. Only 100mbit wired Ethernet and 2.4GHz only, not 5GHz. Booo.And the biggest pain in the ass (and hey Amazon, here's looking at you): Sony STILL makes you sign up for their stupid Bravia service portal to use certain providers, namely Amazon Instant Video.  Confusingly, the Amazon app provides a 5-character code that you'd think would register you on Amazon's site - specifically because they list Sony BRAVIA directly on that page AND also ask for a 5-character code! But no, the code is for another website, BRAVIA branded, (internet.sony.tv/customer - now strangely called "My Essentials", but still branded as "My Bravia" once you sign in) which entails even more convoluted registration hoops.  Stupid, stupid, stupid.  Why are some Sony devices, called Bravia, registered directly through Amazon - while others, NOT called Bravia but when using Amazon, are registered through "My Bravia"? Mind boggling. Marketers: You are a scourge.This is the game you have to play to use Pandora, Amazon and Vudu.A further note: This is also COMPLETELY separate from the Sony Entertainment Network (also known as the Playstation Network) with which you also have to register your device. Why all these disparate services, Sony!??All being said, I admit I'm probably being picky.  At $100, this device does more than anyone would have dreamed even three years ago - and does it very, very well.  It really is one of the best players out there.  That being said, it's 2014, and there's really no excuse for a lot of the annoyances that come with consumer electronics these days, especially from a major brand like Sony. Sony needs to get their marketing department out of their product design and go back to good engineering.So, on the positive side, real quick - I'm just saying what others have said:1. Fast and responsive.2. Picture quality is near perfect3. Audio quality is near perfect4. Discs load fast5. Wi-fi is fast, and streaming is high quality and smooth6. Support for DLNA. Even recognized my Logitech media server (Squeezebox). Nice.7. Two USB ports and mass storage support8. I am liking the move to smaller form factor (despite the weird top panel)9. Dedicated Netflix button is cool.  I'm sure was the result of millions of dollars paid to guys in suits to negotiate what anyone else would consider a five minute decision, but cool nonetheless.10. Plays FLAC (Over USB) and MKV.  Something Sony wouldn't have dreamed of supporting a few years back. Good on them.11. Gracenote support is excellent. Sony acts like this is new / unique to them (it's not) - but it's great.12. Their "Super Wi-Fi" implementation does truly seem to work better.13. Upscaled DVDs look great on it.14. Netflix supports SuperHD on this. Looks great.  Better than my AppleTV and Roku.The jury is still out on:1. 2D to 3D conversion. Not sure why you'd use this. Then again I think 3DTV in general is one of the biggest gimmicks dropped on the buying public since Microsoft Bob, so if you're a 3D fan, ignore what I'm saying.2. 'TV SideView'. Sounds like another proprietary mobile device "enhancement" slash remote app. Perhaps it will alleviate my keyboard complaints. I'll give it a go and report back. We'll see.All in all a great player.  If you're in doubt, this IS the one to get.  But it isn't the walk-on-water device some web reviews are making it out to be.  Well worth the price even at $200. Just a few annoyances.

Both were high quality product, but they were all damaged through the shipping. The seller did not know he had to separate the aluminum plate. The plate rolled and damaged entire content from inside. There are few sellers knowledgeable enough about how to pack a turntable.Finally, I decided to purchase a new one and I was torn between Denon DP-300F, Musichall MMF2.1, Technics MK1200, and Thorens TD-170. All looked good to me. I was almost seduced by the red MMF2.1, but I wanted an automatic - at least auto return. They operate without clicks or hard push. So starting and stopping goes soundless. Even mechanism of starting and stopping that is operated by the kinetic energy of the plate is very much soundless and smooth. It proves a solid design of mechanism from Denon's long experience in designing middle range hi-fi products.2) The tone arm elevator lever is placed in a right place. And the operation is perfect. Only the down movement is well dampened. So the up move is quick and responsive, and down is very smooth.3) The enclosed cartridge is pretty good. It's not as delicate as Shure M97xe, but it delivers a sound that doesn't sound very cheap. It's definitely better than the low-end ortofon cartridge that come with a Thorens.4) The glossy finish is quite satisfying to look at.5) Built-in phono EQ amp is a plus just in case I abandon my Aura VA 100 II and go with an amp that doesn't have phono in.There are things I wished be better:1) Tone arm rest does not have a grip to click and hold. So, I'd need a rubber band when I move the turntable.2) The plate is quite light. Considering belt drive turntables don't need a heavy plate to maintain consistent speed, it's not that big minus.3) There is no ground line. An obsessive high-end user could claim he heard some hum. For me, it means convenience in installation. Probably, it assumed most of the users use built-in phono amp. In that case we don't need any of ground line as we don't need one for a cd player.4) Tone arm is straignt, meaning that I can't use a very traditional head shell. This is not a minus compared to a new MMF or Thorens.5) Buttons are round and give some cheap feel. I'd like more of traditional quality feel buttons.Overall, this turntable features full automatic functions that run smoothly and precisely without sacrificing much to the build quality and the performance at a low end price. If you are a vinyl lover, just go with this.

He has a protector, flashlight-style hands that can help him fight without ever touching you and cool tricks like stopping cars just by aiming at them. I used to love Halloween style stuff but either I'm getting too old for it or getting to be a punk. It looks fun from the television but kinda freaked me out when they were going through--way too much open space. What I liked about the film were all the small parts that made the film interesting to watch (ex. the main male lead coming into his own with his powers--I like that he didn't know how to use them initially; the fight scene with that horrific thing in the truck; the alien species who were out to get the male lead clearly had a sense of humor; that haunted trail; the weird story about the UFO boy). I bought this N900 to replace my Buffalo WHP-300 (wireless N as well) that was unable to stream 1080p movies. Suffice to say I have the N900 streaming 2 1080p FLAC movies from 2 wireless devices in 2 different rooms and it laughs at the thought that I had doubted its capabilities.Anyway, although the N900 is fast, easy to setup, and generally beautiful, it has a few faults that aren't too difficult to overcome. It's huge, but not flashy like other recent Netgear routers. However, my router would constantly drop connections and malfunction (on both LAN AND Wifi connections!!!!) just like some previous Netgear offenders (such as early firmware WNDR3700, 4000 routers).At first I thought, haha fool my once Netgear, but I found a solution. I set the DNS to 8.8.8.8 which fetches DNS from Google instead of my ISP.Lo-and-behold, all those issues other people are getting on a myriad of online forums over dropped connections and slow internet with WNDR3700 and WNDR4500 (N900) routers was completely fixed.So I suggest to you that if your N900 doesn't work perfectly right away and drops connections, change the DNS.Besides the DNS issue I have nothing to complain about, if you want the fastest router you can buy for consumer use and squash your neighbors' puny signals underneath the mighty broadcasting juggernaut from your den, the N900 will fight on your side.

Connection appears perfect.My last advice is if you think you have all your settings correct, CHECK them again, restart your router, then restart your computer. Follow the directions line by line. You should be good. I've only had this an afternoon, so I'll update if anything else comes up. Be patient.UPDATE July 7: Just installed my second camera. It was a breeze. I now have two going on my phone, tablet, and tower computer. The software that comes with it works nicely. It does all I need it to do. Allows multiple cameras and viewing from the internet.Setup is really EASY. When setting up to view from the net you MUST do these things. Assign a port number in the setup page on the IP cameratool. You can assign almost anything. Try 8000, then make the next camera 8001, and so on. NOW, you have a camera with an ip address that is YOUR home IP address followed by :8000 or :8001. That now becomes the IP address of the camera. Go to Starbucks. Type your IP address in with the colon/port number (your ip:8000). There you go. You get the login screen. Log into the camera.If you want to use the software that comes with it, add the camera with that SAME number.I admit I was a bit stumped on the first one, but after playing with it for a week, then adding the scond camera, its a breeze for THOSE OF YOU THAT HAVE SOME CONCEPT OF NETWORKING!!!!!!  If you dont, either hire someone or dont buy this camera.
