review_title: I Dig It. I Dig It A Lot.
review_text: This is the fourth cover I've tried for my Kindle. During that neurotic buying and returning spree, I've discovered what I really want: a slim case that's comfortable to hold when the cover is folded all the way back, something that looks a bit different than a traditional cover, something well-built and sufficiently padded, and something that will allow the Kindle to stand on its own in both landscape and portrait views, while also allowing me to plug in a power cable.Well, you can't have everything - but this Built case is still my favorite. It hits almost all of the criteria I listed: It's slim enough to be comfy to hold while still having enough padding to set my mind at ease; it's a pleasure to hold with the cover flipped around (others have had things that I found uncomfortable to varying degrees); it definitely looks different, with a faux-snakeskin cover that's oddball enough for me without being too hipster; it appears to be well built and, as I said before, padded well. The interior is soft and I have no fear of scratches.Additional high points: the ease with which my Kindle can be put in and taken out of the four mesh strips on the corners that hold it in place. Also, as another reviewer mentioned, there's an indentation in the padding that allows the elastic strap to both stay put and sit flush when it's closed - an excellent touch. No ports or switches are blocked in any way, and I should mention it also has the somewhat ubiquitous magnets that wake and sleep the Kindle automatically.Where it fails to meet my criteria: its inability to stand up in portrait mode (very common issue of course, unless you get one of the rotating cases); the inability to plug it in when it's standing up. The Kindle goes in one way, and when you stand it up (which works very well thanks to the silicone bumpers around the perimeter) the ports are on the bottom. Of course, this also means you can charge it when it's in the case, so that's a tradeoff (yeah, I suppose there could be a hole cut in the spine, but I'm glad there isn't). I've actually solved both of these problems anyway, by buying an inexpensive stand which works great with the Kindle in the case (AmazonBasics Portable Fold-Up Travel Stand).So over all I'm really happy. I've had this remote for about 3 years now and so far I've been able to use it to replace the remote control for every new device I've purchased.  I NEVER try to use the preprogrammed codes, always using the learn function to acquire the programming from the original remote.  It's developed one odd problem over time - the commonly used buttons, such as the channel change buttons, become intermittent and you have to really press hard to get them to operate.  I took the control apart and discovered a fluid substance on the rubber keypad backing where the buttons contact the circuit board. I cleaned the rubber section and the circuit board with a Q tip and Windex and after that the buttons operated as they did when the control was new.  About a year after this problem, it happened again and when I disassembled the remote, I found the same fluid there again.  Another cleaning solved the problem.  I suspect the fluid source is the rubber membrane.  There's never been anything spilled on the remote, so it has to be coming from the inside.  At any rate, the remote continues to operate and since the internal contacts didn't show much sign of wear I suspect it will last another few years.  A good price performer and a great remote (if you are capable of performing the cleanup I described).

Similarly, the auto-focus is so good that combined with the inherent DOF manual focus with this camera is a waste of time -  it's also inconvenient.Overall, its not a P&S; and its not a DSLR. review_title: Very good in their price range, with some advantages over competitors
review_text: My family uses our headphones for music, and I some times make iPhone calls.  My experiences have been with the old apple earbuds, Similarly priced Sony in-ear models, the new Apple earbuds, another in-ear style my wife uses with around-the-ear wraps, and now these.  As I was researching I compared all but the Panasonics.The old Apple earbuds are just terrible -- tinny and fall out and uncomfortable. 'Nuf said.I used the Sony MDR-EX37B model a lot and so did my son and daughter, around $20 and they are much better.  I was mostly happy with them except that when you're in motion the pull of the cord creates a thumping sound.  Both kids managed to break theirs, or lose the removable covers.  But the sound seemed quite good.I find the ones my wife uses for workouts uncomfortable, and the sound is weak.So, figuring that the new Apple earbuds were just ok, I ordered these for listening.  They are very good, far better than the sony model.  The sound is rich and deep as you would expect from an in-ear model, and the materials used seem less prone to the thumping problem. At about the same price, with a microphone, they are a great deal.  I did find that the connection was a little touchy with one ear occasionally dropping out (in particular on an iPad). I think this is likely just a matter of a little breaking in.But as I was comparing all of these options, I was surprised to find that the new Apple earbuds really are outstanding.  They are super-comfortable, with nothing going in the ear, yet stay in place, and have significantly better sound than any of the others -- really clear and nimble sound, not as though it is being forced as I sometimes feel with the in-ear models. I can wear them for hours comfortably. The materials are not sticky, so they stay untangled comparatively well, and they are just smooth at every point of contact.  I know this is a review of the Panasonic model, so I won't dwell on this further ...I think the right conclusion is that the Panasonics are a very good second paid of earbuds for iPhone, etc. They are noticeably better at sound and comfort than similar models at this price point. But if you really want great sound, I am sure there's a step up (and only because the Apple buds, which are god knows how much more expensive, are better) if you are seeking exceptional sound.

review_title: Excellent value in a basic flat screen wall mount
review_text: I ordered this for a friend to help mount his VIZIO 32-inch plasma HDTV on the wall.  The mount came with an extensive set of mounting hardware for compatibility with multiple brands and models of flat screen TVs, and sure enough, one set was a perfect fit for the VIZIO VP322's metric mounting holes.It's pretty basic - two parts mount to the back of the TV, one piece attaches to the wall.  Hook the TV brackets onto the wall mount, tighten a couple of screws to lock it in place and you're done.  The securing screws that fasten the TV bracket to the wall plate are a little hard to reach, but Peerless thoughtfully includes a long Allen screw driver which makes this pretty painless.By the way, for those concerned about whether or nor this will fit your TV, the SF640 mount supports TVs with "mounting patterns" up to 17.73" wide and 12.94" high. This means that the mounting bolt holes in the back of your television can be no more than 17.73 inches apart (width) and no more than 12.94 inches apart (height). If your TV's mounting pattern is larger than this in either dimension then this is not the mount for you. The load capacity of the mount is up to 150 pounds so this should accommodate most flat panel TVs 46 inches or below (assuming the mounting pattern fits your TV and you mount it properly).There is no tilt capability, but for the price this really can't be expected.  All in all, a great value (with a 5-year warranty) and a high quality product.

review_title: More camera than I know what to do with.
review_text: I looked at digital cameras for a few years before selecting the DX7590.  Each year the number of pixels in cameras kept going up while the price stayed about the same.  The first year I was looking a "good" consumer camera had about 3 megapixels, then 4, and now I was looking at cameras with 5 megapixels.  What sold me on this camera was the large lens.  Instead of one of those small lenses that most comparable cameras have this one has a real large glass lens manufactured by a real German lens maker.  Yes, it has all the features you might want if you're an amateur and then some.  I probably will never use the manual override features that allows you to set the shutter time and exposure level, etc., instead of allowing the computer to do it for me.  I'm still a little bewildered by the large array of optional settings for different subjects, but I've taken what I think of as superb photos.I've been taking "snap shots" since my first Brownie camera 50 years ago.  They were all nice for family albums, but never anything that I would say could compete with professional photos.  But all that has changed.  The picture brilliance, clarity, and overall quality that I'm getting outreaches any of my expectations.  Last week I was on a camping trip and took a photo of the early morning fog across the lake.  Yousers!  It looks to me as good as many I've seen in professional photo exhibitions.One problem I'm having is that the 5 megapixel format is so large that I have to shrink the pictures to put them on a web site.  One reason I wanted a digital camera was to be able to put photos on the Internet.  So I switched to the optional 1.8 megapixels photos, and it's still too large for my web site.  Even at 1.8 megapixel setting the photos are brilliant and clear.  It must be the big lens and quality optics.  I tried taking some pictures of flowers, and some of them came out blurry.  I think I'm having trouble holding it still for the close ups.  I guess I need to put it down somewhere or get a mount.  It does have a setting for minimum focal length that is a lot closer than many comparable cameras.  I got really good close up, and then blurry ones.  Between you and me I suspect it's operator error.I keep forgetting that I can take as many pictures as I want for free and discard any I don't need.  I like viewing them full screen on my PC.  The "easy share" base works pretty well.  I have to remember to open the Kodak software and turn on the camera before downloading all the photos to my PC.  I bought some extra memory and that helps.  It says on the screen that I can take 632 pictures at 5 megapixels, or over 1,500 at 1.8 megs.  Maybe it's right. I never take that many.  It's really a lot more camera than I've ever had, or know how to use.  The quality of the pictures is superb.  It's easy to use.

The sound is nice, clean and works beautifully with my DVD player.  It did take me a while to figure out that the DVD setting is set to coaxial by defualt, so I was not getting clear sound while I had it connected through the analog jacks.  I connected the DVD player through the coaxial jack and the sound cleared up.  It is possible to change the method of connection with the remote.I could not get the sound from my TV to go through the RCA unit.  The tuner works well because I used a paper clip at the backend and connected the supplied wired to the end of the paper clip (I am being serious).  Otherwise some stations will not come in clearly.  I'm sure other workarounds can be used.I found that setting the Subwoofer level at Strong gives the best bass which can be done on the Subwoofer button on the remote.  The Level button on the remote will also allow you to increase the volume if it seems to be lacking at the original setting.I had read the reviews on here so I knew what to expect and I can say that I am satisfied with the unit for the price.Edit:6/22/10  After the first month of owning the RCA system I replaced all the speakers with Sony shelf speakers and a Sony subwoofer and it has made all the difference.  It now goes as loud as I need and the sound is crisp and clear.  In other words the RCA receiver works quite well, but the RCA speakers need to be replaced with better ones.

Probably corrupted data issue as nothing will bring a system down like bad data.Google:  Router Power LED Blinks Slowly and Router No Longer WorksSo rather than issue a RECALL on the defective merchandise, they do the next worst thing possible and give you some funky software called TFTP to download and fool around with to get the router re-flashed. A one click solution to read the router's make/model MAC address and current firmware, and auto-magically download the new one and install it while PRESERVING all existing settings.  It should also remember the OLD mac address and use it when you were migrating the settings to a router with a new MAC address.  If their software engineering department can't do that, they need to be replaced starting with the Manager.2) Recalled and Replaced the defective equipment for FREE, send out a new unit, and a postage paid return box for your old unit.  Then use the above software to migrate the settings and old MAC address to the new unit so it works seamless with your existing cable model and service provider.What do you call a router that does not work? Granted, they are not up there with Focal Audio, or even Kenwood Excelon's, but for $50-$70, you really get your money's worth out of them. Normally, I only get butyl rubber surrounds, but at the price, I will not complain.Other speakers I currently have are:Kenwood KFC-1662s - cheap and easy to find. Stock replacements for those not interested in "HiFi".Kenwood KDC-X692 - More expensive than these, and worth it. At more than twice the price of the Rockford's, you can expect a lot, and these deliver. They sound clear and tight, but seem to be missing a few mid-range frequencies. I have to turn them up kind up loud to hear vocals clearly. I use a GPS every day at work.  I travel over 800 miles in a week.  I travel from town to town driving on interstates, 2 lane highways, and neighbor hoods.  I go to county jails, state and federal prisons, hospitals, nursing homes and the like.  I need a GPS in my line of work.I had a Magellan 4370 that could no longer find satellites after only two weeks of service and then froze up.  I returned that GPS for this new 1470.  The power cord broke leaving behind the metal part in the GPS on the first use.  Luckily, I was able to get the metal part out using a pair of pliers and use another USB power cord that I had.  I guess that I just have bad luck with Magellan's.The packaging is rather nice and th unit comes complete with CD, instructions, window mount, power cable and a USB cable too.  (I was surprised to find the USB cable still included.)  The unit turned on, asked some simple questions and then found its location.  I was able to navigate to a restaurant that I had never been to before.If you place the GPS in auto zoom mode, the GPS thinks you only need to see a quarter mile ahead of you.  When driving down the freeway with 9.8 miles till my next turn, the GPS was auto zoomed 1/4 mile.  On the streets, the auto zoom is even closer, measured in 200 to 400 feet range.  I find the auto zoom to close.  You can't even see the next block in front of you.The lane assist is wrong about half the time, which is a great improvement over the 4370, which is more likely to be wrong than correct.The display is very bright, but not nearly as detailed as the 4370, that may be because the 1470 is zoom in so close all the time.  Oh, the traffic service is spotty.  Some times it works, some times it just goes on strike.Multipoint routing only shows your trip from point "A" to point "B", you cannot see the rest of the route, time or millage of your route.  This was very disappointing, the 4370 does a wonderful job, and you can see you whole route.The CPU in the 1470 is fast.On a positive note, the Starbucks coffee shops can be easily found because their logo shows up on the maps screen, and the GPS is very easy to use, but for a person who relies on their GPS, you may want to look at another product.After a few weeks of use, the unit locked up and I returned it.

review_title: A little rough around the edges, but has lots of potential
review_text: I had reluctantly started using the iPhone 4 after many years with Windows Mobile.  I must say that I really enjoy the iPhone experience, and only have a few minor gripes with it.  Recently got an iPad 2, and while it's enjoyable, and great for kids to watch videos on, I found it a little awkward to use as a laptop replacement.So I was very interested in the Touchpad.  Overall, I really like the Touchpad, and it took a little bit of time to get used to it, after using iOS for about one year.  Here's what I like:1) Card-based multitasking is great.  I can close windows and apps very easily, and bring back open ones nicely.  It's a more elegant way to switch between apps than iOS, especially going back and forth between e-mails or web pages.2) Resizable keyboard with number keys on the main keyboard.  Although the iOS keyboard is fine for a phone, it worked poorly for me on an iPad.  I like the Touchpad's much better, opting to reduce it to the small size keyboard.3) Flash works fairly well, although there are some stutters when resizing the browser.  But Amazon cloud player worked, as did Hulu and ABC web sites.4) Synergy - incorporating multiple on-line services such as Facebook, Dropbox, Exchange, and others, makes it very easy to work in the cloud.5) Erasing the device was painless (and maybe too easy?).  But recovery without a PC, such as the iPad was a snap.  The device automatically synced my previously downloaded apps.  Re-enter your passwords for the online services, and you're set.6) Audio sounds really good.  I don't know if the Beats help much, but the speakers sound decent, and with the cheap iPhone headphones, sound better than the iPhone.7) Wireless printing was effortless.  It found my printer, and I was able to print web pages and PDF files easily.  Way easier than with iOS.I do have a few complaints and hopefully many will get corrected very soon:1) I managed to crash the Touchpad a few times doing things like resizing images or starting apps.  There are bugs to be worked out for sure.2) The display rotation is too sensitive.  There were times when it would rotate too easily, but also times where the device wouldn't rotate without a few tries.  Rotation lock, while not a physical switch, proved very useful.3) The screen is a fingerprint magnet.  Fortunately it comes with a cloth.4) Battery life is perhaps a little bit less than an iPad 2, but decent.5) Web browser dragging is annoying when trying to use Flash-based sites.  Instead of clicking on a button, you end up dragging and moving the window.6) At a few points, the screen seems a little unresponsive, or at least not immediately responsive.7) Text selection is not as nice as iOS.  With iOS, you can press and hold, and then move the cursor to where you want it with the magnification.  This type of functionality would help immensely, especially when doing lots of typing.Some people complain that lacking a rear-facing camera and the heavier weight are huge detractors, but I barely notice it.  Sure, it's thicker than and iPad 2 and weighs more, but it's not that big of a deal.  I really don't mind it.  I don't have much need for taking pictures with the Touchpad either.  The phone can do that, and I can copy pictures via Dropbox.A small selection of apps is not too big of a deal at this point, since you can easily go online and use the full desktop version of many services.  Lots of iOS apps are just repackaged web sites.  No big deal.  But a note taking app with which you can hand write or draw would make this a great office tool.  The Evernote app needs to be updated for the larger screen for sure.Overall, the HP Touchpad is a viable contender, especially if HP can get the updates out very soon. There's a lot of potential here, even if it doesn't become the #1 tablet.

*Update 3*I managed to get some useful work out of this piece of mierda by daisy chaining it to my old router. Now, the old router handles all the g band traffic and this one handles only n. Stable in this configuration, but that's hardly a recommendation.*Update 2*I have now owned this router for six months. Unfortunately, the DIR-815 has proven to be unstable on my network of mixed Macs and PCs. Specifically, it started resetting itself every few minutes as soon as I connected a Windows 7 laptop to it. I have now spent literally dozens of hours on the forums and on technical support, updating firmware and drivers, disabling uPnP and other advanced router features, cutting this and that computer out of the network, all to no avail. It's been gathering dust on the shelf for a couple of months, and now goes to the trashcan. Reduced rating to 1 star.*Update 1*I've now had this router for several months. In the interim, My kids have come back home from school. Now that there are up to 7 wireless (all on the n-band) and 2 wired devices vying for connections to this router, I am experiencing some trouble: Specifically, about once every other day I can't connect to the internet at all and need to cycle the power on the router. I'm still investigating and will post updates if I learn anything.I have owned this unit for 1 day.Original review:Summary:Setup had a few glitches, mostly I could never get the "install wizard" CD mounted on my PC but there were a couple of other gotchas that would have taken less time to overcome if the setup documentation was better. All features work, but I haven't really stressed this router yet. I'll post a follow-up when I do.Details:I bought this router to replace an aging router that couldn't keep up with the demands of streaming video in a 4 person household. I was attracted to the DIR-815 because of its features (dual radios) and also because I'm also buying theD-Link Wireless N Dual Band MediaBridge (DAP-1513)to get wired ethernet over to my home theater cabinet. I'm hoping for better compatibility between 2 devices from the same company.Unpacking and setup:The router was a snap to plug in in-place of the existing unit. However, setup was more difficult than it should have been. D-Link has made an attempt at fully automated setup. The provide a "setup wizard CD" with the router. Supposedly, you can just plug the router into your home network, pop the CD into your PC or Mac, and have the "wizard" lead you through the setup process. Well, the CD never mounted on my Windows XP-based PC. So much for the CD. I performed the rest of the setup via the router's browser interface.The setup documentation provided with the router is minimal. I had a few challenges which I overcame without having to call D-Link tech support, but then I'm a computer professional. Here are the rough spots. Most are related to connecting to a Comcast cable modem:WAN setupWAN setup was pretty easy (the default connection protocol, DHCP, is correct) as long as you remember that the MAC address of the PC or router attached to the cable modem is part of their configuration and cannot change (without a call to Comcast). Fortunately, modern routers (including the D-Link) allow you to "fake" any MAC address in the WAN configuration. It even has a handy "clone your PCs MAC" button so you don't have to type the darn' thing. As long as you are working from the same PC as the one you used during the initial cable modem setup, you are golden. I wasn't so I had to go back to the old router's settings to remember the magic number.LAN setupThe Comcast modem hard-wires its LAN-side I.P. address to 192.168.0.1. This is the default I.P. of just about every router on the market. Thanks Comcast! You cannot setup both "sides" (LAN/WAN) of a router with the same I.P. Consequently, you have to choose a different number for your home network. No biggee, just another Gotcha.Wireless setupPretty easy. The option to use a single password for both wireless g and n is cool. IMPORTANT: Believe the router's wizard when it tells you that "hex (0-9, A-F) passords must by 63 characters. If you inadvertently use a password that uses only those characters, it had better be 63 characters or you won't be able to connect wirelessly, and the router won't tell you why.I have now successfully connected via wired, and both wireless radios simultaneously. No dropouts yet.

review_title: Trackman Wheel Just got a Tad Better
review_text: This review is really a comparison of the M570 to my 8 year old Trackman Wheel Wireless. I've been using this Trackman Wheel everyday for the past 8 years, actually hoping that Logitech would have an updated version of this classic mouse. Well, they sort of did. The M570 is the exact form factor to the Trackman Wheel, with the scrolling function falling solely on your right hand thumb. The left, right and wheel fell naturally to my index and middle fingers. Perhaps I was so accustomed to using the Trackman, that it was really no surprise that I felt right at home using the M570. New users might needs some getting used to.The M570 has a matte gray finish with a blue ball, not particularly beautiful, but not ugly either. The M570 does away with the rubber piece on the bottom right side of the Trackman wheel. For me, the rubber piece on the Trackman wheel doesn't improve or help me grip the mouse better since my fingers don't even touch it.The addition of the forward and back button on the M570 was really nice, since I don't have to scroll to a back/forward button or use my keyboard keys to navigate in a browser. What I would really like in this M570 would be hyper-scroll and the wheel being able to tip left and right. That would be very nice, definitely a wish list for me. Besides that, the M570 is definitely a keeper for now.The receiver is the standard Unifying receiver type, which sort of eliminate clutter under my desk and definitely will help laptop users. Besides that, I am setup to accept other wireless Logitech devices in the future. Battery life is extended, even when using one AA size battery. There is also an on-off button on the bottom of the mouse if you want to turn it off manually.In summary, if you are using the classic Trackman Wheel Wireless and wanted something modern but yet still deliver the trackball performance, this product is for you, however, definitely I would like more functionality on the scroll wheel.

review_title: H2 STILL has problems with the wiring!
review_text: Just returned my replacement H2 thru Amazon. I read all of the reviews before I bought the H2, and I guess I'm one of the unlucky ones. But obviously, NZXT is still having problems with the wiring in this case! Specifically, with the 3 3-pin fan controllers, and how they plug into (I guess) the T-shaped molex connector. Both of the cases I got had loose fan connectors that were missing leads. I went on the NZXT forums, and one of their "gurus" tried to help me, but nothing helps when you have bad wiring. On that forum, others were asking the same kinds of questions about the fan controllers on other NZXT case models, so they seem to have a basic design or QC problem when it comes to multiple fan controllers.I have 20+ years of IT experience, so I'm pretty knowledgeable. However, this was my first build-from-scratch, so I read all of the documentation on the case, motherboard, and cpu before I started. It just seems to me that on the higher-end cases that support multiple fans, the manufacturers need to do a better job of documenting the wiring scheme. Gone are the days when you simply plug the 4-pin fan controller onto the motherboard!Next, about NZXT support - I'm not impressed with that either! On a Monday, their phone queue didn't work at all, so I emailed them at "service@nzxt.com" and never received a response. The email didn't bounce back to me, so I assume that's the correct address. After spending 30 minutes in their phone queue on a Tuesday, the support person I talked to simply confirmed what I suspected and agreed that I should return the case thru Amazon.Last, I spent several hours on Amazon researching other PC cases from Fractal Design, Corsair, Cooler Master, and Thermaltake. It's obvious to me that there seems to be no "perfect" case out there, at any price point. Cases by Corsair and Cooler Master at $150 - $200 had negative reviews as well. The H2, at $100, had received good reviews on pcmag.com, as well as here on Amazon. Anyway, I decided to get the Thermaltake RX-I for only $10 more, so I hope my luck improves!

review_title: Great netbook, but make sure it fits your needs
review_text: As I was changing roles, I was turning over my company laptop.  I thought about buying a full size notebook, but decided to give this netbook a try.I custom ordered mine thru HP.  It seems most of the HP 311's sold in the stores had the Atom N270.  Well the Atom N280 is only a $25 upgrade option.  Not much difference probably in performance, but a little helps.I also ordered the netbook with xp and only 1gb of ram, and decided to add the 2gb ram upgrade myself.My order in all, came in under $500.For browsing, and most applications I say this netbook works just fine.  For portable machines I usually prefer the "eraser point" mouse control over the touchpad.  And this netbook only confirms that feeling.  If you tend to rest your palms as you type, you'll find yourself accidentally tapping the touchpad and moving your cursor around.  Palms up, wrists straight, they keyboard works pretty well.  The mouse buttons are a bit stiff and have a loud click sound when in use.  Eventually I forget about it, but it may be a minor annoyance for some.The construction feels pretty solid.  The 11.3 size is probably the sweetspot.  It is small enough that it is very portable and lightweight, yet easier to manage and use than the 10" netbooks.As a gamer, I'm a bit disappointed in the 3-D performance.  That is more a reflection of the ATOM processor.  It does however handle most of the streaming video and ripped DVD performance that other netbooks can not handle.  That is a nice point for me.  This machine seems to be the perfect travel rig.Battery life is pretty good, as I can get about 6 hours of run time.  The LCD screen is a little glossy, but colors are nice and is an improvement from the notebooks I've used in the past.Ultimately, there are more capable gaming machines but they are not nearly as portable.  I give the product overall a 4 star rating.  It will not replace a more powerful notebook, but it fills most duties.  I'm sure somewhere down the line there will be a netbook with more video capabilities but it is hard to find a machine with the perfect size, power and battery life.I've considered trading to a more powerful machine, but the size is what makes me want to keep this netbook.  It's just powerful enough to satisfy most of my needs.

review_title: Decent remote that could have been so much better
review_text: Logitech Harmony 700 Remote Control (Black)I have used Intrigue and Logitech Harmony remotes dating to one of the first, the SST-768, progressing to the 676, the 880 then The One. Now we have the 700. I have seen the 700 called the successor to the 880. I disagree, it's more the successor to the 676 and that series. The One replaces the 880 series. The 700 is far less capable than the 880 and is priced accordingly. The 700 to me, is a case of two steps forward one step back. It just doesn't get it all correct and it should have.First there's the capability, it will replace 6 remotes. That's OK, just not very good in terms of a robust home theatre environment. For a modest setup it should suffice but there's little room for expansion. Then again, maybe if you expand your home theatre you're ready for a new remote too? If you're going to use this in a bedroom or other small environment then 6 is plenty.Next is the design and feel. $125 ($150 MSR) is a lot of money for a remote and the 700 doesn't feel like that's the cost. It has a cheaper feel. The screen is small the plastic doesn't have the feel of upper level plastic. Hold The One, you'll know what I mean by worth the money. The screen. Again it's small, it only shows four items. Menu choices or icons. Most Harmony remotes show six to eight choices. Four is too small. On the other hand the screen is bright and clear. That's a good thing. It's not a touch screen, like the 676 and other Harmony's in this class there are buttons to press adjacent to the screen data. Many like the button approach rather than touch. Those people will rejoice on this choice of design. Also,  this limits how many items can be on the screen and forces you to scroll through the list. You can add 23 icons as favorites on activities that support it. Like "Watch TV". I uploaded an example screen of how icons look. There are a few included in the software but there are many more at the iconharmony web site. You get 6 pages of four icons except for the first page that reserves the upper left space for the "Command/Favorites" choice.  A very good design choice is adding the Red Blue Green Yellow hard buttons to the remote. So many devices use these color buttons that it's good they're there.  The remote feels relatively good in the hand. It's easy to get used to where the buttons are and they're well placed and nicely backlit. If the light goes out just jiggle the remote and the come back on for a programmable period of time.Now I get to my nits that I'd like to pick. The cable that attaches the remote to the charger and computer. Like I said I've had a lot of Harmony remotes and they've all used the same USB mini cable. This one doesn't . I can't use the same cable that is on my desk for a plethora of USB devices.  Nit. The software is the same one all the other remotes use but is constrained. The major nit is you can't rearrange the activities after you set them up. Don't like the order, tough. Another nit is a missing battery indicator. The power lasts a long time, over a week, before needing a charge but I like to know how I stand before the charge me warning shows.All in all this is a decent remote, it just could have been much better or the price point should have been below $100 as a starting point.

review_title: Sorry, This Product Was a Real Disappointment.
review_text: I have been using a JVC XV-SA70BK DVD player for the last couple years.  This player only outputs at 480p.  I recently purchased a Sony HDTV, the top of the line 70XBR950, and was looking forward to upgrading my DVD player to better enjoy the 1080i capabilities of my HDTV.  I jumped at the Zenith unit as soon as it was announced because of it being advertised as an "HD" unit outputting at 1080i through upconversion. During the 20 minutes that my teenage soon and I were able to view the Zenith unit, we concluded, sadly, that the improvement in picture quality as minimal at best and that we would probably return the Zenith for that reason alone. The Zenith's upconversion capabilities are quite weak.  It may the upconversion chip Zenith is using, or it maybe something else in the data stream, but it's not working.  In the past, before buying my Sony HDTV, I have used, happily, both Lumagen and DCDi upconverters/scalars costing thousands of dollars, principally in front projection TV applications, so I am pretty famiiar with the technology and knew what to expect, I thought.  Then, to top off the poor upconversion performance, after 20 minutes of use, the Zenith unit locked up completely. We couldn't stop play or even turn it off without physically pulling out the power cord.  Needless to say, it went right back to Amazon and we went back to our pretty solid, albeit humble, JVC DVD player.  Amazing, really.  Buyer beware.

I'm currently using several of Noctua's fans in various sizes; 120mm, 92mm, and this 80mm fan.Noctua makes an excellent product, but they still can't overcome the immutable fact that smaller computer fans are noisier than larger ones. I installed two of these in push/pull configuration to cool the CPU in my mini tower. There is also a Noctua 120 in there as an active front intake, and one of their 92's for exhaust. All fans blow towards the rear of the case. At full RPMs, I can hear only the sound of air moving from the two larger fans, but there was a clearly audible low drone in the key of 'A', emanating from the center of the motherboard. Thankfully, that sound was easily quieted by using the included low noise adapter cable with its voltage reducing inline resistor, as well as 'SpeedFan' software. And my CPU continues to run at acceptably cool temps  (40/55 Celsius for idle, and when under heavy load).I love Noctua's stuff. And their 80mm fans are quieter than those of other manufacturers (I also own Rosewill, Cooler Master, Vantec 'Stealth' and Thermaltake's 80mm fans). But it is what it is. ALL 80mm fans whine at full RPMs. If you want dead silent, use a larger fan (preferably a Noctua).

First, as for sound quality, they are OK at best.  There is a fair amount of static at even moderate volumes(regardless of the source...I've tried multiple sources and bitrates of files including lossless codecs).  I think I need something with just a little bit more bass as well, without being overbearing.  Also, they aren't as comfortable as the Skull Candy pair, and while I appreciate the hard plastic case because it keeps the wires untangled, it's going to be a bit too large to carry around easily come warm weather.  Right now, I don't have an issue with it, because I can put it in my jacket pocket, but once the need to wear a jacket subsides, I'll have nowhere to put the case.  It's definitely too big to put in the pocket of any of my jeans.  I'm not sure if any set of headphones has a good solution for this problem, but I guess I'll have to keep looking and possibly expand my search to a higher pricing tier.

review_title: How to Have a Happy Wireless Speaker System
review_text: Here's what I've learned about the AR 900mhz wireless speaker system.1) After setup, they work better than I had expected. It appears the system has internal frequency monitoring that allows them to self-adjust, and they do a good job of it. I've gotten very little static even in a high-density neighborhood, and with a houseful of other wireless devices. When static or fuzziness does occur, it seems to be effectively and automatically "dealt with" in a few moments.2) There are a few clever but non-intuitive features that mean you actually need to read the operator's manual on setup, rather than intuit your way through. I thought it was so simple I could just guess, which had me scratching my head for a few minutes wondering why things weren't working. But the answers were all in the manual, such as the need to pre-tune the transmitter appropriately (a blue flashing light on the transmitter will tell you when your tuning is correct), to turn on the speakers with a brief push-and-hold of the volume control, and to turn off the speakers with an extended push-and-hold. Many of the negative comments from other users posted below, such as "When I tried to recharge nonrechargeable alkaline batteries in them, they leaked" (no kidding!) and "I wish there were an on-off button on the speakers" (there is!) and "The speakers would not work until I turned them on" (no kidding!) seem to come from people who blithely ignored the manual.3) Check your output device (whether TV/amplifier/stereo/computer/ipod or other) to see if it has a nonvariable (fixed) line out. That's what these speakers want and need. You can fry the transmitter with a variable line out that's turned up, so be careful if you don't have a fixed line out. My output device, a TV, offered either variable or fixed line out (a menu option) so I had to figure out how to change the TV output to fixed. Setup would have been faster if I'd known about this beforehand.I'm looking forward to adding rechargeable (preferably NiMH) batteries to the speakers and taking advantage of the auto-recharge option afforded by the speaker power supplies. I'd love to move these speakers around the house, completely independent of all wires, including power supply wires.I'm giving these speakers 5 stars because I can't think of any obvious oversights or deficiencies in their design, and because they exceed my expectations in several ways. I used to have to blast our livingroom TV to hear it from the kitchen, and now I can keep the volume at a moderate level right in the kitchen, where I need it. A quick changeover from the TV to the computer allows me to podcast to anywhere within the house. Nice.

I am delighted to report that these headphones will please your noggin in many ways.For the price of these headphones, you will be getting more than your money's worth.  While these are not audiophile or professional quality headphones, the sound quality is still -very- good.  I was surprised to get such clear, deep tones out of headphones that cost so little...drum & bass sounds very nice.  Its bass limit is not as volumous as a professional piece of equipment, but it does seem to have an output limiter that will stop the headphones from maxing out and making that fuzzy static sound, eventually resulting in permanent speaker damage. Sibilance is a frequent problem with many headphone products, but not these... not in the least bit.  They handle treble and tweets with a great deal of clarity, and vocals sound so very nice.  After having used Sony MDR-NC6, Sony MDR-XD100, and Koss R40, this product stands out as #1 in terms of comfort and sound, especially for the price.  Get sucked into these headphones and you won't be disappointed.  Adjust your equalizer to fit the music you like.  Playback will sound just how you want it to.In addition to great sound, these are comfortable as well.  The earphones themselves are made of the standard squishy studio headphone cushioning, though the pads seem to be thicker than usual.  The frame doesn't "pinch" your head either.  Rather, it hugs.  If you've ever used Sony MDR-NC6 before, you'll know what I mean by pinching...a frame so unflexible it presses your ears until they hurt.  Not the ATH T22s... they respect your mellon.  The phones themselves completely enclose the ear, which results in very little sound leak.  The only complaint I have is that the frame arch does not have any padding.I am very pleased with this purchase, and I hope that you may give these things a try once it is time to pick up a new pair of headphones.

Though I have sympathy for everyone who has been having issues with this product, I have been extremely happy with it.I purchased one of these refurbs back in April. We have many wireless devices networked through this router including PCs/laptop/netbooks/servers, NAS/RAID/media devices, streaming bluray players (at the other end of the house), wireless bridges, iPod, cell phone over WiFi, Roku boxes - everything we throw at it works without issue. We also have a second NAS as well as a hub plugged into the LAN ports along with our DSL modem on the WAN port.About 6 weeks ago, I picked up a second one - for $29 I may as well have a spare just in case the first one dies at some point.Update 12/5/2012================Two years later and the original unit has become flakey - DHCP server intermittently doesn't function properly, DNS doesn't work for some connected devices (but will on a powerdown/reboot), router ports are 10/100 and I'm ready to go to gigabit. I picked up the EA2700-RM off the Cisco site - under $50 with free shipping. Still extremely happy that the original refurb was cheap and performed well for long enough.
